title: fix(resolver): take the shared DID resolver instead of building one
body:
Closes KR-19 (their **VTI-19**) — one command fetching `/.well-known/did.jsonl` forty times in five minutes, earning a 429 from the DID host's own rate limiter.

## Two problems, not one

**Twelve call sites each constructed their own `DIDCacheClient`.** A client owns its cache, so the same DID was fetched once per *construction* rather than once per process. `vta-service/src/webvh_cli.rs` alone had five.

**And by calling `DIDCacheClient::new` directly, none of them read `PNM_RESOLVER_URL`.** So an operator who had configured a resolver sidecar — the documented mitigation for exactly this load — did not get it on any of these paths. That env var exists precisely so a single setting reaches every resolver construction without breaking the SDK's public API (see the module doc on `vta-sdk/src/resolver.rs`), and these sites went around it.

The second is the more consequential of the two: the first multiplies fetches, the second removes the thing an operator would reach for to absorb them.

## Why the conversion is behaviour-preserving

Every converted site built

```rust
DIDCacheConfigBuilder::default()
    .with_host_policy(vta_sdk::resolver::webvh_host_policy())
    .build()
```

which is byte-for-byte what `build_did_cache_config(None)` produces. So `shared_did_resolver_from_env()` is a drop-in that additionally honours the env var, and the twelve caches collapse into the one the SDK already keeps per (runtime, sidecar URL, host policy).

## Three sites deliberately left alone

Each looks convertible, and none is:

- **`vtc-service/src/server.rs`** and **`room-host/src/main.rs`** build a plain default with **no host policy**. Converting them would add `webvh_host_policy()` and change which hosts are permitted — a security-relevant change, not a caching one.
- **`pnm-cli/src/bootstrap.rs`** passes `None` **on purpose**. `bootstrap connect` resolves the DID locally so the operator verifies the SCID and signed log on their own machine rather than trusting a sidecar; CLAUDE.md records this explicitly. That `None` is the trust boundary, not an oversight. It is the single most convertible-looking construction in the tree.

This is why each site's config was read rather than the constructor pattern-matched.

## The test that was missing

All of the above now rests on `shared_did_resolver` actually sharing, and nothing pinned that. If sharing broke, every converted site would quietly revert to a private cache with no test failing — the same shape as the bug being fixed.

`two_callers_on_one_runtime_share_one_resolver` asserts on the registry rather than on cache hits: counting fetches against a loopback DID would need the private-host policy and make the test as much about host policy as about sharing.

It is feature-gated (`resolver` sits behind `session`/`didcomm`/`tsp`/…), so I checked it runs in CI's workspace job rather than assuming: it does, via feature unification — 876 tests compile under `--workspace` versus 380 for `-p vta-sdk` alone, which is the discrepancy CLAUDE.md warns about.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — 399 passed, 0 failed
- `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — 1110 passed, 0 failed
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean

No version edits: release-plz owns those here, and a red semver report on this PR would be the report working.

same DID was fetched once per construction rather than once per process,
and a `did:webvh` host saw a burst of requests for what is one logical
operation — enough to earn a 429 from its own rate limiter.

Every one of them built
`DIDCacheConfigBuilder::default().with_host_policy(webvh_host_policy())`,
which is byte-for-byte what `build_did_cache_config(None)` produces, so
taking `shared_did_resolver_from_env()` preserves behaviour and collapses
twelve caches into the one the SDK already keeps per runtime, sidecar URL
and host policy.

It also fixes a second problem those sites had: by calling
`DIDCacheClient::new` directly they never read `PNM_RESOLVER_URL`, so an
operator who had configured a resolver sidecar — the documented mitigation
for exactly this load — did not get it on any of these paths. The env var
existed to spare the SDK's public API, and these call sites went around
it.

Three sites are deliberately left alone, and each looks convertible:

- `vtc-service/src/server.rs` and `room-host/src/main.rs` build a plain
  default with no host policy. Converting them would add
  `webvh_host_policy()` and change which hosts are permitted — a
  security-relevant change, not a caching one, and not one to make inside
  this change.
- `pnm-cli/src/bootstrap.rs` passes `None` on purpose. Bootstrap resolves
  the DID locally so the operator verifies the SCID and signed log on
  their own machine rather than trusting a sidecar; that `None` is the
  trust boundary, not an oversight.

Adds the test that was missing for the property all of this now rests on:
that two callers on one runtime get one resolver. Sharing could have
broken and every converted site would have quietly gone back to a private
cache with nothing failing.

Reported as VTI-19 by the Keyring wallet team, who saw one command fetch
`/.well-known/did.jsonl` forty times in five minutes.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* test(resolver): count shared resolvers for this runtime, not the process

The sharing test asserted `after == before + 1` over the whole registry
and failed in CI. The registry is process-global and every other
`#[tokio::test]` in the binary registers under its own runtime key, so a
total is noisy — and, the part that actually broke it, not monotonic:
`shared_did_resolver` prunes entries whose runtime has ended *before* it
inserts, so a call that adds one entry can also remove several. CI hit
exactly that, pruning a dead entry in the same call that added ours and
leaving the count unchanged.

Count only the entries keyed to the current runtime. That is immune to
what any other test has registered or left behind, and it is the property
the test is about: this runtime asks twice and gets one resolver.

The 0 -> 1 -> still-1 sequence is also what stops it passing vacuously —
if registration were broken the count would stay 0, and if sharing were
broken it would reach 2. An earlier draft proved that by registering a
second key with a different sidecar URL, which put the client in network
mode and made the test spend five seconds waiting on a socket that is not
the subject. It runs in 0.02s without it.

title: test(transport-harness): give the d6 success arm room for a real round trip
body:
`d6_recovers_a_reply_from_an_answering_peer` is flaking in **`Test (workspace)`** — the job this repo's own CI comments call *"the gate that matters"*.

## It is not a new break

| Run | Commit | Result |
|---|---|---|
| [35465791169](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/actions/runs/35465791169) — **main**, 19 Sep 19:54 | `73509892` | **failed on this test** |
| 35466562292 — **main**, 19 Sep 20:10 | `89ebd895` | green |

Same test, opposite outcomes on `main`, sixteen minutes apart. It has also failed twice on #1581, which touches nothing near it — including once on a re-run of identical code, while `Feature combos` went green on that same re-run.

## Why it flakes

The test bounded its reply wait at 5s, with a comment explaining the bound is "generous relative to the orphan tests" because it must cover a real round trip: re-invite → deliver → the peer's reply → the VTA correlating it.

**That bound is a fixture parameter, not the subject.** What the test asserts is the *correlation* — that the answering peer's reply is matched through `pending_replies` and returned, so the coordinator records a success rather than a give-up. The timeout only has to be long enough not to fire first.

At 5s it was also asserting, in effect, that a loaded CI runner completes a TSP round trip within five seconds. It does not reliably do that.

## Why 30s weakens nothing

A reply that never arrives still fails the assertion — it just takes longer to say so. And the timeout path keeps its own dedicated coverage in `d6_drives_recovery_on_a_reply_timeout`, which uses a silent orphan peer and a deliberately short bound, so nothing about timeout behaviour is being relaxed here.

The healthy path is unaffected: the harness still completes in ~7.5s locally, because the wait ends when the reply arrives, not when the bound elapses.

## Why fix it rather than re-run past it

The cost of a flaky test in this job is not the re-run. It is that it teaches people a red `Test (workspace)` means nothing — and this repo already has the incident that follows from that, with six consecutive PRs merging onto a red `main` in September. CLAUDE.md's "a merge is not evidence that anything passed" section exists because of it.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vta-service --features transport-harness transport_harness_tests` — **9/9 pass**
- `cargo clippy -p vta-service --features transport-harness --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean

Test-only; no version edits (release-plz owns those here).

Found while investigating #1581's red, which this unblocks.

title: fix(step-up): route delegated pushes to an approver's own mediator
body:
## What

`approver_mediator` returned `None` for any DID that was not `did:key`, so a `did:webvh` or `did:peer` approver was never pushed to. All four call sites give up at that point — `consent_request.rs:195` and `:329`, `consent.rs:385`, `step_up.rs:856` — and each sits **upstream of everything that would otherwise reach the device**: the TSP attempt, the DIDComm forward, and `trigger_gateway_wake`.

One gate therefore starved three delivery paths at once, which is why the symptom presented from several directions: a consent request that stayed queued, an idle approver that was never roused, and a delegated step-up that fell back to the relay every time.

The predicate now resolves the approver's DID document and reads the mediator from its `DIDCommMessaging` service, matching on service `type` per the workspace transport rules. `did:key` keeps its existing behaviour — it cannot advertise a service, so it routes through the VTA's configured mediator, where the holder registered it.

## Two decisions worth review

**A routable approver never falls back to the configured mediator.** Forwarding to a mediator the approver is not registered with does not reach them, and spends a slot of this VTA's sender-queue allowance to do nothing — the shared-fate shape behind the mediator queue-cap failure. `None` (relay fallback) is the honest answer.

**Resolution is bounded by a 5s timeout.** Every call site awaits this inline on a request path (`step_up.rs:1226`, `:1277`) while the push it gates is documented as best-effort and never a hard dependency, so an approver whose DID host is slow must not hold the caller's response open. The shared `AppState::did_resolver` is used rather than a fresh resolver, so its cache absorbs repeat pushes to the same approver.

## Also

- The three call sites that read `[messaging] mediator_did` under the config read-lock now clone it and drop the lock first: the route decision is network I/O, and holding the lock across it would stall config writers.
- Corrected a warning in `consent_request.rs` that told operators "a non-`did:key` approver produces this" — true before this change, false after.

## Testing

- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — 1770 passed, 0 failed
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- Both reduced-feature clippy runs CI performs (`--features rest`, which has neither `didcomm` nor `tsp`, and `setup,keyring,rest,tsp,cli-synthesis`) — clean
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean
- New unit tests cover the routable-DID route, and that a routable approver does not fall back to our mediator. The existing test pinning the old `did:key`-only behaviour was rewritten against the pure decision function.

## Not covered here

Live validation against a `did:webvh` mediator with a phone-shaped approver — that is the acceptance test for this fix and has not been run yet.

Reported as VTI-26 and VTI-24 by the Keyring wallet team, who hit it with `did:webvh` phone approvers.

title: fix(vta)!: answer the contexts family's declared error codes, and stop distinguishing "not yours" from "not there"
body:
Started as "implement `vta/contexts/delete:notEmpty`". Reading the family's specifications turned it into something larger, because the codes are not the interesting part.

## The leak

Every id-taking task in `vta/contexts/*` checked scope and existence separately, and reported them separately:

```rust
auth.require_context(id)?;                       // 403 — and names the id back
get_context(..).ok_or(AppError::NotFound(..))?;  // 404
```

So a caller scoped to one context learned, from which refusal came back, exactly which other context ids exist. Here is the real thing, captured from the disproving run:

```json
"code": "permissionDenied",
"message": "permission denied: forbidden: no access to context: cov-real"
```

`create_context` had it inverted — parent looked up *before* the scope check — so an unauthorised caller learned a parent was real before being told it couldn't use it.

The specifications require the opposite and say so outright. `vta/contexts/get`: *"deliberately does not distinguish 'does not exist' from 'exists but not yours'"*. `update`, `update-did` and `delete` each repeat it as *"whether or not it exists"*. `create` names `parentNotFound` and ties it to `get`'s reasoning.

## What changed

**`reach_context`** — the family's single answer to "does this caller get to act on this id". Scope, then existence, one `Unreachable` for both. Six operations go through it; `create` gets the same for its parent.

**One `reject_context_error`** maps the typed error to the code the *calling* task declares. The slug is read off the document, so these are all the same match:

| task | code |
|---|---|
| `get` | `vta/contexts/get:notFound` |
| `update` | `vta/contexts/update:notFound` |
| `update-did` | `vta/contexts/update-did:notFound` |
| `preview-delete` | `vta/contexts/preview-delete:notFound` |
| `delete` | `vta/contexts/delete:notFound`, `:notEmpty` |
| `create` | `vta/contexts/create:parentNotFound` |

`From`/`Into` keeps `?` working inside the operations and converts back for the transports that carry a status rather than a Trust-Task code, so REST and DIDComm needed no per-site changes.

**`delete:notEmpty`** lands here too. It rode out as `malformedRequest` — which says the request was wrong, when it was well-formed, understood, and refused for what the context holds. The refusal now counts the whole subtree instead of saying `"associated resources"` (as true of one key as of forty) and carries the counts in `details`.

## Deliberately not changed

**`vta/contexts/secrets` keeps entitlement-before-existence.** Its specification argues that ordering rather than inheriting `get`'s: *"not found is only ever said to a caller already entitled to hear it, so the pair leaks nothing"*. `entitlement_is_checked_before_existence` already pins it. Conflating it would have broken a deliberate design. Its two codes stay unimplemented — `export.rs` has three distinct sources of `NotFound` and that wants reading, not pattern-matching.

**The cheap approach was wrong and I took the typed one.** Mapping every `AppError::NotFound` in these handlers to `<task>:notFound` would have been a few lines — but `delete_context` drives `delete_did_webvh_with`, whose `NotFound` means a DID record is missing. That would answer "no such context" for a DID that vanished mid-cascade.

## Tests

Each confirmed to fail without the fix.

- **`every_contexts_task_answers_its_own_not_found`** — per task, asserts the code *and* that a real-but-unreachable id and an absent one come back identical. Asserted on the emitted document; the refusal being typed internally is not evidence anything puts the code on the wire.
- **`a_delete_without_force_answers_not_empty_on_the_wire`** — same reasoning for `notEmpty` (failed with `taskFailed`).
- The `create` and `delete` pairs at the operations layer assert `to_string()` equality, not just the same variant: a message naming one of them hands back what the variant hides.
- Controls, so neither "always refuses" nor "everything is notFound now" could pass: `an_empty_leaf_needs_no_force`, `top_level_creation_requires_super_admin` (a role question, still `Forbidden`).

## Breaking

A caller scoped elsewhere now gets `notFound` / **404** where it got `permissionDenied` / **403** — on get, update-did, preview-delete, delete, and create's parent. That is the change, not a side effect of it.

`context_admin_cannot_update_other_context_did` asserted the 403. It was right about the authorisation and wrong about what to tell the caller; it now asserts 404 for a real id *and* an absent one, and that the refusal modified nothing.

## Verification

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- webvh-off build (`--no-default-features --features rest,didcomm`) — clean
- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — **128 targets, 0 failures** (re-run after the integration-test update; the prior run was 127 green plus the one expected 403→404 failure).

Expect `semver report` red: `create_context`, `get_context_op`, `update_context`, `update_context_did`, `preview_delete_context` and `delete_context` change their error type.

body:
fix(vta)!: answer the contexts family's declared error codes, and stop distinguishing "not yours" from "not there" (#1580)

The `vta/contexts/*` specifications declare eight extended error codes. The
VTA emitted none of them. Worse than the missing codes: the answers it gave
instead leaked which context ids are real.

## The leak

Every id-taking task checked scope and existence separately, and reported
them separately:

    get_context(..).ok_or(AppError::NotFound(..))?;  // 404

So a caller scoped to one context learned, from the difference between the
two refusals, exactly which other context ids exist. The captured refusal
reads `permission denied: forbidden: no access to context: cov-real` — it
confirms the id and hands it back. `create_context` had the same leak
inverted: it looked the parent up *before* checking scope, so an
unauthorised caller learned a parent was real before being told it could not

`reach_context` is the family's single answer to "does this caller get to
act on this id" — scope, then existence, one `Unreachable` for both. Six
operations go through it; `create` gets the same treatment for its parent.

The operations return a typed `ContextError`, and one `reject_context_error`
maps it to the code the calling task declares — the slug is read off the
document, so `get:notFound`, `update:notFound`, `update-did:notFound`,

`delete:notEmpty` lands here too. It rode out as `malformedRequest`, which
says the request was wrong; it was well-formed, understood, and refused for
what the context holds. The refusal now also counts the whole subtree
instead of saying "associated resources" — as true of one key as of forty —
and carries the counts in `details` so a consumer decides without parsing
English.

## What is deliberately NOT changed

`vta/contexts/secrets` keeps entitlement-before-existence. Its specification
argues that ordering rather than inheriting `get`'s: "not found is only ever
said to a caller already entitled to hear it, so the pair leaks nothing".
`entitlement_is_checked_before_existence` pins it. Its two codes remain
unimplemented — `export.rs` has three distinct sources of `NotFound` and
that wants reading, not pattern-matching.

Mapping every `AppError::NotFound` in these handlers to `<task>:notFound`
was the cheap option and is wrong: `delete_context` drives
`delete_did_webvh_with`, whose `NotFound` means a DID record is missing, and
that would answer "no such context" for a DID that vanished mid-cascade.
Hence the typed error.

## Breaking

A caller scoped elsewhere now receives `notFound` / HTTP 404 where it
received `permissionDenied` / 403, on get, update-did, preview-delete,
delete and create-parent. That is the point of the change, and it is a
change in what existing callers see.

`context_admin_cannot_update_other_context_did` asserted the 403. It was
right about the authorisation and wrong about what to tell the caller; it
now asserts 404 for both a real id and an absent one.

title: fix(ux): take the questions off the screens that were guessing at them
body:
Seven findings from a live UX run, and the answer to most of them is that a screen was asking for something it could work out, or naming a key it had not bound.

## Creating a persona

**The label.** "Label for the new persona:" over an empty box said what to fill in and nothing about what it is for. It now says, in one line, that it is a name for you, that it names the context its keys live in, and that communities are shown the DID instead — and the empty field carries an example (`e.g. Work, Conference, Alice`) as a dimmed placeholder that is gone the moment anything is typed.

> The report suggested `openvtc-alice` as the placeholder, read off the "a context of its own" line on the screen behind. That string is the account's **top context id**, not anything derived from the label, so using it would have taught the wrong thing.

**The path.** The screen put a permanent, public, possibly-taken name next to a random one and left the reader to work out which mattered. The server-assigned outcome is now the whole screen, with the note that a memorable name does not have to live in the DID — an **agent name** points at it and can be changed later. The typed path is still reachable behind `p`; inside that editor Esc means "let the server pick", not "back to the label".

**The context.** Which VTA context a persona is minted into is no longer asked at all. Every persona gets a sub-context of its own, named from its label: it is the only answer that keeps the isolation the sub-context exists for, and it was being put to someone who had just been told what a `did:webvh` path is.

That removal reaches three screens for the price of one. `community_context::context_options` already collapses to a single option for any persona whose keys live somewhere, so the Context row on the join's vetting page and the context field on the new-application form had one reachable value for everything but a brand-new persona. Both are gone; `context_index` stays at 0, which is the value those rows opened on.

## Identifiers on screen

A `did:webvh` is told apart from the next one on its host by its **path**, and every truncation in the tree dropped exactly that:

```
did:webvh:QmZBWtbz1VVTwyFNUHjx8YfL9fZ8XDc6KrBQ66tj9xq6Eh:dids.ic3.dev:firstperson-vtc
did:webvh:QmZBWtbz1VVTwyFNUHjx8YfL9fZ8XDc6KrB...          ← before, at 48
did:webvh:QmZB…q6Eh:dids.ic3.dev:firstperson-vtc          ← after, at 48
```

New `openvtc_core::display::shorten_for_display` gives up the SCID first (via the existing `shorten_webvh`, which parses with `didwebvh-rs` per the repo rule) and only then the middle, spending the remaining budget on the tail. `display_identifier`, `community_label`, `shorten_did`, `membership_profile_label`, `log_did` and the setup/loading screens all go through it.

## Joining

`asdasd` reached the vetting page, failed to resolve, and was offered **"join anyway — the way forward here"**: an offer to address a request to nothing.

- `validate_join_input` returns `Result` now and refuses anything that is neither a DID nor an agent name, naming what was typed. The DID check is deliberately shallow — a method-specific id is the method's business, and refusing a method this build has not heard of would refuse a community OpenVTC can reach.
- A *well-formed* DID that resolves to nothing is a different failure from a community that will not answer, and `learn_over_http` now returns a `NotLearned` enum saying which. An unresolvable DID gets its own page, without the `j` key, saying to check the DID with whoever gave it to you. A **timeout** stays on the resolvable side: slow is not absent (R6.4).

## Vetting

**The frozen screen.** The holder-grant view ends "then press `f` again" — and `f` was not bound there. It is a List-tab verb, and that view is a form mode, where only Esc/Enter/Tab/arrows and a few mode-guarded letters exist. With no field to type in and no rows to move between, Tab and the arrows did nothing visible either, so the whole view read as frozen and only a restart got back to a working `f`. `f` now retries, and the footer names both keys.

**A refusal nobody could see.** `Intake::Refused` sent a reply and no `Notice`, so a vetter whose applicant was turned away saw an empty desk — the one person who can issue a fresh ticket learned nothing. There is now a `Notice::RequestRefused` reaching their activity log (informational, no inbox task), and a shared `queries::request_refusal_words` turns the code into a sentence on **both** ends, in place of `vetting/request:invalidTicket` printed under a vetter's name (R6.4). The `Silent` branch stays silent: it exists so a guesser cannot discover the vetter, and a log line they could provoke would hand them the same discovery from the other side.

> I could not determine the root cause of the reported refusal from the screenshots, and one thing in them is the clue: **the vetter's Tickets count was 0** while the applicant held a link naming him. The only code path that removes a ticket was `d` on the Tickets view — one keypress, next to `u` and `y`, which copy — and everyone already holding that ticket is refused from then on and cannot be told. It is confirmed now, and the confirmation says that is the cost. If it recurs, check first whether the two panes are the same profile.

**Asking a vetter is one field.** The ticket link carries the vetter's DID, so the separate box for it only ever held what the paste was about to overwrite. Ctrl+V works on that field now (it previously typed a literal `v`), and the vetter read out of the link is *shown* rather than typed — seeing where the request is about to go is the check a person can actually make on a string of base64.

> Consequence, chosen deliberately: a spoken short code alone can no longer reach a vetter, since nothing else would carry their DID. `normalise_code` is now unreachable from the applicant UI, and the vetter's own "read it to the person" wording was replaced with "press ⏎ to show its QR code, or u to copy its link" so the two ends do not contradict each other. Core still accepts a `ShortCodeTicket` on the wire, so interop is unchanged.

## Verification

`cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace`, and `cargo test --workspace -- --include-ignored` are all green. New tests cover each finding: the label and path screens' rendering and keys, the persona sub-context, `shorten_for_display` keeping two DIDs on one host apart, `validate_join_input`'s table, the unresolvable-DID page withholding `j`, `f` on the holder-grant view, the one-field request form, and the vetter hearing about a refused request.

Not verified live — this is a TUI change set validated by rendering and key-routing tests, not by a run against the services.

## Pre-merge checklist

```
- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) — no new clients; the resolve keeps its RESOLVE_TIMEOUT
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3) — n/a, no new locks
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1) — the persona mint is unchanged; the ticket delete is local-only and now confirmed
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) — n/a, no new retries
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5) — n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6) — n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*) — no wire types changed; Notice is internal
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*) — an unresolvable community DID now fails closed (no join offered) rather than open
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*) — a refused vetting request now reaches the vetter's log; both ends say what the code means rather than printing it
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1) — the ticket delete persists through the same coalesced save as before, behind a confirmation
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers — none
```

title: ci: filter Feature combos by what it builds, and give it a budget it fits in
body:
Two changes to the longest job on the graph. Asked for as "gate it" and "raise the timeout"; the first turned out to need a split before it was safe.

## The filter could not simply be added

`affects` already gates `Mobile build`, `Enclave build` and both test jobs. `Feature combos` — the most expensive of the lot — had no filter at all, so every docs-only and CLI-only PR waited ~45 minutes for it.

Adding the obvious gate would have been **wrong**. Twenty of its steps name their package with `-p`; one did not:

```
cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings
```

That step builds `pnm-cli`, `cnm-cli`, `vta-mcp` and `vta-mobile-core`, which no `-p` flag in the job mentions. A gate derived from those flags would have been **narrower than the job**, and would have skipped that coverage for a change to one of those crates — a filter that silently covers less than it claims, which is the exact failure `ci-affects.sh`'s own docstring is written against.

So the maximal combination moves to **`Feature combos (all-features)`**, gated on the whole workspace (`vta_tests || vtc_tests` — between them, every crate), so it skips only a change touching no crate at all. Bonus: 4 minutes off the critical path, and the two run in parallel.

## The package list is derived, never written down

`scripts/ci-feature-combo-pkgs.sh` reads the scope out of the job's own `-p` flags. A hand-kept "crates Feature combos covers" would be a second description of what the job's steps already say, and the docstring on `ci-affects.sh` records three incidents from exactly that (#1252, #1256, #1259).

It **refuses** if a `--workspace` step ever reappears in the job, naming the line — because that is precisely what makes the `-p` flags an incomplete account. Verified by putting one back:

```
refusing: the Feature combos job has a --workspace step, so the packages
its -p flags name are not the full set it builds. Move that step to the
features-all job, or this filter will under-cover it:
65:        run: cargo check --workspace --features something
```

## What the gate actually does

Probed with real single-file commits against the derived scope:

| change | verdict |
|---|---|
| `docs/02-vta/rate-limiting.md` | skip — only prose and non-build files changed |
| `pnm-cli/src/setup.rs` | skip |
| `cnm-cli/src/main.rs` | skip |
| `vta-mcp/src/guard.rs` | skip |
| `vta-service/src/lib.rs` | **run** |
| `vtc-service/src/backup.rs` | **run** |

Fail-safe in the direction that costs minutes: `.github/`, `scripts/`, `Cargo.lock`, a root manifest, an unattributable path, or any non-PR event all resolve to **run**.

## And a budget it fits in

~40 minutes of work against a 45-minute ceiling made every run a coin flip. An overrun also doesn't present as a failure — GitHub marks the step that was in flight `cancelled`, which reads as though a human cancelled the run, and #1575 spent three attempts getting one verdict out of it. 60 budgets the tail rather than the mean.

## Not in this PR

The job recompiles the dependency graph for each feature set because `target/` is deliberately uncached (#1133: a source-only change doesn't move `Cargo.lock`, so the key doesn't move and stale workspace artifacts get restored).

That objection is right about `actions/cache` and not about `Swatinem/rust-cache`, which evicts workspace-member artifacts before saving and keeps only dependency ones — the same distinction the existing comment draws when it says the registry cache is safe because it is content-addressed. It's already used in `join-didcomm-soak.yml` and pinned by SHA. Worth measuring separately; the open question is its cache size against the repo's 10 GB allowance, given #891 already showed one fat cache evicting the rest.

## Verification

- `shellcheck scripts/ci-feature-combo-pkgs.sh` — clean
- YAML parses; asserted the gate, the 60-minute budget, the new `affects` output, and that the all-features step left one job and landed in the other
- Guard verified to fire, and the derived scope verified against six real commits

title: feat(vta): report the subtree and the host copies a context delete could not remove
body:
Takes **trust-tasks 0.21.4**, which added the two members the context-delete work needed and had nowhere to put (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#513). Completes #1575 and #1576.

## `subContexts` on the preview

#1576 made every array in the preview the union over the subtree, but the response could not say *which* contexts those arrays covered. So both CLIs and the browser console each derived the list from `contexts/list` and matched paths themselves — three copies of the agent's own cascade rule, none authoritative, sitting in front of an irreversible prompt. They agreed today; nothing kept them agreeing.

The agent decides what its cascade reaches. It now says so, and the consumers read it instead of recomputing it.

## `daemonCleanupErrors` on the delete

A DID whose hosting server would not confirm removing the published log left the deletion reported as a plain success, with the orphan visible only in the agent's own logs — which is the shape of the defect this whole change set started from (#1575). It is the subtree-wide form of the `daemonCleanupError` that `webvh/dids/delete/1.0` already reports for one DID.

`VtaClient::delete_context_with_outcome` returns the response so a caller can see it, mirroring `delete_did_webvh_with_outcome` and, like it, using the **generated** type rather than the hand-written body. The existing `delete_context` stays and documents why the other is usually wanted. Both CLIs print the orphans after the deletion rather than letting a partial success read as a complete one.

## The pin is load-bearing

Not tidying: pinned back to `0.21.3` this **does not compile** — the generated `contexts::delete::v1_0::Response` has no `daemon_cleanup_errors` there. Sibling `trust-tasks-*` crates are already on `"0.21"`, so caret covers them.

## A coverage gap worth naming

`response_coverage::contexts_lifecycle` ran against a **leaf**. `subContexts` was therefore empty, `skip_serializing_if` kept it off the wire, and the response gate would have validated a document that never contained the new member — green, and evidence of nothing about the thing it was supposed to cover.

The fixture now has a sub-context so the member is actually emitted, and the test asserts its value directly rather than trusting the gate's silence. Same failure mode CLAUDE.md records for the response-signing work: coverage of the thing adjacent to the thing.

## Tests

- `preview_names_the_sub_contexts_that_go_with_it` — deepest-first ordering, and `acme-corp` is not a child of `acme`. **Confirmed to fail without the fix** (`left: []`).
- `a_leaf_previews_an_empty_sub_context_list` — the control.
- `a_clean_delete_reports_no_daemon_cleanup_errors` — so "absent means clean" is a decision that was made, not an omission.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — 128 targets, 0 failures
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- webvh-off build (`--no-default-features --features rest,didcomm`) — clean

Expect `semver report` red: the SDK gains members and a method, and `render_delete_context_preview` loses a parameter.

Consumer note: `subContexts` and `daemonCleanupErrors` are optional and `skip_serializing_if` empty, so nothing new appears on the wire in the ordinary case. A **stale Rust consumer** of these two responses would still fail to deserialise one that carries them, since generated response types are `deny_unknown_fields`.

Plugin side: OpenVTC/vta-browser-plugin#262.

title: feat(manager): read the subtree from the agent, and surface a delete that left host copies behind
body:
Follows #261. Takes the two members trust-tasks 0.21.4 added (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#513), served by OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1577.

## The console stops deriving the cascade

#261 named the sub-contexts a delete would take, but had to work them out from `contexts/list` and match paths itself, because `vta/contexts/preview-delete/1.0` had no member for them. It does now (`subContexts`), so `descendantsOf` goes.

This matters beyond tidiness. The agent decides what its cascade reaches; a console that computes that independently is a second implementation of the rule, sitting in front of an irreversible prompt. It agreed today — nothing kept it agreeing, and the disagreement would have shown up as a confirmation dialog that understated what was about to be destroyed.

## A delete that isn't finished says so

`contextDelete` now returns `daemonCleanupErrors`: the DIDs whose records are gone while their published logs may still be served. A success that is not a completed deletion, which the specification says a consumer MUST surface — and which the client was dropping on the floor.

## Tests

The render tests feed `subContexts` through the agent double instead of the records list, so what they pin is the panel's reading of **the agent's answer** rather than its own path matching. Two new core tests cover the cleanup report in both casings.

- `npm run lint` (`tsc -b`, all workspaces) — clean
- `npm test` — 1528 tests across five workspaces, 0 failures
- `npm run build` — clean

## Ordering

Independent of #1577 in the sense that nothing breaks if this lands first: the members are optional, absent reads as empty, and the panel renders correctly either way. But the console only *shows* sub-contexts once an agent on #1577 is serving them, so there is no reason to land this ahead of it.

`vta/contexts/delete/1.0` gained `daemonCleanupErrors`: DIDs whose host
copy the agent could not confirm removing. A success carrying a
non-empty list is not a finished deletion, and the spec says a consumer
MUST surface it, so it is returned rather than dropped.

  • Fragment Refs: Add Refs to <Fragment /> to support composable platform behavior (@​jackpope, @​sebmarkbage, @​eps1lon, @​Dhakshin2007, @​chirokas, @​teamleaderleo, @​fallintoplace: #32465, #32613, #32619, #32654, #32660, #32682, #32722, #32813, #32814, #33056, #33058, #33093, #34069, #34103, #34544, #34545, #37062, #37061, #37060, #36047, #36010, #35642, #35641, #35637, #35630, #34935, #37457, #37408, #37326, #37251, #37171, #37169, #37168, #37167, #37166, #37165, #37164, #37163, #37162, #37161, #37160, #37125, #37063)

New React DOM Features

  • browser(): a new react-dom API that returns a usable which errors during server rendering and resolves in the browser. use(browser()) inside a <Suspense> boundary marks a subtree as browser-only without reporting a recoverable error (@​gnoff: #37143, #37241)
    • Added an onBrowserBailout option to the react-dom/server APIs to observe when a subtree defers to the browser (@​gnoff #37193)

Notable changes

  • Enable Trusted Types API integration (@​rickhanlonii #35816)
  • Transitions now render independently instead of being entangled into a single render, so a slow transition no longer holds up unrelated ones (@​acdlite #37290)
  • Added a DEV-only warning when a component appears to have been unblocked by calling use() conditionally (@​hoxyq, @​eps1lon: #37104, #37203, #37491)

    • Handle non-string function names in Performance Tracks (@​eps1lon #35659)
    • Use minus (-) instead of en dash for removed props in Performance Tracks (@​eps1lon #35649)
    • Handle arrays with bigints in deep objects in Performance Tracks (@​eps1lon #35648)
    • Don't enumerate typed array props in Performance Tracks in DEV (@​UditDewan #36913)
    • Bail out of diffing wide objects and arrays in Performance Tracks (@​eps1lon #34742)
    • Clear potentially large performance measures in DEV (@​hoxyq #34803)

title: fix(vta)!: preview the whole subtree a context delete destroys
body:
> Rebased onto `main` now that #1575 has merged (`83db02f`); base retargeted, so CI runs against `main` for the first time.

`preview_delete_context` collected the named context and nothing else, while `delete_context` cascades the whole subtree. Two functions answering different questions about the same act, and the preview's was the wrong one.

A context whose own keyspaces were empty over children holding keys, DIDs and grants previewed as holding nothing. Every consumer decides from that preview whether the deletion needs `force`, so every consumer decided from the wrong set:

- send `force: false` → the agent refuses, with nothing on screen explaining why; or
- the parent happens to hold one key → `force: true` → an entire unlisted subtree is destroyed under a confirmation listing one key.

The second is how this was reported.

## `collect_subtree_resources`, and why it is not a loop

The ACL classification is the reason. The per-context question is *"does this entry hold **only** this context?"*, which for a subtree gets it backwards: an entry scoped to both `acme` and `acme/eng` looks like it holds another context, so a loop reports it **twice, as merely narrowed** — when deleting `acme` takes both scopes and the entry goes entirely.

Asked once against the whole delete set it comes out as `removed`, which is also where the deletion's own deepest-first cascade converges. Telling an operator that a subject keeps authority it is about to lose completely is the one error this preview must not make.

## The CLIs

Both front-ends prompted off that preview and then passed `force = true` to the deletion regardless, so `vta context delete acme` on a parent that held nothing itself took the subtree **with no prompt at all**.

They now name the sub-contexts — derived locally, since the task has no member for them yet — and count them, and DID templates, toward "does this destroy anything". The renderer never printed `didTemplates` and never counted them either, so a context whose only contents were templates skipped the prompt too.

`render_delete_context_preview` takes `sub_contexts` as a parameter rather than reading it off the preview; when trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#513 lands and the `trust-tasks-rs` pin moves, that becomes `&preview.sub_contexts` and the callers stop computing it.

## Tests

- `preview_reports_what_sub_contexts_hold` — a grandchild's ACL entry, two levels below anything a per-context preview looks at
- `an_acl_entry_scoped_wholly_inside_the_subtree_is_previewed_as_removed` — with a straddling entry and an outside entry as the controls

**Both confirmed to fail against the old preview** (`left: [], right: ["did:key:zBuildBot"]` / `["did:key:zInside"]`).

Breaking: `render_delete_context_preview` gains a `sub_contexts` parameter.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — 128 targets, 0 failures
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean

title: chore(deps): rmcp 3.4, and take the ServerInfo -> ServerConfig rename
body:
## Why

Held back from #25 deliberately — that was an Affinidi-stack bump and this needs a source change, so it belongs on its own.

`rmcp` 3.4 deprecates `ServerInfo`. The migration is **only a rename**: both names are aliases of `InitializeResult`, and `ServerHandler::get_info` still returns the same type. Nothing about the handler's behaviour changes.

## Why upstream renamed it

rmcp#1082: `ServerInfo` collided with the protocol's own `serverInfo` field, which is only the `Implementation` identity — so `server_info.server_info` read as a typo and was not one.

This handler has exactly that line:

```rust
let mut server_info = Implementation::from_build_env();
…
ServerConfig::new(ServerCapabilities::builder().enable_tools().build())
    .with_server_info(server_info)
```

So the comment now says which is which — `ServerConfig` is the whole value (protocol version, capabilities, identity), `server_info` is just the identity — rather than leaving the next reader to work it out.

## Versions

| crate | from | to |
|---|---|---|
| `rmcp` | 3.2.0 | 3.4.0 |
| `rmcp-macros` | 3.3.0 | 3.4.0 |

## Testing

`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` clean (the deprecation warnings this removes were the only ones); 119 tests green.

title: Say what identifierScope is, and that it is not a scope taxonomy
body:
Addresses #5. Prose only, one file, +7. **No schema change and no code change** — see the blast-radius note at the bottom.

## The problem

#5 reported that this framework's `parties[].identifierScope` (`pairwise | public | any`) and the DTG credentials specification's proposed declared correlation scope (`pairwise | community | linked | public`, [`dtgwg-cred-spec#22`](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22)) look like two vocabularies for one axis, with `community` and `linked` having no faithful target here. A witnessed exchange carries credentials under that vocabulary inside Trust Task documents under this one, so the two meet on a single identifier.

Working through it, they are **not** competing vocabularies — but nothing in the text says so, and the member's name actively invites the misreading.

## What this says

**`identifierScope` is a machine-readable restatement of Identifier Correlation and Linkability item 1**, which is a binary rule: an identifier is relationship-scoped, or it is reused across relationships and needs justification. The three values mirror that rule plus abstention. It is not a taxonomy of correlation width and does not claim to be one.

Two consequences, both now stated:

1. **It is declared by a specification, about a party role** — before any identifier exists — not by a holder about an identifier it controls. Where a holder declares something about its own identifier under another specification, the two are assertions about different subjects. Neither overrides the other, and a divergence is not itself a conformance failure. That is what makes the two axes compose rather than compete, and it means #22 can land in any form without this member needing to move.

2. **A bounded-recognisability identifier is a cross-relationship identifier for item 1's purposes.** A VID that one community's members can recognise is reused across relationships, and the joins item 1 forecloses are available to any two of them who compare what they hold. So it is declared `public` and carries the justification obligation in full.

That second point answers the reported `community`/`linked` gap by deciding it rather than by growing the enum. The framework deliberately does not grade width: the bound may be unknown to the parties and may grow, and item 1 does not turn on it. A specification needing to record the bound states it in its justification — which the existing lint already asks for.

It also makes the fail-safe in the following paragraph correct rather than overstated. Treating an unresolvable declaration as "no less correlatable than `public`" is not a bug applied to bounded identifiers; under item 1 a bounded identifier **is** on the `public` side.

## Blast radius

Verified before writing:

- The enum stays at three values. `specs/spec.meta.schema.json` is unchanged, so the 37 `pairwise` and 19 `public` declarations across the registry stay valid.
- `spec.meta.schema.json` is excluded from **both** binding generators by name — `scripts/build-ts-bindings.mjs` (`NOT_PAYLOAD_SCHEMAS`) and `trust-tasks-codegen/src/main.rs`, which walks `payload.schema.json` only. No `IdentifierScope` symbol exists in any `.rs` or `.ts` in the workspace.
- No crate or package version bump, no `codegen-drift`/`bindings-drift` exposure, no struct-literal breakage.

A companion PR carries the same text into `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`'s copy of `SPEC.md` and aligns the meta-schema description.

`npm run render` clean.

title: fix(vta)!: delete a context's did:webvh DIDs off their hosting servers, not just locally
body:
Deleting a context cascaded to its sub-contexts and dropped each DID's local record with `webvh_store::delete_did` plus its log key. That is not a smaller version of deleting the DID; it is a different outcome.

The published log stayed on the hosting server, so **the DID kept resolving for everyone except the agent that owned it**. Credentials the VTA had issued naming it stayed valid, with the only records that could revoke them destroyed. Live sessions authenticated as it kept working. The operator was told the context was deleted, and nothing in the result distinguished the two outcomes.

Reported from the browser console: a context was deleted and a DID in one of its sub-contexts was still present on the hosting service afterwards.

## What changed

Every DID in the subtree now goes through `delete_did_webvh_with` — the same path `pnm did-mgmt dids delete` takes — so the host copy is removed, credentials revoked, sessions ended, and the full key-fragment range cleaned up. `purge_context_resources` no longer deletes DIDs at all: one path, not two, and the weaker one is gone.

| step | `delete_did_webvh` | context cascade (before) | context cascade (now) |
|---|---|---|---|
| blocker pre-flight | yes | no | yes, subtree-wide |
| revoke issued credentials | yes | **no** | yes |
| `delete_log_on_server` | yes | **no** | yes |
| local record + log | yes | yes | yes |
| key records over `next_fragment_id` | yes | partial | yes |
| ACL entry | yes | yes | yes |
| revoke live sessions | yes | **no** | yes |

Three things it needed:

- **`delete_context` takes a `ContextDidCleanup`.** `None` means the caller cannot reach a hosting server, and a context holding DIDs is then refused rather than having its records dropped behind their hosts' backs — the stance `WebvhDeps::delete_cascade` already takes for a single DID. All four transports (REST, DIDComm, trust task, offline CLI) supply one.
- **`DeleteDidOptions::contexts_being_deleted`** narrows the "a context acts as this DID" blocker. Without it the cascade could never delete a context that had an identity; switching the blocker off instead would let a context delete strand an *unrelated* context's DID, so it names the contexts going away rather than suppressing the check.
- **Blockers are collected across the whole subtree and refuse before anything is destroyed.** Per-DID checks inside the loop would delete three contexts' DIDs and refuse on the fourth, which is the half-deletion `vta/contexts/delete/1.0` forbids in as many words.

Ordering is remote-first (R2.1): a local record removed before its host copy is the one state from which the host copy can never be removed.

## Tests

`deleting_a_context_deletes_its_subtree_dids_on_the_hosting_server` mints a hosted DID in a sub-context, force-deletes the parent, and asserts `mock.webvh_host_deletes() == 1`.

**Confirmed to fail against the old behaviour** (`left: 0, right: 1`). That counter is the only witness that separates the two outcomes — an assertion on the local record passes either way, which is exactly why this survived.

`a_context_delete_is_refused_when_an_outside_context_acts_as_one_of_its_dids` pins the narrow form of the blocker exemption, and that nothing is destroyed on the way to the refusal.

## Not in this PR

`vta/contexts/delete/1.0` has no member to carry a partial-success report, so a daemon that refuses a delete is an `ERROR`-level event naming the orphans rather than a wire member. trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#513 proposes `daemonCleanupErrors`; wiring it needs that released and the `trust-tasks-rs` pin moved.

## Pre-merge checklist

- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1)
- [x] Wire types unchanged; no schema movement in this PR (R3.*)
- [x] Logs claim only what was verified; the daemon-side failure is surfaced, not swallowed (R6.*)
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for the cascade ordering (R2.1)

Breaking: `delete_context` gains a parameter and `DeleteDidOptions` gains a lifetime.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — 128 targets, 0 failures
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `--no-default-features` error count unchanged from `main` (4, all pre-existing, none in touched files); the webvh-off path builds clean


---

**Follow-ups in this stack**

- OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1576 — makes the *preview* answer for the subtree too (stacked on this PR)
- OpenVTC/vta-browser-plugin#261 — the console panel that reported this
- trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#513 — `subContexts` + `daemonCleanupErrors`, and the prose making this deletion requirement normative

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.21.4
body:
### Added

- **vta/contexts**: Preview the whole subtree a delete destroys, and report host copies it could not remove

Deleting a context deletes its sub-contexts and everything they hold, to any depth. Neither vta/contexts/delete/1.0 nor its preview said so, and the preview had nowhere to say what the cascade would reach.

  vta/contexts/preview-delete/1.0 gains subContexts, with the existing arrays defined as the union over the whole subtree. The narrower reading — preview the named context alone — is the natural one and is dangerous: a context whose children hold keys and DIDs previews as holding nothing, and a caller deciding whether the delete needs force decides about the wrong thing.

  vta/contexts/delete/1.0 gains daemonCleanupErrors, the subtree-wide form of the daemonCleanupError that vta/webvh/dids/delete/1.0 already reports for a single DID, and now requires that a did:webvh DID in the subtree be deleted the way that task deletes one — published log removed from its hosting server, credentials revoked, authority withdrawn. Removing only the local record is not a deletion: the log keeps resolving for every party except its owner, and the records that could remove it are the ones just destroyed.

  Both members are optional and additive; the refusal and cascade prose describes behaviour that was already implemented but unstated.

body:
Updates the requirements on [affinidi-tdk](https://github.com/affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs) to permit the latest version.
Changelog

Sourced from affinidi-tdk's changelog.

Changelog

All notable changes to this workspace are documented here. The format follows Keep a Changelog, and the workspace crates follow Semantic Versioning.

Per-crate version history is summarised here; for the full code history see git log.

[Unreleased]

Added

  • affinidi-net-guard 0.1.0: one egress guard for URLs an attacker can influence. affinidi-did-web 0.1.5, affinidi-tdk-common 0.6.11.

    A DID names the host a resolver fetches from, and a DID document names the endpoints a client dials, so each is a server-side request forgery primitive unless something refuses internal targets. affinidi-did-web 0.1.4 had the strongest guard in the stack, but it was private to a DID-method crate. It is now a leaf crate under crates/core/ with no affinidi-* dependency, so DID-method crates and external clients can take it without a cycle (ADR 0006).

    The crate enforces two halves, and both are needed. EgressPolicy::vet checks the scheme, userinfo, port, allow-list, special-use names and IP literals; reqwest never consults a resolver for a literal, so this is the only check a literal meets. GuardedResolver checks every address a name resolves to, fails the name on any blocked answer, and pins the connection to the vetted addresses. GuardedClient runs both, with no proxy, finite timeouts, no redirects by default and a capped body read.

    conformance/egress-vectors.v1.json is the vector file the TypeScript and Swift guards will share; the crate's tests run it, including DNS rebinding and redirect cases against local TLS listeners.

    affinidi-did-web now takes its address classification and resolver from the new crate, with its API and name set unchanged. The shared classifier also refuses some non-routable ranges that 0.1.4 accepted; its changelog lists them. affinidi-tdk-common adds create_guarded_http_client(extra_roots, &policy) on the existing platform TLS setup, and re-exports the crate as net_guard.

* chore(deps): take affinidi-tdk 0.16, not 0.14

`#[non_exhaustive]` to `Inbound`, and `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.24.0 -
what affinidi-tdk 0.14 pulls in - constructs that struct with a struct
expression in `transport_adapter.rs`. Its requirement is
`affinidi-messaging-core = "0.1.6"`, so the caret range accepts 0.1.8 and
the SDK stops compiling: `error[E0639]: cannot create non-exhaustive
struct using struct expression`.

Nothing in this repo can fix that from below. We have no Cargo.lock in
git - this is a library, so CI resolves fresh on every run and always
picks up 0.1.8. The only lever is the requirement itself.

0.16.0 moves to `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.26.10, which does not build
`Inbound` by hand, and the three failing jobs go green. affinidi-tdk is a
dev-dependency used by the examples and integration tests, so this
changes nothing for a consumer of the published crate and needs no
CHANGELOG entry.

Every other dependency is already at the newest version its requirement
allows, so no other manifest change was needed.

title: fix(manager): show the subtree a context delete destroys, and ask before taking it
body:
Deleting a context deletes everything below it. The delete panel said nothing about that, and the omission broke in both directions.

**A context holding nothing of its own read as harmless.** The preview rendered "Your agent reports it holds no keys and no DIDs", `needsForce` was false, the panel sent `force: false`, and the agent refused — because sub-contexts exist. The operator was shown a refusal for a deletion the screen had just called harmless.

**A context holding one key of its own read as almost harmless.** `force` went true on the strength of that one key, the confirmation listed it, and the agent destroyed every context below and everything they held. The checkbox read "destroying the keys and DIDs listed above"; the list was one key and the deletion was a subtree.

Both are the same missing fact.

## What changed

The panel names the sub-contexts **first** — they reframe every list under them as the subtree's contents rather than this context's — and decides `force` from all six of the agent's lists, not two.

`contextPreviewDelete` returned three of the six. `aclEntriesRemoved` is the one an operator most needs, since it names the subjects about to lose their authority **outright** rather than merely have it narrowed, and dropping it in the client meant no screen could show it however carefully it was written. It now returns the whole preview as `ContextDeletePreview`, and the panel renders removed-entirely and narrowed as the distinct events the agent already distinguishes.

## Where the sub-contexts come from

Derived from the context list the pane already holds. `vta/contexts/preview-delete/1.0` has no member naming them — trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#513 proposes `subContexts` — and a delete that silently takes sub-contexts is exactly what this prompt exists to prevent, so it is computed rather than left out.

Matching is segment-wise, so `acme-corp` is not read as a child of `acme`. When the member lands this becomes `p.subContexts` and the derivation goes.

## Agent side

The agent's preview under-reported the same way; OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1576 makes it answer for the subtree. This PR is not waiting on it — the six arrays are rendered and counted correctly either way, and with #1576 they carry the subtree's contents rather than only the named context's.

OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1575 is the more serious half: the agent was dropping sub-context DIDs' local records without removing the published log from their hosting server, which is the behaviour that prompted all of this.

## Tests

`tests/contexts-pane-delete.render.test.mts`, four cases:

| test | against the old panel |
|---|---|
| the sub-contexts that go with it are named | **fails** |
| a context holding nothing itself still asks | **fails** |
| grants and templates count as contents | **fails** |
| an empty leaf says so and needs no force | passes — the control |

The control is what keeps the other three from passing vacuously.

## Verification

- `npm run lint` (`tsc -b`, all workspaces) — clean
- `npm test` — 730 tests, 0 failures
- `npm run build` — clean

title: feat(vta/contexts): preview the whole subtree a delete destroys, and report host copies it could not remove
body:
Deleting a context deletes its sub-contexts and everything they hold, to any depth. Neither `vta/contexts/delete/1.0` nor its preview said so, and the preview had nowhere to say what the cascade would reach.

Found from the consumer side: a reference implementation's preview collected the named context alone, so a context whose own keyspaces were empty over children holding keys, DIDs and grants previewed as holding nothing — and every consumer that decides "does this need `force`?" from the preview decided it from the wrong set.

## `vta/contexts/preview-delete/1.0` — `subContexts`

Names the sub-contexts the deletion would remove, with the existing arrays defined as the union over the whole subtree.

The narrower reading is the natural one and is dangerous. A preview scoped to the named context alone reports "holds nothing" for a context whose children hold a great deal, and a caller acting on that answer is deciding about the wrong thing. A preview that under-reports is worse than no preview, because it is a promise the operator acted on.

## `vta/contexts/delete/1.0` — `daemonCleanupErrors`

The subtree-wide form of the `daemonCleanupError` that `vta/webvh/dids/delete/1.0` already reports for a single DID.

The task now also requires that a `did:webvh` DID in the subtree be deleted the way that task deletes one — published log removed from its hosting server, credentials revoked, authority withdrawn. Removing only the local record is not a deletion of it: the log keeps resolving for every party except its owner, and the records that could remove it are the ones just destroyed. This was implemented incorrectly downstream precisely because the task never said which of the two it meant.

## Which side moved

The spec, in both cases. The cascade behaviour was already implemented and simply unstated, and the `subContexts` gap was a real hole in the preview's contract rather than an implementation shortfall. No required member is replaced or removed, so both changes are additive and stay in the `1.0` folder.

## Additive, and what that costs

Both members are optional. The generated Rust binding gets `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Vec::is_empty")]` and a builder setter, so an absent member round-trips unchanged and no struct literal moves.

The known asymmetry applies: a **stale Rust consumer** of either response will fail to deserialise a reply carrying the new member, because generated response types are `deny_unknown_fields`. TypeScript consumers are unaffected unless they have wired the validator seam. Worth stating in the release notes alongside the other members that have landed this way.

No JSON Schema `default` is declared on either — a declared default is materialised by the bindings and breaks round-trip idempotence for existing documents. Absence is described in prose instead.

## Recipe

```
npm run validate                        # 451 specs
cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all
npm run build-ts-bindings
npm run build-go-bindings
npm run build-dart-bindings
npm run check-bindings                  # 451 TS / 446 Rust / 451 Go / 451 Dart — all agree
cargo build --workspace --all-targets   # struct-literal check across the binding crates
cargo test --workspace                  # green
cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features "validate,vta" --lib specs::vta::contexts::preview_delete   # 2 tests
cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features "validate,vta" --lib specs::vta::contexts::delete           # 2 tests
npm run build
```

The preview's `Response` example now carries `subContexts`, so `response_example_1` exercises the new member rather than only proving the schema still parses.

No `Cargo.toml`, `package.json` or `CHANGELOG.md` touched — release-plz owns versions here.

title: feat(join): apply to a community as a second persona
body:
The last of the gaps #355 named. You asked then whether vetting should be one
application per community or several in parallel; the answer was that the
**model already allows several** — `start_application` keys on
`(community, persona)`, so a second persona gets its own application, and being
vetted as one says nothing about another. #355 pinned that in a test.

The join page made it unreachable.

## What was wrong

`KnownVetting` held a single `Option<JoinApplication>`, filled with the first
application found for the community, and:

```rust
pub fn shows_selectors(&self) -> bool {
    self.application.is_none()
}
```

So the moment *any* application existed, the persona chooser vanished and the
vetting row collapsed to "Carry on with your application". From this page there
was no way to apply as anybody else — the capability existed and had no door.

## What it does now

It is a `Vec`. The chooser stays, and which application the page is working
with follows from the persona it is on:

```
Apply for vetting                    under way as alice
   Apply as   alice  (did:key:z6Mk…)  — already applied   ←/→

Apply for vetting                    no application yet
   Apply as   bob    (did:key:z6Mk…)  — no application yet   ←/→
   Context    openvtc/kernel
```

The page still **opens on the application it would have collapsed to** — one
that meets the requirements, else the first — so the common case takes no
keystrokes. The difference is that the others are one arrow key away instead of
unreachable.

Each persona's standing is on its own row, because that is what the reader is
cycling to find out. Putting it only in the route's label two lines up would
make them watch a heading change as a side effect of moving the cursor.

## Three things that had to move together

The row's **label**, its **detail**, and **what Enter does** all answer the same
question — does this persona already have an application — and answering it in
three places is how they drift. `cycle_vetting_choice` previously updated only
`route.state`, which was correct while the answer could never change; now that
it can, a row reading "Carry on with your application" over a persona that has
none would describe a different action from the one it takes.

`vetting_row_words` decides label and detail in one place, used by both
`build_routes` and the cycle handler. The part of the detail that does *not*
depend on the persona — that this community also asks for an invitation — is
kept on the page and re-appended, rather than recomputed from requirements the
handler does not have.

## Two smaller decisions

**"Context" is nested only while a new application would be started.** An
application under way has already answered it, and its face's context is fixed
for the application's whole life, so offering the choice would imply it could
still be changed.

**`selected_application` reads `persona_index`, never the cursor.** The
nested-row count depends on whether the selected persona has an application, and
the cursor position depends on the nested-row count — reading the cursor here
would have made the two define each other.

## Testing

- `cargo test --all-features -- --include-ignored` — all green
- `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all` — clean
- `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps --all-features` — clean

`every_persona_with_an_application_is_reachable_from_the_join` builds two and
asserts both reach the page. `the_vetting_row_follows_the_persona_being_applied_as`
pins all three shapes of the row.

The existing render fixture had to gain a `personas` entry matching its
application: which application the page shows now follows from the persona the
chooser is on, so an application whose persona is not in the list belongs to
nobody the cursor can reach. That is a real invariant, not test scaffolding —
worth knowing if something ever builds `KnownVetting` by hand.

**Not covered:** cycling itself. `cycle_vetting_choice` needs the page's action
harness, so the rebuild-on-cycle path is reasoned about rather than tested —
which is exactly where the old code's bug would have lived.

**Not validated live.**

title: feat(vetting): make a face for this community without leaving the flow
body:
#356 made the picker say which faces cannot make this community's card. This
handles the case it exposed: **none of them can.**

The answer then was to leave the vetting flow, build a face under My Identity,
come back and press `f` again — the out-of-cycle config work this flow has been
folding inline everywhere else (#348, #351).

## The row

The picker gains a last row:

```
This community's card needs  name.legal

▸ OSS Developer  2 attributes  worn now
      shows     email.work, name.preferred
      missing   name.legal — no card for this community
  Work           6 attributes
      shows     name.legal, dob, address.home, …

  Make a face for this community    from attributes you already have
```

A **row rather than a key**, so every way out of this screen is in the list the
eye is already on.

## The form knows what the face is for

```
Make a face for this community

  Name              ▸ _

 This community's card needs  name.legal

  [ ] EMAIL.WORK        email.work
▸ [x] NAME.LEGAL        name.legal      needed here
  [ ] DOB               dob
```

The community has already named the claim types its card must carry, so the
matching attributes open **already ticked**. The holder's decision is usually
just a name.

What is still missing is computed against the **current selection**, not the
pool, so unticking something required says so at the moment of the choice
rather than three steps later at the card preview.

## Composed, never created

The form selects from attributes the pool already holds and never creates one.
Supplying a *value* for a legal name is a different act from arranging which
attributes a face shows, and it belongs with the editor that knows about value
types, sensitivity and masking.

What this form owes the holder instead is to name the claim type **no attribute
can cover**:

```
  missing   name.legal — this face could not make the card
            no attribute of yours is name.legal — add one under My Identity
```

That is a different problem from a claim merely unticked, because ticking harder
will not fix it, and `a_claim_the_pool_cannot_cover_is_named_as_such` pins that
the two do not get conflated.

**This is the deliberate boundary of the PR.** A holder who has never recorded
their legal name still goes to My Identity once. The inline flow covers the
common case — attributes exist, spread across faces that individually fall
short — which is exactly the shape the dry run hit.

## Three smaller decisions

**Creating and wearing are one step.** A face made here exists to be worn by
this application; leaving it created but unworn would put the holder back on the
picker to do what they had just asked for. It reuses the `FaceWorn` outcome, so
the face is recorded on the application (`ChosenFace`, #356) and displayed by
the same paths as one chosen from the list.

**The pool read meets the same holder-grant refusal** the faces read does — the
pool is what a face is built over — and routes it to the same view rather than
passing the agent's paragraph through.

**`other_entries` is empty on the write,** because this creates. `ProfileForm`'s
own doc warns that rebuilding a profile from only the ticked boxes silently
deletes pinned and inline entries; that hazard is real for the general *editor*
and absent here, since there is no existing profile to lose anything from.

## Testing

- `cargo test --all-features` — all green
- `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all` — clean
- `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps --all-features` — clean

Three new tests: the opening selection, the uncoverable case, and that the pool
read's holder refusal lands on the same view.

**Not covered:** the `FaceJob::Create` job itself, which needs a live VTA — the
tests exercise the form's logic and the outcome handling, not the write. The
key wiring (Tab between name and list, Space to tick) is also untested; it goes
through the panel's generic non-List key handler, which has no harness.

**Not validated live.** Nothing here has been run against a real pool.

title: feat(health): say whether this install can read its own faces
body:
The second half of what #354 and VTI #1573/#1574 started. Those made the
refusal *explicable* once it happened; this makes it visible before it does.

## Why a preflight and not a better error

The grant went missing during onboarding (VTI #1573): `--admin-holder` was
granted to the ephemeral setup key, the admin rollover wrote the successor's ACL
row from defaults, and `retire_ephemeral_after_rollover` deleted the row that
held it. Nothing failed at the time. Everything context-scoped kept working.
`openvtc health` reported a clean chain.

It surfaced days later, mid-ceremony, on the one screen that needed it — with a
vetter waiting.

The VTA access section already printed the ACL subject and the grant command.
That is what an operator needs *once they know something is wrong*. Nothing
answered the prior question.

## What it does

One authenticated `persona/profile/list` — metadata only, nothing decrypted —
run **by default** rather than behind a flag, because a check nobody knows to
ask for does not help.

```
Your own identity
  faces            3 readable — this install holds holder authority
```

or:

```
Your own identity
  faces            refused — this install has no holder authority

  Your agent credential administers this context. Your attributes, and the faces
  over them, sit above every context — reaching them is a separate grant:

     pnm acl update did:key:z6Mkhm… --capabilities persona-holder

  It adds authority over your own identity without giving this install any
  authority over other contexts.

  Run it from a super-admin PNM session. Until then nothing that reads
  a face works: personas, the faces a vetter is shown, and the identity
  a community sees when you join.
```

Same `holder_grant_hint` lines as the Identity pane and the Vetting pane, so
there is one rendering of this refusal across three surfaces.

## Two judgement calls

**Exercised, not asked.** `auth/whoami/0.1` returns the effective capability
list and would have been the obvious source — but it has no client method in
vta-sdk 0.43, only a task URI, and a *claim* about a capability is a weaker
answer than using it. Doing the read also means a VTA old enough to have no
capability concept still reports correctly: it refuses in its own words, and
`needs_holder_grant` already matches both wordings.

**Only a confirmed absence fails the run.** An unreachable VTA is already
reported by the chain checks, and failing twice for one cause tells an operator
nothing new — while failing on "unknown" would make every offline run look like
a missing grant. The JSON keeps the distinction:

| state | `granted` |
|---|---|
| refused for want of the grant | `false`, plus `remedy` |
| could not tell | `null`, plus `why` |
| no VTA backend (BIP32) | `null`, `applicable: false` |

`remedy` is the command, not a boolean somebody has to look up how to act on.

## Testing

- `cargo test --all-features` — all green
- `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all` — clean

Two new tests cover the exit-status rule and the absent-vs-unknown distinction.

**Not covered:** `check_holder_authority` itself, which needs a live VTA — the
tests exercise the classification and rendering, not the call. And it has not
been run against an install that is actually missing the grant; the wording was
derived from the refusal text, not observed.

**Cost:** this adds one VTA round trip to every `openvtc health` run on a VTA
profile. It is a single metadata read and the command already opens sessions
under `--recoverable`, but it is no longer free on a profile that never used
faces.
