title: feat(vtc): a VTC provisioned from the v2 template issues hybrid credentials
body:
The last piece. `vtc-host` declares a post-quantum signing slot, the VTA mints
it, the sealed bundle carries it, the VTC stores it and gives it to
`LocalSigner` — so every credential the VTC issues carries a proof from each
key. A verifier that has not migrated checks the `eddsa-jcs-2022` proof; one that
has checks `mldsa44-jcs-2024`; neither needs to know about the other.

Everything before this PR could be in place while credentials still came out
classical-only, which is why the test that matters signs a real credential from
a real stored bundle and looks at the cryptosuites on it.

## `vtc-host` at schemaVersion 2

Three slots: `signing` (ed25519), `ka` (x25519), `pq-signing` (mldsa44, falling
back to ed25519). `#key-0` and `#key-2` are both assertion methods.

**The primary stays Ed25519 and cannot be otherwise** — it signs the did:webvh
log, and didwebvh 1.0 mandates `eddsa-jcs-2022` for log-entry proofs. The
fallback on `pq-signing` is what lets one template serve a VTA that can mint
ML-DSA and one that cannot.

The template moves here rather than in the sealed-variant PR on purpose: the
template is what *activates* the new path, so it lands with the consumer that
can open the result, never before it.

## One reply shape, and what it costs downstream

`VtaReply::Full` now carries `ProvisionResultV2`, and the three runners open
through `response_to_result_v2`, which takes either sealed variant and lifts V1
losslessly. A second `VtaReply` variant was the alternative and would have meant
two names for one event, with every consumer branching on which bundle the VTA
happened to seal — a question none of them has.

**This breaks `affinidi-tdk-rs`'s `mediator-setup` on its next `vta-sdk` bump**,
at two places, and neither is more than a few lines:

  - `sealed_handoff.rs:1167` constructs a `ProvisionResult` literal —
    `provision_from_template_payload` should build a `ProvisionResultV2`, or
    keep returning V1 and be adapted at the `VtaSession::full` boundary.
  - `test_helpers::sample_provision_result` still returns V1;
    `sample_provision_result_v2` is there for the `VtaReply::Full` call sites in
    `app.rs`.

Its *reads* port unchanged: `ProvisionResultV2` has the same `admin_did()`,
`integration_did()`, `integration_key()`, `webvh_log()` and
`authorization_vc()`. `ProvisionResult` and `response_to_result` are untouched
for any consumer that wants to stay on the V1 shape.

## The stored bundle

`VtcKeyBundle` gains `additional_signing_keys`, each carrying its slot, its
algorithm, and its published verification-method id.

- `#[serde(default)]` means every bundle already on disk loads unchanged — which
  is every VTC in the field, all of them provisioned from a v1 template.
- An empty list is skipped on write, so an unchanged VTC writes an unchanged
  bundle.
- `deny_unknown_fields` means the reverse does **not** hold: a bundle written
  with extra keys cannot be read by an older binary, so rolling vtc-service back
  past this change requires re-provisioning. A test states that rather than
  leaving it to be discovered during a rollback.

## Refusing rather than dropping

A stored signing key that cannot be decoded **fails the boot**. The DID document
publishes it as an assertion method, so a VTC that skipped it would issue
credentials a verifier expecting two proofs reads as incomplete, with nothing
anywhere saying why. That is the same judgment `with_additional_key` already
makes at the other end of the chain: a key added for post-quantum protection
that quietly does nothing is the worst outcome available.

The key's algorithm is read from its multicodec by `Secret::from_multibase`, so
this code never enumerates parameter sets; the stored `key_type` is what the
bundle says it is, written by the party that minted it.

## A test whose premise changed

`every_builtin_still_declares_the_historical_key_pair` asserted every built-in
is v1. `vtc-host` no longer is, so it is now checked against what it declares —
including that the historical pair survived unchanged inside the v2 template —
with the v2 built-ins listed by name. Skipping every v2 template instead would
have let a built-in quietly move to v2 and stop being checked at all.

`KeyType` gains `Eq` alongside `PartialEq` (a fieldless enum is trivially `Eq`,
and the stored bundle derives it). Additive.

title: feat(vtc): a VTC provisioned from the v2 template issues hybrid credentials (#1557)
body:
feat(vtc): a VTC provisioned from the v2 template issues hybrid credentials (#1557)

* fix(did-templates): a key slot beyond the historical pair, and the literal it used to publish

`slot_var`'s `{SLOT}_KEY_MB` rule is mechanical, and before this it was
mechanical in one direction only. A `schemaVersion` 2 template could *declare* a
third key slot — a post-quantum signing key beside the classical pair, which is
the shape a hybrid-credential issuer needs — and then could not be loaded,
because the placeholder that slot's own rule produces was rejected:

    Invalid("undeclared placeholder(s) { PQ_SIGNING_KEY_MB } in document
             — add them to requiredVars or optionalVars")

Only `SIGNING_KEY_MB` and `KA_KEY_MB` were ambient, because only those two are
in `RESERVED_VARS`. So `keys` at schemaVersion 2 (#1530) could express exactly
the pair it was introduced to move beyond.

## Following the error's advice published a literal into a write-once log

The advice is the defect. `optionalVars` supplies a **default**, and the
renderer substitutes a default for any name the caller did not supply — and the
minting flow does not supply a slot's key under a name it has never heard of.
So declaring `PQ_SIGNING_KEY_MB` to get past the rejection passed validation
*and rendered*:

    {
      "id": "did:webvh:x#key-2",
      "type": "Multikey",
      "publicKeyMultibase": "PLACEHOLDER-NEVER-SUBSTITUTED"
    }

— inside `assertionMethod`, in a `did:webvh` log that is signed once and cannot
be re-signed. `check_key_slots` already refuses a slot the document never
publishes: a key minted and thrown away. This is the same failure wearing the
other hat, a key published and never minted, and it arrived through the one door
that check does not watch.

## What changes

- `DidTemplate::slot_vars()` — the placeholder names the declared slots occupy,
  built from `key_slots()` rather than a second fixed list. For a v1 template it
  is exactly the two already in `RESERVED_VARS`, so v1 behaviour is untouched;
  it is what lets a v2 template name a third slot at all.
- `check_placeholders_declared` treats those names as ambient. An author cannot
  declare a value they have no way to know.
- `check_slot_vars_not_declared` refuses the reverse — a slot's placeholder in
  `requiredVars` or `optionalVars` — naming the slot and saying why. A v1
  template still gets `ReservedVar` from the check that runs first, unchanged.
- An undeclared placeholder that is *shaped* like a slot's is told to declare a
  **slot**, not a variable. The generic advice pointed at exactly what the new
  check refuses; an error that recommends the defect is worse than no error.

## The state this leaves

A third slot is expressible, and a VTA that cannot yet mint for it fails at
render with `Unresolved` naming the placeholder — rather than emitting a
document with a hole in it. Wiring derivation to the `keys` block is the next
change; until then the loud failure is the correct one.

Found while tracing what stands between a VTC and a second signing key: nothing
in the chain from template to `LocalSigner::with_additional_key` could carry one.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(did-webvh): mint the keys a template's `keys` block asks for

`schemaVersion` 2 templates could declare key algorithms (#1530) and
`derive_entity_keys_with_preference` could honour a preference list (#1532) —
and **nothing connected them.** Both had zero production callers.
`create_did_webvh` called plain `derive_entity_keys`, so a template declaring

    "signing": { "purpose": "signing", "algorithms": ["mldsa44", "ed25519"] }

minted an Ed25519 key and said nothing. Every capability Phase 2 shipped led to
a key nobody could ask for.

The cause is ordering: the template was resolved at *render* time, after the
keys existed. It is resolved before them now — a pure keyspace lookup, so
nothing else changes.

## A did:webvh primary signing key cannot be post-quantum

Found by running it rather than reading it, and it settles the shape of the
whole workstream:

    Invalid cryptosuite MlDsa44Jcs2024: log entry proofs must use eddsa-jcs-2022

The primary key signs the DID log, and didwebvh 1.0 mandates JCS canonicalization
with `eddsa-jcs-2022`. `didwebvh-rs`'s `experimental-pqc` flag would widen that
set and is opt-in for the right reason — a log signed that way is unverifiable by
any conformant resolver. That trades "cannot mint" for "mints a DID nobody can
resolve", so it stays off.

**Post-quantum signing on a did:webvh is therefore a second key, never a
replacement for the first** — which is what `LocalSigner` already assumes, and
what the VTC's HKDF chain (storage, install-token and audit keys all derived from
the Ed25519 seed) forces from the other end.

`log_entry_capable_signing` filters the primary slot's list rather than refusing
it, because that is what a preference list is for: `["mldsa44", "ed25519"]` falls
back exactly as it would for an algorithm this build could not mint. A list with
no classical entry is refused, naming what it asked for and what to do instead.
Silently substituting Ed25519 for a list that never mentioned it is the quiet
downgrade the `keys` block exists to prevent.

## The third slot

`DerivedEntityKeys` gains `additional_signing` — the slot Phase 2 deferred on
the grounds that no consumer existed. Hybrid credentials are that consumer: an
issuer signs with every key it holds, so it needs the classical key and the
post-quantum one at once, which no arity of two can express. Additive to the
existing pair, not a slot map: the arity of the first two is still a true
property worth keeping in the type.

Each extra slot is minted at its **own** BIP-32 path. Sharing the primary's would
make the second key a deterministic function of the first at that index — the
cross-algorithm reuse `derive_ml_dsa_44`'s domain separation exists to prevent,
reintroduced one layer up where that separation cannot see it.

Records are stored under the ids the **published document** gives each key,
found by matching `publicKeyMultibase` — the same rule `minted_vm_ids` already
applies to the pair, so a template numbering its methods any way it likes still
gets records named what its own document says.

## A third live instance of the Phase-2 defect shape

`save_entity_key_records_with_ids` passed `KeyType::Ed25519` as a literal for the
signing key — in the VTA-derived branch, the one a `keys` block steers.
`DerivedEntityKeys` grew `signing_key_type` to stop exactly that; the
caller-supplied branch reads it and this one was missed.

Latent, not live: nothing can mint a non-Ed25519 primary on did:webvh today. The
test says so in as many words, so the first DID method that can does not discover
it far from here.

## Refused rather than ignored

- A **second key-agreement slot**. It would put a second `keyAgreement` entry in
  the document, changing which secret an inbound encrypted message resolves to
  (`select_secret_kid`), and nothing here decides that. The failure would surface
  at a mediator as an undecryptable message.
- **Extra slots against caller-supplied keys.** The VTA mints an extra slot from
  its own seed and may not invent one for a DID whose keys the caller brought.
- An **algorithm name this build does not know**, with the slot that named it —
  the derivation functions only see a `KeyType`, so by then the slot is gone.
- A **minted slot the published document does not carry**. Storing it under a
  guessed id would hide the template/document disagreement that caused it.

## Tests exercise the behaviour, not the plumbing

The end-to-end tests mint a DID and read the **stored key record** back.
`derive_entity_keys_with_preference` existed, was tested, and had no caller — a
test that stopped at the plumbing would have passed throughout.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(sealed-transfer): a template-bootstrap variant that can carry a second signing key

The last structural blocker on hybrid credentials. `LocalSigner` has signed with
every key it holds since #1553, and since the previous PR a VTA mints whatever
the template's `keys` block asks for — but nothing could *deliver* a second key
to a consumer, because there was no field to put it in.

## Why a new variant, measured rather than assumed

`DidKeyMaterial` and `TemplateBootstrapPayload` both carry
`#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`. Adding a third key field was tried against
`main` first:

    unknown field `pq_signing_key`, expected one of `did`, `signing_key`, `ka_key`

Every existing opener rejects the whole payload, with a message that reads like a
corrupted bundle of a format it believes it understands. The workspace rule
(CLAUDE.md, "Sealed-transfer is the only secret-bearing wire format") says add a
variant instead, and the failure that produces is the better one — it names the
thing the opener does not know:

    unknown variant `template_bootstrap_v2`, expected one of `admin_credential`, …

## Fixed pair plus additional, not a flat slot list

`DidKeyMaterialV2` keeps `signing_key` and `ka_key` structural and adds
`additional_signing_keys`. Two facts make that the right shape rather than the
tidy one:

- **A did:webvh's primary signing key signs its log**, and didwebvh 1.0 mandates
  `eddsa-jcs-2022` for log-entry proofs. It is Ed25519 and cannot be otherwise.
- **The VTC derives its storage key, install-token signer and audit key from that
  same Ed25519 seed.** A bundle able to omit it is a bundle able to brick the
  consumer.

So post-quantum signing is an addition, never a substitution — which is also the
shape `LocalSigner` already has, so the chain from template to signature is one
idea end to end. A flat list was the alternative and is the slot map Phase 2
deliberately rejected for `DerivedEntityKeys`: the arity of the first two is a
true property worth keeping in the type.

`SlotKeyPair` carries both `slot` — the join back to the template declaration
that asked for the key — and `key_type`, read from the stored key record rather
than inferred from the multicodec. Phase 2's recurring defect was a type asserted
where it should have been carried.

## The shape follows the template

A producer emits V2 only when the DID actually holds a key beyond the pair, which
only a template declaring an extra slot produces. **Every v1 template — which is
all thirteen built-ins — keeps sealing `TemplateBootstrap` byte-identically.**

Blast radius on existing openers is therefore zero, including `mediator-setup` in
affinidi-tdk-rs, a real cross-repo consumer: `didcomm-mediator` is v1, so it
never sees the new variant. Both directions are pinned by tests that mint through
the real flow and open the real bundle, because "which variant did the VTA
choose" is the contract and no amount of testing the payload types in isolation
shows it.

Same no-migration property as the proof rule one layer up: one key emits a proof
object, several emit an array. The wire shape follows what is there; nothing has
a flag to set.

## Reading both shapes through one path

`response_to_result_v2` accepts either variant and returns the V2 shape, lifting
V1 through `DidKeyMaterialV2::from_v1`. That lift is total and not a guess: V1
has exactly two slots, `signing` and `ka`, by the format's definition. The one
thing V1 does not state is each key's algorithm, so it is read from the
multicodec prefix — the only carrier V1 has — via a new
`KeyType::from_public_multibase` built from the same exhaustive match as
`multicodec_public`, so the two cannot drift.

A key whose prefix names no algorithm this build knows is **refused, not
defaulted**. Defaulting to Ed25519 would put the mislabelling `key_type` exists
to prevent one layer further down, where nothing would catch it.

`ProvisionResult` and `response_to_result` are untouched — that type's `payload`
field is public API another repository already reads, and widening it would break
those consumers for a capability they have not asked for. A V2 bundle reaching
the old entry point is `WrongPayload`: the caller asked for the shape it can
install and got another, and silently dropping the extra key would defeat the
point of having asked.

## Not included

`vtc-host` stays at schemaVersion 1. The template is what *activates* this path,
so it moves with the consumer that can open the result — the VTC's key bundle and
boot path — not before it.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(vtc): a VTC provisioned from the v2 template issues hybrid credentials

The last piece. `vtc-host` declares a post-quantum signing slot, the VTA mints
it, the sealed bundle carries it, the VTC stores it and gives it to
`LocalSigner` — so every credential the VTC issues carries a proof from each
key. A verifier that has not migrated checks the `eddsa-jcs-2022` proof; one that
has checks `mldsa44-jcs-2024`; neither needs to know about the other.

Everything before this PR could be in place while credentials still came out
classical-only, which is why the test that matters signs a real credential from
a real stored bundle and looks at the cryptosuites on it.

## `vtc-host` at schemaVersion 2

Three slots: `signing` (ed25519), `ka` (x25519), `pq-signing` (mldsa44, falling
back to ed25519). `#key-0` and `#key-2` are both assertion methods.

**The primary stays Ed25519 and cannot be otherwise** — it signs the did:webvh
log, and didwebvh 1.0 mandates `eddsa-jcs-2022` for log-entry proofs. The
fallback on `pq-signing` is what lets one template serve a VTA that can mint
ML-DSA and one that cannot.

The template moves here rather than in the sealed-variant PR on purpose: the
template is what *activates* the new path, so it lands with the consumer that
can open the result, never before it.

## One reply shape, and what it costs downstream

`VtaReply::Full` now carries `ProvisionResultV2`, and the three runners open
through `response_to_result_v2`, which takes either sealed variant and lifts V1
losslessly. A second `VtaReply` variant was the alternative and would have meant
two names for one event, with every consumer branching on which bundle the VTA
happened to seal — a question none of them has.

**This breaks `affinidi-tdk-rs`'s `mediator-setup` on its next `vta-sdk` bump**,
at two places, and neither is more than a few lines:

  - `sealed_handoff.rs:1167` constructs a `ProvisionResult` literal —
    `provision_from_template_payload` should build a `ProvisionResultV2`, or
    keep returning V1 and be adapted at the `VtaSession::full` boundary.
  - `test_helpers::sample_provision_result` still returns V1;
    `sample_provision_result_v2` is there for the `VtaReply::Full` call sites in
    `app.rs`.

Its *reads* port unchanged: `ProvisionResultV2` has the same `admin_did()`,
`integration_did()`, `integration_key()`, `webvh_log()` and
`authorization_vc()`. `ProvisionResult` and `response_to_result` are untouched
for any consumer that wants to stay on the V1 shape.

## The stored bundle

`VtcKeyBundle` gains `additional_signing_keys`, each carrying its slot, its
algorithm, and its published verification-method id.

- `#[serde(default)]` means every bundle already on disk loads unchanged — which
  is every VTC in the field, all of them provisioned from a v1 template.
- An empty list is skipped on write, so an unchanged VTC writes an unchanged
  bundle.
- `deny_unknown_fields` means the reverse does **not** hold: a bundle written
  with extra keys cannot be read by an older binary, so rolling vtc-service back
  past this change requires re-provisioning. A test states that rather than
  leaving it to be discovered during a rollback.

## Refusing rather than dropping

A stored signing key that cannot be decoded **fails the boot**. The DID document
publishes it as an assertion method, so a VTC that skipped it would issue
credentials a verifier expecting two proofs reads as incomplete, with nothing
anywhere saying why. That is the same judgment `with_additional_key` already
makes at the other end of the chain: a key added for post-quantum protection
that quietly does nothing is the worst outcome available.

The key's algorithm is read from its multicodec by `Secret::from_multibase`, so
this code never enumerates parameter sets; the stored `key_type` is what the
bundle says it is, written by the party that minted it.

## A test whose premise changed

`every_builtin_still_declares_the_historical_key_pair` asserted every built-in
is v1. `vtc-host` no longer is, so it is now checked against what it declares —
including that the historical pair survived unchanged inside the v2 template —
with the v2 built-ins listed by name. Skipping every v2 template instead would
have let a built-in quietly move to v2 and stop being checked at all.

`KeyType` gains `Eq` alongside `PartialEq` (a fieldless enum is trivially `Eq`,
and the stored bundle derives it). Additive.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

feat(sealed-transfer): a template-bootstrap variant that can carry a second signing key (#1556)

* fix(did-templates): a key slot beyond the historical pair, and the literal it used to publish

`slot_var`'s `{SLOT}_KEY_MB` rule is mechanical, and before this it was
mechanical in one direction only. A `schemaVersion` 2 template could *declare* a
third key slot — a post-quantum signing key beside the classical pair, which is
the shape a hybrid-credential issuer needs — and then could not be loaded,
because the placeholder that slot's own rule produces was rejected:

    Invalid("undeclared placeholder(s) { PQ_SIGNING_KEY_MB } in document
             — add them to requiredVars or optionalVars")

Only `SIGNING_KEY_MB` and `KA_KEY_MB` were ambient, because only those two are
in `RESERVED_VARS`. So `keys` at schemaVersion 2 (#1530) could express exactly
the pair it was introduced to move beyond.

## Following the error's advice published a literal into a write-once log

The advice is the defect. `optionalVars` supplies a **default**, and the
renderer substitutes a default for any name the caller did not supply — and the
minting flow does not supply a slot's key under a name it has never heard of.
So declaring `PQ_SIGNING_KEY_MB` to get past the rejection passed validation
*and rendered*:

    {
      "id": "did:webvh:x#key-2",
      "type": "Multikey",
      "publicKeyMultibase": "PLACEHOLDER-NEVER-SUBSTITUTED"
    }

— inside `assertionMethod`, in a `did:webvh` log that is signed once and cannot
be re-signed. `check_key_slots` already refuses a slot the document never
publishes: a key minted and thrown away. This is the same failure wearing the
other hat, a key published and never minted, and it arrived through the one door
that check does not watch.

## What changes

- `DidTemplate::slot_vars()` — the placeholder names the declared slots occupy,
  built from `key_slots()` rather than a second fixed list. For a v1 template it
  is exactly the two already in `RESERVED_VARS`, so v1 behaviour is untouched;
  it is what lets a v2 template name a third slot at all.
- `check_placeholders_declared` treats those names as ambient. An author cannot
  declare a value they have no way to know.
- `check_slot_vars_not_declared` refuses the reverse — a slot's placeholder in
  `requiredVars` or `optionalVars` — naming the slot and saying why. A v1
  template still gets `ReservedVar` from the check that runs first, unchanged.
- An undeclared placeholder that is *shaped* like a slot's is told to declare a
  **slot**, not a variable. The generic advice pointed at exactly what the new
  check refuses; an error that recommends the defect is worse than no error.

A third slot is expressible, and a VTA that cannot yet mint for it fails at
render with `Unresolved` naming the placeholder — rather than emitting a
document with a hole in it. Wiring derivation to the `keys` block is the next
change; until then the loud failure is the correct one.

in the chain from template to `LocalSigner::with_additional_key` could carry one.

only a template declaring an extra slot produces. **Every v1 template — which is
all thirteen built-ins — keeps sealing `TemplateBootstrap` byte-identically.**

Blast radius on existing openers is therefore zero, including `mediator-setup` in
affinidi-tdk-rs, a real cross-repo consumer: `didcomm-mediator` is v1, so it
never sees the new variant. Both directions are pinned by tests that mint through
the real flow and open the real bundle, because "which variant did the VTA
choose" is the contract and no amount of testing the payload types in isolation
shows it.

Same no-migration property as the proof rule one layer up: one key emits a proof
object, several emit an array. The wire shape follows what is there; nothing has
a flag to set.

## Reading both shapes through one path

`response_to_result_v2` accepts either variant and returns the V2 shape, lifting
V1 through `DidKeyMaterialV2::from_v1`. That lift is total and not a guess: V1
has exactly two slots, `signing` and `ka`, by the format's definition. The one
thing V1 does not state is each key's algorithm, so it is read from the
multicodec prefix — the only carrier V1 has — via a new
`KeyType::from_public_multibase` built from the same exhaustive match as
`multicodec_public`, so the two cannot drift.

A key whose prefix names no algorithm this build knows is **refused, not
defaulted**. Defaulting to Ed25519 would put the mislabelling `key_type` exists
to prevent one layer further down, where nothing would catch it.

`ProvisionResult` and `response_to_result` are untouched — that type's `payload`
field is public API another repository already reads, and widening it would break
those consumers for a capability they have not asked for. A V2 bundle reaching
the old entry point is `WrongPayload`: the caller asked for the shape it can
install and got another, and silently dropping the extra key would defeat the
point of having asked.

## Not included

`vtc-host` stays at schemaVersion 1. The template is what *activates* this path,
so it moves with the consumer that can open the result — the VTC's key bundle and
boot path — not before it.

title: feat(did-webvh): mint the keys a template's `keys` block asks for
body:
`schemaVersion` 2 templates could declare key algorithms (#1530) and
`derive_entity_keys_with_preference` could honour a preference list (#1532) —
and **nothing connected them.** Both had zero production callers.
`create_did_webvh` called plain `derive_entity_keys`, so a template declaring

    "signing": { "purpose": "signing", "algorithms": ["mldsa44", "ed25519"] }

minted an Ed25519 key and said nothing. Every capability Phase 2 shipped led to
a key nobody could ask for.

The cause is ordering: the template was resolved at *render* time, after the
keys existed. It is resolved before them now — a pure keyspace lookup, so
nothing else changes.

## A did:webvh primary signing key cannot be post-quantum

Found by running it rather than reading it, and it settles the shape of the
whole workstream:

    Invalid cryptosuite MlDsa44Jcs2024: log entry proofs must use eddsa-jcs-2022

The primary key signs the DID log, and didwebvh 1.0 mandates JCS canonicalization
with `eddsa-jcs-2022`. `didwebvh-rs`'s `experimental-pqc` flag would widen that
set and is opt-in for the right reason — a log signed that way is unverifiable by
any conformant resolver. That trades "cannot mint" for "mints a DID nobody can
resolve", so it stays off.

**Post-quantum signing on a did:webvh is therefore a second key, never a
replacement for the first** — which is what `LocalSigner` already assumes, and
what the VTC's HKDF chain (storage, install-token and audit keys all derived from
the Ed25519 seed) forces from the other end.

`log_entry_capable_signing` filters the primary slot's list rather than refusing
it, because that is what a preference list is for: `["mldsa44", "ed25519"]` falls
back exactly as it would for an algorithm this build could not mint. A list with
no classical entry is refused, naming what it asked for and what to do instead.
Silently substituting Ed25519 for a list that never mentioned it is the quiet
downgrade the `keys` block exists to prevent.

## The third slot

`DerivedEntityKeys` gains `additional_signing` — the slot Phase 2 deferred on
the grounds that no consumer existed. Hybrid credentials are that consumer: an
issuer signs with every key it holds, so it needs the classical key and the
post-quantum one at once, which no arity of two can express. Additive to the
existing pair, not a slot map: the arity of the first two is still a true
property worth keeping in the type.

Each extra slot is minted at its **own** BIP-32 path. Sharing the primary's would
make the second key a deterministic function of the first at that index — the
cross-algorithm reuse `derive_ml_dsa_44`'s domain separation exists to prevent,
reintroduced one layer up where that separation cannot see it.

Records are stored under the ids the **published document** gives each key,
found by matching `publicKeyMultibase` — the same rule `minted_vm_ids` already
applies to the pair, so a template numbering its methods any way it likes still
gets records named what its own document says.

## A third live instance of the Phase-2 defect shape

`save_entity_key_records_with_ids` passed `KeyType::Ed25519` as a literal for the
signing key — in the VTA-derived branch, the one a `keys` block steers.
`DerivedEntityKeys` grew `signing_key_type` to stop exactly that; the
caller-supplied branch reads it and this one was missed.

Latent, not live: nothing can mint a non-Ed25519 primary on did:webvh today. The
test says so in as many words, so the first DID method that can does not discover
it far from here.

## Refused rather than ignored

- A **second key-agreement slot**. It would put a second `keyAgreement` entry in
  the document, changing which secret an inbound encrypted message resolves to
  (`select_secret_kid`), and nothing here decides that. The failure would surface
  at a mediator as an undecryptable message.
- **Extra slots against caller-supplied keys.** The VTA mints an extra slot from
  its own seed and may not invent one for a DID whose keys the caller brought.
- An **algorithm name this build does not know**, with the slot that named it —
  the derivation functions only see a `KeyType`, so by then the slot is gone.
- A **minted slot the published document does not carry**. Storing it under a
  guessed id would hide the template/document disagreement that caused it.

## Tests exercise the behaviour, not the plumbing

The end-to-end tests mint a DID and read the **stored key record** back.
`derive_entity_keys_with_preference` existed, was tested, and had no caller — a
test that stopped at the plumbing would have passed throughout.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: feat(did-webvh): mint the keys a template's `keys` block asks for (#1555)
body:
feat(did-webvh): mint the keys a template's `keys` block asks for (#1555)

* fix(did-templates): a key slot beyond the historical pair, and the literal it used to publish

`slot_var`'s `{SLOT}_KEY_MB` rule is mechanical, and before this it was
mechanical in one direction only. A `schemaVersion` 2 template could *declare* a
third key slot — a post-quantum signing key beside the classical pair, which is
the shape a hybrid-credential issuer needs — and then could not be loaded,
because the placeholder that slot's own rule produces was rejected:

    Invalid("undeclared placeholder(s) { PQ_SIGNING_KEY_MB } in document
             — add them to requiredVars or optionalVars")

Only `SIGNING_KEY_MB` and `KA_KEY_MB` were ambient, because only those two are
in `RESERVED_VARS`. So `keys` at schemaVersion 2 (#1530) could express exactly
the pair it was introduced to move beyond.

## Following the error's advice published a literal into a write-once log

The advice is the defect. `optionalVars` supplies a **default**, and the
renderer substitutes a default for any name the caller did not supply — and the
minting flow does not supply a slot's key under a name it has never heard of.
So declaring `PQ_SIGNING_KEY_MB` to get past the rejection passed validation
*and rendered*:

    {
      "id": "did:webvh:x#key-2",
      "type": "Multikey",
      "publicKeyMultibase": "PLACEHOLDER-NEVER-SUBSTITUTED"
    }

— inside `assertionMethod`, in a `did:webvh` log that is signed once and cannot
be re-signed. `check_key_slots` already refuses a slot the document never
publishes: a key minted and thrown away. This is the same failure wearing the
other hat, a key published and never minted, and it arrived through the one door
that check does not watch.

## What changes

- `DidTemplate::slot_vars()` — the placeholder names the declared slots occupy,
  built from `key_slots()` rather than a second fixed list. For a v1 template it
  is exactly the two already in `RESERVED_VARS`, so v1 behaviour is untouched;
  it is what lets a v2 template name a third slot at all.
- `check_placeholders_declared` treats those names as ambient. An author cannot
  declare a value they have no way to know.
- `check_slot_vars_not_declared` refuses the reverse — a slot's placeholder in
  `requiredVars` or `optionalVars` — naming the slot and saying why. A v1
  template still gets `ReservedVar` from the check that runs first, unchanged.
- An undeclared placeholder that is *shaped* like a slot's is told to declare a
  **slot**, not a variable. The generic advice pointed at exactly what the new
  check refuses; an error that recommends the defect is worse than no error.

## The state this leaves

A third slot is expressible, and a VTA that cannot yet mint for it fails at
render with `Unresolved` naming the placeholder — rather than emitting a
document with a hole in it. Wiring derivation to the `keys` block is the next
change; until then the loud failure is the correct one.

Found while tracing what stands between a VTC and a second signing key: nothing
in the chain from template to `LocalSigner::with_additional_key` could carry one.

title: fix(theme): scope the remembered theme choice per profile
body:
## The bug

Running two OpenVTC instances under different local profiles and changing the theme in one **changed it in all of them** — and, via a live file-watcher, repainted the other *running* instances immediately.

## Root cause

The theme choice was kept in a single `<config>/tui.toml` shared by every profile (this was intentional — "how the TUI looks is the person's, not the account's"), while every other profile-scoped surface encodes the profile into its filename. So two instances differing only by `--profile` read and wrote the same file.

**Blast radius (what else crossed profiles):** only the cosmetic theme keys (`theme`, `auto_dark`, `auto_light`) and a transient `last-startup-failure.txt` crash report. Everything that matters — secrets/keyring, the whole config + account/community data, log settings, the process lock — is already correctly isolated per profile.

## The fix (theme now fully per-profile)

- `Roots` gains a `profile`; the choice file is `tui.toml` for the `default` profile and `tui-{profile}.toml` otherwise, mirroring the `config-{profile}.json` convention. The theme **library** (`themes/`) stays shared — it's authored content, not a per-profile setting.
- `main.rs` resolves the profile **before** choosing the theme (profile resolution factored into a `resolve_profile` helper). Its informational messages now print with the default palette since the theme isn't chosen yet — a rare, acceptable trade.
- The TUI settings theme actions and the `openvtc theme` CLI both read/write the running profile's file. The live watcher watches that file, so two instances of the **same** profile still stay in sync while different profiles no longer cross.
- Fixed the other cross-profile collision too: the startup crash report is now `last-startup-failure-{profile}.txt` (unsuffixed for `default`).

## Tests / gates
- New `settings_file_is_scoped_per_profile` unit test (default → `tui.toml`, named → `tui-{profile}.toml`, two profiles differ).
- `cargo fmt`, `clippy --all-targets --all-features`, `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc`, and full `cargo test` (694 core + 611 openvtc + census) all pass.

## Note
This reverses a previously-intentional design (theme as a person-level, cross-profile preference) in favour of strict per-profile isolation, per the reporter's requirement that instances be fully isolated.

title: Default relationship communication to pairwise R-DIDs and govern P-DID fallback
body:
Surfaced by an external RAHP/DRARM assessment of the Cypress release
(sankarshanmukhopadhyay/rahp-toolkit#18, finding `OVTC-RAHP-04`). Confirmed as
reported.

## Problem

Pairwise relationship identity is opt-in, and the fallback is the persona DID.

- TUI request form: `generate_r_did` defaults to `false`
  (`openvtc/src/state_handler/relationship_actions.rs:1056`); the user has to
  find and toggle the checkbox on field 3 to get privacy.
- TUI inbox accept: `a` accepts **without** an R-DID, `A` accepts **with** one
  (`openvtc/src/ui/pages/main/mod.rs:914-930`). The convenient key is the
  linkable one.
- CLI: requires `--generate-did` (`docs/relationships-vrcs.md:60-66`), which
  states plainly that without an R-DID, subsequent communication uses the P-DID.

So the safe path is the one the operator has to know to ask for, on a decision
whose consequences are invisible at the moment they make it.

## Why this is worse here than the generic pattern

The assessment scores this as stable-identifier correlation. In our case the
stable identifier is a **published, resolvable `did:webvh`** that frequently
carries a verified agent name. Two counterparties do not need traffic analysis
to correlate the same persona across contexts — they compare a string, and can
then resolve it to a named identity. The linkage is not merely possible, it is
a lookup.

That argues for flipping the default rather than warning on the fallback.

## Proposed change

1. **Default `generate_r_did` to `true`** on the request form and make the
   R-DID-generating accept the primary key binding in the inbox. Keep the
   P-DID path available, deliberately chosen, and labelled with what it costs.
2. **CLI:** make R-DID generation the default and introduce an explicit opt-out
   flag rather than an opt-in one. `--generate-did` becomes a no-op that warns,
   for one release, so existing scripts do not silently change meaning in the
   other direction.
3. **No silent revert.** Once a relationship has an R-DID, subsequent messages
   must not fall back to the P-DID — define the bootstrap-to-pairwise migration
   point and assert it. A fallback that can re-expose the P-DID mid-relationship
   defeats the default.
4. **Test:** given two relationships established from the same persona, assert
   that protocol-visible identifiers do not permit the two counterparties to
   correlate them.
5. **Docs:** update `docs/relationships-vrcs.md` — the current text presents the
   R-DID as an optional privacy extra rather than the norm.

## Upstream question

Whether VTC should *require* pairwise identifiers for relationship
communication rather than leaving it to client defaults is a protocol question
for `verifiable-trust-infrastructure`. If it does, this issue reduces to
conformance. Raising it there separately; this change stands either way.

## Acceptance

- A new relationship request and a new relationship acceptance both mint an
  R-DID with no extra keystroke.
- Choosing the P-DID path is possible and states the linkability cost at the
  point of choice.
- A relationship with an R-DID never emits the P-DID on a subsequent message.

title: feat(relationships): honor a community's relationshipIdentifierDefault (#241)
body:
Advances #241.

## What was already done

Investigating #241 against current `main`, the substantive pairwise work has landed:
- **#254** made pairwise the default and added the no-revert guard.
- **#255** issues the VRC under the relationship R-DID (not the persona), signed with the R-DID's own key.

And two facts bound the rest:
- OpenVTC **never publishes VRCs to the VTC relationship graph** (no `POST /v1/relationships`; VRCs are exchanged peer-to-peer over DIDComm), so the VTI #1061 PoP/`VrcPublishAuthorization`/graph machinery does not apply to this client.
- The one spec-aligned client behaviour still missing: OpenVTC never read a community's declared **`relationshipIdentifierDefault`**, so it always defaulted to pairwise regardless of what a community published.

## This change

Reads `relationshipIdentifierDefault` (`attributed` | `pairwise`) and uses it to seed the new-relationship form's mint default — a **soft default, still user-overridable**, exactly as the spec frames it ("read by clients before minting, not a gate"; absent ⇒ pairwise).

- **Model:** `RelationshipIdentifierDefault { Attributed, Pairwise }` + an optional field on `CommunityRecord`, threaded through the serde shadow + `From` + `new_pending` so older configs load unchanged.
- **Fetch:** `join::send_community_profile_show` sends an empty-payload `vtc/community/profile/show/0.1` Trust Task, using the exact DIDComm/TSP plumbing as the join-status poll; the reply is threaded and handled inbound. Type URIs are pulled from `trust-tasks-rs` so they can't drift from the schema.
- **Store:** `messaging::handle_community_profile_show_response` records the declared value on every membership of the sending VTC (it's a community-level property), read via a JSON pointer so a `deny_unknown_fields`/`non_exhaustive` `CommunityProfileView` can't fail the read over a field we don't need. Anti-spoof: only a community we actually hold a membership with may set it.
- **Trigger:** a `community_profile_poll` driver asks each Active community **once per session** — keyed on "already asked", not "value still unknown", so a community that declares nothing (a permanently `None` value) is not polled every tick forever (R1.4) — capped per tick.
- **Consume:** `default_generate_r_did` seeds the form from the working community (`state.selected_community`, falling back to the default working membership): `attributed` ⇒ persona DID, everything else (pairwise / undeclared / State-A) ⇒ pairwise.
- **Guardrail:** the inbound-gate census lists the new response type so the gate and dispatcher can't silently drift.

## Tests
- **Core:** the handler records attributed/pairwise, leaves undeclared/unrecognised as `None` (pairwise default), and ignores a response from a VTC we hold no membership with.
- **openvtc:** `default_generate_r_did` returns the persona DID only for an `attributed` working community; pairwise otherwise and in State-A. The pacer asks once per session and re-enables after a leave. The census admits the new type.
- `cargo fmt`, `clippy --all-targets --all-features`, `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc`, full `cargo test` all clean.

## Not in scope / follow-ups
- The PoP / `VrcPublishAuthorization` / graph-publish path (OpenVTC doesn't publish to the graph).
- Migrating the home-grown `MessageType::VRCIssued` flow onto the standard `vrc/relationships/{propose,issue}` specs (a separate conformance refactor).
- A "your community prefers X" hint on the form's identifier toggle (the default already encodes the preference; the toggle label is currently static).

## Live-validation limitation
The MockVta transport harness is WIP/blocked, so an end-to-end fetch against a real VTC isn't runnable here. The request/response types come from the pinned `trust-tasks-rs` 0.21.3 and the send/receive plumbing is the proven `join-requests/status` path; a live smoke against a VTC that declares `attributed` is a recommended follow-up once a harness is available.

title: Bind taskContext to the published Trust Tasks mechanisms, and secure credentials with Data Integrity
body:
The credential-side half of splitting #18 across the three specifications, as planned on #18 once the VTI repository existed. **#18 stays open until these three merge**, then closes pointing at them.

| Part | PR |
|---|---|
| Credentials (this PR) | this one |
| Trust Tasks | trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#15 |
| VTI | trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#33 |
| Executable evidence | [Keyring `ref-07g-outcome-evidence-pairing`](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/c3a7f1d2a547d7a602cf93b87f5672d7a158d4c1/tsp-reference/ref-07g-outcome-evidence-pairing) |

**Merge order: trust-tasks-spec#15 first.** This PR links to the `#evidence-that-a-cited-exchange-completed` anchor that PR creates; merging this one first leaves a dead link in the published Working Draft. This PR and the VTI one can merge in either order once it is in.

@talltree @sankarshanmukhopadhyay — tagging you as the authors of the #39 scope guidance this split implements, and @talltree for the review on #18 that asked for it. @stormer78 — the Trust Tasks PR carries your trust-tasks-tf#173 follow-ups.

## How the split was decided

Two rules already on the record, applied as written:

- **Scope guidance** from [dtgwg-cred-tf discussion #39](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-tf/discussions/39) (Drummond, agreed by Sankarshan): credentials define types, properties and high-level requirements and *reference* the other specifications; Trust Tasks defines processing, ceremony and evidence requirements. VTI, created afterwards, owns what holds only across a composition.
- **The review on #18**: Trust Task Context Binding detail belongs in the Trust Tasks specification; ZK proof types do not belong in the credential specification.

And one rule for this split: everything in #18 is carried unless other work has already superseded it.

## Where each part of #18 went

| #18 content | Now |
|---|---|
| `digestMultibase` for the VWC | **Already on main** (#19) |
| `z`/`u` multibase headers | **Superseded** — main requires base58btc `z` only |
| Framework 0.4 permalinks; the "Trust Tasks core specification" term | **Dropped** — the framework is published; cited directly |
| "id locates, digest binds"; `proofValue` rejected as binder | **Already in Trust Tasks 0.5.0** (via trust-tasks-tf#173) — cited |
| `taskContext` = innermost exchange's initiating `id` | **This PR** — property definition, citing Trust Tasks |
| `taskDigestMultibase` | **This PR** — Base Structure, `dtg:witnessed` profile, profile item 6 |
| `DataIntegrityProof` + `eddsa-jcs-2022` RECOMMENDED | **This PR** — `proof` property and examples |
| `bbs-2023`, proof sets, selective-disclosure trade-off | **Not carried** — outside the credential spec per the #18 review; this PR only states that a selective-disclosure mechanism is carried in addition to the proof |
| Qualifying Trust Task specification profile | **Trust Tasks** — Specification Requirements item 20, updated with the three changes from trust-tasks-tf#173 |
| Pairing checklist; errors as failure evidence | **Trust Tasks** — *Evidence That a Cited Exchange Completed* |
| Holder ships outcome evidence | **This PR** (holder MUST), **Trust Tasks** (SHOULD carry), **VTI** (VTI-CMP-023) |
| Verifier MUST NOT infer completion | **This PR** keeps it, pointing at Trust Tasks and VTI |
| Related Specifications; #11 | **This PR** and **VTI** (citations fixed both ways) |

## What changed here

- **`taskContext`** is the initiating document's `id` of the innermost attesting exchange. Base Structure said `threadId`, which contradicts the published Trust Tasks rule.
- **`taskDigestMultibase`** is defined. `witness/session/submit/0.1` and `vetting/session/0.1` already require it and say its schema *"belongs to DTG Core Credentials"*.
- **Outcome Interpretability** keeps its MUST NOT and points at the Trust Tasks checks and VTI; the holder conformance item follows.
- **Related Specifications** lists Trust Tasks and VTI as published; DTG Core Trust Task Protocols stays planned for DTG-specific task specifications. The two remaining "planned Protocols" mentions (VMC lifecycle, VDC invocation) are untouched — their referents still don't exist. Resolves #11.
- **`proof`** is `DataIntegrityProof` with `eddsa-jcs-2022` RECOMMENDED; all examples updated (#17 item 3).
- **Minimum compatible version** keeps `0.4.0` for naming and binding, with the outcome-evidence minimum recorded as pending until trust-tasks-spec#15 is released under a Document Status.

## Found while splitting — recorded, not addressed here

1. **#18's own text rejects the real witness ceremony.** "The originating request's Type URI with `#response`" can't match `witness/session` → `witness/session/submit#response`. The Trust Tasks PR replaces it with a declared outcome-evidence type ([rung](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/c3a7f1d2a547d7a602cf93b87f5672d7a158d4c1/tsp-reference/ref-07g-outcome-evidence-pairing), Act 4).
2. **Keyring's verifier accepts a cancelled session's control `#response` and a holder-signed `#response` as completion** ([rung](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/c3a7f1d2a547d7a602cf93b87f5672d7a158d4c1/tsp-reference/ref-07g-outcome-evidence-pairing), Act 3). A Keyring fix, not a spec one.
3. **The witness spec's "evidence issuer is the credential issuer" does not generalize** — vetting's response is signed by the applicant, not the vetter who issues the statement. The Trust Tasks rule uses the initiating document's `recipient`.
4. **VTI uses "witness" only for a DID-log host service**, while a VWC witness issues credentials. Worth a terminology pass at some point; nothing here depends on it.
5. **The minimum-version values stay pending** until the Trust Tasks definition is released under a Document Status.

## For review

- Reviewed internally on our fork before proposing here; @bmiller59 is credited as co-author for the #15 material redistributed into this PR.
- Rendered with `npm run render` — no errors, every new anchor resolves.
- Open PRs #55 and #50 touch `spec/body.md` as well; I checked this branch merges cleanly with both, and the anchors this PR references survive #55's restructuring.

title: Keep credential validity and exchange completion apart
body:
The VTI half of splitting [trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#18](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/18) across the three specifications, following the scope guidance in [dtgwg-cred-tf#39](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-tf/discussions/39). The full redistribution map is in the credentials PR.

| Part | PR |
|---|---|
| VTI (this PR) | this one |
| Trust Tasks | trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#15 |
| Credentials | trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#56 |

**Merge order: trust-tasks-spec#15 first.** This PR cites the *Evidence That a Cited Exchange Completed* section that PR adds, through `[TRUST-TASKS]`. This PR and the credentials one can merge in either order once it is in.

@talltree @sankarshanmukhopadhyay — tagging you as the authors of the #39 scope guidance this split implements. @stormer78 — the Trust Tasks PR carries your trust-tasks-tf#173 follow-ups.

## Why here

Credential validity is decided under the credential specification; whether the exchange a credential cites completed is decided under Trust Tasks, over documents the credential does not contain. Keeping a relying party from reading the first as the second is a property of the composition — the kind VTI-CMP-001 says this specification owns.

## What this adds

- **VTI-CMP-022 / 023** (Semantic completion) — a credential citing an exchange is not completion evidence without outcome evidence satisfying the Trust Tasks checks; where a decision depends on completion, the evidence travels with the presentation.
- **VTI-CMP-064** (Privacy across composition) — outcome evidence counts among the durable correlators of VTI-CMP-062: whole Trust Task documents disclose the exchange's and both parties' identifiers regardless of the credential's own proof mechanism.
- **VTI-CRD-032** — successful credential verification does not establish completion; pointer to VTI-CMP-022.
- **References** — the `[DTG-CRED]` and `[TRUST-TASKS]` citations are fixed; the intro's cross-specification note records the minimum Document Status of each as pending the release of the definitions this depends on.
- **Appendix E, Family 2** — required by VTI-CMP-120 for new composition requirements: propositions, counter-cases, `JOINTLY-OWNED`, and [Keyring `ref-07g`](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/c3a7f1d2a547d7a602cf93b87f5672d7a158d4c1/tsp-reference/ref-07g-outcome-evidence-pairing) as the pressure test for the second proposition.

## Notes for review

- **Requirement identifiers** follow the numbering blocks already in use in each section; the editor may renumber.
- **Appendix E and #32.** Family 2 is recorded here as VTI-CMP-120 currently requires, with Appendix E in its present (informative) form. #32 questions whether that appendix should be reclassified or restructured; if it is, this entry moves with it. The entry carries that note inline.
- **Terminology, not addressed here:** this specification uses "witness" for a DID-log host service, while a witnessed credential's witness issues credentials. Worth a pass at some point; nothing in this PR depends on it.
- Rendered with `npm run render` — no errors, no duplicate identifiers.
- Reviewed internally on our fork before proposing here; @bmiller59 is credited as co-author, and the Appendix E note is his.

title: Define outcome evidence for a cited exchange
body:
The Trust Tasks half of splitting [trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#18](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/18) across the three specifications, following the scope guidance in [dtgwg-cred-tf#39](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-tf/discussions/39) and the review on #18. The full redistribution map is in the credentials PR.

| Part | PR |
|---|---|
| Trust Tasks (this PR) | this one |
| Credentials | trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#56 |
| VTI | trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#33 |

**Merge order: this PR first.** dtgwg-cred-spec#56 links directly to the `#evidence-that-a-cited-exchange-completed` anchor this PR creates; merging it before this one leaves a dead link in a published Working Draft. The credentials and VTI PRs can merge in either order once this is in.

@talltree @sankarshanmukhopadhyay — tagging you as the authors of the #39 scope guidance this split implements. @stormer78 — item 20 below is where your three follow-ups from the trust-tasks-tf#173 closing comment land.

## Why here

Trust Tasks 0.5.0 already absorbed most of #18's reasoning through trust-tasks-tf#173: naming the innermost exchange by its initiating `id`, the task digest, `inResponseTo`, the document lifecycle. What it does not define is whether a **cited exchange completed**. That rule lives today in #18 and, separately, in `witness/session/submit/0.1` and `vetting/session/0.1` — none of which generalizes on its own.

Under the #39 scope guidance, a credential specification defines its types, properties and high-level requirements and references the specifications that define the rest; processing, ceremony and evidence requirements belong here.

## What this adds

- **Evidence That a Cited Exchange Completed** — four checks: the citation binds the initiating document; the terminal's `threadId` pairs through the initiating document; the terminal's type is the **declared** outcome-evidence response; it is signed by the initiating document's **`recipient`**.
- **Specification Requirements item 20** — a citable specification declares its outcome-evidence response, with a payload schema, proof REQUIRED, `issuedAt` required, and `durable` retention. This is where Glenn's three follow-ups from the #173 closing comment land: the `cancelled` terminal state, items 17 and 18, and the empty `#response`.
- **Privacy Considerations item 6**, the **outcome evidence** term, and VTI as an informative reference.

## Evidence

[Keyring `ref-07g-outcome-evidence-pairing`](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/c3a7f1d2a547d7a602cf93b87f5672d7a158d4c1/tsp-reference/ref-07g-outcome-evidence-pairing) runs seven exchanges — witness, vetting, a minted thread, a cancellation, a self-signed response, an error, a counterfeit — through the witness spec's rule, Keyring's verifier, #18's text, and this rule, using real Trust Task documents and `eddsa-jcs-2022` proofs. Only this rule gets all seven right.

| Exchange | witness spec | Keyring | #18 | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| witness ceremony | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ false negative | ✓ |
| vetting ceremony | ✗ (out of scope) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| minted `threadId` | ✗ (out of scope) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| cancelled (control `#response`) | ✗ | ✓ false positive | ✗ | ✗ |
| holder-signed `#response` | ✗ | ✓ false positive | ✗ | ✗ |
| error / counterfeit | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ |

The two false positives are a Keyring bug, tracked on our side, not a change proposed here.

## Notes for review

- `witness/session/submit` and `vetting/session` stay consistent with this section for their own exchanges; the registry specs are not edited here. `witness/session/submit/0.1` still states its own pairing rule ("evidence issuer = credential issuer"), which agrees with this general rule only because the witness case makes issuer and recipient coincide — a follow-up issue on dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf will propose it cite this section instead.
- **No Document Status bump** — bumps have been their own PR. A follow-up will bump it and fill in the minimum-version notes that dtgwg-cred-spec#56 and dtgwg-vti-spec#33 currently record as pending.
- Rendered with `npm run render` — no errors.
- Reviewed internally on our fork before proposing here; @bmiller59 is credited as co-author for the material carried over from his review.

title: feat(communities): persist and surface decision evidence for rejected/removed membership (#240)
body:
Resolves #240.

Both of that issue's upstream blockers have since landed — the poll now carries the rejection code/reason/time (VTI #1058, closing #1052) and the removal notice exists (VTI #1053, `vtc/members/removal-notice/0.1`, in vta-sdk 0.39) — so the client work the issue scoped is now buildable end to end.

## What this does

A `Rejected`/`Removed` membership used to record only *that* it ended. The code, reason, authority and time each inbound path carried went to a `info!`/`warn!` line and were discarded; `reject()`/`remove()` took no arguments and `CommunityRecord` had nowhere to keep them. This persists that evidence and shows it.

### Core
- New `DecisionEvidence` on `CommunityRecord`, set by `reject(evidence)` / `remove(evidence)`. Every field is optional; an all-absent value is a deliberate **"no reason given"**, distinct from a record that predates the field. Threaded through the struct, its serde shadow and the `From` impl so older configs keep loading.
- All four reject paths now record what they carry:
  - `deny` verdict → code + reason
  - FORBIDDEN problem-report → code + comment
  - join-denial trust-task-error → code + message
  - status poll → code + reason + `decidedAt` (the recovery path for a missed live verdict)
- The `deny` arm also adopts the VTC's request id and stamps `receipt_at`, matching the refer/request_more arms — the inconsistency the issue's scoping flagged. A denial is a correlated response, not a dropped submit.
- New `handle_member_removal_notice` for `vtc/members/removal-notice/0.1` — the **first** path that can move a membership to `Removed`. Unsolicited, so it correlates by sender + the persona it names, transitions only an *Active* membership (a stale notice can't clobber a `Left` the member chose), and persists authority / reason / time / disposition.

### UI
- `CommunitySummary` gains a `DecisionSummary`; the community detail block renders a `Reason:` row (always — "no reason given" when none), plus decided-by / decided-at / code / record rows when carried.

### Guardrail
- The inbound-gate census lists the removal-notice type, so the gate and the dispatcher can't silently drift (a routed-but-ungated type is a silent drop).

## On "deciding authority"
Only a removal notice names an independently-attestable authority (`decidedBy`). A join rejection's issuer is unsigned and applicant-influenced, so `decided_by` stays `None` there rather than being shown as if it were attestable — noted in the field docs and the UI.

## Tests
- Core: evidence persisted on each of the four reject paths; the empty-poll path lands as present-but-empty ("no reason given"); the `deny` arm acknowledges + adopts the id; removal notice removes an Active member with full evidence, keeps an omitted reason absent, and ignores an unknown-persona / non-Active target.
- UI: a terminal row renders its evidence; an evidence-free one reads "no reason given".
- Gate: the census admits the removal-notice type.

`cargo fmt`, `clippy --all-targets --all-features`, and `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc` are clean.

title: Persist and surface decision evidence for rejected or removed community membership
body:
Surfaced by an external RAHP/DRARM assessment of the Cypress release
(sankarshanmukhopadhyay/rahp-toolkit#18, finding `OVTC-RAHP-03`). This issue
covers the **client half** only; the governance half (appeal, review,
restoration) belongs in VTC/VTI and is tracked separately.

## Problem

When a VTC rejects a join request or removes an active member, the decision
evidence reaches us on the wire and we throw it away.

VTC returns a typed reject code plus a reason
(`vtc-service/src/messaging.rs:974` in `verifiable-trust-infrastructure`). All
four inbound paths in `openvtc-core/src/messaging.rs` have that code and reason
in hand:

- `:308` — `status: "rejected"` on a join-status reply
- `:392` — `VerdictEffect::Deny`, which even logs `code` and `reason`
- `:473` — `FORBIDDEN` problem-report (invitation not accepted)
- `:564` — join-denial `trust-task-error`, which logs `code` and `detail`

Each one then calls `record.reject()`, and
`CommunityRecord::reject()` / `remove()` take **no arguments**
(`openvtc-core/src/config/account.rs:441-454`). They set a status and clear
`acknowledged`. Nothing else is persisted.

The net effect for the operator: a community flips to `Rejected` or `Removed`,
the actions-required badge lights up, they press a key to acknowledge it — and
the *why* exists only in a `tracing` line they will never see. There is no
record of who decided, on what basis, or when. Acknowledging an outcome you
cannot inspect is not meaningful acknowledgement.

`Expired` has the same shape but is client-generated, so it is less severe —
still worth carrying the timeout basis for consistency.

## Proposed change

1. Give `reject()` and `remove()` a decision-evidence argument and persist it on
   `CommunityRecord`:
   - deciding authority (the VTC DID that sent the decision)
   - decision code (typed) and human-readable reason
   - decision timestamp (theirs if present, ours as received otherwise)
   - the inbound path it arrived on, so the evidence is reconstructable
2. Surface it wherever the terminal state is shown — the communities list detail
   view and the actions-required notice — not only in the acknowledge prompt.
3. Keep it stable across the config round-trip (serde) so history survives a
   restart; inactive records are already retained for re-join
   (`docs/design/multi-community-support.md` R-S-1), and the evidence should be
   retained with them.
4. Where no reason is supplied by the VTC, say so explicitly ("no reason given")
   rather than rendering an empty field — absence of a reason is itself
   information the operator should see.

## Out of scope

Appeal/review endpoints, policy-version context, and correction/restoration
semantics after an overturned decision. Those need the governing layer to define
them first; this issue makes OpenVTC ready to surface them.

## Acceptance

- A rejected join and a removal each persist and display authority, code, reason
  and timestamp.
- A decision arriving with no reason renders explicitly as such.
- Round-trip test: evidence survives save/load.
- No decision evidence is lost between the four inbound paths — a test per path.

title: feat(credentials): the VTC signs with every key it holds, and can hold a post-quantum one
body:
Issuance — the other half of hybrid credentials, after #1548/#1550 taught
verification to read a proof set. `LocalSigner` holds a list of signing keys
rather than one, and both sign paths go through `sign_multi`, so a credential
carries one proof per key under the cryptosuite that key's own type selects.

## The feature flag that made all of this unreachable

Writing the tests found it, and it is the most consequential thing here:

```toml
affinidi-data-integrity = "0.7"        # no features — `ml-dsa` OFF
```

`CryptoSuite::default_for_key_type`'s ML-DSA arm is `#[cfg(feature = "ml-dsa")]`.
Without the feature it returns `None`, the signer falls back to `EddsaJcs2022`,
and signing fails with:

```
key type MlDsa44 is not compatible with cryptosuite EddsaJcs2022
```

**The VTC could not produce a post-quantum credential proof under any
circumstances** — and explained itself by naming Ed25519.

The PQC plan caught *exactly this trap* for `affinidi-secrets-resolver` — pinned
with no features, so `Secret::generate_ml_dsa_44` was not compiled — and it was
fixed. Nobody checked whether the same applied to `affinidi-data-integrity`. It
did. Every capability built above it (ML-DSA key derivation, template `keys`
blocks, the resolver reading declared types) led to a key that could not sign a
credential in this build.

That is the "built, tested, and unreachable" finding this plan opened with, one
layer further down than anyone looked.

## No migration, by construction

**One key emits a bare proof object; several emit an array.**

A VTC that has never been given a post-quantum key issues byte-identically to
what it always has — so nothing downstream had to be updated first, and no
stored bundle is rewritten. The number of proofs simply follows the number of
keys.

A test pins the single-key shape deliberately: the day it starts emitting a
one-element array, every existing consumer of a VTC credential is affected at
once, and that would be a *silent* change to a wire format.

`sign_multi` pins `created` once across the batch, so two proofs on one
credential cannot disagree about when it was signed — also tested, because
otherwise the first proof carries t0 and the second t0+ms, which is a gift to
anyone diffing two proofs meant to describe one signing event.

## Still to come

**Nothing yet gives the VTC a second key.** That needs the `vtc-host` template at
`schemaVersion` 2 declaring a post-quantum signing slot, and `VtcKeyBundle` grown
to carry it — that bundle has the same two-fixed-slots shape `DerivedEntityKeys`
had before #1532. `with_additional_key` is the seam that work will use.

A key whose type has no Data Integrity cryptosuite (ML-DSA-65/87, which W3C
defines no suites for) fails **loudly** at signing rather than being dropped
here — a key added for post-quantum protection that quietly did nothing is the
worst outcome available. affinidi-tdk-rs#818 makes that failure say why.

## Verification

VTC and workspace suites clean; clippy `-D warnings` clean; rustfmt clean;
lockfile self-pin guard clean (the feature change pulls in no duplicate). Seven
signer tests, four of them new, including the hybrid round trip.

title: feat(tsp): adopt TSP Rev 3 as a first-class citizen
body:
## What

Makes openvtc speak **TSP Rev 3** end to end. Rev 3 §7.2.2 gates application
traffic on a recorded relationship — a peer with none has its messages silently
dropped — so every leg openvtc drives now forms the relationship, answers
inbound control, and persists relationship state across restarts.

Validated live against an updated (Rev 3) VTA.

## Changes

| Area | What |
|------|------|
| **Deps** | 0.42.1 frontier: `vta-sdk 0.42.1`, `affinidi-tdk 0.16`, `affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.26.7`, `affinidi-messaging-core 0.1.8`, `affinidi-tsp 0.2.1`, `trust-tasks-rs 0.21.3`, `vta-service 0.32` (dev). Single-copy graph. `dtg-credentials 0.9.1` (WD-02: `digest` → `digestMultibase`) — vta-sdk 0.42 now depends on it, so it is no longer openvtc-only. Rationale comments rewritten. |
| **Send (VTC)** | `send_trust_task` forms the §7.2.2 relationship (idempotent, `None`-guarded) before the Trust Task. |
| **Send (VTA)** | `enable_tsp_if_advertised` now **relates** after `enable_tsp_trust_tasks` (via vta-sdk 0.42.1's `relate_tsp_trust_task_leg`) — the `connect_auto` + enable two-step needs the explicit relate that `connect_didcomm_with_tsp` does internally. |
| **Receive** | Live path recognises `InboundKind::RelationshipControl` (SDK adapter records it); stored path migrates `unpack` → `unpack_message` with full `InboundTsp` branching. |
| **Durable store** | Config-backed `RelationshipKv` → SDK `PersistentRelationshipStore`, injected into every ATM, hydrated at startup, persisted into `ProtectedConfig` on a coalesced dirty signal. Separate from the DIDComm relationship model. |
| **UI** | New "TSP Relationships" pane — per-community relationship state, live-updated. |
| **Health** | `openvtc health` reports each community's TSP relationship state, naming the "no relationship → Trust Task dropped by the gate" case. |

## Upstream this depended on (all landed)

- **did-git-sign 0.4.12** (VGI, on vta-sdk 0.42) — without it the graph carried a stale `messaging-sdk 0.24` that would not compile against the shared `messaging-core 0.1.8`.
- **vta-sdk 0.42.1 / #1547** — exposed `relate_tsp_trust_task_leg` so openvtc's two-step VTA connect can form the §7.2.2 relationship. Coordinated with the sessions owning `client/mod.rs` and the vtc-service D4/D6 recovery work; no collisions.

## Testing

All CI gates green: `cargo test --workspace` (19 suites, 0 failed), `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, `fmt --check`, `RUSTDOCFLAGS=-D warnings cargo doc`, `cargo deny check sources`, `cargo tree -d` single-node.

Per `vti-stack-development-guide.md`: outbound clients keep finite timeouts (**R1.2**; TSP discovery bounded at 5s); error text distinguishes unreachable / auth / contract (**R6.4**; the relate/enable/discovery arms each log their own reason); endpoint shapes verified against the current SDK rather than assumed (**R3.6**).

## Follow-ups (not blockers)

- **Relate-failure rollback**: on a rare relate failure the VTA leg is attached-but-unrelated; `disable_tsp_trust_tasks` is private in vta-sdk, so we log and rely on the next VTA connect re-relating (openvtc rebuilds the runtime client per operation). A public `disable` would let us roll straight back to DIDComm.
- **WS5 accept/cancel actions**: the pane is read-only status; inbound invites are recorded automatically. Active accept/cancel would reuse the same off-loop pattern.

* feat(tsp): adopt TSP Rev 3 relationship management

Rev 3 §7.2.2 gates application traffic on a recorded relationship: a peer the
endpoint holds none with has its messages silently dropped. Adopt it on every
leg openvtc drives, and persist it so a restart does not forfeit it.

- Send (tsp.rs): form the relationship (`form_relationship_routed`, idempotent,
  `None`-guarded) before a VTC Trust Task, or the VTC drops it with no reply.

  keeps it out of the Trust Task mapper; the stored path migrates `unpack` ->
  `unpack_message` with full `InboundTsp` branching (record control, drop
  padding).
- Durable store (tsp_store.rs): a config-backed `RelationshipKv` wrapped in the
  SDK's `PersistentRelationshipStore`, injected into every ATM, hydrated at
  startup and mirrored into `ProtectedConfig` on a coalesced dirty signal — so a
  §7.2.2 relationship survives a restart rather than being re-formed (or its
  peer's traffic dropped until it is). Kept separate from the DIDComm
  relationship model.

title: docs(tsp): record that send_nested is cross-mediator-only (§7.2)
body:
Records an empirically-verified correction to §7 so the next person doesn't repeat a flip that doesn't work.

## What was found

The "smallest increment" some scoping suggested — flip a single-intermediary send seam from `send_routed(&[mediator, recipient])` to `send_nested_routed(&[mediator], recipient)` — **fails at pack time**:

```
couldn't pack routed TSP message: invalid message: a routed message requires at least one onward hop
```

`send_nested_routed` requires a **≥2-hop** route (`[our_mediator, recipient_mediator]`), because the privacy it buys is "an intermediary *before* the recipient's mediator never learns the recipient." On one shared mediator there are no earlier intermediaries — nothing to hide — so the API rightly refuses it. (Verified by flipping `TspSession::send_document` and running `tsp_round_trip`, then reverting.)

This matches what `tsp-vs-didcomm-trust-task-surface.md` (#1545) reasoned from first principles: **the metadata-privacy benefit is multi-hop-only.**

## What §7.2 now records

- Single-mediator (every current seam, every test) stays on `send_routed`.
- The real increment is **topology-aware** cross-mediator nesting: resolve the peer's mediator DID (already exposed), and only when it differs from ours use `send_nested_routed([our_mediator, peer_mediator], recipient)`.
- It **must land with a two-mediator test** — a single-mediator test would take the `send_routed` branch and prove nothing. Deferred until that harness/topology exists, rather than ship an untested cross-mediator path.

Docs-only.

title: feat(credentials): every VTC verification path reads a proof set
body:
The follow-up #1548 promised. All six remaining single-proof readers are
converted, so **no `vtc-service` path now rejects a hybrid credential as
malformed**.

## Three had a latent bug the array case would have hidden

`recognition/verify` (both sites) and `routes/relationships` read
`verificationMethod` off the **raw JSON**:

```rust
let vm = proof_value.get("verificationMethod").and_then(|v| v.as_str())
```

For an array that is `None` — so on a hybrid document the issuer-binding check
was not merely unperformed, it was **unreachable**. Each now reads the parsed
proof's own field.

This is the argument for having done these one at a time rather than as a bulk
edit, which is what I said in #1548 and it turned out to be the right call: a
mechanical swap of the parse line would have left three binding checks reading a
field that no longer existed.

## Two needed more than a swap

**`credentials/exchange/verify`** derives `holder_did` from the proof and uses it
downstream. It now comes from `accept_any`, which has already refused a set whose
verifying proofs disagree about the signer — so there is exactly one answer
rather than "whichever proof came first". `proof_purpose` is checked on *every*
proof: a presentation carrying one `authentication` proof beside an
`assertionMethod` one is ambiguous about what the holder attested, and the
permissive reading is the dangerous one.

**`routes/members/personhood`** resolves the holder's DID document once and looks
up each proof's own verification method within it. A hybrid holder's two keys are
both found, and no proof can reference a method belonging to another DID because
the document searched is always the holder's.

## The status list deserves its own note

`recognition/verify`'s second site verifies a **status list** — the document that
decides whether a credential is revoked. A proof set mixing issuers there is
exactly the substitution attack the URL-based issuer check immediately above it
already refuses, so binding every proof to the list's own issuer closes the same
hole by the other route.

## Still not converted, deliberately

`vta-sdk/src/provision_integration/{credential,template_verify}.rs` — VTA-issued
bootstrap credentials, one-shot and sealed, opened once and archived, where a
hybrid proof set is not a realistic shape. The helper lives in `vtc-service`, and
promoting it to `vta-sdk` for two call sites that will not use the capability is
not worth the published-API surface.

## Verification

VTC and workspace suites clean; clippy `-D warnings` clean; rustfmt clean.

## Phase 3

| | |
|---|---|
| affinidi-tdk-rs#818 | a key with no cryptosuite is refused by name |
| #1548 | verification can read a proof set — helper + 2 paths |
| this | the remaining 6, so the VTC accepts hybrid credentials everywhere |
| next | **issuance** — which needs the VTC to hold a second key, and therefore a `schemaVersion` 2 `vtc-host` template |

That last dependency closes a loop worth noting: Phase 3's issuance half is only
possible because Phase 2 taught templates to declare which algorithms their keys
use.
