title: vta-service-v0.33.0
body:
### Added

- **vta-sdk**: A TSP client re-forms a dropped relationship and retries a safe task ([#1544](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1544))

TSP Rev 3 §7.2.2 is symmetric and silent: if the VTA loses its half of a
  relationship (idle eviction, key rotation, a fresh redeploy) it *drops* the
  peer's next frame with no reply. A fresh `pnm` process recovers on its own
  because it re-invites every run ([#1540](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1540)). A client whose relationship store still
  reads "related" — a long-lived process, or a durable store — never re-invites
  (`relate` short-circuits on the local state) and just times out, forever.

  This wires the client-side send-path self-repair — the first consumer of
  `affinidi-messaging-sdk`'s `reset_relationship` in this workspace, and design
  note `tsp-relationship-recovery.md`'s D4. `VtaClient::dispatch_trust_task` now
  treats a TSP reply-timeout as a possible §7.2.2 drop and, across all three leg
  shapes (pure, multiplexed, separate), re-forms the relationship — reset the
  local half to `None`, re-invite through the existing `relate` — leaning on D2's
  reconcile transition so the reset is safe even when the peer had not actually
  forgotten.

  The resend is gated on `vta_sdk::retry_safety`, because a §7.2.2 drop is
  indistinguishable from a lost reply and a blind resend is only safe when a second
  execution does no harm: a `ReadOnly`/`RetrySafe` task is resent once here; a
  `Keyed`/`KeyedSecret`/unknown task is *healed* (so the next attempt lands) but
  its resend is left to `VtaClient::idempotent`, the one retry owner that holds a
  stable key. So this never double-executes a mutation and never stacks a second
  retry loop on the idempotency one. It is the synchronous, per-call form — a
  single inline retry, no single-flight/backoff coordinator (that stays for the
  D6 outbox integration).

- **tsp**: The VTC persists + answers TSP relationships and relates before sending to the registry (Rev 3 §7.2.2) ([#1543](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1543))

The VTC is a server like the VTA, but its TSP was half-wired: it drove the
  delivery layer yet built the ATM with a bare `ATMConfig::builder().build()`
  (in-memory relationship store, wiped on restart), its `handle_tsp` had no
  relationship-control answering arm, and `MessagingRegistryClient` sent Trust
  Tasks to the trust-registry with a plain `send_routed` and no relationship. So
  the registry §7.2.2-dropped every frame ("no relationship with ...trust-registry"),
  and a VTC restart would have dropped the registry's replies too.

  Bring the VTC to VTA parity:

    - Lift the durable relationship-store adapter (`KeyspaceRelationshipKv` +
      `maintenance_loop`) out of `vta-service` into a shared, feature-gated
      `vti_common::relationship_store`, alongside `VtiOutboxStore`. `vta-service`
      now re-exports it and keeps only its VTA-specific §7.2.2 drop telemetry.
    - Inject the store into the VTC ATM (`with_relationship_store`) over a new
      `tsp_relationships` keyspace — distinct from the VTC's social-graph
      `relationships`, and excluded from backup (transport state). Spawn the
      boot-enumerate + idle-eviction maintenance loop once at startup.
    - `handle_tsp` now answers `InboundKind::RelationshipControl` via a
      `decide_control` policy (accept an invite, record an accept, answer a
      cancel) — the ACL gate stays at the Trust Task layer.
    - `MessagingRegistryClient` sends over `send_reestablishing`: it forms the
      relationship (sends an invite) when readiness demands, then sends the
      payload (§3.6). A `TODO(D4)` marks the reply-timeout reset that belongs at
      the correlated-reply wait site.

  This is the sender-and-responder half of the same recovery work already landed
  in `vta-service` and the trust-registry. The `VtaClient`/`SessionStore` Auto
  path is a different client and was handled separately ([#1540](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1540)).

- **did-templates**: Clients carry a post-quantum template on the task version that can hold it ([#1542](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1542))

The last piece of Phase 2. A `keys` block now travels end to end: authored by an
  operator, sent on a task version that can express it, accepted by the VTA,
  minted with the right algorithm, recorded as what it is, published in the
  document, and read correctly by a verifier.

title: feat(vta-service): re-form a dropped TSP relationship on the outbound send path (D6)
body:
Completes the TSP relationship-recovery series on the **VTA outbound send path** — **D6** in `tsp-relationship-recovery.md`. The coordinator-grade counterpart to the client-side per-call self-repair (#1544), following the transport-surface decision (#1545: multi-hop TSP is required, so this recovery work is justified investment).

## What

Every VTA server-initiated TSP send funnels through `operations::outbound::send_tsp`. On a reply-timeout — the §7.2.2 silent-drop signature — it now drives the upstream single-flight `RecoveryCoordinator`:

- One shared coordinator on `AppState`, keyed `(our_vid, their_vid)`.
- `begin` → **`Start`**: reset our stale local half (safe against a false positive via D2's reconcile), then for a **`retry_safety`-safe** task re-invite + resend once (`send_reestablishing`); a task that could double-execute is only healed (re-invited, no resend) — same gate as #1544.
- **`InFlight`**: a concurrent send to the same lost peer coalesces onto the one re-invite (no invite storm).
- **`Backoff`/`GiveUp`**: cap a genuinely-down peer.

New on `TspTransport`: `reset_relationship`, `send_reestablishing`, `relate`, `our_vid`. The reply timeout becomes a `TspSender` field (default = the 30s const) only so a test can shorten it.

## Tests

`test_support::transport_harness_tests`, against a routable-but-silent orphan peer with a short timeout:
- **`d6_drives_recovery_on_a_reply_timeout`** — the coordinator is consulted and one recovery runs.
- **`d6_coalesces_concurrent_recoveries`** — two concurrent recoveries for one peer record **one** attempt (single-flight).

Both **non-vacuous by construction**: no coordinator call ⇒ zero attempts (fails #1); no coalescing ⇒ two attempts (fails #2).

## Coordination / scope

- The **VTC registry** seam is handled separately (reset-only) by `feat/vtc-tsp-d4-reset` (session devel-b4). This PR is the VTA seam only; the coordinator can wrap the registry client as a consumer later without touching that file.
- Honest gap: a full **end-to-end success-path** test (a responding peer that recovers a reply) needs a responding-peer harness and is a noted follow-up. The reply-success arm here is the trivial passthrough over the SDK-tested `send_reestablishing`; what this PR proves is the novel D6 orchestration (coordinator consulted, single-flight, cap, reset+reestablish driven).

## Verification

`cargo check` (tsp + default), `fmt`, `clippy -D warnings` (lib + tests) all clean; the two D6 tests pass. No public-API/semver change (`AppState` field is `cfg(tsp)`, `TspTransport` methods additive).

title: vti-common-v0.19.1
body:
### Added

- **tsp**: The VTC persists + answers TSP relationships and relates before sending to the registry (Rev 3 §7.2.2) ([#1543](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1543))

The VTC is a server like the VTA, but its TSP was half-wired: it drove the
  delivery layer yet built the ATM with a bare `ATMConfig::builder().build()`
  (in-memory relationship store, wiped on restart), its `handle_tsp` had no
  relationship-control answering arm, and `MessagingRegistryClient` sent Trust
  Tasks to the trust-registry with a plain `send_routed` and no relationship. So
  the registry §7.2.2-dropped every frame ("no relationship with ...trust-registry"),
  and a VTC restart would have dropped the registry's replies too.

  Bring the VTC to VTA parity:

    - Lift the durable relationship-store adapter (`KeyspaceRelationshipKv` +
      `maintenance_loop`) out of `vta-service` into a shared, feature-gated
      `vti_common::relationship_store`, alongside `VtiOutboxStore`. `vta-service`
      now re-exports it and keeps only its VTA-specific §7.2.2 drop telemetry.
    - Inject the store into the VTC ATM (`with_relationship_store`) over a new
      `tsp_relationships` keyspace — distinct from the VTC's social-graph
      `relationships`, and excluded from backup (transport state). Spawn the
      boot-enumerate + idle-eviction maintenance loop once at startup.
    - `handle_tsp` now answers `InboundKind::RelationshipControl` via a
      `decide_control` policy (accept an invite, record an accept, answer a
      cancel) — the ACL gate stays at the Trust Task layer.
    - `MessagingRegistryClient` sends over `send_reestablishing`: it forms the
      relationship (sends an invite) when readiness demands, then sends the
      payload (§3.6). A `TODO(D4)` marks the reply-timeout reset that belongs at
      the correlated-reply wait site.

  This is the sender-and-responder half of the same recovery work already landed
  in `vta-service` and the trust-registry. The `VtaClient`/`SessionStore` Auto
  path is a different client and was handled separately ([#1540](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1540)).

title: vta-sdk-v0.42.1
body:
### Added

- **vta-sdk**: Expose relate_tsp_trust_task_leg for the connect_auto + enable two-step ([#1547](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1547))

OpenVTC's `connect_auto` + `enable_tsp_trust_tasks` two-step attaches the TSP
  Trust-Task leg but has no public way to form the Rev 3 §7.2.2 relationship for
  it, so a Rev 3 VTA silently drops the consumer's first Trust Task. The only
  relate was `pub(crate) relate_trust_task_leg`, reachable only from inside the
  crate via `connect_didcomm_with_tsp` (which relates internally).

  Add a thin public wrapper, `relate_tsp_trust_task_leg`, over that existing
  idempotent (state-read guarded) internal relate. No behavior change: it forwards
  verbatim, so calling it after `enable_tsp_trust_tasks` forms the relationship,
  and it is a no-op when the Trust-Task surface is not on TSP.

- **vta-sdk**: A TSP client re-forms a dropped relationship and retries a safe task ([#1544](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1544))

TSP Rev 3 §7.2.2 is symmetric and silent: if the VTA loses its half of a
  relationship (idle eviction, key rotation, a fresh redeploy) it *drops* the
  peer's next frame with no reply. A fresh `pnm` process recovers on its own
  because it re-invites every run ([#1540](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1540)). A client whose relationship store still
  reads "related" — a long-lived process, or a durable store — never re-invites
  (`relate` short-circuits on the local state) and just times out, forever.

  This wires the client-side send-path self-repair — the first consumer of
  `affinidi-messaging-sdk`'s `reset_relationship` in this workspace, and design
  note `tsp-relationship-recovery.md`'s D4. `VtaClient::dispatch_trust_task` now
  treats a TSP reply-timeout as a possible §7.2.2 drop and, across all three leg
  shapes (pure, multiplexed, separate), re-forms the relationship — reset the
  local half to `None`, re-invite through the existing `relate` — leaning on D2's
  reconcile transition so the reset is safe even when the peer had not actually
  forgotten.

  The resend is gated on `vta_sdk::retry_safety`, because a §7.2.2 drop is
  indistinguishable from a lost reply and a blind resend is only safe when a second
  execution does no harm: a `ReadOnly`/`RetrySafe` task is resent once here; a
  `Keyed`/`KeyedSecret`/unknown task is *healed* (so the next attempt lands) but
  its resend is left to `VtaClient::idempotent`, the one retry owner that holds a
  stable key. So this never double-executes a mutation and never stacks a second
  retry loop on the idempotency one. It is the synchronous, per-call form — a
  single inline retry, no single-flight/backoff coordinator (that stays for the
  D6 outbox integration).

- **did-templates**: Clients carry a post-quantum template on the task version that can hold it ([#1542](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1542))

The last piece of Phase 2. A `keys` block now travels end to end: authored by an
  operator, sent on a task version that can express it, accepted by the VTA,
  minted with the right algorithm, recorded as what it is, published in the
  document, and read correctly by a verifier.

title: feat(credentials): verification can read a document carrying more than one proof
body:
Groundwork for hybrid credentials — and deliberately the **verification** half
first.

A credential signed with both Ed25519 and ML-DSA-44 arrives as a JSON **array**,
and every verification path here did:

```rust
serde_json::from_value::<DataIntegrityProof>(proof_value.clone())
```

…which fails on an array. So a hybrid credential was rejected as *malformed* by
this stack — including one it had issued itself, had issuance been wired first.
That is why verification moves first, and it is a checked fact rather than a
convention: I established it before writing anything.

`affinidi-data-integrity` has had `sign_multi` / `verify_multi` since it was
written, with **zero consumers** anywhere in this workspace. This is the first.

## Two rules that are not about cryptography

**Every proof is bound to the issuer before any signature is verified.** A proof
naming someone else is not a failed signature — it is a document claiming the
wrong author — and it must not become reachable merely by being the one that
happens to verify.

**All proofs that verify must name the same issuer.** A document carrying a valid
proof from Alice and a valid proof from Mallory is not "verified" in any sense
one answer can express; a caller handed one `Ok` and one DID would reasonably
assume one signer. The test covers this with **both signatures genuinely valid**,
which is what makes it worth refusing — and it closes the obvious trick of
appending a proof from a party the reader trusts more.

`RequireAny` is the acceptance rule: during transition a verifier is *expected*
not to understand every suite present, so demanding all of them would make a
post-quantum proof a liability to the classical verifier that cannot check it.
Tightening to `RequireAll` once the fleet holds PQC keys is a policy change, not
a code one.

## Scope — stated rather than implied

**This does not yet mean the stack accepts hybrid credentials.** Two paths are
converted (`LocalSigner::verify`, invitation verification). Six are not:

```
vtc-service/src/members/inbound_vmc.rs:348
vtc-service/src/recognition/verify.rs:277, :531
vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs:1606
vtc-service/src/routes/members/personhood.rs:690
vtc-service/src/credentials/exchange/verify.rs:433
```

Each is a third-party credential path with its own issuer binding and error
handling. Converting six of those in bulk is how a security check gets quietly
weakened, so they get a focused follow-up.

**Safe to land in this state** because nothing issues a hybrid credential yet, so
no path can currently receive one. The value of landing it separately is that the
two rules above are established *once*, and the remaining six reuse them rather
than each inventing an answer.

`vta-sdk/src/provision_integration/{credential,template_verify}.rs` also read a
single proof and are deliberately excluded — VTA-issued bootstrap credentials,
one-shot and sealed, where a hybrid proof set is not a realistic shape.

## Verification

VTC and workspace suites clean; clippy `-D warnings` clean; rustfmt clean; seven
new tests covering the acceptance rules, malformed-proof indexing, and the
empty-array-vs-unsigned distinction.

## Phase 3 so far

| | |
|---|---|
| affinidi-tdk-rs#818 | a key with no cryptosuite is refused by name (and the plan's "silent fallback" corrected — it was never silent) |
| this | verification can read a proof set |
| next | the remaining six verification paths, then issuance — which needs the VTC to hold a second key, and therefore a `schemaVersion` 2 `vtc-host` template |

feat(credentials): verification can read a document carrying more than one proof (#1548)

Groundwork for hybrid credentials, and deliberately the verification half
first: a credential signed with both Ed25519 and ML-DSA-44 arrives as a JSON
**array**, and every verification path here did

    serde_json::from_value::<DataIntegrityProof>(proof_value.clone())

which fails on an array. So a hybrid credential was rejected as malformed — by
this stack, including one it had issued itself, had issuance been wired first.
That is why verification moves before issuance, and it is a fact rather than a
convention: it was checked before anything was written.

`affinidi-data-integrity` has had `sign_multi` / `verify_multi` since it was
written, with zero consumers anywhere in this workspace. This is the first.

## Two rules that are not about cryptography

**Every proof is bound to the issuer before any signature is verified.** A proof
naming someone else is not a failed signature — it is a document claiming the
wrong author — and it must not become reachable merely by being the one that
happens to verify.

**All proofs that verify must name the same issuer.** A document carrying a
valid proof from Alice and a valid proof from Mallory is not "verified" in any
sense one answer can express, and a caller handed one `Ok` and one DID would
reasonably assume one signer. The test covers it with BOTH signatures genuinely
valid, which is what makes it worth refusing; it also closes the obvious trick of
appending a proof from a party the reader trusts more.

`RequireAny` is the acceptance rule. During the transition a verifier is
expected not to understand every suite on a document, so demanding all of them
would make a post-quantum proof a liability to the classical verifier that
cannot check it. Tightening to `RequireAll` once the fleet holds PQC keys is a
policy change, not a code one.

## Scope, stated rather than implied

Two paths are converted: `LocalSigner::verify` and invitation verification.
**Six are not**, and this does NOT yet mean the stack accepts hybrid
credentials:

    vtc-service/src/members/inbound_vmc.rs:348
    vtc-service/src/recognition/verify.rs:277, :531
    vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs:1606
    vtc-service/src/routes/members/personhood.rs:690
    vtc-service/src/credentials/exchange/verify.rs:433

Each is a third-party credential path with its own issuer binding and error
handling. Converting six of those in bulk is how a security check gets quietly
weakened, so they get a focused follow-up that can attend to each.

Safe to land in this state because nothing issues a hybrid credential yet, so no
path can receive one. The value of landing it separately is that the two rules
above are established once, and the remaining six reuse them rather than each
inventing an answer.

`vta-sdk/src/provision_integration/{credential,template_verify}.rs` also read a
single proof and are deliberately excluded: those are VTA-issued bootstrap
credentials, one-shot and sealed, where a hybrid proof set is not a realistic
shape.

VTC and workspace suites clean; clippy clean under `-D warnings`; rustfmt clean.

title: feat(vta-sdk): expose relate_tsp_trust_task_leg for the connect_auto + enable two-step
body:
## Why

OpenVTC forms a two-transport client with the `connect_auto` + `enable_tsp_trust_tasks` two-step: `connect_auto` builds the DIDComm client, `enable_tsp_trust_tasks` multiplexes the TSP Trust-Task leg onto its session. But there was no **public** way to then form the Rev 3 **§7.2.2** relationship for that leg. The only relate is `pub(crate) async fn relate_trust_task_leg`, reachable from inside the crate only (via `connect_didcomm_with_tsp`, which relates internally). So a consumer on the two-step path attaches the leg but never relates it, and a **Rev 3 VTA silently drops the consumer's first Trust Task** — the relationship is what authorises the session's application messages.

## The change

A thin **public wrapper** on `impl VtaClient`, forwarding verbatim to the existing internal relate:

```rust
#[cfg(all(feature = "session", feature = "tsp"))]
pub async fn relate_tsp_trust_task_leg(&self, vta_did: &str) -> Result<(), VtaError> {
    self.relate_trust_task_leg(vta_did).await
}
```

- **No behavior change.** It calls the same idempotent (state-read guarded) internal relate `connect_didcomm_with_tsp` already uses, so calling it after `enable_tsp_trust_tasks` is safe, and it is a no-op when the Trust-Task surface is not on TSP.
- `relate_trust_task_leg`'s visibility and body are **unchanged**; no version field touched (release-plz derives the bump).

## Reviewers

- Coordinated with **PNM-VTA** (owns `client/mod.rs`; #1540 made `relate_trust_task_leg` `pub(crate)`).
- Conventional-commit `feat`, so after merge **release-plz's Release PR cuts the vta-sdk minor**.

## Verification

- `cargo build -p vta-sdk --all-features` and `--features session,tsp` — both clean.
- `cargo test -p vta-sdk --all-features` — all pass (incl. doctests).
- `cargo clippy -p vta-sdk --all-features -- -D warnings` — clean.
- `cargo fmt -p vta-sdk --check` — clean.

title: feat(tsp): the VTC registry client re-forms a dropped relationship on a reply timeout (D4)
body:
## Why

Rev 3 §7.2.2 is symmetric and silent: if the trust-registry loses its half of the relationship (a fresh or reset durable store, idle eviction, key rotation), it drops the VTC's next Trust Task with no reply. Since #1543 the VTC **persists** its relationship half — so once it reads "related" it never re-invites (`send_reestablishing` reads `SendReadiness::Ready` and sends directly), and every send to the registry then times out, forever. This is a real, observed failure: the registry logs `discarded: no relationship with …trust-registry` on every VTC send while the VTC sits on a stale "related" half.

## What

`MessagingRegistryClient::round_trip` now treats a TSP reply-timeout as a possible §7.2.2 drop and resets our local relationship half (`atm.tsp().reset_relationship`), so the syncer's next attempt re-invites: `send_tsp`'s `send_reestablishing` then reads `SendReadiness::Reestablish` and forms the relationship before sending. The reset is safe against a false positive (the registry was merely slow) because a fresh invite over a relationship it actually kept reconciles via D2 rather than erroring.

One file: `vtc-service/src/registry/messaging.rs`.

## Coordination / boundaries

- This is the registry client's analogue of `VtaClient`'s self-repair (**#1544**), which runs in a different client (`VtaClient::dispatch_trust_task`) and does not reach `MessagingRegistryClient`. No shared file; confirmed with that PR's author.
- **Timeout detection is structural** (the `tokio::time::timeout` fired), not a forked error-string matcher — so no second `is_tsp_reply_timeout`.
- **Reset state only — never resend inline.** The syncer's existing backoff stays the single retry owner (per the "retry has exactly one owner" R-rule), so a mutation is never double-executed and there's no `retry_safety` gate to duplicate.
- `round_trip`/`send_tsp` signatures are unchanged, so a future recovery coordinator (D6) can wrap this client as a consumer without touching this file.

## Verification (offline)

- `cargo build -p vtc-service --features tsp` — green.
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets` with `--features tsp` and default, `-- -D warnings` — green.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean.
- `cargo test --lib -p vtc-service --features tsp registry::` — 99 pass, 0 fail.

title: feat(vta-sdk): a TSP client re-forms a dropped relationship and retries a safe task
body:
Follow-up to #1540. That fix made a **fresh** `pnm` process recover a lost TSP relationship (it re-invites every run). This closes the same gap for a client that **doesn't** restart.

## The gap

TSP Rev 3 §7.2.2 is symmetric and silent: if the VTA loses its half of a relationship (idle eviction, key rotation, a fresh redeploy) it *drops* the peer's next frame with no reply. A client whose relationship store still reads "related" — a long-lived process, or a durable store — never re-invites (`relate` short-circuits on the local state), so the send is dropped and the call just times out, forever.

## What this does

Wires the **client-side send-path self-repair** — the first consumer of `affinidi-messaging-sdk`'s `reset_relationship` in this workspace, and design note `tsp-relationship-recovery.md`'s **D4**. `VtaClient::dispatch_trust_task` now treats a TSP reply-timeout as a possible §7.2.2 drop and, across all three leg shapes (pure `Tsp`, multiplexed, separate), re-forms the relationship:

- reset the local half to `None`, then re-invite through the existing `relate` — leaning on **D2**'s reconcile transition so the reset is safe even if the peer had *not* actually forgotten (the fresh invite lands on its live half and is re-accepted, not errored).

## The safety gate

A §7.2.2 drop is indistinguishable from a lost reply, so a blind resend is only safe when a second execution does no harm. The resend is gated on `vta_sdk::retry_safety`:

- **`ReadOnly`/`RetrySafe`** (e.g. `acl/grant`) → resent once here.
- **`Keyed`/`KeyedSecret`/unknown** → *healed* (so the next attempt lands) but the resend is left to `VtaClient::idempotent`, the one retry owner that holds a stable key.

So this never double-executes a mutation and never stacks a second retry loop on the idempotency one. It is the **synchronous, per-call** form — a single inline retry, no single-flight/backoff coordinator (that stays for the D6 outbox integration).

## API

- New: `DIDCommSession::force_relate_tsp`, `TspSession::force_relate`, `VtaError::is_tsp_reply_timeout` (matching a shared `TSP_REPLY_TIMEOUT_PREFIX` const so the timeout producer and the detector can't drift), `MockVta::forget_tsp_relationship` (test seam). All additive — no breaking change.

## Test

`tests/e2e/tests/tsp_self_repair_on_drop.rs`: a dual `VtaClient` whose VTA has forgotten its half recovers a `RetrySafe` grant in **one call**. **Non-vacuous** — neutering the self-repair reproduces the bare `timed out waiting for the TSP reply` (verified, and the VTA logs the `discarded: no relationship` drop).

## Verification

- New test + full TSP e2e group green (`tsp_self_repair_on_drop`, `tsp_dual_client_reply`, `tsp_vtaclient_relate`, `tsp_vta_trust_task`, `tsp_dual_leg`); `vta-sdk` 603 lib tests green; default (non-`tsp`) build clean; `cargo fmt` clean; clippy clean on the changed files.

## Docs

Design note `tsp-relationship-recovery.md` D4 updated to record the client-side wiring (and that it's the per-call form, not the coordinator).

title: docs(tsp): record the Trust-Task-surface transport decision (multi-hop required)
body:
Decision record: the PNM<->VTA Trust-Task surface stays on **TSP** (not a DIDComm fallback), decided on the *benefit* — metadata-private multi-hop routing — rather than the friction of the relationship-recovery bug series (#1527 / #1537 / #1540 / #1544).

**Decision:** multi-hop TSP is a **requirement**. So the §7.2.2 relationship layer is the price of a benefit we *will* collect, and the D1–D9 recovery work is justified investment, not speculative rent.

**Consequences recorded for the roadmap:**
- The send seams call `send_routed(&[mediator, recipient])` today — a *single* intermediary, i.e. routed delivery, not the metadata-private multi-hop wrap. Delivering the benefit means wiring the seams to `send_nested` / route discovery (already the designed stance in `tsp-enablement.md`: use upstream routing, don't build onion routing ourselves).
- **D6** coordinator recovery (single-flight, backoff, herd control) becomes non-optional at multi-hop / fleet scale; the per-call self-repair (#1544) only covers single-mediator.
- D7–D9 hardening warranted for the same reason.

Also clarifies what the relationship layer *is* (admission) vs what it is **not** (authentication — intrinsic to the envelope; authorization — the ACL), since conflating them is what made the cost/benefit hard to weigh.

Docs-only.

title: feat(tsp): the VTC persists + answers TSP relationships and relates before sending to the registry (Rev 3 §7.2.2)
body:
## Why

The VTC is a server like the VTA, but its TSP was half-wired. It drove the delivery layer (`DidCommTransport`/`MessagingService`) yet built its ATM with a bare `ATMConfig::builder().build()` — **no relationship store** — had **no answering arm** in `handle_tsp`, and its `MessagingRegistryClient` sent Trust Tasks to the trust-registry with a plain `send_routed`. So the registry §7.2.2-dropped every VTC Trust Task (`discarded: no relationship with …trust-registry`) — a real, observed failure once the registry started enforcing §7.2.2.

This brings the VTC to VTA parity: persist + answer inbound relationships, and relate-before-send as the initiator to the registry.

Companion to the registry-side fix (affinidi-trust-registry-rs #135) and distinct from #1540 (which fixed the `VtaClient`/`SessionStore` Auto path — a different client that doesn't cover `MessagingRegistryClient`).

## What changed

- **Shared adapter → `vti-common`.** `KeyspaceRelationshipKv` (impl `RelationshipKv`) + `build_relationship_store` + `maintenance_loop` now live in `vti-common/src/relationship_store.rs`, next to `VtiOutboxStore`, behind a new **off-by-default `tsp` feature** (keeps `affinidi-messaging-sdk` out of non-TSP consumers). `vta-service` re-exports them under their historical names and keeps its VTA-only §7.2.2 drop-telemetry — no vta-service call-site changes.
- **VTC responder side.** `build_messaging` injects `with_relationship_store` over a **new `tsp_relationships` keyspace** (distinct from the VTC's social-graph `RELATIONSHIPS`), the maintenance loop is spawned once at startup, and `handle_tsp` answers `InboundKind::RelationshipControl` via `decide_control` → `accept_relationship`/`cancel_relationship` (mirrors the VTA; no ACL check in the control path).
- **VTC initiator side.** `MessagingRegistryClient::send_tsp` uses `send_reestablishing`, forming the §7.2.2 relationship (sending an invite) when readiness demands, with the payload riding after per §3.6.

## Reviewer notes

- **D4 reply-timeout reset is TODO'd**, not built — it belongs at the correlated-reply wait site (there's no reply to time out inside the send). Not needed for the first-contact fix; it hardens the case where the registry restarts and forgets its half after a relationship existed. Fast-follow.
- New keyspace is in `ALL` + `EXCLUDED_FROM_BACKUP`; census count 30→31.

## Verification (offline)

- Build (`vti-common --features tsp`, vta-service, vtc-service) — green.
- `cargo clippy … --all-targets -- -D warnings` — green.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean.
- `cargo test --lib -p vti-common --features tsp` — 461 pass. `-p vtc-service --features tsp` — 1035 pass; the 4 `admin_ui::tests` failures are the offline `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD=1` empty-asset panic (unrelated; green in CI where the UI is built).
- Not run locally: the server-spinning `-p vtc-service` integration tests and the `-p vtc-client` job — for CI.

The VTC is a server like the VTA, but its TSP was half-wired: it drove the

title: feat(did-templates): clients carry a post-quantum template on the task version that can hold it
body:
**The last piece of Phase 2.** A `keys` block now travels end to end: authored by
an operator, sent on a task version that can express it, accepted by the VTA,
minted with the right algorithm, recorded as what it is, published in the
document, and read correctly by a verifier.

## The task version follows the template version

`create` and `update` pick their URI from `template.schema_version` rather than
always sending 3.0:

| Template | Task URI | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `schemaVersion` 1 | **2.0** | nothing 2.0 cannot express, so demanding 3.0 buys nothing and costs compatibility with every VTA deployed before 3.0 |
| `schemaVersion` 2 | **3.0** | genuinely cannot travel on 2.0 |

A caller sending a v2 template to an older VTA gets `UnsupportedType` naming the
version. That is the **correct** answer rather than an obstacle — an older VTA
could not mint the keys that template asks for either, so failing at the wire is
better than succeeding into a DID that is not what was asked for.

Reads go to 3.0 unconditionally, because a 2.0 read now refuses to return a v2
record — a client pinned to 2.0 could not see post-quantum templates at all.

## A gap #1538 left, closed here

Worth calling out because it is mine. That PR's ceiling guarded what a caller
could **send**, not what the service would **return**.

A `schemaVersion` 2 template fetched through a 2.0 read came back carrying a
`keys` block, under a response schema that pins `schemaVersion` to `const: 1` and
sets `additionalProperties: false`. The caller received a document its own
specification says cannot exist.

`list` refuses the whole listing rather than filtering it. Quietly dropping v2
templates would be worse than an error: an operator would see a list with the
post-quantum templates missing and conclude they had never been created.

## Censuses, again

`retry_safety` required the new URIs classified, and `ALL_URIS` required them
registered before a classification was allowed to name them. Both mechanical —
recorded because the pair together is what stops a URI being served, retried or
classified without the other two knowing.

One e2e test failed **correctly**: its scripted responder answered `list/2.0`
while the client had moved to 3.0, so it returned `no handler`. Moved to 3.0 with
a note, so a future reader hitting that finds the reason rather than assuming the
responder is broken.

## Verification

Workspace and VTC suites clean; clippy `-D warnings` clean; rustfmt clean.

## Phase 2 complete

| | PR |
|---|---|
| Verifiers read the declared key type | #1528 |
| `keys` block, `schemaVersion` 2 | #1530 |
| Derived keys carry their algorithm | #1532 |
| Operators can create PQC keys; two-axis labelling | #1535 |
| The wire shape at 3.0 | dtgwg#508 |
| The VTA accepts 3.0 | #1538 |
| Clients send it | this |

A recurring shape across all of them, worth recording: **almost every defect was
a type asserted where it should have been carried** — the resolver hardcoding
`Ed25519`, `save_key_record` hardcoding it again, the task URI being the only
carrier of the spec version. Each was invisible while one algorithm existed, and
each would have surfaced far from its cause the moment a second one did.

3.0 existed, for templates those VTAs serve perfectly well. A `schemaVersion` 1
template has nothing 2.0 cannot express, so demanding 3.0 buys nothing and costs
compatibility. A `schemaVersion` 2 template genuinely cannot travel on 2.0, so
demanding 3.0 turns a silent failure into `UnsupportedType` naming the version —
and an older VTA could not mint the keys that template asks for either, so the
refusal is the correct answer rather than an obstacle.

Reads go to 3.0 unconditionally, because a 2.0 read now refuses to return a v2
record: a client pinned to 2.0 could not see post-quantum templates at all.

## A gap #1538 left, closed here

That PR's ceiling guarded what a caller could SEND and not what the service
would RETURN. A `schemaVersion` 2 template fetched through a 2.0 read came back
carrying a `keys` block, under a response schema that pins `schemaVersion` to
`const: 1` and sets `additionalProperties: false` — the caller received a
document its own specification says cannot exist.

`list` refuses the whole listing rather than filtering. Quietly dropping v2
templates would be worse than an error: an operator would see a list with the
post-quantum templates missing and conclude they had never been created.

## Censuses, again

`retry_safety` required the new URIs classified, and `ALL_URIS` required them
registered before a classification was allowed to name them. Both are
mechanical; recording them because the pair together is what stops a URI being
served, retried or classified without the other two knowing.

One e2e test failed correctly: its scripted responder answered `list/2.0` while
the client had moved to 3.0, so it returned `no handler`. Moved, with a note —
a future reader hitting that should find the reason rather than assume the
responder is broken.

Workspace and VTC suites clean; clippy clean under `-D warnings`; rustfmt clean.

title: build(deps): take vta-sdk 0.42 so did-git-sign can publish (unblocks OpenVTC)
body:
## What & why

Moves the workspace onto the **vta-sdk 0.42** frontier that VTI main deploys and
that **OpenVTC's rev3 line already pins directly** (`vta-sdk 0.42.0`).

This is the "moves first" edge. While `did-git-sign` declared `^0.39`, an
OpenVTC build that took vta-sdk 0.42 directly still dragged a **second, broken
vta-sdk 0.39 copy** in through this crate — the exact duplicate state OpenVTC's
manifest records having escaped. Publishing this workspace on 0.42 lets that
duplicate collapse to a single node in the consumer. One row here is one row
there.

## Version changes

| dependency | from | to | note |
|---|---|---|---|
| workspace `version` | 0.4.11 | **0.4.12** | so the crates republish |
| `vta-sdk` | 0.39 | **0.42** | the frontier |
| `affinidi-tdk` | 0.14 | **0.16** | what vta-sdk 0.42 declares |
| `trql-client` | 0.17 | **0.18** | registry release cut for this move; declares `trust-tasks-rs ^0.21`, closing the split the 0.36 step opened knowingly |
| `affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk` | 0.8.37 | 0.8.37 (floor unchanged; resolves 0.8.38) | SSRF floor kept |

Transitively via `cargo update`:
- `trust-tasks-rs` 0.19.4 **+** 0.20.7 → single **0.21.3**
- `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.24.0 → **0.26.7**
- `didwebvh-rs` stays **0.7.0**

The root `Cargo.toml` pin-rationale comments are updated to record the 0.42 move
(trql-client and vta-sdk blocks) in the house style.

## Code changes

**None.** The bump crosses three minors (0.39 → 0.42) but needs no source
change: `did-git-sign` reaches the VTA through `connect_auto` and takes display
names, and `verify-trust` never talks to a VTA (takes only `agent-names`), so
the `client`/`session`/`didcomm` surface those minors reshaped is not named
anywhere in this workspace.

## Single-node confirmation

`cargo tree -i vta-sdk`:

```
vta-sdk v0.42.0
├── did-git-sign v0.4.12
└── verify-trust v0.4.12
```

`cargo tree -d` shows **none** of `vta-sdk` / `trust-tasks-rs` / `didwebvh-rs`
duplicated (only the pre-existing crypto-crate duplicates: aead 0.5/0.6, aes
0.8/0.9, from the pgp vs. hpke split — unrelated to this bump).

## Checks

- `cargo build --workspace` — OK
- `cargo test --workspace` — OK (all suites pass, 0 failed)
- `cargo test -p did-git-sign --features insecure-policy-bypass` — OK
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean

Do **not** just merge-and-forget: after merging, push a **`v0.4.12`** tag to
trigger `publish.yml`. That published `did-git-sign 0.4.12` is what unblocks
OpenVTC's rev3 line.

title: fix(vta-sdk): the Auto connect path forms the TSP relationship it cannot reply without
body:
## What

`pnm acl create` (and every Trust Task over the dual DIDComm+TSP `Auto` transport) timed out with `tsp transport error: timed out waiting for the TSP reply`, while the VTA logged the operation as a success (`outcome="success"`, `TSP trust-task dispatched status=200 OK`). The grant ran; only the acknowledgement was lost.

## Root cause

TSP Rev 3 §7.2.2 is a **symmetric** relationship gate: an endpoint silently *drops* an application frame from a VID it holds no relationship with — and that includes the **client dropping the VTA's reply**.

`SessionStore::connect`'s dual-transport `Auto` path (`session.rs::attach_tsp_leg_bounded`) attached the Trust-Task TSP leg via `enable_tsp_trust_tasks` but **never called `relate`** — unlike `VtaClient::connect_didcomm_with_tsp`, which #1527 fixed. A fresh `pnm` process uses the SDK's **in-memory** relationship store and starts at `None` every run, so:

- the request still landed, because the **VTA's durable store** remembered an earlier handshake and admitted it;
- the VTA dispatched and replied `200 OK`;
- the client had no relationship to open the reply under, so it dropped it as `no relationship with did:key:…` (its own VID) and timed out.

This path had **no test coverage** — nothing exercised `SessionStore::connect`'s dual `Auto` connect — which is why it shipped even though #1527 and #1525 (the VTA answering arm) are both present.

## Fix

- `attach_tsp_leg_bounded` now forms the §7.2.2 relationship after attaching the leg (both the multiplexed and separate-mediator shapes), mirroring `connect_didcomm_with_tsp`.
- On failure it reverts to a pure DIDComm client (`disable_tsp_trust_tasks`) so the `Auto` fallback ("trust tasks stay on DIDComm") is real, rather than returning a relationship-less leg that drops every reply.
- `relate_trust_task_leg` is now `pub(crate)`; `disable_tsp_trust_tasks` is new.

## Test

Adds `tests/e2e/tests/tsp_dual_client_reply.rs`: a **multiplexed dual `VtaClient`** runs a real `acl/grant` against `MockVta::start_with_transports` and asserts the reply is admitted — the exact `pnm acl create` symptom. **Vacuity-checked**: neutering the relate makes `create_acl` time out (~32s), so the test genuinely depends on the relationship.

## Verification

- New test passes; TSP e2e group green (`tsp_dual_client_reply`, `tsp_vtaclient_relate`, `tsp_dual_leg`, `tsp_vta_trust_task`); `vta-sdk` lib tests green; `cargo fmt` clean; clippy clean on the changed files.
- No public-API/semver change — the new methods are `pub(crate)`, the changed function is private.

title: feat(did-templates): the VTA accepts did-templates 3.0 alongside 2.0
body:
**Fourth of the Phase 2 sequence**, and the server half of dtgwg#508. Registers
`create`, `update`, `get` and `list` at 3.0 — the versions whose template schema
can carry a `keys` block — and bumps `trust-tasks-rs` to 0.21.3, the release that
publishes them.

`delete` and `render` are deliberately absent: neither carries a template shape,
so neither gained a 3.0.

## Not a cutover, and not an ad-hoc dual-accept

This surface's precedent is a **clean cutover** — the twelve 1.0 URIs were
dropped in the change that introduced 2.0. That was right there: 1.0 carried two
competing scope hierarchies, so keeping it meant keeping the ambiguity.

It is wrong here. **2.0 has no defect.** It simply cannot express a post-quantum
template, and remains a correct way to manage a v1 one. A cutover would force
every client to update in lockstep with the VTA for no safety gain.

So this uses the mechanism the repo already has for exactly this case —
`SUPERSEDED_TASKS`. Both versions dispatch, a 2.0 response carries
`supersededBy` so the caller learns where to go, and the usage counter lets
removal wait on an **observed zero** rather than a guessed date.

I'd been weighing cutover against dual-accept and was about to pick one by
argument; the repo had already answered it, and
`every_dual_accepted_spec_marks_its_older_forms_superseded` enforces the
invariant I was going to assert by hand.

## The ceiling — the part nothing else would catch

`parse_payload` is plain serde on a hand-rolled body type. There is **no
per-version schema validation at runtime**, so the task URI is the only thing
carrying the spec version. Once 2.0 and 3.0 reach one handler they are
indistinguishable inside it, and a 2.0 caller could send a `schemaVersion` 2
template with a `keys` block — which `vta/_shared/0.1` forbids by pinning
`schemaVersion` to `const: 1`.

The service would be quietly more permissive than the specification it
publishes, and nothing would notice: the conformance fixtures check payload
shapes, not which URI dispatched them.

So the handler reads its own dispatching URI and holds the template to what that
version can express. An unrecognised version gets the **narrow** ceiling —
defaulting permissive would mean a future version silently accepting templates it
never promised to, invisibly.

## Three things the conformance census caught

Each would have shipped:

| | Caught |
|---|---|
| 1 | **Serving 3.0 URIs against a registry that did not know them** — VTI pinned `trust-tasks-rs` 0.21.1; the specs are in 0.21.3 |
| 2 | **A made-up spec URI in my own test fixture** — twice, including the bare stem, because the produced-URI census greps source for spec-URI literals |
| 3 | **Four dispatched URIs with no witness** |

(2) is now derived from `TASK_DID_TEMPLATES_CREATE_3_0` by stripping the version,
so no literal exists and the test survives the URI moving. Worth knowing: **you
cannot write a fake spec URI in this codebase, even in a test.**

On (3), the judgment that mattered: the new witnesses carry a **`schemaVersion` 2
template**, not the existing v1 fixture. A 3.0 witness carrying a v1 template
would pass the sweep while proving nothing about the `keys` block 3.0 exists for
— and would keep passing if that block were dropped from the published schema
entirely. The fixture publishes both key slots, so it also exercises #1530's rule
that a declared slot whose placeholder never appears is refused.

## Verification

Workspace and VTC suites clean; clippy `-D warnings` clean; rustfmt clean; all
nine conformance tests pass including the witness sweep.

## What remains

PR 5 — the CLI emitting 3.0 — finishes Phase 2. After that a template can
declare post-quantum keys end to end: authored by an operator, accepted by the
VTA, minted with the right algorithm, recorded as what it is, published in the
document, and read correctly by a verifier.

title: vta-service-v0.32.0
body:
### Added

- **tsp**: Surface §7.2.2 relationship-gate drops as telemetry (D8) ([#1536](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1536))

The event that was invisible when the recovery workstream's incident happened — an inbound TSP application message dropped because the VTA holds no relationship with the sender — is now a queryable telemetry event, so a spike is an operational alarm rather than a scatter of error logs (design note tsp-relationship-recovery.md, D8).

  - vti-common: new TelemetryKind::TspRelationshipDropped (BREAKING — the enum is not non_exhaustive; carries a count field). No internal exhaustive match breaks — all sites construct.

  - vta-service build_messaging injects an Arc<AtomicU64> into the ATM via with_relationship_drop_counter (affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.26.7); the SDK gate increments it on every drop.

  - A drop_telemetry_loop spawned ONCE at server startup samples the counter each minute and records a TspRelationshipDropped event with the delta. Spawned beside the eviction sweep, not in build_messaging (which re-runs per reconnect).

  tsp-gated; non-tsp build unaffected. release-plz owns the version bump (the semver-report red is expected for the breaking variant).

- **tsp**: Durable-store maintenance — boot enumerate + idle eviction sweep (D6/D9) ([#1534](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1534))

Wires the D6/D9 SDK cores (affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.26.6) into the VTA:

  - KeyspaceRelationshipKv gains scan_prefix over the keyspace's prefix_iter_raw (keys are plaintext, values decrypted — the invariant the sweep relies on).

  - maintenance_loop logs how many TSP relationships survived a restart (D9 observability) then periodically evicts idle ones (D6/D5, 7-day default).

  - Spawned ONCE at server startup over its own store handle on the relationships keyspace — deliberately NOT in build_messaging, which re-runs per mediator reconnect and would leak a sweep task per reconnect.

  Bumps the sdk lock to 0.26.6 (affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#815). tsp-gated; non-tsp build unaffected. Design: docs/05-design-notes/tsp-relationship-recovery.md (D6/D9).

- **keys**: A derived key carries the algorithm it was minted with ([#1532](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1532))

* feat(keys)!: a derived key carries the algorithm it was minted with

  `DerivedEntityKeys` gains `signing_key_type` / `ka_key_type`, and
  `derive_entity_keys_with_preference` mints the first algorithm a template's
  `keys` block asks for that this build can produce.

title: vta-keyspaces-v0.2.9
body:
### Added

- **tsp**: Persist TSP relationship state across restarts ([#1531](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1531))

* feat(tsp): persist TSP relationship state across restarts

  Rev 3 §7.2.2 has an endpoint silently drop application traffic from a VID it holds no relationship with. Every VTA ATM::new builds ATMConfig::builder().build() with no relationship store, so it gets the SDK's in-memory default — wiped on restart. A restarted VTA therefore forgets every TSP peer and drops their traffic until each re-handshakes, with no visible error (the failure that started this workstream).

  This injects a durable RelationshipStore backed by an encrypted fjall keyspace:

title: fix(core): raise vti-didcomm-js floor to ^0.10.0 for long-framed TSP replies
body:
A `keys/list` with **no context filter** timed out in the management console (`tsp: timed out awaiting reply frame`), while per-context queries worked. The VTA logged the reply sent successfully — `count=50 total=94`, `200 OK` — but the wallet saw no frame.

## Root cause

Through `@openvtc/vti-didcomm-js` 0.8.x, the inbound demux (`_onFrame` in `mediator-transport.js`) classified TSP by `text.startsWith("-E")` — the qb64 spelling of the **short** `-E` count code. Spec Rev 3, which this wallet now speaks, widened that count to cover the ciphertext, so any TSP message past ~12 KB is framed with the six-byte **long** count code and its text starts `--E`. `"--E…".startsWith("-E")` is false, so a large reply was handed to the DIDComm unpacker, thrown out as a poison frame, and — because the throw returns before the ack — **never acked**, so the mediator redelivered it on every reconnect while the waiter timed out.

`keys/list` with no context filter returns a full page of key records, crosses the threshold, and was silently lost. Per-context replies (small, short-framed) were unaffected. The empty error (no "last inbound frame declined" suffix) confirmed the frame never reached the TSP layer at all.

## Fix

Bump `@openvtc/pnm-core`s `@openvtc/vti-didcomm-js` dependency `^0.8.0` → `^0.10.0`. 0.10.0 (OpenVTC/vti-didcomm-js#24) moves the classifier into `isTspFrameText`, matching both `-E` and `--E`. No plugin source change is needed — the bug was entirely in the library.

Records the `^0.10.0` floor as a correctness constraint in `CLAUDE.md`, beside the existing `^0.6.2` persist-before-ack floor.

## Test fix from the same release

`tests/did.egress-socket.mjs`s non-vacuity **control** failed — not from the demux fix, but from an unrelated hardening in 0.9+: the resolver now runs its own `net-guard` on `did:webvh` resolution by default, so a bare `vtiResolve(did, {})` is refused before it dials. The control relied on the resolver dialling a loopback listener to prove the fixture is reachable. It now relaxes the dependencys policy (`allowInsecure` + `allowPrivate`) to keep proving that; the two real guard tests are unchanged and still refuse first with this repos `assertResolvableWebvhHost`. Verified empirically: no-policy → `BlockedEndpointError`, 0 dials; permissive → 1 dial.

## Verification

- `npm run build` clean (both `background.js` and `manager.js` bundles).
- `npm test` — **1521 pass, 0 fail**.
- Depends on: OpenVTC/vti-didcomm-js#24 (merged) + 0.10.0 published to npm (done).

title: fix(mediator-transport): route long-framed TSP messages, which Rev 3 made real
body:
The inbound demux classified TSP by `text.startsWith("-E")` — the qb64 spelling of the **short** `-E` count code. TSP spec Rev 3 widened that count to cover all signable content (the ciphertext included), so any message past 4095 quadlets (~12 KB) is framed with the six-byte **long** count code and its text starts `--E`. `"--E…".startsWith("-E")` is false, so every large Rev 3 message went to the DIDComm unpacker instead of the TSP consumer.

## Why it was silent in the worst direction

A TSP frame handed to `unpackInbound` throws, is reported as a poison frame, and — because the throw returns before `_dispatchTspFrame` — is **never acked**. The mediator keeps its copy and redelivers it on every reconnect, forever, while the consumer that wanted it never hears. A message that loops is harder to notice than one that errors.

Nothing could have caught this before Rev 3 existed: Rev 2s `-E` count covered only the envelope header — a couple of dozen quadlets whatever the message size — so it could not produce a long frame at all.

## Observed symptom

A wallet on this library (0.8.0) doing `keys/list` with no context filter timed out with a bare `tsp: timed out awaiting reply frame` (no "frame declined" suffix — the frame never reached the TSP layer), while the VTA logged the reply sent successfully (`count=50 total=94`, `status=200 OK`). Per-context queries (small replies, short-framed) worked; the all-contexts reply crossed ~12 KB and was long-framed, so it was dropped.

## The fix

`src/tsp-frame.js` now owns the predicate — `isTspFrameText` for the qb64 form the mediator delivers, `isTspFrameBytes` for qb2 — matching both short `-E` and long `--E` framing, rather than an inline `startsWith`. It is a module because the rule is not obvious from the expression and has a deliberate exclusion: Rev 2s long form `-0E…` (a superseded CESR v2 draft) is **not** matched, because nothing can emit it.

Reading Rev 2 is unaffected — Rev 2 messages are short-framed and start `-E` exactly as before. The framing question and the revision question are independent; this library answers only the first (it is key-blind for TSP and hands bytes to a consumer that decides the rest).

## Cross-repo note (R4.1)

The same predicate exists in the mediator (`affinidi_tsp::is_tsp`) and in the wallet codec (`@openvtc/vti-tsp-js`s `isTsp`), both fixed for this reason. These are independent implementations of one wire contract — deliberately not solved by sharing code, which would only make them agree on a shared mistake.

## Tests

Test heads are bytes from real messages packed by vti-tsp-js 0.3.0, pinned rather than imported so this library takes no dependency on the other implementation. Reverting the predicate to `["-E"]` fails three of them — the classifier test, the routing test, and the ack test (routing a frame without acking it still loses the message).

Ships as **0.10.0** (CHANGELOG + `package.json` bumped in this commit).

title: fix(tsp): form a relationship before the health Trust-Ping
body:
## The live bug

`pnm health`'s TSP Trust-Ping still fails against a VTA on Rev 3, with the VTA logging:
```
TSP message from did:key:… discarded: no relationship with did:webvh:…glenn-vta
```
This is the exact failure that opened the whole recovery workstream — and it's **client-side**: the session-identity probe sent the ping *application* message with **no prior relationship**, so the VTA correctly dropped it under §7.2.2.

## Why the recovery machinery didn't already cover it

Everything on the *VTA* side is in place: the answering arm (VTI#1525 — accepts inbound invites), the durable store (#1531), the D2 reconcile transition (`affinidi-tsp 0.2.1`). The one missing link was that the client **never sent the invite**. `TspPingSession::relate` existed but was never wired into the probe.

## Fix

Call `session.relate(vta_did)` before the pings in the probe's session-identity path:
- The VTA's answering arm accepts the invite; an invite already admits the messages that follow it (§3.6), so the ping is admitted and the pong returns.
- `relate` is **idempotent by state read** (skips when a relationship already admits application messages), so a persisted relationship is a no-op.
- On repeat runs the client's fresh invite lands over the VTA's *persisted* relationship and is handled by the **D2 reconcile transition** — no `InvalidTransition`.
- The cold `--fresh` probe is untouched (it deliberately tests the relationship-free §3 routed send via `probe_send`).

## Testing

Compiles + clippy (`-p pnm-cli --features tsp --all-targets`) clean; fmt clean. This is the change that should make @glenn's live Trust-Ping go green — worth a re-test against the latest VTA once merged.

title: feat(tsp)!: surface §7.2.2 relationship-gate drops as telemetry (D8)
body:
Makes the D8 alarm **queryable** in the VTA — the one event that was invisible when the recovery workstream's incident happened (an inbound TSP application message dropped because the VTA holds no relationship with the sender) is now a telemetry event, so a spike is an operational signal rather than a scatter of error logs.

## What
- **`vti-common`**: new `TelemetryKind::TspRelationshipDropped` — ⚠️ **breaking** (the enum isn't `#[non_exhaustive]`). No internal exhaustive match breaks; every site constructs. Carries a `count` field.
- **`vta-service`**: `build_messaging` injects an `Arc<AtomicU64>` into the ATM via `with_relationship_drop_counter` (affinidi-messaging-sdk **0.26.7**, [affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#816](https://github.com/affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs/pull/816)); the SDK gate increments it at both discard sites.
- A **`drop_telemetry_loop`** spawned **once at server startup** (beside the eviction sweep, *not* in `build_messaging` which re-runs per reconnect) samples the counter each minute and records a `TspRelationshipDropped` event with the delta.

## Notes
- `tsp`-gated; non-`tsp` build unaffected. Clippy (tsp + non-tsp, `--all-targets -D warnings`) clean; fmt clean.
- **release-plz owns the version** — no version edited here; the semver-report red is expected and correct for the breaking variant.
- Completes the observability half of D8 end-to-end (SDK counter #816 → VTA telemetry). `pnm services report`-style queries can now surface relationship-drop spikes.

Coordinating separately with the affinidi-webvh-service session on the `DIDCommService` facade additions (`tsp_ensure_relationship` + `with_relationship_store`) that let facade consumers like webvh get the same durable-store + re-invite behaviour — that's the next piece.

title: feat(keys): an operator can create a post-quantum key, and see which axis it protects
body:
Two gaps, the first of which made everything upstream unusable in practice.

## `keys create` could not make a PQC key

The VTA has been able to derive ML-DSA-44/65 since #1505, and since #1532 the
derived key carries its own algorithm so the stored record is right. But the CLI
matched exactly three strings:

```rust
"ed25519" | "x25519" | "p256" => ...,
other => Err("unknown key type '{other}', expected ed25519, x25519, or p256")
```

**Every post-quantum capability in the stack sat behind a front door that could
not ask for it.** `pnm keys create --key-type mldsa44` now works.

`keys import` deliberately still refuses them — **and says why**. The VTA
validates imported key material per algorithm and has no ML-DSA checker, so
offering it here would take an operator's private key and fail at the far end.
The refusal names the gap and points at `keys create`, instead of the generic
"expected ed25519, x25519, or p256", which reads as *no such algorithm* and
sends someone looking in the wrong place. The gap is real and server-side.

## "Is this post-quantum?" has no single answer

`QuantumPosture` makes that structural rather than something to remember.

Signature resistance and confidentiality resistance are **separate facts** on
different timetables, and today the second is false almost everywhere: an
identity can sign with ML-DSA-44 while still agreeing keys with X25519.
Collapsing them into one badge is wrong in the direction that matters — a reader
shown "post-quantum" for that identity has been told its recorded traffic is safe
from harvest-now-decrypt-later, and it is not.

So every label names its axis, and a test holds them to it:

```
Key Type:  mldsa44 (post-quantum signing)
Key Type:  x25519 (classical key agreement)
```

Two deliberate omissions:

- **No `PostQuantumKeyAgreement` variant.** Nothing a DID document publishes can
  answer that axis affirmatively today — the hybrid KEM lives in the TSP
  transport, not in a verification method. Adding the variant before that is true
  would let a renderer claim something nothing can do.
- **No wildcard arm in `posture()`.** `#[non_exhaustive]` binds other crates, not
  this one, so a new key type breaks the match on purpose. The default that would
  otherwise be inherited ("classical") is a claim about security, and the wrong
  one for the next PQC algorithm added.

## Verification

Workspace and VTC suites clean; clippy `-D warnings` clean; rustfmt clean; three
new tests. The mapping is pinned as a table because a drifted entry fails nothing
at compile time — it just tells an operator their classical key is post-quantum.

## Where this sits

Not in the original Phase 2 sequence — picked up because it was unblocked while
the spec release landed, and because it turned out to be the gap that made the
rest inert. Phase 2 so far: #1528 (verifiers read the declared key type), #1530
(templates declare algorithms), #1532 (derived keys carry theirs), dtgwg#508 (the
wire shape at 3.0), this. Next is the VTA accepting 3.0.

title: feat(tsp): durable-store maintenance — boot enumerate + idle eviction sweep (D6/D9)
body:
Wires the D6/D9 SDK cores ([affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#815](https://github.com/affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs/pull/815), `affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.26.6`) into the VTA.

## What
- **`KeyspaceRelationshipKv::scan_prefix`** over the keyspace's `prefix_iter_raw` — keys are plaintext, values are transparently decrypted (`vti-common` store: "keys remain plaintext for prefix scans"), which is exactly the invariant the sweep relies on: `decode_rel_key` reads the plaintext key, `serde_json` reads the decrypted value.
- **`maintenance_loop`** — on boot logs how many TSP relationships survived the restart (D9 observability; a non-zero count is the durable store doing its job), then periodically `evict_idle`s (D6/D5, 7-day default, 6h sweep interval).
- **Spawned once at server startup**, over its own store handle on the `relationships` keyspace — **deliberately not in `build_messaging`**, which re-runs on every mediator reconnect and would leak a sweep task per reconnect (the lifecycle trap the mediator-connection supervisor is written to avoid).

## Notes
- `tsp`-gated; non-`tsp` build unaffected. `cargo check`/`clippy -p vta-service --features tsp --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean; fmt clean.
- Bumps the sdk lock to 0.26.6.
- Design: [`docs/05-design-notes/tsp-relationship-recovery.md`](docs/05-design-notes/tsp-relationship-recovery.md) (D6/D9).

Remaining recovery follow-ups (tracked in the note): the §7.2.2 drop-counter metric (needs a small SDK gate hook) and the client-side mid-session recovery loop (`vta-sdk`, makes the D4/D6 `RecoveryCoordinator` live).

title: Drop the informative credential categories; keep Edge Credentials as a class
body:
Implements the decision recorded in #28 (https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/28#issuecomment-5696470196): drop the informative categories, keep Edge Credentials as a section and a defined term because it is a normative class rather than a category.

**Why edge stays and annotation goes.** A grouping earns a heading only if the specification says something about the group that it does not say about each member. Edge Verifiability, the VSC's profile-versus-type test, the `dtg:witnessed` profile and the VRC, VMC and VDC glossary entries all depend on the edge credential class. Nothing depended on the annotation category: its preamble was one sentence, its glossary entry said it annotates an edge, which was already untrue of the VSC, and its only other use was the VAC preamble explaining why the VAC was not in it.

**Changes**

- Abstract and Introduction list the seven types flat, with the VRC, VMC and VDC described as edge credentials that form a bi-directional pair. The "descriptive only" caveat goes.
- Taxonomy drops the mermaid diagram. Without the category nodes it duplicated the formal W3C type hierarchy printed directly beneath it, which never had categories.
- Edge Credentials preamble states the bilateral test once: an edge credential is one half of a pair whose relationship is only established when the counterparty issues the other half; every other credential is complete on the issuer's signature alone; a statement that would need the counterparty's agreement is an edge credential, not a VSC predicate profile.
- Annotation Credentials heading and its placement editor's note removed. VPC and VSC promoted to top-level sections in place, with the VSC's subsections promoted one level to match.
- VAC preamble loses the paragraph justifying its standalone placement and no longer contrasts itself with an annotation credential.
- Glossary: `DTG annotation credential` deleted. VPC and VSC entries become "a DTG credential that". `DTG credential` no longer lists three WD01 subtypes.
- `CONTEXT.md` updated to match.

**Not changed.** No schema, type string or `@context` change. `DTG edge credential` and the Edge Credentials section are unchanged apart from the added preamble paragraph. Every section still has either no subsections or more than one.

**Outline after this PR:** Edge Credentials (VRC, VMC, VDC, Edge Verifiability), VIC, VPC, VSC, VAC.

Closes #28.

A **list** rather than a single value, because a fleet does not migrate
atomically: that says *mint ML-DSA-44 where the implementation can and Ed25519
otherwise*, so one template serves a VTA with post-quantum support and one
without.

This is the wire shape for work already implemented in VTI (#1528, #1530,
#1532); the implementation went first so the spec describes something that runs.

## Why a new shared version rather than an edit

`DidTemplate` lives in `_shared/0.1`, which the shipped **1.0 and 2.0** specs
reference. Editing it in place would retroactively change what those versions
mean — the thing versioning exists to prevent. `_shared/0.2` follows the
precedent `credentials` and `device` already set, and 1.0/2.0 keep pointing at
0.1.

## Why four task families, not two

`create` and `update` carry a `DidTemplate`; **`get` and `list` return a
`DidTemplateRecord`**, which flattens the same fields. A stored v2 template
fetched through `get/2.0` would fail validation, so all four move together —
otherwise a template can be written and not read back.

## The change is breaking, for a stronger reason than expected

`additionalProperties: false` on both definitions is the obvious half. The
decisive half:

```json
"schemaVersion": { "type": "integer", "const": 1 }
```

The 0.1 schema **cannot express a v2 template at all**. 0.2 widens this to
`enum: [1, 2]`.

Note `DidTemplateRecord` duplicates `DidTemplate`'s properties rather than
`$ref`-ing them, so both definitions carry the change — worth knowing for
whoever edits this next.

## Two requirements the prose makes normative

- **An implementation MUST NOT substitute an algorithm absent from the list.**
  Running out of candidates is an error, never a silent downgrade — otherwise a
  deployment intended to be post-quantum ships classical keys with nothing
  reporting it. `minItems: 1` is the same rule at the schema level: an empty
  list would express no preference and inherit whatever the implementation
  happened to default to.
- **An implementation MUST refuse a declared slot whose placeholder never
  appears in `document`.** The key would be minted and never published, so
  verifiers keep seeing only the keys that are, while the operator believes the
  template migrated.

The slot→placeholder rule is explicit (`{SLOT_UPPERCASE}_KEY_MB`) and chosen so
`signing` and `ka` produce the two names a v1 template already uses. **A v1
template is exactly a v2 template whose keys block is
`{signing: [ed25519], ka: [x25519]}`** — so an implementation reads both through
one path, and adopting v2 cannot change how a v1 template renders.

## Generated bindings

All four regenerated in this PR. One effect worth flagging because it touches a
file this change does not otherwise edit: a *second* version of a shared schema
makes the TypeScript generator disambiguate its hoisted names, so `DidTemplate`
in `_shared/components.ts` became `DidTemplate_VtaV0_1`.

**Not a break** — the 0.1 module re-exports the old name and the package root
only ever exposed namespaces (`DidTemplateShared_v0_1.DidTemplate`) — but it was
verified rather than assumed, since TypeScript is repeatedly the side where a
change that is additive everywhere else turns out not to be.

## Verification

- `npm run build` + `npm run validate` — clean, 451 specs
- `npm run check-bindings` — 451 specs against **451 TS, 446 Rust, 451 Go and
  451 Dart** modules, all agreeing
- `cargo build --workspace --all-targets` + 45 test suites — green

The `$defs.Response` warnings on the new 3.0 files are inherited verbatim from
2.0, which carries them too — pre-existing debt copied forward with the version,
not new. Fixing that class is a separate, wider change.

pre-existing debt. The 2.0 files these were copied from are on that list; new

title: docs(tsp): D6–D9 recovery cores prototyped + service-wiring plan
body:
Updates the recovery design note to reflect the **D6–D9 decision cores** landed in [affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#815](https://github.com/affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs/pull/815), and records the service-wiring plan.

## Cores now in the SDK (#815)
- **D6/D8** `RecoveryCoordinator` (async single-flight over `RecoveryState` + `BackoffPolicy`) with `RecoveryMetrics { attempts, successes, give_ups }`.
- **D6/D9** `RelationshipKv::scan_prefix`, `PersistentRelationshipStore::{evict_idle, forget, established_relationships}`.
- **D7** `InviteRateLimiter`.

## Two wiring findings recorded
- **The timeout→recovery loop belongs client-side** (`vta-sdk`/`pnm-cli`), where correlated sends originate — exactly where the original bug appeared (a `pnm health` TSP ping timing out). A responder VTA rarely initiates a correlated TSP round-trip, so its recovery is mostly D1 (durable store, done) + D2 (auto re-accept, done).
- **The VTA eviction sweep must be spawned once at server startup, not in `build_messaging`** — which re-runs on every mediator reconnect. A sweep task holds the store `Arc` and doesn't depend on the socket, so spawning it per-reconnect leaks one sweep per reconnect (the task-lifecycle trap the mediator-connection note warns about). It needs a concrete `Arc<PersistentRelationshipStore<..>>` kept beside the `Arc<dyn RelationshipStore>` handed to the ATM.

Docs-only. The service/client wiring (VTA sweep + drop-counter metric; client recovery loop + proactive reconcile) follows once #815 publishes.

title: feat(tsp): pack TSP Rev 3 natively, read Rev 3 and Rev 2
body:
## What this is

The plugin side of the TSP Rev 2 → Rev 3 cutover. The wallet now **packs Rev 3
and only Rev 3**, and **reads Rev 3 or Rev 2** by dispatching on the version
marker the wire carries. This is the plugin half of a coordinated cutover; the
VTA half — making Rev 3 the default it reads and packs — landed in VTI
`verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1512` (`feat(tsp)!: adopt Rev 3`, merged
2026-09-16); the VTA answers inbound relationship invites as of
`verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1525`. So this branch is safe to merge without
dropping the wallet's outbound TSP to REST at the receiver.

Before this, the wallet's Rev-3 frames were unreadable by a VTA still on
affinidi-tsp 0.1.x, so the TSP channel silently fell through to REST
(`tsp-channel.ts` — "a VTA still on affinidi-tsp 0.1.x cannot read what we
send; that is the cutover, not a bug"). With the VTA now reading Rev 3, TSP to
the VTA completes end-to-end.

## Design (per CLAUDE.md's TSP Rev 2 exception)

- **We pack Rev 3 unconditionally.** There is no dual-accept *arm*, no
  `if (rev === 2)` branch on the pack path, and no negotiation — an outbound
  message has nothing to read, so nothing to negotiate.
- **Rev 2 is a frozen, decode-only codec** in its own directory
  (`packages/tsp-js/src/rev2/reader.ts`), reached by dispatching on the version
  marker (`revision.ts` → `peekRevision`, reads ≤9 bytes, touches no key). It
  exists because TSP is a ToIP spec with implementations nobody here controls
  (the reference `tsp_sdk` shipped Rev 3 in 0.10.0 while others are still on
  Rev 2) — **not** for the VTA, which cuts over with us. It is deleted whole,
  with its arm of the dispatcher, the day the last Rev 2 peer is gone.
- **Rev 3 requires relationships before application messages** (§7.2.2), so
  `packInvite`/`unpack` XRFI/XRFA relationship forming was added
  (`tsp-js/src/relationship.ts`, `core/src/vta/tsp-relationship.ts`).

This is the one legitimate exception to this repo's "no compat folds" rule, and
it stays one precisely because a peer we do not control is on the far side of
Rev 2 — for the VTA and the mediator the answer is no, and no second version
arm belongs anywhere else in the tree.

## Scope

- `packages/tsp-js`: Rev 3 codec (`rev3/{control,direct,envelope,fields,payload}.ts`),
  Rev 2 decode-only reader, `revision.ts` dispatcher, `relationship.ts`, CESR
  wire + HPKE additions, spec Appendix A vectors + interop/dispatch tests.
- `packages/core`: `vta/tsp-channel.ts` (Rev 3 pack, dual read), new
  `vta/tsp-relationship.ts`, `vta/index.ts` export, `@openvtc/vti-tsp-js` bumped
  to `^0.3.0`, `tests/tsp.relationship.mjs`.
- `CLAUDE.md`: the TSP Rev 2 exception documented as the sole compat-fold
  carve-out.

## Verification

- `npm run build` — clean; `dist/manager.js` and `dist/background.js` each a
  single chunk (MV3 + admin-guard invariants hold).
- `npm test` — **1,521 pass / 0 fail** (tsp-js 124, core 656, extension 726,
  demo-rp 6, reviewer-demo 9). Includes the real spec Appendix A (YTSP-AAC)
  vectors re-packed byte for byte and the Rev 2/Rev 3 dispatch tests.

## Pre-merge checklist (vti-stack-development-guide §9)

- [x] No new `reqwest::Client::new()` / bare `fetch()`; all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) — N/A to this diff; TSP goes over the existing injected transport.
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) — relationship forming is guarded "at most once at a time".
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6) — inbound persist-before-ack path untouched.
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*) — TSP is CESR/binary; revision dispatched on the wire version marker, errors matched on stable `code` (`E_TSP_REVISION`), not strings (R3.7).
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*) — an unreadable/unrecognised revision throws rather than guessing.
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*)
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1)
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers — the Rev 2 decode-only codec is the documented exception to "no compat folds"; see CLAUDE.md and the design note above.
