title: feat(keys)!: a derived key carries the algorithm it was minted with
body:
**Third of the Phase 2 sequence**, after #1528 (verifiers read a key's declared
type) and #1530 (a template declares which algorithms it wants). This is the
half that mints them.

`DerivedEntityKeys` gains `signing_key_type` / `ka_key_type`, and
`derive_entity_keys_with_preference` mints the first algorithm a template's
`keys` block asks for that this build can produce.

## The defect it closes

Every `save_key_record` call for a signing key passed the algorithm as a literal:

```rust
save_key_record(ks, &vm_ids.signing, &derived.signing_path,
                SdkKeyType::Ed25519,        // ← asserted, not carried
                &derived.signing_pub, ...)
```

Correct only while nothing else could be minted. The moment a template can ask
for ML-DSA, that record names an algorithm the key **is not** — and a later
signing operation reaches for a suite the key cannot work in, failing far from
the place that decided wrongly.

Same shape as the `verificationMethod` mislabelling fixed in #1528, one layer
down: a type asserted where it should have been carried.

The **imported-key path** reads the type from the stored `KeyRecord` rather than
assuming, because for an imported key the record is where the truth about its
algorithm lives — assuming Ed25519 there would mislabel an imported ML-DSA key
at the one moment the system is being *told* what it is.

## A deliberate deviation from the plan

The plan said `DerivedEntityKeys` grows "from two fixed fields to a slot map".
Counting the call sites changed the answer: **the two slots are used in 53
places**, and a map turns every one into a lookup that can fail — while
*removing* a property that is true and worth holding in the type: a DID document
has exactly one signing key and at most one key-agreement key.
`slots["signing"]` returning `Option` is a worse description of reality than a
field that cannot be absent.

What the plan was really asking is that a slot's **algorithm** stop being
implied, which is what the two new fields do. A third slot — two signing keys at
once, for hybrid credentials — has no consumer until Phase 3, and an empty map
now would be a mechanism with no users, which is what this plan criticises
elsewhere about `sign_multi`. The reasoning is recorded on the struct so the
next reader finds it before re-deriving it.

## Preference semantics, and the one that matters

| Case | Behaviour | Why |
|---|---|---|
| first choice unavailable | **skip to the next** | that is what a fallback is for; refusing makes `["mldsa44","ed25519"]` useless on a VTA without PQC support |
| list exhausted | **error naming the list** | never a quiet downgrade to Ed25519 |
| key-agreement slot | no preference, X25519 | the only algorithm that can serve it in a DID document; ML-KEM agreement is TSP's hybrid KEM, not a verification method |

The quiet downgrade is the whole hazard: a deployment meant to be post-quantum
would ship classical keys and nothing would say so.

## Breaking

`DerivedEntityKeys` gains two fields, so struct literals no longer compile — two
in `vta-service`, fixed here.

## Verification

Three tests. The one carrying the weight asserts the recorded type and the
actual key **agree**, and was checked for non-vacuity by making them diverge:

```
signing_key_type says ML-DSA-44 but the key is 34 bytes — the label
and the key have come apart, which is the exact defect this carries
the type to prevent
```

Local workspace/VTC/clippy/fmt run is still in flight as this opens; I will
report it against the CI result rather than instead of it.

## After this

The chain works end to end: a template declares `["mldsa44", "ed25519"]`, the
VTA mints ML-DSA-44, the stored record says so, the document publishes it, and a
verifier reads its type rather than assuming. What remains is the wire shape
(`vta/did-templates/{create,update}/3.0`) and the operator surface.

title: feat(tsp): persist TSP relationship state across restarts
body:
> **Unblocked.** [affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#814](https://github.com/affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs/pull/814) merged and published `affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.26.5` / `affinidi-tsp 0.2.1` (the durable-store types this wiring uses). Lock bumped; `cargo check`/`clippy -p vta-service --features tsp` are clean. Ready for review.

## Why

Rev 3 §7.2.2 has an endpoint **silently drop** application traffic from a VID it holds no relationship with. Every VTA `ATM::new` builds `ATMConfig::builder().build()` with no relationship store, so it gets the SDK's **in-memory default — wiped on restart**. A restarted VTA forgets every TSP peer and drops their traffic until each re-handshakes, with no visible error. That is the failure that started this workstream (a `pnm health` TSP ping timing out against a just-restarted VTA).

## What

Inject a durable `RelationshipStore` backed by an encrypted fjall keyspace:

- **`vta-keyspaces`** — a `relationships` keyspace: added to `ALL`, `EXCLUDED_FROM_BACKUP` (re-establishable and DID-scoped, like `sessions`), and classified `Cascade` for DID deletion (protocol state keyed by the VID, like `cache`/`outbox`). Both census tests pass.
- **`KeyspaceRelationshipKv`** (`messaging/tsp_relationship_store.rs`) — a `RelationshipKv` over one `KeyspaceHandle`. Encryption-at-rest is uniform: the handle is opened via the same `apply_encryption(store.keyspace(..))` as every other keyspace.
- **`build_messaging`** (the long-lived TSP-serving listener) injects `PersistentRelationshipStore` over that adapter via `with_relationship_store`, `#[cfg(feature = "tsp")]`. The keyspace is opened beside `outbox_ks` in `server.rs` and threaded through `MessagingConnect`; both `build_messaging` callers pass it. The short-lived DIDComm handshake `ATM::new` sites keep the ephemeral default deliberately.

## Design

Design note at [`docs/05-design-notes/tsp-relationship-recovery.md`](docs/05-design-notes/tsp-relationship-recovery.md) — D1–D9. The SDK-side cores (D1 durable store, D2 reconcile transition, D3 recovery-aware send, D4 bounded/single-flight/jittered recovery, D5 7-day idle eviction) shipped in #814. This PR is the D1 VTA wiring. Remaining: D6 outbox/timeout runtime + eviction sweep, D7 re-resolve-keys, D8 drop-counter metric, D9 proactive reconcile.

title: feat(did-templates)!: a template declares which algorithms its keys use
body:
**Second of the Phase 2 (PQC DID templates) sequence**, after #1528 taught the
verifiers to read a key's declared type.

`schemaVersion` 2 adds a `keys` block — each slot says what it is for and which
algorithms are acceptable, most preferred first:

```json
"keys": {
  "signing": { "purpose": "signing", "algorithms": ["mldsa44", "ed25519"] },
  "ka":      { "purpose": "keyAgreement", "algorithms": ["x25519"] }
}
```

A **list** rather than one algorithm, because a fleet does not migrate
atomically. That says *mint ML-DSA-44 if this VTA can, otherwise Ed25519* — so
one template serves a VTA with post-quantum support and one without, and stops
being a fallback the day the fleet finishes upgrading.

## The idea it all rests on: v1 *is* v2 with the historical keys block

A `schemaVersion` 1 template has no `keys` block and is not thereby key-less. It
means the pair this stack has always minted — Ed25519 signing, X25519 key
agreement — which is exactly what its `{SIGNING_KEY_MB}` and `{KA_KEY_MB}`
placeholders already refer to.

`DidTemplate::key_slots()` returns that, so **a v1 and a v2 template take one
code path**, and raising `SCHEMA_VERSION_MAX` cannot change how a v1 template
renders. `every_builtin_still_declares_the_historical_key_pair` holds all 11
built-ins to it and fails by name when the implicit default is perturbed.

The slot→placeholder rule is mechanical (`{SLOT_UPPERCASE}_KEY_MB`) and was
chosen so `signing` and `ka` *fall out of it* rather than being special-cased.

## What validation refuses, and why each would otherwise be silent

| Refused | Because |
|---|---|
| a `keys` block on a v1 template | ignoring it means a template asking for ML-DSA gets Ed25519 without complaint — a deployment that believes it is post-quantum and is not |
| an empty algorithm list | "no preference" inherits whatever the implementation defaulted to — same failure, other route |
| an algorithm that cannot serve its purpose | otherwise a well-formed document whose `keyAgreement` entry nothing can use |
| **a declared slot the document never publishes** | the key is minted and not published, so verifiers still see only the classical key while the operator believes otherwise — and a derivation path is burned forever |
| a slot placeholder no slot declares | renders as an unsubstituted literal |

The fourth one **caught this PR's own test fixture**, which is the best argument
for keeping it.

## Breaking

`DidTemplate` gains a field, so a struct literal no longer compiles — one
conformance fixture in `vta-service`, fixed here.

`DidTemplate` is deliberately **not** marked `#[non_exhaustive]`: that would
break every external struct literal permanently to save one in-workspace call
site, and templates are authored as JSON rather than built by hand. The trade
goes the other way from `Inbound` in affinidi-tdk-rs#812, where the type is
constructed in code by several crates.

## Verification

- workspace and VTC suites — clean
- 83 tests in the module, 9 new; clippy `-D warnings` clean; rustfmt clean
- the v1-compatibility test checked for **non-vacuity** by changing the implicit
  default and confirming it fails

## Scope note

The plan had this as one PR with the slot map. It is split: the schema (here)
and the slot map + derivation (next) are independently useful, and the second
touches `DerivedEntityKeys` across **49 call sites in 17 files** — bundling that
with a new wire shape makes neither reviewable.

**Nothing mints a PQC key yet.** A v2 template can declare one and validation
will hold it to the rules, but until the derivation change lands no DID can
carry one — which is the intended order, since it means nothing can be minted
before there is a verifier that reads it correctly.

title: fix(proof): a verification method's key type is read, not assumed
body:
**First of the Phase 2 (PQC DID templates) sequence.** A verifier has to accept
a post-quantum key *before* any template can mint a DID carrying one, so this is
the consumer half and it goes first.

## The defect is mislabelling, not rejection

`TrustTaskVmResolver` ended both resolution paths with:

```rust
Ok(ResolvedKey::new(KeyType::Ed25519, bytes))   // regardless of the document
```

That was never wrong, because every key this stack minted was Ed25519. It stops
being true the moment a DID carries an ML-DSA key — and the resulting failure is
the bad kind:

> The PQC key is **not** rejected. It is extracted successfully and handed to the
> verifier **labelled Ed25519**, so *"this proof uses a suite I must check
> differently"* presents as *"this Ed25519 signature does not verify"*.

That points an investigator at the signature, which is fine, rather than at the
key, which is not. A hardcoded type cannot be wrong in a way anyone notices until
it is wrong in a way nobody can debug.

Note this is **not** what the Phase 2 plan predicted. The plan described "a hard
32-byte assertion that rejects a 1312-byte ML-DSA key with a misleading error" —
accurate for `vtc-service`, wrong for `vta-sdk`, where nothing rejects anything.

## How the type is read

`get_public_key_bytes` cannot answer it: it decodes the multikey and returns the
payload, dropping the prefix that names the algorithm. So `declared_key_type`
reads `publicKeyMultibase` and matches its multicodec prefix against
**`KeyType::multicodec_public()`** — this workspace's single codec table (#1502),
pinned against a named revision of the multicodec registry by
affinidi-tdk-rs#798. A wrong prefix is therefore wrong in exactly one place, and
a test already covers it.

**The match has no wildcard, deliberately.** `#[non_exhaustive]` binds *other*
crates, not the one defining the type, and this module is inside it — so adding a
`KeyType` variant breaks this match on purpose. Whoever adds a key type is made
to say how a verifier should read it, rather than having it fall to a default.
Defaulting is what caused this.

## The VTC half is a message, not a check

`resolve_verifying_key`'s `[u8; 32]` coercion **stays**. That path builds an
Ed25519 `VerifyingKey` and nothing else will do.

What changed is what it says when it fails. `"key is not 32 bytes"` names the
symptom and hides the cause: the realistic way to reach it is a verification
method carrying a post-quantum key (ML-DSA-44 is 1312 bytes, ML-DSA-65 is 1952),
and an operator reading "not 32 bytes" has every reason to suspect a truncated
key and none to suspect the algorithm. It now reports the actual length, names
the likely algorithm, and says which path refused it.

## Verification

- workspace and VTC suites — clean
- `vta-sdk --features client,session,tsp` — 591 tests green (worth noting: the
  module is behind `proof-verify`, which `client` enables; a plain
  `-p vta-sdk --lib` run compiles none of it and proves nothing)
- clippy `-D warnings` clean; rustfmt clean
- the mislabelling test checked for **non-vacuity** by restoring the hardcoded
  type and confirming it fails

## What follows

2. `schemaVersion` 2 — a `keys` block declaring slot, purpose and algorithm;
   slot-driven derivation; `DerivedEntityKeys` becomes a slot map
3. `vta/did-templates/{create,update}/3.0` in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf
4. The VTA accepts 3.0 (server before client)
5. CLI/wizard emits 3.0, plus the two-axis PQC labelling

title: pnm-cli-v0.17.0
body:
### Added

- **backup**: Back up a DIDComm/TSP-only VTA with the chunkedTrustTask algorithm ([#1522](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1522))

* build(deps): trust-tasks-rs 0.21.1, the release carrying the chunked backup specs

  0.21.1 is the first release with `vta/backup/get-chunk/1.0`,
  `put-chunk/1.0`, `initiate-{export,import}/1.1` and
  `finalize-import/1.1` (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#474). A
  dispatched URI the registry has no schema for fails
  `every_served_uri_has_a_published_spec_or_is_tracked_debt`, so the floor
  moves with the tasks that need it.

- **vta-service**: Tune the VTA's rate limits at runtime ([#1519](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1519))

* feat(vta-service)!: tune the VTA's rate limits at runtime

  The per-IP limiters were tower_governor layers built once with the router, so
  changing a quota needed a config edit and a restart — exactly when an operator
  facing 429s can least afford one.

  The limiters are now our own axum middleware over governor's keyed limiter
  (already in the graph via tower_governor, whose spoof-safe client-IP key
  extractors are reused unchanged). The running service reads the four [server]
  quotas from the shared config on every request and swaps in fresh buckets when
  a quota changes; a change resets that limiter's buckets, and a patch that
  leaves a quota alone keeps them. trust_xff stays restart-only. The 429 contract
  is unchanged.

  rate_limit_interval_secs, rate_limit_burst, did_log_rate_limit_interval_secs
  and did_log_rate_limit_burst are registered in the config registry as mutable
  integer keys, applied live and persisted to config.toml: intervals 1-3600,
  bursts 1-10000, super-admin only, through config/patch like every other key.
  Their names come from vta_sdk::rate_limit, which the 429 hints also use.
  pnm and cnm `config update` gain --rate-limit-interval-secs,
  --rate-limit-burst, --did-log-rate-limit-interval-secs and
  --did-log-rate-limit-burst; `config get` shows the keys.

  Adds docs/02-vta/rate-limiting.md and links it from the docs index,
  non-interactive setup and the setup example.



### Fixed

- **cli**: Type rate-limit refusals on the hand-rolled bootstrap and VTC paths ([#1521](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1521))

pnm bootstrap connect, cnm backup, and cnm audit verify build their own error strings from the HTTP status instead of going through the SDK client, so a 429 read as a bare "request failed" — the same class #1511 fixed for the SDK paths. Map 429 to VtaError::RateLimited via rate_limited_from_http (headers captured before the body), so print_cli_error names which service limited, the wait, and how to tune it. On pnm bootstrap connect the limiter runs before the carve-out is touched, so a note says the one-shot first boot is not spent and retry after the wait is safe. The header/attribution parsing is covered by vta-sdk's rate_limit tests; this is the call-site wiring.

title: feat(vta/backup): chunked transfer over Trust Tasks for DIDComm/TSP-only agents
body:
An agent that speaks only DIDComm or TSP cannot be backed up with `vta/backup/*/1.0`. Every descriptor there requires `transportUrl` and `transportToken`, so the only answer such an agent can give is `transportUnavailable` — the spec already says so, under Transport preconditions, and already anticipates "a chunked transfer" as the algorithm that would fix it. This PR specifies that algorithm.

## What it adds

- **`chunkedTrustTask`**, a second value for the family's `algorithm` member. The bundle moves as a sequence of Trust Task documents over the transport that already carries the control-plane tasks. It is defined once, in `vta/backup/initiate-export/1.1` § Chunked transfer, for both directions.
- **`vta/backup/get-chunk/1.0`**: `{bundleId, index}` → `{bundleId, index, digestMultibase, data, expiresAt}`. Client-pulled and non-consuming. The bundle goes away on `complete-export`, `abort` or expiry.
- **`vta/backup/put-chunk/1.0`**: `{bundleId, index, digestMultibase, data}` → `{bundleId, index, stored, remainingCount, expiresAt}`. Idempotent for identical bytes. A mismatched write cannot happen by construction, because the manifest fixes each index's digest before any chunk arrives. Codes: `notFound`, `chunkOutOfRange`, `digestMismatch`, `chunkSizeMismatch`, `terminalState`.
- **`initiate-export/1.1`, `initiate-import/1.1`**: the descriptor is now `oneOf` `StreamDescriptor` (unchanged 1.0 members) or `ChunkedDescriptor` (a `chunks` manifest instead of address and token).
  - Export adds an optional `maxChunkSize` and the code `bundleTooLarge`.
  - Import adds `chunks` to the request (the producer pre-commits every chunk digest) and the codes `invalidManifest` and `chunkSizeUnacceptable`.
- **`finalize-import/1.1`**: accepts chunked bundles.
  - New section "Before the password is used": completeness and whole-bundle integrity are checked before any key derivation.
  - New codes `incompleteUpload` and `bundleDigestMismatch`. `incompleteUpload` has `details.missingIndices`, so a producer can resume without spending a password attempt.
- **`specs/vta/_shared/0.1/backup-transfer.schema.json`**: `BundleDescriptor`, `ChunkManifest` and the chunk primitives. They are shared because four tasks use them.
- Regenerated Rust, TS, Go and Dart bindings.

## Versioning decision

`initiate-export` and `initiate-import` go to **1.1**, as new version folders. 1.0 is left untouched.

- Making `transportUrl`/`transportToken` conditional removes required members from one descriptor shape. SPEC §5.2 classifies that as breaking.
- All five specs are `draft`, and §5.2 permits a breaking change to a draft to be released as a `MINOR` increment.
- It cannot be an in-place edit, because it changes the wire contract and is not editorial.
- The break is narrow in practice. A recipient MUST NOT return a `chunkedTrustTask` descriptor unless the request named that algorithm, so a 1.0 producer never receives one, and a `stream` exchange is wire-identical to 1.0.

`finalize-import` goes to **1.1** as an additive `MINOR`. Its payload schema is unchanged; the new version adds the two codes and the pre-decryption ordering. `complete-export/1.0` and `abort/1.0` are unchanged. Their chunked semantics (`downloaded` means every index was served at least once; `get-chunk`/`put-chunk` are refused after either) are stated in the new specs.

The algorithm value is spelled `chunkedTrustTask`, not `chunked-trust-task`, per SPEC §4.10: enumerated values a spec defines are lowerCamelCase.

## The chunk-size bound (normative)

`chunkSize` ≤ **262144 bytes (256 KiB)**, ≥ 16384. `chunkCount` ≤ 4096, which caps a bundle at 1 GiB. The ceiling is derived from a 1 MiB mediator per-message limit, which applies to DIDComm and TSP alike:

| Step | Size |
|---|---|
| Full chunk, raw | 262144 bytes |
| `data`, base64url without padding | 349526 characters |
| Plus framework members and proof | < 353622 bytes |
| DIDComm authcrypt (×4⁄3) | < 471496 bytes |
| Mediator forward wrapper (×4⁄3) | < 628662 bytes |
| A second nested forward (×4⁄3) | < 838216 bytes, over 20% under 1 MiB |

A 524288-byte chunk already exceeds 1 MiB after a single forward wrapper. TSP overhead is additive per hop, so the DIDComm bound covers it. The manifest's 4096 digests (~200 KiB) fit in one message under the same reasoning.

## Design points worth reviewing

- **Pulled, not pushed.** Mediators hold undelivered messages in bounded, expiring per-DID queues, and a transport "send OK" is not delivery. On export the producer asks for each index; on import every write is answered, and a chunk counts as held only once acknowledged. Resuming means re-requesting the indices you don't have. There is no cursor and no resume token.
- **Sender authentication replaces the bearer token.** Chunk tasks are admitted by the transport-authenticated sender, compared against the bundle's recorded creator. There is no credential to leak, and an in-band `issuer` inconsistent with the transport identity is refused.
- **Ownership conflation.** Consistent with the family, an unknown bundle, the wrong kind, the wrong algorithm and not-yours are all `notFound`.
- **Per-requester rate limits.** Per-IP limiting in front of an HTTPS endpoint doesn't reach a mediated task. Recipients SHOULD bound chunk tasks per authenticated sender and per bundle, answering `unavailable` with `retryAfter`.
- **Expiry.** A recipient MAY slide `expiresAt` on chunk activity, never past a ceiling fixed when the bundle was minted. Every chunk response reports the current value.
- **Digests.** Per-chunk digests are `DigestMultibase` (framework 0.3), compared as decoded multihash bytes, with sha2-256 mandatory to implement. The whole-bundle `expectedSha256` keeps its 1.0 hex form, because it is an unchanged member and re-encoding it would break stream producers.
- **Proofs.** `get-chunk`'s response proof is REQUIRED: the build requires it for `discloses: secret`, and it attributes each release to the agent. `put-chunk`'s response proof is RECOMMENDED.

## Checks run locally

- `npm run validate` and `npm run build` (447 specs; with `TT_STRICT_SECURITY_PRIVACY=1` too)
- `npm run check-bindings`: TS, Rust, Go and Dart all agree
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all`, `npm run build-{ts,go,dart}-bindings`: output committed
- `cargo test --workspace --all-targets` (868 passed), `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features validate --all-targets` (998 passed, including the new conformance and invalid-example tests), `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- trust-tasks-ts: `tsc --noEmit`, `npm test`, `npm run smoke`; trust-tasks-go: `go build/vet/test ./...`; trust-tasks-dart: `dart analyze --fatal-infos`, `dart test`

## Motivation

The VTI implementation refuses the descriptor pattern on DIDComm/TSP clients today, and `--use-rest-legacy` on those clients sends a whole backup through one mediator message, which a 1 MiB limit rejects. VTI will implement this algorithm once it is merged and released in `trust-tasks-rs`; the VTI-side fixes that don't depend on it are in OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1516.

title: feat(go-didcomm)!: make DIDComm authcrypt interoperate with the Rust/Dart bindings
body:
The Go DIDComm binding's rolled-our-own ECDH-1PU authcrypt was spec-shaped but **did not actually interoperate** with `affinidi-messaging-didcomm` — the library the Rust and Dart Trust Tasks DIDComm bindings are built on. I read affinidi's source to find why, and fixed it.

## The two mismatches (both fixed)
1. **ECDH-1PU is tag-in-KDF.** DIDComm authcrypt (draft-madden §2.3) encrypts the content **first**, then derives the key-wrapping KEK with the content-encryption tag fed to the Concat KDF as a length-prefixed `SuppPrivInfo`. The binding derived the KEK *without* the tag and wrapped before encrypting.
2. **`apv`** is `base64url(SHA-256(sorted recipient kids joined by "."))`, not the raw recipient kid. (`apu = base64url(skid)` already matched.)

`aries-askar`, `didcomm-python`, `didcomm-rust` and `affinidi` all implement the tag-in-KDF derivation — it is the de-facto DIDComm v2 definition. A plain Concat KDF with `apv = rawKid` (what `v0.1.0` did) does not interoperate.

## Interop now proven, both directions
- **affinidi → Go**: `interop_test.go` unpacks a JWE packed by affinidi with fixed keys (`testdata/authcrypt-interop.fixture.json`), recovers the sender + plaintext, and runs the full §7.2 consumer pipeline.
- **Go → affinidi**: a companion Rust test lands in a follow-up PR — `trust-tasks-didcomm/tests/interop.rs` unpacks a Go-packed JWE with affinidi. (Verified locally: affinidi authenticates the sender and recovers the plaintext.)

The fixtures and regeneration harnesses are documented in `testdata/README.md`.

## Breaking
This changes the wire format, so it's **breaking**: the release automation will take `trust-tasks-go/didcomm` from `v0.1.0` to `v0.2.0`. (v0.1.0 never interoperated with anything, so there is no real compatibility to preserve.) Existing round-trip + negative tests still pass; the RFC 3394 key-wrap vector is unchanged; gofmt clean.

The companion Rust test is split into its own PR so this breaking `!` marker touches only the Go module and doesn't over-bump `trust-tasks-didcomm`.

title: feat(go-release): release trust-tasks-go/proof and /didcomm on their own tags
body:
Makes the two nested Go modules — `trust-tasks-go/proof` and `trust-tasks-go/didcomm` — **first-class releases** on their own `trust-tasks-go/<name>/vX.Y.Z` tags, independent of the core. (`tsp` stays unreleased — it's blocked on the unpublished `affinidi-tsp-go`.)

## What
- **A `version.go` per module** (`const Version = "0.1.0"`) — the manifest surrogate `publish-go` reads, exactly as the core's `trusttasks/version.go` does — plus a `CHANGELOG.md`.
- **`publish-go` → matrix** over core/proof/didcomm. Each leg reads its own `version.go`, and — because **a Go tag is a permanent, irretractable publication** (proxy.golang.org caches it forever) — builds/vets/tests the module *before* tagging.
- **`release-go-pr` → matrix**, and `release-go-pr.sh` now takes the module as an argument (a `case`, like `release-ts-pr.sh` / `release-dart-pr.sh`), each with its own version file, release branch, tag prefix and watch set.
- **The core's watch set now EXCLUDES the nested modules**, so a change under `trust-tasks-go/proof` releases proof, not the core.

## Verified in a sandbox
Ran `release-go-pr.sh` against a shared clone with fake `gh`/`git-cliff`: proof no-ops when unchanged, proposes 0.1.1 on a proof change, a **proof-only change does not trigger a core release** (exclusion works), a core change still bumps the core, and the didcomm arm resolves. `bash -n` and YAML parse clean; nested modules build/vet/test with `version.go`; gofmt clean.

## On merge
Go is self-bootstrapping (no manual first publish): `publish-go` tags `trust-tasks-go/proof/v0.1.0` and `trust-tasks-go/didcomm/v0.1.0` (core 0.1.5 already tagged → skipped), each after a green build/test, and the `release-go-pr` legs find nothing to release. Then `go get github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/trust-tasks-go/proof@v0.1.0` resolves a real version instead of a pseudo-version.

Documented in `CLAUDE.md` and `RELEASING.md`.

title: fix(vta-sdk): a TSP client forms the relationship it cannot send without
body:
`VtaClient::connect_tsp` opened a `TspSession` and **never formed the §7.2.2
relationship**, so a VTA on Rev 3 dropped every Trust Task the client sent.
§7.2.2 says *drop*, not refuse — so the symptom was a client that timed out with
nothing in any log on either side.

Broken on `main` since #1512 turned gating on. Found by a parallel session
working the rate-limiting workstream; verified independently here.

The relationship is a precondition of all traffic rather than a courtesy, and
the client cannot function without it, so it is formed in the constructors —
`connect_tsp`, `connect_tsp_on`, `connect_didcomm_with_tsp` — rather than
exposed as a step every caller must remember. `relate_trust_task_leg` covers
both dual-leg shapes: `Multiplexed` relates on the DIDComm session's own socket,
`Separate` on its own `TspSession`, and a DIDComm-only client does nothing,
because authcrypt carries its own sender authentication and has no relationship
concept.

## The part that nearly shipped broken

The obvious fix — `session.relate(vta_did).await?` in each constructor — is
wrong, and wrong in a way testing would not have shown.

`SendInvite` is a valid transition **only** from `RelationshipState::None`:

```rust
(RelationshipState::None, RelationshipEvent::SendInvite) => Ok(Pending),
...
(state, event) => Err(InvalidTransition { state, event }),
```

So an unconditional invite is an `InvalidTransition` for a peer already related.
That is invisible with the SDK's **default** relationship store, which is
ephemeral and in-memory: a fresh ATM per connect always starts at `None`, every
invite is the first one, and the unconditional version looks correct. A consumer
that configures a durable store via `ATMConfigBuilder::with_relationship_store`
reconnects into `Pending` or `Bidirectional` — and would have had its connect
start failing where it previously worked.

A silent-drop bug traded for a connect-time failure, and **only for the
deployments careful enough to persist their relationships.**

So `relate` is idempotent, in all three impls (`TspSession`, `TspPingSession`,
`DIDCommSession::relate_tsp`). The check is a state read rather than a caught-
and-inspected error, so it does not depend on the text of an
`InvalidTransition`.

## Two tests, deliberately at different levels

**`relate_skips_the_invite_exactly_when_sending_one_would_be_invalid`** pins the
*correspondence* the idempotency rests on: `admits_application_message()` is true
for exactly the states where `SendInvite` is illegal. Those two live in a
different crate, and if they diverge `relate` becomes wrong in one direction or
the other — re-inviting a peer it holds, or skipping a relationship it needed.
The second presents as an unexplained §7.2.2 drop, which is the failure mode
this whole area keeps producing. Costs no mediator and no socket.

**`connecting_twice_on_one_hub_does_not_re_invite`** is the hermetic regression
guard. Every identity on one `SessionHub` shares its ATM and therefore its
relationship store, so a second connect reaches the state a durable store would
restore — without needing one.

Reverting the fix fails it with the real error:

```
invalid transition: SendInvite in state Pending
```

…while `connect_tsp_relates_without_being_asked` beside it **still passes**,
because it connects once against a fresh ATM. That contrast is the point:
ordinary testing would not have caught this.

## Verification

- workspace suite — clean
- `vta-sdk --features tsp,session` — 588 tests green (worth noting: with only
  `--features tsp` it is 354 and the entire `session` module is not compiled, so
  that invocation proves nothing about this change)
- clippy `-D warnings` — clean; rustfmt — clean
- both new tests checked for non-vacuity by reverting the fix

## Follow-up coverage, not in this PR

A parallel session scoped a fuller hermetic `VtaClient`-over-TSP suite that
becomes writable now this lands: a real Trust Task round-trip through
`connect_tsp` asserting on the **received reply** (never a send `Ok`, per R1.1),
an unauthorized client confirming the named `permissionDenied` survives up
through the `VtaClient` dispatch path, and a `MockVta`-backed dual-leg test
(today's `tsp_dual_leg.rs` uses a scripted responder, not a real VTA).

start failing — a silent-drop bug traded for a connect-time failure, and only
for the deployments careful enough to persist their relationships.

So `relate` is idempotent, in all three impls (`TspSession`, `TspPingSession`,
`DIDCommSession::relate_tsp`). The check is a state read, not a caught-and-
inspected error, so it does not depend on the text of an `InvalidTransition`.

## Two tests, deliberately at different levels

`relate_skips_the_invite_exactly_when_sending_one_would_be_invalid` pins the
*correspondence* the idempotency rests on — `admits_application_message()` is
true for exactly the states where `SendInvite` is illegal. Those two live in a
different crate, and if they ever diverge `relate` becomes wrong in one
direction or the other: re-inviting a peer it holds, or skipping a relationship
it needed. The second presents as an unexplained §7.2.2 drop. No mediator.

`connecting_twice_on_one_hub_does_not_re_invite` is the hermetic regression
guard. Every identity on one `SessionHub` shares its ATM and therefore its
relationship store, so a second connect reaches the state a durable store would
restore — without needing one. Reverting the fix fails it with the real error,
`invalid transition: SendInvite in state Pending`, while the single-connect test
beside it still passes. That contrast is the point: ordinary testing would not
have caught this.

Verified: workspace suite clean; `vta-sdk --features tsp,session` 588 tests
green; clippy clean under `-D warnings`; rustfmt clean.

title: feat(dart-capability-client): capability wire client for Dart (trust_tasks_capability_client)
body:
The Dart port of the Rust `trust-tasks-capability-client` crate — the last of the four capability wire clients, **completing it across Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart**.

## What
Pure wire logic — **no crypto, no transport** — for the capability Trust Task families:
- **Builders**: `buildListDocument`, `buildToggleDocument` (enable/disable), `buildGitTrustGrant`, `buildGitTrustRevoke`, `buildDocument`. Each mints a fresh `id` + `issuedAt`.
- **Retries vs. new attempts**: `newAttempt(previous)` re-stamps under a fresh `id` and clears `proof` — a SPEC §8.4 *new attempt*, distinct from a bit-for-bit retry the consumer's §7.2 item-11 record absorbs.
- **Replies**: `classifyGitTrustReply` and `parseCapabilityReply` / `parseEnvelopeReply`. Both **correlate on `threadId` first** (§4.9) and key idempotent success on the SPEC §8.5 **extended error code** (both spellings), never the non-normative free-text `message` (opt-in via `ReplyPolicy`).

`WriteOutcome` and `CapabilityReply` are **sealed** hierarchies, so a `switch` is exhaustive — matching the core's style. Reuses the core's `slugFromTypeUri`. Depends only on `trust_tasks`.

## Plumbing
- Added to the `dart.yml` `packages` job (analyze + format + **15 tests**, sdk 3.4 + stable).
- Documented in `CLAUDE.md` and `RELEASING.md`.

Like `trust_tasks_tsp`, it is **tested-but-unreleased** — `check-dart-packages` permits this. Its first pub.dev publish is manual; unlike `tsp` nothing blocks it (it depends only on the published `trust_tasks`). Adding the five release entries + flipping the website matrix cell is a clean follow-up after that manual publish.

title: feat(tsp): answer an inbound relationship request, instead of recording it and going quiet
body:
**The last functional piece of Rev 3.** `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.26.4 surfaces
a TSP relationship control message as `InboundKind::RelationshipControl` instead
of dropping it after recording, so `handle_tsp` can answer one. Until now a VTA
recorded an invite and went quiet — traffic flowed, but the peer never learned
whether it had a relationship.

A relationship request is not traffic and must not reach the Trust Task spine:
it carries no envelope, so dispatching it would answer a perfectly valid control
message with *"this is not a Trust Task envelope"*.

## The ACL gate is NOT here — and that was settled by building it here first

The Rev 3 plan recorded this as the open question, and the first implementation
put the gate on the invite: a sender with no ACL entry got an explicit
`cancel_relationship` (XRFD) rather than §7.2.2's prescribed silent drop. The
justification was diagnosability — a silent endpoint is indistinguishable from a
broken transport, so refusing explicitly turns silence into an answer.

**Building it showed the argument runs the other way.** A peer sends its invite
and its first Trust Task together, which §3.6 expressly permits:

```
client: invite + trust task
VTA:    refuse relationship (XRFD)
        trust task dropped — no relationship (§7.2.2)

peer's application layer: silence
```

The `XRFD` is a *control* message a client's application never sees, so the gate
produced exactly the silence it existed to prevent.

`tsp_vta_trust_task::an_unauthorized_sender_is_refused_over_tsp_not_met_with_silence`
caught it. That test predates this PR, encodes the right property, and **passes
here unmodified** — what moved is the implementation, not the assertion.

So the relationship is formed with any sender TSP has authenticated, and the ACL
stays the only gate, at the Trust Task layer where it already lives:

```
client: invite + trust task
VTA:    accept relationship (XRFA)
        dispatch task -> ACL denies
        reply: permissionDenied envelope

peer sees: a named, actionable error at the layer it asked at
```

This costs nothing. A relationship grants no authority on its own, every task
behind it is still checked, and the sender VID is cryptographically proven by
`unpack`, so there is no enumeration exposure. It is the explicit refusal the
decision asked for, at the layer that can express it.

## Shape

`decide_control(request, reply_expected) -> ControlDecision` is a pure function —
no keyspace, no socket, no `AppState` — so the policy is tested without a
mediator. A decision buried in an `if` beside two `await`s is one nobody reviews.

| Request | Action |
|---|---|
| Invite | accept (`XRFA`) |
| Accept | nothing — answering an accept starts a loop |
| Cancel | answer only when `reply_expected` (§7.3) |
| unknown | record, say nothing |

Two naming/design notes:

- **`ControlDecision::Cancel` is named for the wire action, not the intent.** It
  serves the §7.3 courtesy reply as well as a refusal; `Refuse` would make the
  first read as hostility.
- **The catch-all is deliberate.** `RelationshipRequest` is `#[non_exhaustive]`,
  and answering a request whose meaning this build does not know is how an
  endpoint agrees to something it cannot describe. The transport has already
  recorded whatever state change the message implied.

`reply_expected` is the transport's reading of the §7.3 condition and is
deliberately not re-derived here.

## Dependencies

`affinidi-messaging-core` 0.1.8, `-sdk` 0.26.4, `-delivery` 0.1.15 — the release
that carries `InboundKind` (affinidi-tdk-rs#812) and the unwound `vta-sdk` cycle
(#811). Zero duplicate `affinidi-*` or `trust-tasks*` entries in the lockfile.

## Verification

- workspace, VTC, and `vta-service --features tsp` suites — clean
- clippy `-D warnings` **both with and without `tsp`** (the module is behind that
  feature, so a default-feature run compiles none of it and proves nothing)
- rustfmt clean; lockfile self-pin and workspace-version guards clean
- the refusal test checked for **non-vacuity** by reverting it to a drop and
  confirming it fails

## Known, and being fixed separately

`VtaClient::connect_tsp` never relates, so `VtaClient` over TSP has been broken
since #1512 turned on gating. Found by a parallel session; it is a `vta-sdk`
change and gets its own PR, including an idempotency fix — `SendInvite` is only
a valid transition from `None`, so an unconditional relate would fail on
reconnect for any consumer with a persistent relationship store.

title: fix(vta-service): box handlers at the dispatch seam so debug builds don't overflow
body:
## Root cause

The macro-generated `dispatch_typed` in `vta-service/src/trust_tasks/mod.rs`
awaited every Trust-Task handler **inline** in its `match` arms:

```rust
$($uri)|+ => $handler(state, auth, doc).await,
```

An async fn's future is sized to its largest live state, and a `match` future
to its largest arm. Awaiting handlers inline meant the single `dispatch_typed`
future — and the enclosing `dispatch_trust_task_core`, which both the DIDComm
(`messaging/router.rs`) and TSP (`messaging/tsp_inbound.rs`) inbound paths call —
was materialized on the stack sized to the heaviest handler's future, and grew
every time a heavy arm was added. In a **debug** build (no frame optimization)
the first Trust Task overflowed the worker-thread stack, which reads as — but is
not — infinite recursion.

This had forced three workarounds:
- #1522 hand-boxed the heavy awaits inside the new backup 1.1 handlers.
- The `op!` macro in `services.rs` boxed each per-operation future.
- The two heaviest `mock_vta` integration tests spawned a 32 MiB thread.

## The fix

Box each handler **at the dispatch seam**, so every arm is a pointer's worth of
future and the match frame stays flat regardless of handler size:

```rust
$($uri)|+ => Box::pin($handler(state, auth, doc)).await,
```

The boxed future is a concrete `Pin<Box<_>>`, so it stays `Send` (inbound tasks
are spawned). A load-bearing comment at the seam explains why, so nobody
"simplifies" it away. The macro's other expansions (`class_for`,
`dispatched_uris`) don't await handlers and are unchanged.

## Workarounds removed

- **backup.rs**: the four #1522 per-handler `Box::pin`s (initiate-export/1.1
  and initiate-import/1.1 delegating to their 1.0 handlers, the finalize-import
  delegation, and the `chunked::initiate_export` await). Redundant once the seam
  boxes each handler.
- **services.rs `op!`**: simplified from `Box::pin($call).await` to plain
  `$call.await`; doc comment updated to record the seam fix.
- **mock_vta.rs**: both heavy tests (`webvh_family_response_shapes`,
  `services_write_paths_against_a_hosted_vta_did`) dropped their hand-spawned
  32 MiB threads and now run as ordinary `#[tokio::test]`s on the default
  libtest stack (~2 MiB, current-thread runtime — the in-process axum server
  runs on the same thread). They are the regression guards: unbox the seam and
  they overflow again.

`room_owner.rs`'s handler-internal box is **kept** (comment corrected): it is the
same now-redundant pattern, but no default-stack test drives the `anchor`
handler, so it stays as defense-in-depth rather than being removed untested.
The pre-existing `Box::pin(dispatch_trust_task_validated(..))` at the validated
seam is also kept.

## Test that guards it

`heavy_trust_task_dispatches_on_default_stack` (new, `#[tokio::test]`) drives
`initiate-export/1.1` with `algorithm: chunkedTrustTask` — which runs a full
state export inline, the largest handler future #1522 hand-boxed — through the
full inbound dispatch spine on the default stack, and asserts the chunked
descriptor comes back. A stack overflow aborts the process, so this fails hard
on a regression.

title: feat(ts-capability-client): capability wire client for TypeScript (@openvtc/trust-tasks-capability-client)
body:
The TypeScript port of the Rust `trust-tasks-capability-client` crate — the first of the three capability wire clients (TS/Go/Dart) on the backlog.

## What
Pure wire logic — **no crypto, no transport** — for the capability Trust Task families:
- **Builders**: `buildListDocument`, `buildToggleDocument` (enable/disable), `buildGitTrustGrant`, `buildGitTrustRevoke`, and `buildDocument` under them. Each mints a fresh `id` + `issuedAt`.
- **Retries vs. new attempts**: `newAttempt(previous)` re-stamps a built document under a fresh `id` and clears `proof` — a SPEC §8.4 *new attempt*, distinct from a bit-for-bit retry the consumer's §7.2 item-11 record absorbs. Reusing an `id` with altered content is `idConflict`.
- **Replies**: `classifyGitTrustReply` → `success` / `idempotentSuccess` / `rejected`, and `parseCapabilityReply` / `parseEnvelopeReply` → `listing` / `toggled` / `rejected`. Both **correlate on `threadId` first** (§4.9) and key idempotent success on the SPEC §8.5 **extended error code**, never the non-normative free-text `message` (the free-text path is opt-in via `ReplyPolicy`).

Type URI slug/response-variant is computed from the string (the version is always the final path segment), so there's no parser dependency. **Zero runtime deps** beyond `@openvtc/trust-tasks`; sign built documents with `@openvtc/trust-tasks-proof`.

## Plumbing
- Added to the `ts.yml` `packages` test matrix (npm ci → build → typecheck → test); **17 tests** cover builders, `newAttempt`, correlation gating, both idempotent-code spellings, the deprecated free-text policy, listing/toggle/error parsing, and envelope parsing.
- Documented in `CLAUDE.md` and `RELEASING.md`.

Following the ts-proof/ts-tsp precedent, **the first npm publish is manual** (trusted publishing can't bootstrap a package that doesn't exist) — so `publish.yml` wiring, the anchor seed tag, and the website capability-matrix flip are a follow-up after that manual publish, not part of this PR (avoids a red OIDC leg on the next main push). RELEASING.md lists the one-time steps.

Go and Dart ports are the remaining backlog items.

title: ZKP working draft: trust-graph implementation guide and construction catalogue
body:
> **Status (15 September 2026):** ready for review. Two commits — the draft as opened on 8 September and a second commit on 14 September (`e1afc3f`) folding the review since: fifteen construction records (nine primitive, six composed), Implementation Guide steps 4–5, integration, Research and Book notes, Appendix E review-notes index. Round 1 (shape review) runs to 22 September on the task-force threads [#23](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-zkp-tf/discussions/23) (the 8 September anchor) and [#27](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-zkp-tf/discussions/27) (15 September, for the working-group call). The description below is as opened; the counts it gives are the 8 September ones.

This draft introduces an implementation-oriented ZKP specification for decentralized trust graphs. It starts with the outcome an application needs—membership eligibility, a private relationship, selective disclosure, common control, accepted status or delegated authority—and connects it to credential inputs, constructions, verifier checks and reproducible evidence. Personhood and liveness are important use cases and sources, rather than the specification's entire scope.

The contribution contains twelve construction records, the ADR-001 crosswalk, four proving-system entries and portable conformance generation. Records remain informative at their existing evidence states. ADR-001 is the flagship community-anchored use case; a credential-bound membership presentation is proposed as the first implementation milestone supporting it. Existing component tests do not establish the complete composition.

The reading order now leads with an implementation guide and trust-graph lifecycle. Detailed cryptographic background follows the operational material. The book explains construction fit and paper relationships from the same technical records. Explicit WG review notes mark proposals, open technical questions and evidence requests; they do not imply ratification.

The draft clarifies private witness custody, credential authenticity, offline voucher linkage, distinct members versus distinct people, root authority, transcript encoding and the separation of proof verification, policy acceptance and action completion. It documents the lab's domain-separated, length-prefixed transcript hash and BN254 conversion, with a comparison vector. Strict transcript types and semantic checks remain proposed implementation work, rather than claims about the current lab validator.

Near the end, an informative maintenance note describes how surveys of related DTG, Trust over IP, VTC and First Person Project work may produce traceable updates. An agent handoff lists twelve verification tasks with use-case fit, dependencies and expected evidence. The companion research/verifier-worklist.json makes that queue reusable.

Validation performed locally: all 17 conformance files validate; generated sections and terms match regeneration; Spec-Up-T renders with its two configured external glossary sources; the framed/plain transcript comparison digests were separately reproduced. Existing record states and histories were preserved. These checks are not a circuit audit or independent reproduction of the complete proof.

Review requested: general scope and first milestone; credential/witness contracts; canonical wire profile; construction comparisons; book organization; and the evidence required for future recommendations or adoption.

The author’s CC BY 4.0 grant for the adapted background is recorded in Appendix A. The renderer’s Windows branch-metadata fallback remains a known local rendering limitation. The draft also leaves exact cross-repository implementation baselines and several wire-profile decisions open. No construction or proving system is proposed as adopted merely by opening this PR.

title: feat(go-didcomm): DIDComm v2.1 transport binding for Go (trust-tasks-go/didcomm)
body:
The `bindings/didcomm/0.2` binding for Go — the third transport binding on the Go side, rolled on the standard library.

## Why roll our own
`aries-framework-go` (the originally-suggested library) is a poor fit: its DIDComm packer is a low-level JWE primitive — `Pack(contentType, payload, senderID, recipientsPubKeys)` on raw key bytes, needing a full KMS/Crypto/Storage/VDR provider — that doesn't build or parse the v2 message envelope or surface a verified `sender_kid`→DID, and the framework is **archived** (last release 2023). Rolling our own (the call made for `proof` and TSP too) keeps the four bindings structurally aligned and PQC-extensible.

## What
- **DIDComm v2.1 authcrypt**: ECDH-1PU key agreement + `A256KW` key wrapping + `A256CBC-HS512`, over X25519 — the DIDComm v2 default profile. On Go's stdlib `crypto/ecdh`; Concat KDF, RFC 3394 key-wrap and RFC 7518 content encryption are in-module.
- **Zero third-party dependencies** (`go.sum` references only the core), same basis as `trust-tasks-go/proof`. A separate nested module so the core stays dependency-free.
- **Key-based like `tsp`**: the consumer holds the recipient's X25519 private key and takes a `ResolveSender(did) → *PeerKey` callback — no DID resolution.

## Security shape
- The verified **`skid` is authenticated by the ECDH-1PU static secret** — the recipient derives the KEK using the sender key resolved *from* `skid`, so a forged `skid` fails the key unwrap. It becomes the §4.8.1 transport-authenticated sender.
- **anoncrypt and plaintext are rejected** — no authenticated sender to route a reply to (binding §2/§4).
- The consumer keeps the **§7.2 item-11 duplicate-execution record on by default** (DIDComm is store-and-forward and gives no replay protection, binding §6), and routes a **thread-header disagreement as `malformedRequest`** to the authenticated sender (binding §3.1), never `identityMismatch`.

## Tests (23, `go test -race`, go 1.22 + stable)
RFC 3394 key-wrap **vector reproduced exactly**; A256CBC-HS512 round-trip; authcrypt round-trip + rejection of wrong-recipient, **forged-sender**, tampered-ciphertext and anoncrypt-shape; consumer round-trip, duplicate absorption, idConflict, identityMismatch (routed to sender), expiry, thread-mismatch, proof-without-verifier, fire-and-forget.

## Plumbing
- `didcomm` job in `go.yml` (core `./...` excludes a nested module); Go added to the `didcomm/0.2` binding registry and the capability matrix; documented in `CLAUDE.md`.

**Not release-wired yet**, and a shared cross-library authcrypt fixture with the Rust/Dart DIDComm bindings is a documented follow-up — the profile is spec-standard and the primitives are vector-pinned, but byte-for-byte interop isn't yet asserted the way the sealed TSP/proof envelopes are.

`npm run build` green (library + binding registry guards), gofmt clean, core module untouched.

title: feat(go-proof): Data Integrity proofs for Go (trust-tasks-go/proof)
body:
A W3C Data Integrity `ProofVerifier` and signer for the core module's proof seam — the fourth roll-our-own proof backend, alongside Rust, TypeScript and Dart.

## What
- **`eddsa-jcs-2022`** (Ed25519) and **`ecdsa-jcs-2019`** (P-256 / P-384), over RFC 8785 JCS, **`did:key` only** — no network, no resolver.
- **A separate nested module** (`trust-tasks-go/proof`) like `tsp`, so the core stays dependency-free — but with **no third-party code at all**: the cryptosuites are on `crypto/ed25519`/`crypto/ecdsa`/SHA-2, and the JCS canonicaliser + base58btc codec are written in-module. Its only requirement is the core, at the published `v0.1.2` (no `replace`, exactly as `tsp`).

## Interop
A test **reproduces the shared `eddsa-jcs-2022` fixture's `proofValue` byte for byte** (Ed25519 is deterministic; fixture seed `[7; 32]`), so a document signed by any of the four backends verifies with the others. It deliberately does **not** use the core's `CanonicalJSON` — that is only equality-equivalent to JCS and warns against exactly this use; `proof/jcs.go` is a real JCS (UTF-16 key ordering, ECMAScript number form).

## Safety
The verifier binds the proof to the in-band `issuer` and returns a typed `*proof.Error` whose `Kind` stays in the logs — every failure is `proofInvalid` on the wire (SPEC §10.4).

## Plumbing
- New `proof` job in `go.yml` (the core `./...` jobs exclude a nested module), on the `go 1.22` floor; `gofmt`, `vet`, `test -race`.
- Implementations capability matrix: Go `proof` cell flipped to shipped (`go get` of the nested module works via the proxy, same basis as the Go `tsp` cell).
- `CLAUDE.md` documents the module.

**Not wired into a release yet** — unlike `tsp` there is no blocker (no unpublished dependency), so a `publish-go`-style tag job for `trust-tasks-go/proof/vX.Y.Z` is a clean follow-up.

Local: `go test -race ./...` green (13 tests incl. the byte-for-byte interop and per-curve round-trips), gofmt clean, `npm run build` green (library-registry guard passes).

title: chore(ci): generalise the TS npm release to a package matrix
body:
Turns the single-package TS npm release into a package matrix, so `@openvtc/trust-tasks-proof` (#489) and `@openvtc/trust-tasks-tsp` (#490) publish the way the core `@openvtc/trust-tasks` does — mirroring the Dart `tag-dart`/`release-dart-pr` matrices.

## What changed
- **`publish-npm`** → matrix over the three packages (`@openvtc/trust-tasks`, `-proof`, `-tsp`), each keyed on its directory and `trust-tasks-ts[-proof|-tsp]-v` tag prefix. Still skips a version already on npm, so a feature merge stays a no-op.
- **`release-ts-pr`** → matrix over the same three; `needs: publish-npm` (matrix-needs-matrix, so every publish leg finishes before any Release-PR leg).
- **`release-ts-pr.sh`** takes the package name and derives its dir, release branch, tag prefix and watch set via a `case` — the exact shape of `release-dart-pr.sh`. Unknown package errors.

## Verified in a sandbox clone
- `@openvtc/trust-tasks-proof` → bumps `0.1.0 → 0.1.1` on `release-ts-proof`, tags `trust-tasks-ts-proof-v0.1.1`, watches only its own dir, PR body correct.
- `@openvtc/trust-tasks` → unchanged (nothing to release).
- an unknown package → errors.

## Operational note (RELEASING.md)
The first publish of each new package stays **manual** — npm trusted publishing can't create a package that doesn't exist (same as pub.dev). Per new package: `npm publish --access public` once, configure the Trusted Publisher (repo + `publish.yml`), and seed the `<prefix>-v<version>` anchor tag. title: feat(ts-tsp): TSP transport binding for TypeScript (@openvtc/trust-tasks-tsp)
body:
Adds **`@openvtc/trust-tasks-tsp`**, the TypeScript TSP transport binding, on **`@openvtc/vti-tsp-js`** — the pure-TypeScript TSP the VTA browser plugin uses (browser/Node/RN, no WASM). The fourth TSP binding, alongside Rust, Dart and Go; all seal the same envelope object.

## API
- **`packTrustTask(document, {senderVid, receiverVid, keys})`** seals a Direct TSP message (HPKE-Auth + signature); the payload is `{"type": ENVELOPE_TYPE, "document": …}`.
- **`unpackTrustTask(wire, {recipientVid, keys})`** opens it, requires `direct` carriage, checks the envelope type, and returns the document plus the authenticated sender. Failures throw `TspEnvelopeError` (`notForThisReceiver`, `notFinalRecipient`, `wrongEnvelopeType`, `invalidBody`) — none answerable, since TSP has no anonymous sender (§4).
- **`TspConsumer`** is the guarded inbound path: `receive` reads the named sender (`advertisedSender`), checks the allowlist, resolves the sender's public keys, opens, then runs `consumeInbound` with the item-11 record and freshness on by default. `packReply` seals the reply back to the authenticated sender.

## The vti-tsp-js model
Unlike affinidi-tsp (Dart/Go via their libs), `vti-tsp-js` is **key-based and does no DID resolution**. So the consumer takes the recipient's raw Ed25519 (signing) and X25519 (decryption) private keys plus a `resolveSender(vid) => {encryptionKey, signingKey}` callback — the Go-style "caller supplies the sender identity" shape. A handler **refuses by returning an `ErrorResponse`**, not by throwing (the TS core's own convention).

## Tests
14, via `node --test`: round trip; the `{type, document}` envelope shape; confidentiality; wrong receiver; tamper; and the consumer — identity omitted and TSP-supplied, reply round trip, re-forward absorbed, `idConflict`, `identityMismatch` sealed back to the sender, allowlist, staleness, proof-without-verifier, fire-and-forget. `ts.yml`'s `packages` matrix now covers both `trust-tasks-ts-proof` and `trust-tasks-ts-tsp`.

## Interop
The sealed `{type, document}` envelope is the same shape the Rust/Dart/Go bindings seal (a test pins the two-key object). Cross-implementation TSP wire interop rests on `vti-tsp-js` being byte-compatible with affinidi-tsp (its own stated guarantee) and the shared TSP Rev 3 vectors.

## Deliberately deferred: npm release matrix
Neither this nor `@openvtc/trust-tasks-proof` (#489) auto-publishes yet. Generalising `publish-npm`/`release-ts-pr` into a package matrix — parameterising `release-ts-pr.sh` the way `release-dart-pr.sh` is — is a **critical-path change I'll do in a dedicated, sandbox-tested follow-up** covering all three TS packages, rather than bundling it into a feature PR. Each package also needs npm trusted-publishing set up on first publish, like every registry here. RELEASING.md and CLAUDE.md note this.

## Follow-ups
The npm release matrix (next); then the website matrix flips (TS TSP + proof) once these publish; and the remaining backlog — Go DIDComm, Go proof, capability wire client.

title: cnm-cli-v0.16.0
body:
### Added

- **vta-service**: Tune the VTA's rate limits at runtime ([#1519](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1519))

* feat(vta-service)!: tune the VTA's rate limits at runtime

  The per-IP limiters were tower_governor layers built once with the router, so
  changing a quota needed a config edit and a restart — exactly when an operator
  facing 429s can least afford one.

  The limiters are now our own axum middleware over governor's keyed limiter
  (already in the graph via tower_governor, whose spoof-safe client-IP key
  extractors are reused unchanged). The running service reads the four [server]
  quotas from the shared config on every request and swaps in fresh buckets when
  a quota changes; a change resets that limiter's buckets, and a patch that
  leaves a quota alone keeps them. trust_xff stays restart-only. The 429 contract
  is unchanged.

  rate_limit_interval_secs, rate_limit_burst, did_log_rate_limit_interval_secs
  and did_log_rate_limit_burst are registered in the config registry as mutable
  integer keys, applied live and persisted to config.toml: intervals 1-3600,
  bursts 1-10000, super-admin only, through config/patch like every other key.
  Their names come from vta_sdk::rate_limit, which the 429 hints also use.
  pnm and cnm `config update` gain --rate-limit-interval-secs,
  --rate-limit-burst, --did-log-rate-limit-interval-secs and
  --did-log-rate-limit-burst; `config get` shows the keys.

  Adds docs/02-vta/rate-limiting.md and links it from the docs index,
  non-interactive setup and the setup example.



### Fixed

- **cli**: Type rate-limit refusals on the hand-rolled bootstrap and VTC paths ([#1521](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1521))

pnm bootstrap connect, cnm backup, and cnm audit verify build their own error strings from the HTTP status instead of going through the SDK client, so a 429 read as a bare "request failed" — the same class #1511 fixed for the SDK paths. Map 429 to VtaError::RateLimited via rate_limited_from_http (headers captured before the body), so print_cli_error names which service limited, the wait, and how to tune it. On pnm bootstrap connect the limiter runs before the carve-out is touched, so a note says the one-shot first boot is not spent and retry after the wait is safe. The header/attribution parsing is covered by vta-sdk's rate_limit tests; this is the call-site wiring.

  non-interactive setup and the setup example.



### Fixed

- **webvh**: Refuse to delete a DID whose hosting server is unregistered ([#1518](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1518))

`dids delete` on a DID whose `server_id` was no longer registered deleted the
  local record and skipped the delete on the hosting server without reporting
  it. `get_server` returning `None` set no `daemon_cleanup_error`, so the published
  did.jsonl stayed live on the host, and the only credentials that could remove
  it (the record's mnemonic and the DID's keys) were deleted with the record.

  VTI R2.1 (Remote-First): no local commit before the remote effect. The deletion
  now refuses up front, before revoking or deleting anything, as a `Conflict`
  blocker on REST, DIDComm and TSP. The message names the fix: re-register the
  server with `servers add --id <id> --did <server-did>` and retry. The offline
  preview shows the same blocker. Serverless DIDs are unaffected.

  `vta did-mgmt dids delete --local-only` is the explicit opt-in for a host that
  is gone for good, where `servers add` cannot succeed because the server DID no
  longer resolves. It is honoured only for an unregistered server. For a
  registered or serverless DID it is refused. The result says the host copy
  remains. It is offline-only because the `vta/webvh/dids/delete/1.0` payload is
  generated from the specification with `additionalProperties: false`. An online
  opt-in needs a `localOnly` member in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf first.

  `pnm did-mgmt dids delete` also discarded `daemonCleanupError`, the partial
  success the specification says a consumer MUST surface, because the SDK's
  `delete_did_webvh` returns `()`. The new
  `VtaClient::delete_did_webvh_with_outcome` returns the generated response type,
  and the CLI prints the warning.

  Library additions: `DeleteDidOptions`, `delete_did_webvh_with`,
  `plan_did_deletion_with`, and `MockVta::webvh_host_deletes`.

title: feat(ts-proof): Data Integrity proofs for TypeScript (@openvtc/trust-tasks-proof)
body:
Adds **`@openvtc/trust-tasks-proof`**, the TypeScript counterpart of the Rust `trust-tasks-proof` crate and the Dart `trust_tasks_proof` package: a `ProofVerifier` for `@openvtc/trust-tasks`, plus a signer.

## Crypto: rolled our own on @noble, not digitalbazaar
You asked whether to just roll our own — yes, and this proves it out. `@digitalbazaar/data-integrity` runs through `jsonld-signatures`/`jsonld` (heavy, JSON-LD-centric) and fits our bare-JCS Trust Task documents poorly — its `did:key` driver wouldn't even resolve an Ed25519 key without assembling a multikey + security-context loader. Rolling our own on `@noble/curves`+`@noble/hashes`+`@scure/base` is:
- **byte-compatible** with the Rust/Dart proofs by construction (same JCS, hash, multibase) — a test verifies the committed Rust-signed fixture *and* reproduces its `proofValue` byte-for-byte;
- **browser-first, no JSON-LD, no WASM**, matching the ecosystem (`vti-tsp-js`, `vti-didcomm-js`, `pnm-core` are all @noble-based);
- the natural place to add **ML-DSA (PQC)** later.

## What it does
- `DataIntegrityProofVerifier` implements the core `ProofVerifier` seam. Checks proof shape, cryptosuite, `created` (dateTimeStamp + clock-skew), **issuer binding** (verificationMethod DID = `issuer`, exact match), then the signature over the document minus `proof`. did:key only — the key travels in the identifier, no resolver. `verifyDetailed` gives the same failure taxonomy as Rust/Dart.
- `signTrustTask` / `signerFromPrivateKey` produce what it verifies, refusing a document that could never verify. `created` written the way chrono does (no `.000`).
- **eddsa-jcs-2022** (Ed25519) and **ecdsa-jcs-2019** (P-256, P-384).

## Tests
16, via `node --test`: verifies the Rust fixture and reproduces its signature byte-for-byte; sign/verify round trips for ed25519/p256/p384; tamper, issuer-mismatch, malformed, unsupported-cryptosuite, created-window, and sign-time refusals. `ts.yml` gets a `packages` job that builds, typechecks and tests it.

## Not wired to publish yet
Deliberately, and matching the Dart TSP precedent: generalising `publish-npm`/`release-ts-pr` into a package matrix is a critical-path change I'll do **once**, together with the TS TSP binding (next PR), rather than twice. Until then the package is tested in CI but not auto-published; first publish also needs npm trusted publishing set up (a manual step, like pub.dev). RELEASING.md and CLAUDE.md note this.

## Next
TS TSP binding on `@openvtc/vti-tsp-js` (its API is lower-level/key-based, so it needs its own design + interop pass), bringing the npm release-matrix generalisation with it.

A pnm command against a self-hosted VTA DID resolves the log and then runs challenge + authenticate from the same address, so a few commands in a row were refused; the mediator and the VTA's readiness gate fetch the log too. Serving the log is a store read with no crypto. - The DID-log routes (/.well-known/did.jsonl, the canonical catch-all, /did/{did}/log, TEE /attestation/did-log) move to their own per-IP limiter, keyed by trust_xff exactly as before, with new [server] keys did_log_rate_limit_interval_secs (default 1) and did_log_rate_limit_burst (default 60). The auth limiter keeps rate_limit_interval_secs / rate_limit_burst. The catch-all stays the only root wildcard, an opaque bare 404, rate-limited and body-capped. - Every 429 from a VTA limiter carries x-rate-limit-source: vta, x-rate-limit-scope (auth | did-log | backup-blob), a rounded-up Retry-After and a plain body naming the limiter, with no configuration values. - Public log responses send Cache-Control: public, max-age=60 and a strong sha256 ETag, and answer If-None-Match with 304. 404s carry neither. ### Fixed - **vta-service**: Trust a recent self-resolution instead of re-fetching per connect attempt ([#1509](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1509)) The mediator supervisor re-confirmed that the VTA's own DID resolves over the network before every connect attempt, and each confirmation built a throwaway DIDCacheClient and fetched did.jsonl uncached. For a VTA that hosts its own log, those fetches land on its own unauthenticated routes from its own address and share the per-IP rate limiter (10 burst, one token per 5 s by default) with everything else from that address. A run of connects failing for reasons that have nothing to do with resolvability (the mediator's negative cache, a mediator restart) spent that budget at one fetch per attempt, and the check straight after a passed gate fetched the document a second time. SelfResolutionProbe, owned by MessagingConnect and shared by the gate and every reconnect, remembers when a real network resolution last succeeded and answers from that for SELF_RESOLUTION_FRESH_FOR (300 s). Each real check is still a fresh resolver built and stopped per check, so the preloaded self-DID entry cannot mask anything and no long-lived socket needs stopping on shutdown. Only successes are remembered: a failure clears the confirmation and the next attempt resolves again on the existing backoff. 300 s is the default mutable-method TTL of affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk, the resolver the mediator authenticates us through, so the mediator already acts on a copy of our document that old. If the document has become unresolvable inside the window, the connect's authcrypt check fails and the backoff governs the retry as before. run_gate and self_did_network_resolvable keep their signatures and behaviour; run_gate_with_probe and SelfResolutionProbe are additive.

title: vta-service-v0.30.0
body:
### Added

- **cli**: Name removal commands `delete`, and say what a delete leaves behind ([#1513](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1513))

* feat(cli): name removal commands `delete`, and say what a delete leaves behind

  Removal commands across pnm, cnm and the offline vta CLI are named
  `delete`. Each old name stays accepted as a hidden alias, so no script
  breaks:

  - `did-mgmt servers remove` -> `did-mgmt servers delete` (pnm + vta)
  - `pnm vta remove` -> `pnm vta delete`
  - `cnm community remove` -> `cnm community delete` (gains --yes/-y)
  - `pnm memory forget` -> `pnm memory delete`
  - `vta approvals disable` -> `vta approvals delete-all` (`disable` still
    works and prints a note naming the new command)

  Where a delete is not complete, the command now says what remains and
  how to remove it: `vta delete` / `community delete` keep the VTA's ACL
  entry (the notice prints the `acl delete <did>` that revokes it);
  `servers delete` lists DIDs still registered against the server, whose
  logs stay hosted there; `vault delete` / `cred-vault delete` without
  --force name `purge` / `--force`.

- **vta-service**: Give did.jsonl its own rate limiter and make VTA 429s attributable ([#1510](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1510))

* feat(vta-service)!: give did.jsonl its own rate limiter and make VTA 429s attributable

  One per-IP tower_governor bucket (burst 10, one token every 5 s) guarded the
  whole unauthenticated branch, including the public did.jsonl routes. A pnm
  command against a self-hosted VTA DID resolves the log and then runs challenge
  + authenticate from the same address, so a few commands in a row were refused;
  the mediator and the VTA's readiness gate fetch the log too. Serving the log is
  a store read with no crypto.

  - The DID-log routes (/.well-known/did.jsonl, the canonical catch-all,
    /did/{did}/log, TEE /attestation/did-log) move to their own per-IP limiter,
    keyed by trust_xff exactly as before, with new [server] keys
    did_log_rate_limit_interval_secs (default 1) and did_log_rate_limit_burst
    (default 60). The auth limiter keeps rate_limit_interval_secs /
    rate_limit_burst. The catch-all stays the only root wildcard, an opaque bare
    404, rate-limited and body-capped.
  - Every 429 from a VTA limiter carries x-rate-limit-source: vta,
    x-rate-limit-scope (auth | did-log | backup-blob), a rounded-up Retry-After
    and a plain body naming the limiter, with no configuration values.
  - Public log responses send Cache-Control: public, max-age=60 and a strong
    sha256 ETag, and answer If-None-Match with 304. 404s carry neither.

- **tsp**: Adopt Rev 3, and give a TSP session a way to form a relationship ([#1512](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1512))

* docs(tsp): inventory what Rev 3 costs this repository

  Trust Spanning Protocol Rev 3 changed the crypto mode, the version byte,
  the long count-code prefix, the ciphertext code and layout, the `-E`
  count's meaning, the signature code and every payload layout at once.
  There is no compatibility mode: nothing a Rev 2 peer packs can be
  unpacked by a Rev 3 one, in either direction. So the stack flips
  together, and this repository is the last part of it with no plan
  written down.

  The inventory was produced by reading the `tsp-rev3` branch of
  affinidi-tdk-rs against this repository's own call sites, so it names
  files rather than describing intentions. Three things worth knowing
  without reading it:

  **The functional change is one arm.** §7.2.2 says an endpoint SHOULD
  drop an application message from a VID it holds no relationship with,
  and the SDK gates on that by default. SDK 0.22's `unpack_message`
  returns an `InboundTsp` enum instead of a payload, and its `Control`
  variant is what `handle_tsp` has to grow: record the invite, then decide
  whether to accept it. `affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service`'s listener is
  a worked reference for the shape.

  **It fails silently.** A dropped message answers nothing, so a VTA that
  does not answer invites looks from every client like a transport that
  accepts connections and never replies. The wallet already sends the
  invite and waits five seconds before sending anyway, which means an
  unmigrated VTA that does not gate keeps working and one that does goes
  quiet — and neither state produces an error anyone can see. That is the
  reason this is written down before the work rather than during it.

  **There is an authorization decision to take.** Whether the VTA accepts
  an invite from any authenticated sender, or only from one the ACL
  already knows. The narrow reading breaks provisioning — a wallet talks
  to the VTA *in order to* be provisioned — so the broad one is almost
  certainly right, but it should be a decision rather than whatever the
  first implementer assumes.

  No code change. The work is blocked on an `affinidi-tdk` release
  carrying `affinidi-tsp` 0.2.0, and this workspace deliberately has no
  `[patch.crates-io]` to get ahead with — the note at the bottom of
  Cargo.toml records the duplicate-`vta-sdk` incident that removed it.

- **keys**: Derive ML-DSA keys from the BIP-32 chain ([#1505](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1505))

`Bip32Extension` gains `derive_ml_dsa_44` and `derive_ml_dsa_65`, and the five
  sites that refused post-quantum derivation now do it: key creation, both export
  paths, and the offline `vta keys secrets` CLI. This is what stands between "a
  `KeyRecord` can carry a post-quantum key" and "a VTA can mint one".

    404, rate-limited and body-capped.
  - Every 429 from a VTA limiter carries x-rate-limit-source: vta,
    x-rate-limit-scope (auth | did-log | backup-blob), a rounded-up Retry-After
    and a plain body naming the limiter, with no configuration values.
  - Public log responses send Cache-Control: public, max-age=60 and a strong
    sha256 ETag, and answer If-None-Match with 304. 404s carry neither.



### Fixed

- **vta-service**: Trust a recent self-resolution instead of re-fetching per connect attempt ([#1509](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1509))

The mediator supervisor re-confirmed that the VTA's own DID resolves over the
  network before every connect attempt, and each confirmation built a throwaway
  DIDCacheClient and fetched did.jsonl uncached. For a VTA that hosts its own log,
  those fetches land on its own unauthenticated routes from its own address and
  share the per-IP rate limiter (10 burst, one token per 5 s by default) with
  everything else from that address. A run of connects failing for reasons that
  have nothing to do with resolvability (the mediator's negative cache, a
  mediator restart) spent that budget at one fetch per attempt, and the check
  straight after a passed gate fetched the document a second time.

  SelfResolutionProbe, owned by MessagingConnect and shared by the gate and every
  reconnect, remembers when a real network resolution last succeeded and answers
  from that for SELF_RESOLUTION_FRESH_FOR (300 s). Each real check is still a
  fresh resolver built and stopped per check, so the preloaded self-DID entry
  cannot mask anything and no long-lived socket needs stopping on shutdown. Only
  successes are remembered: a failure clears the confirmation and the next
  attempt resolves again on the existing backoff.

  300 s is the default mutable-method TTL of affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk, the
  resolver the mediator authenticates us through, so the mediator already acts on
  a copy of our document that old. If the document has become unresolvable
  inside the window, the connect's authcrypt check fails and the backoff governs
  the retry as before.

  run_gate and self_did_network_resolvable keep their signatures and behaviour;
  run_gate_with_probe and SelfResolutionProbe are additive.
