title: feat(cli): name removal commands `delete`, and say what a delete leaves behind
body:
Removal commands across `pnm`, `cnm` and the offline `vta` CLI are now named `delete`. Every old name still parses, as a hidden alias, so no script breaks. That's why the title has no `!`: the syntax the CLIs accept only grows, and no published crate's public API changes. `vta-cli-common` keeps `cmd_webvh_server_remove` / `cmd_memory_forget` under their existing names for that reason. Trust Task URIs are unchanged (`spec/vta/webvh/servers/remove/1.0` is a specification name).

Where a `delete` doesn't delete everything, the command now prints a notice saying what remains and the command that removes it.

## Renamed

| Old | New | Old name kept as | Notice added |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pnm did-mgmt servers remove <id>` | `pnm did-mgmt servers delete <id>` | hidden alias `remove` | Lists DIDs still registered against the server, notes their logs are still hosted there, and prints the `servers add --id … --did …` + `dids delete` sequence that removes them completely. The lookup is best-effort, and the delete never refuses. |
| `vta did-mgmt servers remove <id>` (offline) | `vta did-mgmt servers delete <id>` | hidden alias `remove` | same, read from the local store |
| `pnm vta remove <slug>` | `pnm vta delete <slug>` | hidden alias `remove` | Only the local connection and credential are deleted. The VTA's ACL entry remains, and the notice prints `pnm acl delete <client-did>`, with a warning not to run it for the VTA's only admin |
| `cnm community remove <name>` | `cnm community delete <name>` (+ `--yes/-y`, hidden `--force`) | hidden alias `remove` | same, with `cnm acl delete <client-did>` |
| `pnm memory forget <key>` | `pnm memory delete <key>` | hidden alias `forget` (`delete` used to be the hidden alias) | — |
| `vta approvals disable` | `vta approvals delete-all` | hidden subcommand `disable`, which prints a note naming `delete-all` and then runs it | — |
| internal `WebvhCommands::RemoveServer` (pnm + vta) | `DeleteServer` | n/a (not user-facing) | — |

`pnm vault delete` / `pnm cred-vault delete` without `--force` now also print how to delete right away: `vault purge <id>` (or `vault delete <id> --force`). `vault purge` / `cred-vault purge` stay visible. Their help text now says they do the same thing as `delete --force`, which the server handler confirms: `force: true` and `purge` both call the same hard delete.

### Judgement calls
- **`vta vault wipe` keeps its name.** It is a bulk hard delete, like `pnm memory wipe`, and cli-style.md now allows a bulk verb as long as the help text says it deletes every entry. Its confirmation flag becomes `--yes` (hidden `--force`), because it was a consent flag, not a "skip the soft delete" flag.
- **`vta approvals delete-all`, not `delete --all`.** There is no `delete <one>` to pair with `--all`: deleting a single rule is `remove`, which keeps its verb (below).
- **No refusal on `servers delete` with DIDs still registered.** A refusal would change what the Trust Task does, and would break any script that deletes such a server today. It prints the notice instead. See the follow-up below: that notice matters more than it first appears.

## Kept the verb (not deletion)

| Command | Why |
|---|---|
| `pnm approvals remove`, `approvals approvers remove` (and offline `vta approvals remove`) | Edits a list inside one policy row; the row survives |
| `pnm did-mgmt agent-names remove` | Releases a name claim, next to `enable`/`disable`. Help now says the released name can be claimed by any DID, and points to `disable` to park it |
| `pnm keys revoke` / `cnm keys revoke` | Changes a key's lifecycle state |
| `cnm vetting vetters revoke` | Credential revocation |
| `pnm device disable` / `device wipe` | The device stays on record; `wipe` is a remote-wipe instruction, not record deletion |
| `services * disable` | Withdraws an advertisement, and `rollback` can restore it |
| `services didcomm drain cancel` | Stops a pending process |
| `auth logout` | Ends a session |

## `--force` / `--yes` rule (written up in `docs/04-reference/cli-style.md`)

- `--yes` / `-y` skips a confirmation prompt, or is the consent a non-interactive run gives. It never changes what gets deleted.
- On a delete, `--force` means skip the soft delete, and only where a soft path exists (`vault delete`, `cred-vault delete`).
- Prompt-skipping commands that used to take `--force` / `-f` still accept them as hidden aliases of `--yes`:
  - `pnm contexts delete`, `cnm contexts delete`, `vta contexts delete` (`--force`, `-f`)
  - `pnm vta delete` (`--force`)
  - `vta did-mgmt dids delete` (`--force`)
  - `vta vault wipe` (`--force`)
  - `pnm memory wipe` (already did; now also takes `-y`)
- The other uses of `--force` are not about deletion and are unchanged: `backup export --force` (overwrite the output file), `did-mgmt dids register --force` (take over a slot), `services didcomm {enable,update} --force` (skip the handshake), `vta vault seed --force` (overwrite an entry).

## Knock-on
- Hints in `pnm-cli/src/setup.rs` now name `pnm vta delete`. One of them also pointed at `pnm vta show {slug}`, which doesn't exist; it now says `pnm --vta {slug} vta info`.
- Docs updated: `docs/02-vta/{approvals,non-interactive-setup,personal-ai-agents}.md`, `docs/05-design-notes/{pnm-setup-deferred-vta-did,approvals-convergence}.md`, `pnm-cli/README.md`, `cnm-cli/README.md`.
- Parse tests cover every new name, every kept alias, and each `--yes`/`--force`/`-f` spelling (pnm, cnm, vta). `vta-service/tests/approvals_breakglass_cli.rs` now drives `delete-all`, and has a new test showing `disable` still deletes everything and names `delete-all`.

## Follow-up found, not fixed here
`dids delete` on a DID whose server id is no longer registered removes the local record and **skips the delete on the hosting server without reporting it**. In `operations::did_webvh` `delete_did`, `get_server` returning `None` sets no `daemon_cleanup_error`, so the log is left orphaned on the host and nothing is reported. The `servers delete` notice tells operators to re-add the server before deleting such DIDs. The operation itself should probably report the skip, but that is a server-side behaviour change and out of scope for a naming PR.

The root `CLAUDE.md` still says `vta approvals {list,remove,disable}` in the approvals section. I left it for a maintainer to update.

## Verification
All run on the branch after rebasing onto `origin/main` at e7c70ef3 (#1511):
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean
- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast`: exit 0, 123 test binaries and doc-test runs, 4406 tests passed, 0 failed. All the new parse tests and approvals break-glass tests ran and passed.
- `vtc-service` / `vtc-client` were not run; this PR changes neither.

title: feat(vta-service)!: give did.jsonl its own rate limiter and make VTA 429s attributable
body:
## Diagnosis

`routes::apply_unauth_governor` put **one** per-IP `tower_governor` bucket (default burst 10, one token every 5 s) in front of the whole unauthenticated branch — the auth endpoints *and* the public `did.jsonl` routes (`/.well-known/did.jsonl`, the `/{*did_log_path}` catch-all, `/did/{did}/log`, TEE `/attestation/did-log`).

For a VTA that hosts its own `did:webvh` log, every `pnm` command resolves the VTA DID (an uncached `did.jsonl` GET) and then runs challenge + authenticate from the same address — 3 of the 10 tokens — so a few commands in a row got 429. The mediator and the VTA's own readiness gate fetch the log too. Serving the log is a store read with no crypto; it was spending a budget sized for endpoints that do crypto on caller input. The 429 itself was tower_governor's bare `Too Many Requests! Wait for Ns`, which gave an operator no way to tell the VTA's limiter from a mediator's or a proxy's.

## What changed

**Separate limiters** (`vta-service/src/routes/rate_limit.rs`, new). Each branch gets its own per-IP buckets, still keyed by `trust_xff` exactly as before (`PeerIpKeyExtractor` / `SmartIpKeyExtractor`):

| scope | routes | quota |
|---|---|---|
| `auth` | auth challenge/authenticate/refresh, passkey login, `/bootstrap/request`, TEE attestation reports | `rate_limit_interval_secs` / `rate_limit_burst` (5 / 10, unchanged) |
| `did-log` | `/.well-known/did.jsonl`, the canonical catch-all, `/did/{did}/log`, TEE `/attestation/did-log` | **new** `did_log_rate_limit_interval_secs` / `did_log_rate_limit_burst` (1 / 60) |
| `backup-blob` | `/backup/blob/*` | auth quota, own bucket (as before) |

The catch-all stays the only root wildcard, still answers an opaque bare 404, and is still rate-limited (now on `did-log`) and body-capped at `UNAUTH_BODY_SIZE`. `/attestation/did-log` moved with the other log routes — same public log, same cheap read.

**Attributable 429s.** Every 429 any VTA limiter produces now carries:

- `x-rate-limit-source: vta` — **a client contract; do not rename.**
- `x-rate-limit-scope: auth | did-log | backup-blob`
- `retry-after: <secs>` (rounded *up*, never 0 — tower_governor truncates, so a client honouring it was being refused again) and the legacy `x-ratelimit-after` with the same value
- `application/json` body — no configuration values:

```json
{"error":"rate_limited","limiter":"did-log","message":"Too Many Requests: rejected by the VTA's `did-log` rate limiter. Retry after 3 s.","retryAfterSecs":3}
```

This is the server half of the contract #1511 (`vta_sdk::rate_limit`, merged) reads: the header name and the legacy wait header come from `vta_sdk::rate_limit::{SOURCE_HEADER, LEGACY_RETRY_AFTER_HEADER}` rather than literals, and a test asserts `RateLimitSource::from_source_header(Some("vta"))` is `Vta`, so server and client cannot drift. The config key names this PR adds are the ones `vta_sdk::rate_limit::{VTA_DID_LOG_INTERVAL_KEY, VTA_DID_LOG_BURST_KEY}` already name. Implemented through `GovernorLayer::error_handler`; the key-extraction 500 is unchanged.

**Cacheable logs.** The public log responses now send `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60` and a strong `ETag` (`"sha256-<hex>"` over the log bytes), and answer a matching `If-None-Match` (exact, list, weak form or `*`) with `304` and no body. 60 s is well inside the 300 s that `affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk` (the resolver the mediator and clients use) already caches a `did:webvh` document for, so an HTTP cache adds no staleness a verifier does not already accept; the log is append-only, so a cached copy is at worst missing the newest entry. Caching headers are only ever set on 200/304 — a 404 stays byte-identical to axum's default, so they cannot fingerprint the DID configuration.

## Config / compatibility

- `vta-config::ServerConfig` gains `did_log_rate_limit_interval_secs` and `did_log_rate_limit_burst` (serde defaults, so existing `config.toml` files load unchanged). `ServerConfig` is not `#[non_exhaustive]`, so a struct literal elsewhere breaks — hence the `!`.
- `vta-service`: `routes::router_with_cors(origins, trust_xff, interval_secs, burst)` → `router_with_cors(origins, trust_xff, RateLimits)`; the `pub(crate)` `UNAUTH_INTERVAL_SECS` / `UNAUTH_BURST` consts moved into `routes::rate_limit`. New public `routes::rate_limit` module (`Limiter`, `Quota`, `RateLimits`, header-name consts).
- `vta setup` (interactive) writes the new defaults; `vta setup --from` already takes `[server]` as a `ServerConfig`, so the keys flow through.
- Zero in either new key clamps to 1, like the existing keys.
- Operationally: the auth budget is unchanged; `did.jsonl` fetches simply stop spending it.

Runtime tuning of all four keys and operator docs follow in a stacked PR.

## Tests

- `routes::rate_limit::tests` — a did-log burst does not spend the auth budget and vice versa (two limiters merged into one router, same shape as `build_api_router`); per-IP isolation; the full 429 contract (headers, `retry-after ≥ 1`, exact JSON body); the source label is what the SDK reads as `Vta`; zero clamp for all four keys; defaults match `ServerConfig::default()`.
- `tests/api_integration.rs` — end-to-end on the real router: a `did.jsonl` flood (both the well-known route and the catch-all) trips `did-log` no earlier than its 60 burst and leaves the same IP's full auth burst; an auth flood leaves `did.jsonl` reachable; the existing auth and backup-blob 429 tests now also assert `x-rate-limit-source` / `x-rate-limit-scope`.
- `routes::self_hosted_did::tests` — strong ETag + `max-age=60` on 200; 304 with no body for exact / listed / weak / `*`; a stale tag gets the full log; the tag changes when the log grows; 404s carry no caching headers even with `If-None-Match: *`.
- `vta-config` — the new keys default, parse, and are not flagged as unknown.
- The existing `rate_limit_tests` (tower_governor interval-vs-rate semantics) and `zero_rate_limit_config_is_clamped_not_panicked` are kept.

## Verification (local, on this branch, rebased on `main` at #1511)

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `cargo fmt --all -- --check` | clean |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` | clean |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` | clean |
| `cargo clippy -p vta-service --no-default-features --features rest --all-targets -- -D warnings` | clean |
| `cargo clippy -p vta-service --no-default-features --features setup,keyring,rest,tsp,cli-synthesis --all-targets -- -D warnings` | clean |
| `cargo check -p vta-service --no-default-features --features tee,rest,didcomm` | clean |
| `cargo check -p vta-service --no-default-features --features rest,didcomm` | clean |
| `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` | 4414 passed, 0 failed (123 test binaries) |
| `cargo test -p vta-service --no-default-features --features tee,rest,didcomm --lib routes::` | 53 passed (before the rebase onto #1511; the TEE path is unchanged by it) |

`vtc-service` is untouched and its separate job was not run.

title: fix(vta-service): trust a recent self-resolution instead of re-fetching per connect attempt
body:
## Root cause

A VTA that self-hosts its `did:webvh` log could trip its own per-IP unauthenticated rate limiter (default burst 10, one token per 5 s, shared with `/auth/*`).

Part of the resolution volume came from the mediator supervisor. `MessagingConnect::supervise` called `readiness::self_did_network_resolvable` before **every** connect attempt. `self_did_resolves` deliberately builds a throwaway `DIDCacheClient` per call, so that the startup-preloaded self-DID entry can't mask real network resolvability. As a result every check was an uncached GET of the VTA's own `did.jsonl`, sent directly or through the resolver sidecar.

When connects keep failing for reasons unrelated to resolvability, the supervisor retries every ≤60 s at the reconnect cap, and every retry fetched the document again. The mediator's own negative cache (the "classic" failure the reconnect loop exists for) and a mediator restart are both such reasons. The first reconnect check straight after a passed gate also fetched the document a second time.

## Change

- Add `readiness::SelfResolutionProbe`. `MessagingConnect::run` creates one and shares it between the gate (`run_gate_with_probe`) and every reconnect check. It records when a **real** network resolution last succeeded and answers from that record for `SELF_RESOLUTION_FRESH_FOR` = 300 s.
- A real check still goes through `self_did_resolves`: a fresh resolver, built and `stop()`ped per check. So:
  - the preloaded self-DID entry and the long-lived resolver's cache still can't satisfy it;
  - no long-lived network-mode client exists that would need stopping on shutdown;
  - the invariants from the "Mediator connection" section of CLAUDE.md are untouched: nothing new on the startup path, `build_messaging` teardown unchanged, `MIN_HEALTHY_SESSION` unchanged.
- Only successes are remembered. A failed check clears the confirmation, so an unresolvable VTA re-probes on every attempt under the existing backoff.
- The gate's own retries are never short-circuited. Until the gate passes, every attempt is a real resolution.

### Why 300 s

300 s is the default TTL for mutable methods (`did:web`, `did:webvh`) in `affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk`, which is the resolver the mediator authenticates us through. The mediator therefore already acts on a copy of our document up to 300 s old, and trusting our own positive observation for the same window adds no staleness that the mediator doesn't already accept.

If the document becomes unresolvable inside the window, the connect's authcrypt check fails and the backoff governs the retry, as before. A window longer than the mediator's cache is where a stale "yes" could hide a real change, so the bound stops there. A test pins the constant.

Net effect: during a run of successful self-resolutions, the probe costs at most one fetch per 300 s instead of one per connect attempt.

## Compatibility

Additive only. `run_gate` and `self_did_network_resolvable` keep their signatures and stateless behaviour, and `SelfResolutionProbe`, `run_gate_with_probe` and `SELF_RESOLUTION_FRESH_FOR` are new. There is no `!`.

Docs: `docs/02-vta/mediator-connection.md` §2 and the `MediatorReadinessConfig::reconnect` doc comment now describe the window. The CLAUDE.md "Mediator connection" line "re-confirming self-resolution before every attempt" is still true: every attempt still checks, but a recent success now answers the check. I left CLAUDE.md alone.

The SDK half of the same churn (throwaway resolvers per CLI call) is a separate, independent PR.

## Tests

In `messaging::readiness::tests`, driven through an injected probe:
- `consecutive_successful_checks_fetch_once_within_the_window`: 4 checks, 1 real resolution.
- `a_failed_check_is_not_remembered`: failures resolve each time, and the first success then resolves too.
- `a_success_expires_after_the_window`: past the window a check resolves again, and a failure there is not masked.
- `a_gate_pass_answers_the_first_reconnect_check`
- `did_key_probe_is_ready_without_resolving`
- `freshness_window_does_not_outlive_the_mediator_resolver_cache`

## Verification (local, macOS)

Re-run after rebasing onto #1511, on a tree with this commit plus the SDK PR #1517:
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean
- `cargo clippy -p vta-service --no-default-features --features rest --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean
- `cargo clippy -p vta-service --no-default-features --features setup,keyring,rest,tsp,cli-synthesis --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean. The same three clippy runs were also clean on this branch alone.
- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast`: 4406 passed, 0 failed, 50 ignored (vtc-service/vtc-client: 1644 passed, 0 failed)

fix(vta-service): trust a recent self-resolution instead of re-fetching per connect attempt (#1509)

The mediator supervisor re-confirmed that the VTA's own DID resolves over the
network before every connect attempt, and each confirmation built a throwaway
DIDCacheClient and fetched did.jsonl uncached. For a VTA that hosts its own log,
those fetches land on its own unauthenticated routes from its own address and
share the per-IP rate limiter (10 burst, one token per 5 s by default) with
everything else from that address. A run of connects failing for reasons that
have nothing to do with resolvability (the mediator's negative cache, a
mediator restart) spent that budget at one fetch per attempt, and the check
straight after a passed gate fetched the document a second time.

SelfResolutionProbe, owned by MessagingConnect and shared by the gate and every
reconnect, remembers when a real network resolution last succeeded and answers
from that for SELF_RESOLUTION_FRESH_FOR (300 s). Each real check is still a
fresh resolver built and stopped per check, so the preloaded self-DID entry
cannot mask anything and no long-lived socket needs stopping on shutdown. Only
successes are remembered: a failure clears the confirmation and the next
attempt resolves again on the existing backoff.

300 s is the default mutable-method TTL of affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk, the
resolver the mediator authenticates us through, so the mediator already acts on
a copy of our document that old. If the document has become unresolvable
inside the window, the connect's authcrypt check fails and the backoff governs
the retry as before.

run_gate and self_did_network_resolvable keep their signatures and behaviour;
run_gate_with_probe and SelfResolutionProbe are additive.

title: feat(tsp)!: adopt Rev 3, and give a TSP session a way to form a relationship
body:
Puts this repository on TSP Rev 3, and fixes the two things adopting Rev 3
semantics turned out to require. Rev 3 has **no compatibility mode** — nothing a
Rev 2 peer packs can be unpacked by a Rev 3 one, in either direction — so the
stack flips together and this is the last Rust repository in the chain.

`affinidi-tdk` 0.14 → 0.16, `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.24 → 0.26.1,
`affinidi-messaging-test-mediator` 0.7 → 0.9, `trust-tasks` → 0.21.

## Why this is also the unlock for the `vta-sdk` cycle

`[patch.crates-io]` maps `affinidi-messaging-core` to the workspace copy, so the
**registry** copy of `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.24 — in the graph only because
of the `vta-sdk` cycle — compiles against it. That means the cycle **freezes
`affinidi-messaging-core`'s API against a published crate nobody can edit**: any
required field added to `Inbound` breaks it.

Two escapes were tested and neither works. Gating `vta` out of the mediator's
default features does not clear the duplicate (`mediator-setup` depends on
`vta-sdk` unconditionally), and gating it out of `mediator-setup` is not viable
either — 65 call sites, the tool's whole bootstrap flow.

What does clear it is releasing `vta-sdk` built against the current line, which
is what merging this makes possible. `scripts/check-lockfile-self-pins.sh`
reports *no workspace crate pulled back in from crates.io*, and the lockfile
carries no duplicate `affinidi-*` or `trust-tasks*` entry.

## The rule that came out of the test failures

`TspSession::pump_once` called `unpack_bytes` and skipped what it could not
read. So a relationship control message was **never recorded**, and §7.2.2 then
discarded every application message that followed — drops, not refuses, so the
symptom is a peer that times out with nothing in the log.

That is the same defect as affinidi-tdk-rs#800 fixed in the mediator adapter.
`pump_once` is the second instance and `tsp_binding_pair`'s hand-rolled VTA-side
pickup loop is the third, which makes it worth stating as a rule rather than a
fix:

> **Under Rev 3 a raw `atm.tsp().unpack` loop is wrong wherever it appears.**
> That signature cannot say a frame is a control message, and skipping one
> silently costs every frame that follows.

All three now use `unpack_message`, record control, and skip padding and `XCTL`
by name with no catch-all arm.

## A TSP session could not form a relationship at all

`TspSession`, `TspPingSession` and `DIDCommSession`'s TSP leg had no way to send
an invite. Under Rev 2 that was survivable; under Rev 3 the control exchange is
a precondition of every application message, so the session cannot talk to
anything. `relate` / `relate_tsp` is a missing capability, not test scaffolding.

Nothing to await: the peer records the invite on arrival and
`admits_application_message` is true for any state but `None` — §3.6 lets a
sender pack user data alongside its invite — so traffic flows without an accept,
and the sender's own `Pending` admits the reply.

## Two traps worth knowing

**`form_relationship_routed` does not route the invite.** "Routed" names the
reply path an invite advertises (§7.2.4); `send_control` sends direct either
way. Switching to it to fix a 403 changed nothing.

**The invite is a direct message, and the fixture default refuses those.**
`local_direct_delivery_allowed` defaults to `false`, so every TSP fixture needed
it enabled or the relationship could never be formed — surfacing as
`e.p.direct_delivery.denied`, which reads as a transport fault rather than a
missing flag. Twelve mediator builders across four end-to-end test files and the
VTC test harness.

## ⚠️ What this does NOT do, and the window it opens

**It does not answer invites.** A VTA or VTC records one and admits the traffic,
but whether to *accept* is an authorization decision, and `Inbound` still has no
way to carry a message kind to the layer that would make it. That is a breaking
change to `affinidi-messaging-core`, blocked until the stale
`affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.24 leaves the graph — which releasing `vta-sdk` from
this branch is what does.

So merging this puts VTI on Rev 3 **semantics** — §7.2.2 relationship gating, on
by default — while nothing can yet answer. Concretely:

- `vta-service` has `tsp` **off** by default, so a default VTA is unaffected.
- **`vtc-service` and `pnm-cli` have it on**, and `vtc-service` receives inbound
  TSP (`messaging.rs:430`). The VTC is the surface that would go quiet against a
  peer that has not first sent an invite.
- VTI sets no `tsp_relationship_gating`, so it takes the SDK default (gated).

This is unavoidable in ordering: the fix needs `vta-sdk` released, and that needs
this merged. **The window is in code, not in production** — but it is real, and a
deployment should not be cut from this commit alone. The follow-up is the
`InboundTsp::Control` arm, ACL-gated, refusing explicitly via
`cancel_relationship` (XRFD) rather than silently, so an unauthorized peer is
told rather than dropped.

## Verification

- **122 workspace suites** green — CI's
  `--workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client` job, `--no-fail-fast`.
- **62 suites / 1644 tests** green in the separate `-p vtc-service -p vtc-client`
  job.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean.
- All five repository guards pass: lockfile self-pins, workspace version reqs,
  authz context types, Nitro member census, workflow action pins.

Note the `semver report` check is expected to be red — this changes public API
in `vta-sdk`, and release-plz reads the same signal into the Release PR. Per
RELEASING.md, no version is edited here.

title: feat(tsp)!: adopt Rev 3, and give a TSP session a way to form a relationship (#1512)
body:
feat(tsp)!: adopt Rev 3, and give a TSP session a way to form a relationship (#1512)

* docs(tsp): inventory what Rev 3 costs this repository

Trust Spanning Protocol Rev 3 changed the crypto mode, the version byte,
the long count-code prefix, the ciphertext code and layout, the `-E`
count's meaning, the signature code and every payload layout at once.
There is no compatibility mode: nothing a Rev 2 peer packs can be
unpacked by a Rev 3 one, in either direction. So the stack flips
together, and this repository is the last part of it with no plan
written down.

The inventory was produced by reading the `tsp-rev3` branch of
affinidi-tdk-rs against this repository's own call sites, so it names
files rather than describing intentions. Three things worth knowing
without reading it:

**The functional change is one arm.** §7.2.2 says an endpoint SHOULD
drop an application message from a VID it holds no relationship with,
and the SDK gates on that by default. SDK 0.22's `unpack_message`
returns an `InboundTsp` enum instead of a payload, and its `Control`
variant is what `handle_tsp` has to grow: record the invite, then decide
whether to accept it. `affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service`'s listener is
a worked reference for the shape.

**It fails silently.** A dropped message answers nothing, so a VTA that
does not answer invites looks from every client like a transport that
accepts connections and never replies. The wallet already sends the
invite and waits five seconds before sending anyway, which means an
unmigrated VTA that does not gate keeps working and one that does goes
quiet — and neither state produces an error anyone can see. That is the
reason this is written down before the work rather than during it.

**There is an authorization decision to take.** Whether the VTA accepts
an invite from any authenticated sender, or only from one the ACL
already knows. The narrow reading breaks provisioning — a wallet talks
to the VTA *in order to* be provisioned — so the broad one is almost
certainly right, but it should be a decision rather than whatever the
first implementer assumes.

No code change. The work is blocked on an `affinidi-tdk` release
carrying `affinidi-tsp` 0.2.0, and this workspace deliberately has no
`[patch.crates-io]` to get ahead with — the note at the bottom of
Cargo.toml records the duplicate-`vta-sdk` incident that removed it.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* build(deps): move the affinidi pins to the Rev 3 release

The first half of the cut-over: `affinidi-tdk` 0.14 -> 0.15,
`affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.24 -> 0.25 and `affinidi-messaging-test-mediator`
0.7 -> 0.8, across nine manifests. The commit that follows carries them the
rest of the way (0.16 / 0.26.1 / 0.9) once the upstream blocker below was
cleared; they are kept apart because the blocker is worth recording against the
code that found it.

Each of those was found by a duplicate rather than by reading, and the order
mattered: the first bump left both versions resolving, because a stale pin
elsewhere kept the old one alive and the build stayed green against it. A
`cargo check` that passes is not evidence the old version is gone — only
`cargo tree -i <crate>@<old>` is, and it has to be run under `--all-features`,
since three of these were reachable only there.

## The blocker: a fourth repository, which no inventory recorded

`docs/05-design-notes/tsp-rev3-migration.md` says this repository is blocked on
an `affinidi-tdk` release carrying `affinidi-tsp` 0.2.0. That release has
landed, and it is not sufficient.

`trust-tasks-tsp` — the Trust Tasks TSP transport binding, which `vta-sdk` and
`vta-service` both depend on — pins `affinidi-tsp = "0.1"`. So the graph still
resolves `affinidi-tsp` 0.1.15 beside 0.2.0, which is the one state this
cut-over must not reach: two TSP implementations at two revisions in one
binary, with no compatibility between them. Everything else here is single-
versioned; this one is not.

Fixing it upstream was not a one-line bump. Moving `trust-tasks-tsp` to
`affinidi-tsp` 0.2 pulls `affinidi-did-common` 0.4, which collided with a
stale 0.3.x line that `affinidi-did-resolver-traits`, `affinidi-did-web` and
`affinidi-meeting-place` still held through `trust-tasks-proof`'s
dev-dependencies. That 0.3.x line did not merely duplicate — it **failed to
compile** in the resulting graph (`JWK::new` and `OctectParams::new` are gone,
an `ssi-jwk` skew), and floating every one of those crates to its newest patch
did not clear it.

So the chain is four repositories, not three: affinidi-tdk-rs -> dtgwg-trust-
tasks-tf (`trust-tasks-tsp`) -> here -> the JS clients. Both upstream hops have
since shipped — dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#466 moved the binding to Rev 3 and #467
released `trust-tasks` 0.21 — which is what lets the next commit finish the
move. The migration note's three-repository chain is corrected there.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(tsp)!: adopt Rev 3, and give a TSP session a way to form a relationship

Completes the dependency move — `affinidi-tdk` 0.16, `messaging-sdk` 0.26.1,
`test-mediator` 0.9, `trust-tasks` 0.21 — and fixes what adopting Rev 3
semantics exposed. **Zero duplicate `affinidi-*` or `trust-tasks*` crates in the
graph**, which is what lets `vta-sdk` be released against the current line and
unwind the cycle that has been re-breaking `[patch.crates-io]` since 0.20.

## The same defect as affinidi-tdk-rs#800, in two more places

`TspSession::pump_once` called `unpack_bytes` and skipped what it could not
read: `continue; // not sealed to us / TSP control traffic`. So a relationship
control message was **never recorded**, and §7.2.2 then discarded every
application message that followed. Drops, not refuses — nothing goes back — so
the symptom is a peer that times out with nothing in the log.

#800 fixed this in the mediator adapter. `TspSession::pump_once` is the second
path that had it and `tsp_binding_pair`'s hand-rolled VTA-side pickup loop is
the third, so it is worth stating as a rule rather than a fix: **under Rev 3 a
raw `atm.tsp().unpack` loop is wrong**, because that signature cannot say a
frame is a control message, and skipping one silently costs you everything that
follows. All three are fixed the same way — `unpack_message`, record control,
skip padding and `XCTL` by name, no catch-all arm.

## A TSP session could not form a relationship at all

`TspSession`, `TspPingSession` and `DIDCommSession`'s TSP leg had no way to send
an invite. Under Rev 2 that was survivable; under Rev 3 it means the session
cannot talk to anything, because §7.2.2 makes the control exchange a
precondition of every application message. So `relate` / `relate_tsp` is a
missing capability rather than test scaffolding.

Nothing to await: the peer records the invite on arrival and
`admits_application_message` is true for any state but `None` — §3.6 lets a
sender pack user data alongside its invite — so traffic flows without an accept,
and the sender's own `Pending` admits the reply.

## Two things the tests taught, both worth writing down

**`form_relationship_routed` does not route the invite.** "Routed" names the
reply path an invite advertises (§7.2.4); `send_control` sends direct either
way. Switching to it to fix a 403 changed nothing.

**The invite is a direct message, and the fixture default refuses those.**
`local_direct_delivery_allowed` defaults to `false`, so every TSP fixture needed
it enabled or the relationship could never be formed —
`e.p.direct_delivery.denied`, which reads as a transport fault rather than a
missing flag. Thirteen mediator builders: four end-to-end test files and both
test harnesses. `MockVta::start_with_transports` was the awkward one — it used
`TestMediator::spawn()`, the shorthand that takes no builder, so it had to be
opened up before the flag could be set at all.

## What #1508 cost, arriving from the other direction

`tsp_vta_trust_task.rs` landed on `main` while this branch was open, and its
three end-to-end tests were written against Rev 2 — a client that simply sends.
Under §7.2.2 the VTA drops those frames before the spine sees them, so all three
fail as *silence*, which is precisely the symptom #1507's own `expect` messages
describe. Same presentation, different cause, and no way for either branch to
have seen it alone.

`an_unauthorized_sender_is_refused_over_tsp_not_met_with_silence` needed more
than a mechanical fix. It asserts that an ungranted sender gets
`permissionDenied` rather than nothing — but under Rev 3 an *unrelated* sender
is dropped before authorization is consulted, so without a relationship the test
would eventually pass for the wrong reason. Forming the relationship first is
what keeps it aimed at the ACL rather than at the transport gate, and the test
now says so.

## What this does not do

It does not answer invites. A VTA or VTC records one and admits the traffic, but
whether to *accept* is an authorization decision, and `Inbound` still has no way
to carry a message kind to the layer that would make it — that is a breaking
change to `affinidi-messaging-core`, blocked until the registry copy of
`affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.24 leaves the graph. Releasing `vta-sdk` from this
branch is what removes it.

Measured by CI on the merged tree: **123 workspace suites / 4397 tests** and
**62 VTC suites / 1644 tests**, no failures. Clippy clean under
`--all-targets -- -D warnings`; rustfmt clean; feature combos, MSRV, both Docker
images, the enclave and mobile builds all green.

All five repository guards pass. `check-lockfile-self-pins.sh` reports *no
workspace crate pulled back in from crates.io*, which is the cycle being gone
rather than merely tolerated, and the lockfile carries no duplicate
`affinidi-*` or `trust-tasks*` entry.

The semver report is red and none of it is from this change: `VtaError`'s new
`RateLimited` variant and the `vta-service` signature changes came from #1509 /
#1510 / #1511, which are already on `main` and ahead of the published baselines
the report compares against.

title: fix(tsp-js): raise MAX_HOPS to 64 so longer routes interoperate
body:
This PR targets `feat/tsp-rev2-rev3-dual-handler`, like #249 and #250.

`MAX_HOPS` was 10. It caps `packRouted` and decoding any hop list or reply path (`decodeVidList`, and the Rev 2 reader). The TSP specification sets no maximum; the ToIP reference has no limit, affinidi-tsp-go allows 64 and Dart 32. As a result, tsp-js refused 12-hop routes that every other implementation opens.

This raises the limit to 64, matching affinidi-tsp-go and the matching affinidi-tsp change. It still bounds a hostile hop count, and is still enforced on both pack and decode.

- New test: a 64-hop route packs and opens with its hops intact. 65 is still rejected.
- tsp-js `npm test`: 112 pass. core `tests/tsp.*.mjs`: 33 pass.
- Conformance suite (OpenVTC/tsp-conformance) with this branch and the affinidi-tsp change: interop is 893 pass, 0 fail (previously 25 hop-limit failures).

title: feat(dart-https): HTTPS transport binding for Dart (trust_tasks_https)
body:
Adds **`trust_tasks_https`**, the HTTPS transport binding (`bindings/https/0.2`) for Dart, and the Dart counterpart of the Rust `trust-tasks-https` crate. This is the second of the three agreed Dart packages; DIDComm v2 comes next.

## Client: `HttpsClient`
- POSTs to `<base>/trust-tasks`, ignoring a trailing slash on the base (§6.1).
- Fills in `issuer`, `recipient` and `issuedAt` when the request leaves them unset.
- Returns a response only if it belongs to this request: same thread, the request's type with `#response`, issued by the server and addressed to this client.
- Reads a non-2xx JSON body as a `trust-task-error` before treating it as a plain HTTP failure (§4).
- Failures come as one sealed exception type. A `202` or `204` is reported as a duplicate the server already accepted, not as an error.
- `sendAck` handles fire-and-forget specs. An optional `responseVerifier` requires a verified proof on every response.
- Built on `package:http`, so it runs on the web and in Flutter.

## Server: `HttpsServer`
- Takes a plain `HttpsRequest` and returns an `HttpsReply`, so it isn't tied to one HTTP framework.
- `package:trust_tasks_https/io.dart` serves it with `dart:io`. It enforces the 256 KiB body limit on chunked bodies as they're read, and applies a 30-second request timeout. It's a separate library so the client keeps web support.
- Checks run in the same order as `trust-tasks-https/src/server.rs`, so both servers refuse a document for the same reason:
  1. Method, path, content type and body size.
  2. Parse, bearer token and route lookup.
  3. Identity, expiry and freshness.
  4. **Attribution gate:** a request with no recognised token and no proof is refused (§5).
  5. The DID-method pre-screen.
  6. `consumeInbound`: proof, spec policy, the duplicate-execution claim, then the handler.
- **Proofs are verified over the JSON as received.** Verifying the re-encoded typed document drops payload members the generated type doesn't model, which breaks valid signatures.
- Statuses follow §4. The identity-related codes all share 422. A contested identity with no authenticated sender gets the same answer as an unparseable body.
- Duplicates (§5.1):
  - A byte-for-byte resend gets the first response without running the handler again.
  - A refusal that isn't retryable is replayed with its original status.
  - A duplicate still executing gets 202; a fire-and-forget duplicate gets 204.
  - A different document under the same `id` is `idConflict` (409).
  - If the replay store can't be reached, the server fails closed with `unavailable` (503).
  - If the handler throws, the claim is released, so a resend runs again.
- `enableDiscovery()` answers `trust-task-discovery`, refuses unauthenticated callers unless `public: true`, and supports slug-pattern filters.
- Differences from Rust:
  - Discovery lists the routes at request time. Rust's `enable_discovery` takes a snapshot, so routes added later are missed.
  - Discovery reports `frameworkVersion` as `0.5`; the Rust registry still defaults to `0.2`.

## Interop (run, not assumed)
Using the Rust crate's own `server_demo` and `client_demo`, with `trust_tasks_proof` signing and verifying on the Dart side:

| Direction | Result |
|---|---|
| Dart client → Rust `server_demo`, signed `acl/grant` | ✓ response; the retry gets the same response and the handler runs once; a document whose signature no longer matches gets 422 `proofInvalid` |
| Rust `client_demo` → Dart server, signed `acl/grant` including optional `label` and `reason` | ✓ response |

## Tests
54 in total: carriage, identity and suppression, the attribution gate, proofs, all duplicate cases, discovery, the §4 status table, client response binding and error handling, and a real-socket round trip including the chunked-body limit.

## pana
150/160 on this branch. The only miss is the repository-URL check, which can't pass until the package is on `main`. Unlike `trust_tasks_proof`, this package doesn't depend on `ssi` and so avoids `pqcrypto`; documentation scores full marks. It supports all 6 platforms.

## Plumbing
- `dart.yml`: a new job runs the package's tests on SDK 3.3 and on stable.
- `publish.yml`: `trust_tasks_https` added to the tag and Release PR jobs.
- `publish-dart.yml`: new tag pattern and package case.
- `release-dart-pr.sh`: new package case.
- Website: the Dart HTTPS cell changes from ◐ `package:http` to ● `trust_tasks_https`.
- RELEASING.md, CLAUDE.md and GETTING-STARTED.md updated.
- Also corrects `trust_tasks_proof`'s pubspec description, which was written before `signTrustTask` existed. That will release as a `trust_tasks_proof` patch.

## After merge (maintainer)
1. Run `dart pub publish` from `trust-tasks-dart-https/`.
2. On pub.dev's Admin tab, enable GitHub Actions publishing with tag pattern `trust-tasks-dart-https-v{{version}}`.

title: ci: build all five implementations and gate on unexplained failures and regressions
body:
Adds `.github/workflows/conformance.yml`. It checks out affinidi-tdk-rs, vta-browser-plugin (tsp-js), affinidi-tsp-go and affinidi-tsp-dart next to the suite, builds every driver from source, and runs the full matrix.

- **Triggers:** push to `main`, pull requests, a weekly run, and `workflow_dispatch` with a ref input for each repo.
- **Seed:** the run id, so each run uses fresh keys and the report records the seed.
- **Gate:** a new runner option, `--gate known`, is non-zero in three cases:
  - a failure that no entry in `findings.toml` explains (a new disagreement);
  - a failure that matches a finding marked `fixed` (a regression);
  - a driver that did not build or start.

  `make run` keeps `--gate all`.
- **`findings.toml`:** three findings are now marked `fixed`: the XSCS body (#803/#249), the accepter's reply digest (#804) and accept correlation (#250). Findings that match nothing are printed as a note.
- **Outputs:** the job summary shows the report summary, and the report plus driver logs are uploaded as the `conformance-report` artifact.

Checked locally against the current merged code: 0 unexplained failures, exit 0. With affinidi-tsp built from a checkout that predates #804, the gate reports `REGRESSION (affinidi-accepter-forgets-reply-digest)` and exits 1.

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.21.1
body:
### Added

- **vta/backup**: Chunked transfer over Trust Tasks for DIDComm/TSP-only agents ([#474](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/474))

`vta/backup/*/1.0` required every descriptor to carry `transportUrl` and
  `transportToken`, so an agent reachable only over DIDComm or TSP could
  answer an export or import with nothing but `transportUnavailable`. This
  specifies the `chunkedTrustTask` algorithm the 1.0 prose anticipated.

  - `vta/backup/get-chunk/1.0` (client-pulled, non-consuming) and
    `vta/backup/put-chunk/1.0` (idempotent per index, checked against a
    pre-committed manifest).
  - `initiate-export/1.1` and `initiate-import/1.1`: the descriptor is a
    `oneOf` of the unchanged stream shape and a chunked shape carrying a
    manifest (chunkSize, chunkCount, per-chunk DigestMultibase) instead of
    an address and a bearer token. Released as a MINOR under SPEC §5.2's
    draft rule; a recipient must not return a chunked descriptor unless it
    was asked for one, so a stream exchange is wire-identical to 1.0.
  - `finalize-import/1.1`: completeness and whole-bundle integrity are
    checked before the password is used; adds `incompleteUpload` (with the
    missing indices, for resume) and `bundleDigestMismatch`.
  - `specs/vta/_shared/0.1/backup-transfer.schema.json` holds the shapes
    the four tasks share.

  The chunk-size ceiling is normative at 262144 bytes: the largest power
  of two whose chunk document survives base64url, DIDComm authcrypt and
  two nested forward wrappers under a 1 MiB mediator message limit.
  chunkCount is capped at 4096 so the manifest fits in one message too.

title: feat(dart-proof): Data Integrity proofs for Dart (trust_tasks_proof)
body:
Adds **`trust_tasks_proof`**, a new pub.dev package: W3C Data Integrity proofs for `package:trust_tasks`, built on Affinidi's `package:ssi`. It is the Dart counterpart of the Rust `trust-tasks-proof` crate. This is the first of the three Dart packages agreed (proof, then HTTPS, then DIDComm v2).

## What it does

- **`DataIntegrityProofVerifier`** plugs into `ProofPolicy.verify`. It handles `eddsa-jcs-2022` and `ecdsa-jcs-2019` (P-256, P-384) and checks the proof in the same order as the Rust crate:
  - the proof has the right shape;
  - the cryptosuite is allowed;
  - `created` is a timestamp with `Z` or an offset, at most 60s in the future;
  - **the proof is bound to the issuer**: the DID in `verificationMethod` must equal `issuer`;
  - the signature verifies.
- `verifyDetailed` explains a failure using the same categories as Rust (`malformedProof`, `issuerMismatch`, `unsupportedCryptosuite`, `signatureInvalid`). That detail is for logs only; the peer still gets a plain `proofInvalid`.
- `.forDidKey()` resolves keys locally with no network access. `.withResolver(r)` handles other DID methods.
- **`signTrustTask`** refuses to sign a document that could never verify (no issuer, or an issuer the key doesn't control). It builds the proof itself rather than calling ssi's generators, because ssi's generators wrote `created` without a timezone before 4.3.0.

## Interop (tested, not assumed)

| Direction | Result |
|---|---|
| Rust `trust-tasks-proof` signs → Dart verifies | ✓ committed fixture |
| Dart signs → Rust matches | ✓ same Ed25519 key, document and `created` give **the same `proofValue`, byte for byte** (test) |
| Dart signs → `affinidi-data-integrity` 0.7.11 verifies | ✓ eddsa-jcs-2022, ✓ ecdsa-jcs-2019 P-256, ✗ P-384 (the Rust crate only allows P-256 for that suite; noted in the README) |

## Dependency range

`ssi: ">=3.9.6 <5.0.0"` covers two major versions on purpose. `package:didcomm` requires ssi 3, so a package that needed ssi 4 could never be installed alongside the upcoming DIDComm transport. CI runs the tests with ssi pinned to 3.9.6 as well as with whatever version pub picks. The minimum is 3.9.6 because ssi 3.9.0–3.9.5 no longer compile against `x25519` 0.1.2. No ML-DSA support, because those verifiers only exist in ssi 4.

## Release plumbing, generalised to multiple Dart packages

- `dart.yml`: new `packages` job covering proof on SDK 3.6, on stable, and on stable with ssi 3.9.6.
- `publish.yml`: `tag-dart` and `release-dart-pr` now run once per package, one at a time, core first. Before tagging, `tag-dart` removes `pubspec_overrides.yaml` with `git rm`, so each release is checked against the **published** `trust_tasks`. A plain `rm` makes the publish dry run exit 65.
- `publish-dart.yml`: accepts both tag patterns, picks the package directory from the tag, and **does nothing if that version is already on pub.dev**. That stops a hand-published first version from turning into a failed run.
- `scripts/release-dart-pr.sh <package>`: tested in a sandbox clone for both packages. Proof moves only `version:`; core still moves `version:` and `packageVersion`. That test caught and fixed a top-level `return` in the inline Node code.
- Website: the Dart "Data Integrity verifier" cell changes from ◐ `ssi` to ● `trust_tasks_proof`.
- RELEASING.md, CLAUDE.md and GETTING-STARTED.md are updated.

## After merge (needs a maintainer)

1. Run `dart pub publish` from `trust-tasks-dart-proof/`. pub.dev only accepts a brand-new package from a user, not from CI.
2. On the package's Admin tab, enable publishing from GitHub Actions for `trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf` with tag pattern `trust-tasks-dart-proof-v{{version}}`.

## Known score ceiling

pana scores this **150/160** once merged. The repository-URL check can only pass once this is on `main`. The documentation check fails because `pqcrypto` 0.4.1, a third-party dependency of ssi 4, ships a `dartdoc_options.yaml` that points at a file it doesn't publish. That breaks dartdoc for every package that depends on it; `ssi` loses the same 10 points on pub.dev. It can only be fixed upstream.

title: feat(sdk)!: type rate-limit refusals and say who sent them
body:
## Problem

When a did:webvh host rate-limits a resolver (HTTP 429), the resolver gets `DIDWebVHError::NetworkError { status_code: Some(429), .. }` and turns it into `ResolverError::ResolutionFailed(String)`, which becomes `DIDCacheError::DIDError(String)`. The status is lost on the way. Consumers such as the VTA/CLI and the mediator can't tell "the host rate-limited us" apart from "the DID is invalid", so operators see confusing errors. did:web and did:scid (vh) lost the status the same way.

The single-flight made this worse. It shared successes only, so when the leader failed, each waiter became the next leader and fetched again. N concurrent resolutions of a rate-limited DID sent the host N requests, one after another.

## Change

- **`affinidi-did-resolver-traits` 0.1.4**: adds `ResolverError::NetworkFetch(NetworkFetchError)`. `NetworkFetchError { url: Option<String>, status: Option<u16>, message }` is `#[non_exhaustive]`, so a `retry_after` field can be added later without a breaking release. It has builder methods and `is_rate_limited()`. The error text reads `DID host <url> rate-limited resolution (HTTP 429)`.
- **`affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk` 0.8.38**:
  - Adds `DIDCacheError::NetworkFetch(NetworkFetchError)` (re-exported from `errors`) and makes `DIDCacheError` `Clone`.
  - did:webvh `NetworkError`, did:scid's wrapped `NetworkError`, did:web `ResolutionFailed { status, url }` and did:web `Http` now map to `NetworkFetch`. A body read that fails after a 200 records `status: None`.
  - Single-flight (new `single_flight.rs`, used by both the DID map and the agent-name map): waiters now get the leader's error instead of fetching again. The error is not cached. Leadership is released on drop.
  - **Also fixed:** before, a cancelled leader (a caller's `timeout(...)` around `resolve`) left its map entry behind with a closed channel. Every later resolution of that DID then spun on it without yielding. `cancelled_leader_does_not_wedge_later_resolutions` holds this.

## Semver

Both enums are already `#[non_exhaustive]`, so the new variants don't break compilation. These are patch bumps per ADR 0003.

**The behaviour does change:** these fetch failures used to be `DIDError`, and their message text is different now. The CHANGELOG calls this out.

## Not typed yet (documented in the CHANGELOG)

- **`Retry-After`:** neither `didwebvh-rs` 0.7 (`download_file` returns only the status) nor `affinidi-did-web` keeps response headers.
- **Network mode:** the cache server sends errors to clients as text, so they still arrive as `TransportError(String)`. Fixing that needs a websocket protocol change.
- **did:webs and did:ebsi:** they build the status into their own error strings, so their failures are still `DIDError`.

## Tests

- `tests/network_fetch_errors.rs`: a loopback server answers did:webvh requests with 429 or 404. The tests check the typed error and its text. They also run 8 concurrent resolutions and check that **exactly 1** request reaches the host, then that a later resolution fetches again.
- I confirmed both regression tests fail against the previous logic: the concurrency test saw 8 requests instead of 1, and the cancellation test hit its 5s timeout.
- Unit tests cover the mapping helpers and `NetworkFetchError`.

## Verification (local)

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: clean.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` (with `RUSTFLAGS="-D warnings --cfg tracing_unstable"`): clean.
- cache-sdk clippy with `local`, `local,did-scid` and `local,network,did-webvh`, no default features: clean.
- `cargo clippy -p affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk --all-features` fails on an **existing** `collapsible_if` at `lib.rs:519` (`resolve_shortcuts`). This PR doesn't touch that line, and CI doesn't run that build.
- Tests pass for cache-sdk (default, `--all-features`, and `agent-names,network`), resolver-traits, cache-server, tdk-common and tdk-test-support, all with `--locked`.
- `check-version-bumps.sh`, `check-changelogs.sh` and `check-workspace-duplicates.sh` all pass.
- `Cargo.lock` also picks up the `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.26.1 entry, which was already bumped on main but missing from the lock.

title: feat(sdk)!: type rate-limit refusals and say who sent them (#1511)
body:
feat(sdk)!: type rate-limit refusals and say who sent them (#1511)

A 429 became VtaError::Other("429: Too Many Requests"), with no hint and
the Retry-After header discarded; through the boxed session auth path it
became VtaError::Auth, telling the operator to re-authenticate.

Add VtaError::RateLimited { limited_by, retry_after, limiter, url } with a
non_exhaustive RateLimitSource (Vta, Vtc, Mediator, DidHost, Upstream) read
from the x-rate-limit-source header; an unlabelled 429 is Upstream (proxy,
load balancer, or older VTA). Every VTA HTTP status mapping in the SDK now
reads headers. idempotent retries a rate limit whose wait fits
MAX_RETRY_AFTER and surfaces a longer one at once. The CLI renders who
refused, how long to wait, and which knob to turn; every key name lives in
vta_sdk::rate_limit.

Breaking: new variant on VtaError, and from_http maps 429 to RateLimited.

title: fix(tsp-js): resolveAccept, so an accept for an invite never sent is not adopted
body:
This PR targets `feat/tsp-rev2-rev3-dual-handler`, like #249.

`tsp-js` ships its relationship rules as pure functions, but none of them compared an accept's Digest with the invite we sent. `transition(pending, "receiveAccept")` only sees the state, so a client that relied on the library's rules would adopt an accept for an invite it never sent (§7.2.2).

- **tsp-js:** new `resolveAccept(state, answeredDigest, ourInviteDigest)` returns `adopt` or `ignore`, mirroring `resolveCancel`. It is exported, and the README and CHANGELOG are updated.
- **core:** `ensureRelationship` already made this check inline, so the wallet was not affected. It now calls `resolveAccept`, and a new test covers an accept that names the wrong digest.

This was found by the cross-implementation TSP Rev 3 conformance suite, where it failed in 5 cases. With this branch, the suite's relationship cases pass across all 5 implementations (250/250).

- core `tests/tsp.*.mjs`: 33 pass.

title: fix(tsp-js): refuse an XSCS/XCTL body that is not exactly one Bytes primitive
body:
This PR targets `feat/tsp-rev2-rev3-dual-handler`, where Rev 3 lives; it isn't on `main` yet.

`decodePayloadFrame` read an XSCS/XCTL body as its first primitive. It dropped anything else in the `-A##` stream without an error and ignored data after the stream.

The body must now be an `-A##` stream that ends the payload frame and holds exactly one Bytes primitive. That is the form used by the spec's vectors and the ToIP reference (`tsp_sdk` 0.11). Everything else throws: an `-H##` group, a second primitive, or trailing data.

Context: [tswg-tsp-specification#77](https://github.com/trustoverip/tswg-tsp-specification/issues/77). Found by the cross-implementation TSP Rev 3 conformance suite.

title: fix(dart): take trust_tasks to 160/160 on pub.dev
body:
pub.dev scored the published `trust_tasks` 0.1.0 at **140/160**. Two specific deductions, both fixed.

## `-10` "The package description is too long."

196 characters against pub.dev's 60–180 window (search results only render the first part, which is why it scores as a failed pubspec check rather than a style note). Now **148**, with the window recorded in a comment so the next edit doesn't silently fall outside it.

## `-10` "No example found."

Adds `example/main.dart` — runnable, not illustrative. It decodes an inbound document, runs it through `consumeInbound` against the generated `acl/grant` policy, and delivers it three times to show both halves of SPEC §7.2 item 11:

```
first delivery    : handled -> https://trusttasks.org/spec/acl/grant/0.1#response
identical resend  : duplicate (already executed, inFlight=false)
escalated resend  : rejected -> idConflict
handler ran 1 time(s) — the effect happened exactly once.
```

Making it runnable is what caught a bug in it: the first draft omitted the proof `acl/grant` declares REQUIRED, so all three deliveries returned `proofRequired` and the "example" demonstrated a rejection instead of the pipeline.

## Verified with the real scorer

`pana` 0.23.19 — the analyzer pub.dev runs — against this branch:

```
## ✓ Follow Dart file conventions (30 / 30)
### [*] 10/10 points: Provide a valid `pubspec.yaml`      ← was 0
## ✓ Provide documentation (20 / 20)
### [*] 10/10 points: Package has an example              ← was 0
## ✓ Platform support (20 / 20)
## ✓ Pass static analysis (50 / 50)
## ✓ Support up-to-date dependencies (40 / 40)
Points: 160/160.
```

title: feat(site): list all four client libraries with a capability matrix
body:
`/implementations` was titled **"trust-tasks for Rust."** and described one library. Accurate when Rust was the only one; once TypeScript, Go and Dart shipped it became a nav entry labelled "Implementations" pointing at a page about a single implementation — and a developer browsing trusttasks.org had no way to discover the other three existed.

## What changed

- **`/implementations`** is now the index across all four libraries, with a capability matrix.
- **`/implementations/rust`** is the Rust crate-by-crate walkthrough, linked from the index.
- **`website/assets/libraries.js`** — new hand-maintained registry of the libraries and what each supports.
- **`checkLibraryRegistry()`** in `scripts/build-registry.mjs` — so this list cannot rot like the others have.

## The matrix is the point

"Which languages are there" is a list. "Can I do TSP from Dart" is the question a reader actually arrives with, and until now the honest answer — **transport bindings ship in Rust only** — was discoverable solely by reading the source tree.

Core rows are uniform across all four because `check-bindings` makes them so. The transport rows are where the libraries genuinely differ, and each ticked cell names the package behind it:

| | Rust | TypeScript | Go | Dart |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Core (types, §7.2, schemas, freshness, replay, errors) | ● | ● | ● | ● |
| Transport seam | ● | ● | ● | ● |
| TSP / HTTPS / DIDComm v2 / DIDComm v1 | ● | — | — | — |
| Push | — | — | — | — |
| Data Integrity verifier · capability client | ● | — | — | — |

A dash means the library doesn't *ship* that capability, not that it's unreachable — the page says so explicitly, because the `ProofVerifier` seam being unfilled is a deliberate design choice rather than a gap.

## A guard, because this is the fifth hand-maintained list

`CLAUDE.md` documents this failure mode four times over (`data.js` categories, `spec.meta.schema.json` slugs, `bindings.js` bindings, binding prose). This list makes the strongest claim of any of them — it tells someone choosing a language what they can build — so it gets a guard with three rules, each tamper-tested:

1. A library's `dir`, and every package it names under `transports`, must exist in the tree.
2. A `binding:*` capability must name the package providing it — no unverifiable ticks.
3. Every binding under `bindings/<slug>/` must have a matrix row (the `checkBindingRegistry()` guarantee, applied here).

Each failure names the fix. Rule 3 currently catches `push`, which has a row and no implementation anywhere — rendered honestly as a full row of dashes.

## No version numbers, deliberately

Every install line uses its registry's own "latest" idiom (`cargo add`, `npm install`, `go get`, `dart pub add`). The ecosystem entry this replaces claimed *"Tracking framework 0.2 (0.2.x crate line)"* while the workspace was at **0.21** — a list that cannot state a version cannot state a stale one. Same fix removes a pinned `= "0.2"` Cargo snippet from the Rust page.

## Also corrects the Rust page's arithmetic

Stale since `didcomm-v1` landed: it claimed "seven crates" and "three transport bindings" and rendered six cards. Nine crates publish — the facade, `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` and `trust-tasks-ceremony` were all missing.

## Verified

Loaded in a browser against the local server, not just built:

- both routes render; nav tab stays lit on the deep dive
- `§7.2` / `§8.1` references linkify; binding rows link to their binding specs
- console clean, no errors
- `npm run build` and `npm run validate` pass

title: Structural issues in categorization of DTG credentials
body:
In reviewing @martipos PR https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/16, I realized we have an issue with spec as currently structured in Working Draft 01. 

We refer to "three functional categories" of DTG creds because at the proposal stage, we actually had three categories (with multiple members in each category). However, once we realized we only needed one verifiable invitation credential (VIC), we don't actually have three categories, only two:

1. Edge Credentials (VRCs and VMCs) 
2. Annotation Credentials (VWCs, VPCs, VECs)

Fixing this would also address the editorial issue that section "8. Invitation Credentials" currently only has just one subsection, "8.1. VIC (Verifiable Invitation Credential)". As a general rule, a spec should never have a section with only one subsection.

My proposed fix:

1. Move what is currently (in Working Draft 01) section "9. Annotation Credentials" to become the new section 8 (so it immediately follows section "7. Edge Credentials"). That way we cover the two categories of DTG credentials first in sections 7 and 8.
2. Change what is currently section "8. Invitation Credentials" to become the new section 9.
3. Change the name to "9. VIC (Verifiable Invitation Credential)".
4. Just include in section 9 the content of what is currently section 8.1.

title: docs(dart): record what the first pub.dev publish attempt actually did
body:
Two corrections to `RELEASING.md`, both from **observing** the release that #470 triggered rather than reasoning about it.

## 1. `RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN` is set

This file said "**Not currently set**", and I repeated that when describing the Dart release path — including a warning that the release tag would not trigger the publish workflow.

That is wrong. `tag-dart` pushed `trust-tasks-dart-v0.1.0` and `publish-dart.yml` **did** trigger, which the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot cause. The no-PAT warning in `tag-dart` did not fire, confirming the PAT was used.

## 2. The first version really must be published by hand — with evidence

The claim was previously an inference from the pub.dev docs. It is now observed. The tag triggered `publish-dart.yml`, which ran the entire pipeline correctly:

```
Publishing trust_tasks 0.1.0 to https://pub.dev:
...
Total compressed archive size: 853 KB.
Validating package...
Uploading...
Message from server: Only users are allowed to upload new packages.
```

Dry run clean, archive validated, upload attempted, refused only at the new-package gate. **Nothing was published and nothing is broken** — a Dart tag is an anchor, not a publication, unlike a Go one.

## 3. A consequence worth knowing before anyone tries to verify the automation

`trust-tasks-dart-v0.1.0` now exists, and pub.dev will not accept a second upload of a version it already has. So once `0.1.0` is published by hand, re-pushing that tag proves nothing — the first release the automation performs end to end will be **`0.1.1`**.

Docs only; no behaviour change.

## Still outstanding for a maintainer

1. `dart pub publish` from `trust-tasks-dart/`, signed in as a user.
2. Enable automated publishing on the package's Admin tab: repository `trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`, tag pattern `trust-tasks-dart-v{{version}}`.

title: feat(dart): Dart bindings and SPEC §7.2 runtime for Trust Tasks
body:
Adds **`trust-tasks-dart`**, published to pub.dev as **`trust_tasks`** — the fourth reference implementation alongside `trust-tasks-rs`, `@openvtc/trust-tasks` and `trust-tasks-go`.

Scoped to parity with the Go and TypeScript packages: generated types, the §7.2 pipeline, conformance tests, drift CI and release automation. No transport bindings — see the note at the end.

## What is here

| | |
|---|---|
| `scripts/build-dart-bindings.mjs` | emits one self-contained Dart library per schema; runs `dart format` on its own output |
| `trust-tasks-dart/lib/specs/**` | 509 generated libraries |
| `trust-tasks-dart/lib/src/runtime/**` | hand-written: envelope, §7.2 pipeline, §8.3/§8.5 codes, JCS canonicalization + SHA-256, freshness, replay guard, transport seam |
| `trust-tasks-dart/test/` | 74 tests mirroring the Go and TypeScript suites, plus a smoke test over a *generated* library |
| `.github/workflows/dart.yml` | drift, analyze + format, test — matrixed over Dart 3.3 (the declared floor) and stable |
| `scripts/release-dart-pr.sh`, `tag-dart`, `publish-dart.yml` | the publishing half |

`dart analyze --fatal-infos` is clean across all 509 generated libraries plus the runtime — the generated tree is held to the same lint bar as hand-written code, with no exclusions. `dart pub publish --dry-run` reports 0 warnings.

## Cross-language conformance

`npm run check-bindings` is now **four-way**:

```
Bindings conformance: 442 specifications checked against 442 TypeScript,
437 Rust, 442 Go and 442 Dart modules — all agree.
```

863 policy blocks and 863 schema documents compared, zero disagreements. As with Go, the `$ref` inliner and the policy derivation are **independent implementations** rather than imports, for the reason the file headers give — sharing them would reduce the comparison to asserting a resolver agrees with itself. Verified by tampering: a flipped policy flag and an altered schema description are both caught and both sides named.

The check also now asserts that `version:` in `pubspec.yaml` and `packageVersion` in `lib/src/runtime/version.dart` agree. **Not hypothetical** — the first draft of the rewrite in `release-dart-pr.sh` used a regex that could not match a version containing dots, so it silently rewrote nothing. Caught before it shipped; the guard stops it recurring.

## Three decisions specific to Dart

**The package library exports the runtime only.** Dart's `export` is flat — there is no `export * as Foo` — so exporting 500 generated libraries from one barrel would collide on the first shared `Ext`. A consumer imports one specification directly and prefixes it. Please don't "fix" this in review by adding spec exports to the barrel.

**Closed value sets are `extension type`s over `String`, not `enum`s.** A Dart `enum` *throws* on a value it does not know, so a peer on a newer MINOR would crash the parse — squarely against SPEC §5.2's forward-compatibility requirement. An extension type is zero-cost, erases to `String`, keeps `==` and the named constants, and carries an unrecognised value through. This puts Dart with Rust's `#[non_exhaustive]` and Go's named string type; TypeScript's closed union remains the one side where adding a standard code is breaking.

**The outcome type is a sealed hierarchy**, so a `switch` over it is exhaustive and the compiler names a missing case. Safe to close because outcomes are produced by this library and never parsed from a peer — unlike the wire values in `codes.dart`.

Dart also gets one thing right that Go needed a workaround for: a nullable `List<String>?` distinguishes absent from present-and-empty natively, so `acl`'s `allowedKeys` needs no pointer-to-slice trick. `test/smoke_test.dart` pins it.

## Publishing — needs two one-time manual steps

pub.dev only accepts an automated publish when the workflow run was **triggered by a tag push**, which it verifies in the OIDC token's claims. So unlike the other three there is no publishing from the push-to-`main` trigger: `tag-dart` verifies and tags, and `publish-dart.yml` — triggered by that tag — publishes via the Dart team's reusable workflow.

Before the first automated release:

1. **Publish `trust_tasks` 0.1.0 by hand** — `dart pub publish` from `trust-tasks-dart/`, signed in as a publisher. A package that does not exist yet has no Admin tab to configure, so this one cannot be automated.
2. **Enable automated publishing** on the package's Admin tab: repository `trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`, tag pattern `trust-tasks-dart-v{{version}}`.

> ⚠️ A tag pushed by the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` does **not** trigger a workflow. Without `RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN` set, the release tag lands and nothing publishes. `tag-dart` warns explicitly when that happens, and the fix is to re-push the tag from a workstation.

I have not touched pub.dev or pushed any tag.

## On transports, and what this means for scope

The Affinidi Dart TDK covers more than I expected, and the gap is specific:

| binding | Dart |
|---|---|
| proof (Data Integrity) | ✅ `ssi` 4.2.0 — JCS, `eddsa-jcs-2022`, ML-DSA-44 |
| DIDComm v2 | ✅ `didcomm` 2.3.4 + `affinidi_tdk_didcomm_mediator_client` |
| HTTPS | ✅ `package:http` |
| **TSP** | ❌ nothing in the 38-package set |

So Dart transports are a realistic next PR for three of the four, but TSP — which `ecosystem.js` calls the *preferred* binding — has no Dart implementation to wrap. Worth deciding deliberately rather than discovering later.

## Checks run locally

- `npm run build-dart-bindings` — idempotent, `dart format`-clean
- `dart analyze --fatal-infos` — no issues (509 generated + runtime + tests)
- `dart format --set-exit-if-changed .` — 0 changed
- `dart test` — 74 passing
- `dart pub publish --dry-run` — 0 warnings
- `npm run check-bindings` — 442 specs, four languages, all agree
- `npm run validate` — 442 specs, 72 shared schemas

* fix(dart): make generated formatting deterministic and keep the 3.3 floor

Two CI failures on the Dart jobs, both real.

`dart format` picks its style from the code's language version, which it infers
from the enclosing package's *resolved* config in `.dart_tool/`. With no
resolution it falls back to the newest version it knows, and since Dart 3.13
that selects the new "tall" style. So the generator produced differently
formatted output depending on whether anyone had run `dart pub get` — passing

check derives the same value the same way, so neither depends on ambient state.

unresolvable. The package's own floor is 3.3 because that is the release that
introduced extension types, which the generated closed-value types use; a dev
dependency must not narrow what consumers can build against. Dart 3.3 is Flutter
3.19 and 3.5 is Flutter 3.24, so the difference is not academic. Took
`lints: ^4` instead.

title: test(tsp): drive a Trust Task through a running VTA over TSP
body:
Follow-up to #1507, which fixed a TSP defect nothing could have caught.

## The gap

Every TSP test in `tests/e2e` stops **below** the VTA:

| test | what it proves |
|---|---|
| `tsp_round_trip` | the mediator routes a frame between two accounts |
| `tsp_dual_leg` | one socket carries both protocols |
| `tsp_binding_pair` | the envelope survives a round trip |
| `tsp_ping_correlation` | a probe measures its own reply |

The VTA-side unit tests are their mirror image: `tsp_inbound::dispatch_one` is
exercised with a `{}` body that never reaches a handler, and asserts only that
*some* reply envelope comes back.

So the join between them — a real Trust Task, dispatched by a running VTA,
answered over the same mediator socket — was covered from both sides and by
nothing. #1507 is what that cost: the VTA sealed its outbound TSP frames on a
profile built with no mediator, so every send died inside the SDK with
`Config error: No Mediator is configured for this Profile`, while inbound replies
kept working (they seal on a different profile). The VTA looked healthy right up
until it had to start a conversation.

## What this adds

`tests/e2e/tests/tsp_vta_trust_task.rs`, on `MockVta::start_with_transports` — a
whole VTA on an embedded `TestMediator`, hermetic, no network, so it runs in CI
unignored.

- **`a_tsp_sealed_secret_is_unsealed_by_a_running_vta`** — the headline. Seals a
  `VaultSecret` to the VTA as a TSP Direct message, carries it inside a signed
  `vault/upsert/0.3` sent over TSP, and asserts the entry was **created** and
  **attributed to the proven sender VID** — not merely that no error came back.

  This is the assertion `trust_tasks::vault::tsp_unseal_tests` says outright it
  cannot make: *"the unpack-success path needs runtime verification against a
  real TSP message."* That path had never run since it was added in #594,
  because the profile it used could not unseal either — `TspOps::unpack_bytes`
  calls `ATMProfile::dids()`, which has no answer without a mediator.

- **`an_unauthorized_sender_is_refused_over_tsp_not_met_with_silence`** — asserts
  `permissionDenied` specifically, so a `malformedRequest` (never reached the
  authorization check) fails. `dispatch_one`'s unit test proves the refusal is
  *built*; this proves it is sealed, routed and delivered. A refusal that cannot
  be sent is indistinguishable, from the client, from being ignored — which is
  the shape #1507 actually produced.

- **`the_reply_threads_to_the_request_that_asked_for_it`** — the mediator inbox
  is durable and flushes on connect, so "a frame arrived" is weaker than it
  looks; `tsp_ping_correlation` documents a health probe that passed on a
  previous run's backlog.

## Falsified, not assumed

Reintroducing the mediator-less reply profile in `handle_tsp` fails all three
with the production error verbatim:

```
WARN vta_service::messaging::service: failed to send TSP reply
  recipient=did:key:z6Mku… error=Config error: No Mediator is configured for this Profile

test a_tsp_sealed_secret_is_unsealed_by_a_running_vta ... FAILED
test an_unauthorized_sender_is_refused_over_tsp_not_met_with_silence ... FAILED
test the_reply_threads_to_the_request_that_asked_for_it ... FAILED
```

## Harness change

`MockVta::register_mediator_account` — the one addition. A counterparty needs a
mediator account **and** an ACL grant, and they are different permissions in
different places: the mediator decides who may connect and be routed to, the VTA
decides what they may ask for. Without the account the VTA's reply is accepted by
the mediator and then dropped, which looks exactly like the VTA not answering.

`tests/e2e` gains `vta-service/transport-harness` and `trust-tasks-rs`.

## Four preconditions worth knowing

Each refuses the request before any handler runs, and none is obvious from the
call site. All four are recorded in the test's comments:

1. **`issuedAt` is mandatory** — SPEC §7.2, it bounds the duplicate-execution
   record. Omitting it is a cheap way to write a test that looks like it
   exercises a handler and never reaches one.
2. **`recipient` must be in-band** — "specification declares recipient REQUIRED
   but the document carries no in-band recipient".
3. **The task declares `proof` REQUIRED, and TSP's sender proof does not
   substitute for it.** The transport proves who sealed the frame; the
   Data-Integrity proof binds the document. The spine wants both.
4. **The wire `SiteTarget` discriminator is camelCase** (`webOrigin`). The
   internal `vti_common::vault::SiteTarget` is kebab, and that is *not* a
   mismatch — `trust_tasks::wire_v0_2` translates at the boundary. Schema
   validation runs on the wire document, so a kebab `kind` is refused as
   `malformedRequest` and never reaches a handler, which reads like a handler
   bug and is not one.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast`
  — **123 targets, 4375 tests, 0 failures** (was 122/4351)
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean

Tests only; no production code changes beyond the `pub` test-support helper.

test(tsp): drive a Trust Task through a running VTA over TSP (#1508)

Every TSP test in `tests/e2e` stopped below the VTA — `tsp_round_trip` proves

title: docs(go): the Go module seeds its own release tag
body:
Corrects guidance I added in #468, which was wrong about an operation that cannot be undone.

`RELEASING.md` told a reader to hand-seed `trust-tasks-go/v<version>` alongside the crate and npm anchors, and `scripts/release-go-pr.sh` said the same in its error message.

## Why it was wrong

`publish-go` does not measure from a prior tag the way `release-go-pr` does. It reads `const Version`, asks whether `trust-tasks-go/v<Version>` exists, and writes it when it does not — so the first push to `main` carrying the module publishes it **and** writes the anchor in one step. `release-go-pr` runs `needs: publish-go`, so by the time it looks there is always a tag.

That is exactly what happened on #468: `publish-go` verified the tree, pushed `trust-tasks-go/v0.1.0` at the merge commit, and `release-go-pr` then correctly reported nothing to release. All six jobs in `publish.yml` were green.

## Why it mattered

Hand-tagging is not merely unnecessary here, it is the riskier path:

- a Go tag **is** the publication — `proxy.golang.org` caches it permanently and it cannot be retracted, only superseded;
- tagging from a local checkout skips the `go build` / `go vet` / `go test` that `publish-go` runs *before* it tags.

So the old instructions pointed at a manual, unverified route to an irreversible action.

## Changes

- `RELEASING.md` — drops the Go tag from the one-time seeding block, adds a short section explaining why there is nothing to seed and why hand-tagging is wrong.
- `scripts/release-go-pr.sh` — the "no tag exists" error now says to re-run `publish-go` rather than to seed by hand, and explains why.
- `CLAUDE.md` — one-line correction to the pointer at RELEASING.md.

Docs only; no behaviour change.

## Verified against the live module

```
$ go get github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/trust-tasks-go@v0.1.0
go: added ...trust-tasks-go v0.1.0

runtime version:   0.1.0
first delivery:    handled
  response type:   https://trusttasks.org/spec/acl/grant/0.1#response
identical resend:  duplicate (§7.2 item 11)
```
