title: feat(vtc): browse the recognition graph, from either side of it
body:
feat(vtc): browse the recognition graph, from either side of it

#1493 added `GET /v1/registry/records` and its client and left the table
unwritten. This is the table: a **Trust records** card that enumerates the
graph from the registry, or from what this community believes it published.

The two views are a toggle rather than two cards, because the useful act is
switching between them — the drift summary above says *that* they disagree, and
this says *how*.

- A registry read is a live round trip every time and the card is not polled.
  The specification forbids serving that view from a cache, so an unreachable
  registry is an error here rather than a quietly substituted list, and a page
  left open must not become steady load on a third party. Refresh is deliberate.
- The assertion column has three states. `recognized` and `authorized` each
  appear only on the record type that carries them, and an absent one means the
  record makes no such assertion — not `false`. Rendering "not authorised"
  against a recognition record would invent a refusal the registry never made.

Also fixes two spans I shipped unstyled in #1489 and #1493. Both used a bare
`warn` class, and `.warn` exists only scoped — `.finding.warn`,
`.stat-tile-foot.warn`, `.vet-note.warn` — so neither rendered. The drift row's
direction, which is the field that decides which way an operator acts, was
plain text indistinguishable from the benign case; the failed job's
`unsupportedType` tell likewise. Both now use `.chip`, which is what this
console uses for status in a table.

The chip is also better than what was intended. Colouring 200 characters of
registry error text says "something here is bad" without saying what; a
"version skew" chip beside it names the one reading that changes what an
operator does next.

## `vta-sdk`

## [0.38.2](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-sdk-v0.38.1...vta-sdk-v0.38.2) — 2026-09-15 ### Added - **vtc**: Retry and discard a failed sync job from the console ([#1493](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1493)) The queue became visible in #1487 and comparable against the registry in #1489, and in both the answer to "so fix it" was: stop the daemon and run a CLI. The mutation could not be a route, because binding a `spec/vtc/registry/…` Trust Task URI ahead of its upstream specification is what `trust_task_manifest.rs` refuses. trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#460 specified the family and trust-tasks-rs 0.20.6 publishes it, so the four tasks bind and the buttons work: - `GET /v1/registry/sync-jobs` `…/sync-jobs/list/0.1` - `POST /v1/registry/sync-jobs/retry` `…/sync-jobs/retry/0.1` - `POST /v1/registry/sync-jobs/discard` `…/sync-jobs/discard/0.1` - `GET /v1/registry/records` `…/records/list/0.1` The offline `vtc sync-jobs` CLI stays. It is the break-glass path for a daemon that will not start, which is exactly when an HTTP route is no use, and both surfaces go through `sync_jobs_cli::requeue` and the same eligibility rule, so "only a Failed row may move" is written once. Where the two deliberately differ is in how they refuse. Retry *reports* an ineligible row (`skipped`, with `notFailed` or `notFound`) rather than failing, so one row the reconciler picked up cannot defeat a bulk retry, and a job swept between the page load and the click is an ordinary race. Discard *raises* 409/404, because the request names exactly one job and there is no partial outcome to describe. Bulk retry is `allFailed: true` rather than an omitted `jobId` — a client bug that drops the identifier must not become a bulk operation — and discard has no bulk form at all. Two census gates caught real defects on the way, both worth recording: - `generated_wire_types_census` rejected the two query structs I had written by hand. It was right: they restated `…/list/0.1`'s payload. The handlers now take the generated `Payload` as the `Query` extractor, and the OpenAPI parameters are declared inline rather than derived from a mirror. - `every_bound_published_uri_has_a_witness` required a conformance fixture per bound URI. Added four, transcribed from what the handlers build — including that a failed job carries no `nextAttemptAt`, because it has no schedule and claiming one would be the response asserting something untrue. Every `#[non_exhaustive]` generated enum is matched with an explicit refusal rather than a catch-all that guesses. A future spec release naming a fourth retry target must not be silently read as one of the existing two. ### Fixed - **tsp**: Every client seals Trust Tasks in the binding envelope ([#1488](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1488)) #1478 gave the VTA's TSP receiver the published `trust-tasks-tsp` binding and cut the browser wallet over with it. Every Rust client kept sealing the bare document, so the VTA refused all of them: refused a TSP frame that is not a binding envelope reason=TSP payload is not a `…/binding/tsp/0.1/envelope` envelope (got `…/spec/messaging/ping/0.1`) A TSP trust ping, and `keys/export-secret/0.1` from openvtc, are the two that were reported; the cause is one missing call, in the send funnels every TSP client in this workspace goes through — `TspSession::send_document` (so `announce`, `request`, and the mobile approver), `DIDCommSession:: send_tsp_document` (so `request_tsp`, so every `VtaClient` trust task on TSP), and the two `TspPingSession` probes behind `pnm health`.
## `vti-secrets`
## [0.3.8](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vti-secrets-v0.3.7...vti-secrets-v0.3.8) — 2026-09-15 ### Fixed - **deps**: Bound aws-smithy-types below 1.7, which breaks aws-smithy-json 0.63 ([#1485](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1485)) A fresh dependency resolution stopped compiling: error[E0308]: expected `DocumentObject`, found `HashMap` --> aws-smithy-json-0.63.0/src/codec/deserializer.rs:707:37 error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `&_` not covered --> aws-smithy-json-0.63.0/src/serialize.rs:36:15 `aws-smithy-types` 1.7.0 changed `Document::Object` from `HashMap` to a new `DocumentObject`, and added a variant to an enum that is `#[non_exhaustive]` — a breaking change shipped as a MINOR bump. `aws-smithy-json` 0.63.0 declares `aws-smithy-types = "^1.6.1"`, which admits 1.7.0 and then does not compile against it. Cargo unifies `aws-smithy-types` to one version across the graph but keeps both `aws-smithy-json` 0.63 and 0.64 — 0.x minors are incompatible majors — so the two coexist and only the 0.63 copy breaks. We have both because `aws-sdk-secretsmanager` 1.116.0 moved to json `^0.64.0` while `aws-config` 1.12.0, its newest release, still wants `^0.63.0`. Both reach us: `vti-secrets` behind `aws-secrets`, and `vta-tee` unconditionally, so a plain `cargo build --workspace` is affected as well as the secrets path. Cargo.lock already held 1.6.3, so committed builds were never affected and only a lockless resolution broke — which is what `cargo install --path` does unless given `--locked`. That is how this was met: cargo install --path vtc-service --no-default-features \ --features setup,website,admin-ui,aws-secrets,tsp `--locked` remains the right flag for a reproducible install. This bound is what keeps `cargo update` and a lockless build honest too. The bound is declared once in `[workspace.dependencies]` with the reasoning, and referenced from the two crates that pull `aws-config` — Cargo only honours a version requirement from a crate that declares it, so a workspace entry alone would constrain nothing. Neither crate calls it. `>= 1.6.1, < 1.7` rather than `= 1.6.3`: 1.6.1 is aws-smithy-json 0.63.0's own floor, and the upper bound excludes the break without freezing out patch releases in the working line. **Remove it when `aws-config` ships a release on json 0.64.** Verified, on this branch: - without the bound, a lockless resolve picks aws-smithy-types 1.7.0 with aws-smithy-json 0.63.0 AND 0.64.0 — the failing combination - with it, a lockless resolve picks 1.6.3, json 0.63.0 alone, and backs aws-sdk-secretsmanager off to 1.115.0 - Cargo.lock moves by two lines, both dependency edges; no version churn - `cargo check -p vti-secrets --no-default-features --features aws-secrets` and `cargo check -p vtc-service --no-default-features --features setup,website,admin-ui,aws-secrets,tsp` both pass

## [0.28.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-service-v0.27.1...vta-service-v0.28.0) — 2026-09-15 ### Fixed - **tsp**: Every client seals Trust Tasks in the binding envelope ([#1488](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1488)) #1478 gave the VTA's TSP receiver the published `trust-tasks-tsp` binding and cut the browser wallet over with it. title: Adopt semantic versioning for Document Status, distinct from Version
body:
`spec/header.md` currently has two fields that read as if they mean the same thing but shouldn't:

```
_Version:_ 1.0
_Document Status:_ Working Draft 02
```

Proposal: keep them meaning two different things, explicitly.

- **`_Version:_`** — the version of the *specification* the Working Drafts are converging toward (e.g. `1.0`). Changes rarely — only when the spec itself is re-targeted.
- **`_Document Status:_`** — the semantic version of *this Working Draft*, as `Working Draft MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` (e.g. `Working Draft 0.3.0`), not a bare incrementing ordinal like `02`. Bump MINOR for a draft with new normative content (what "WD02 → WD03" already means informally today), PATCH for a post-publication editorial/errata fix that changes no normative meaning, and hold MAJOR at `0` until the spec reaches an approved/stable milestone.

This gives every citation something to pin precisely ("as of WD 0.3.1") instead of the current ordinal, which can't distinguish an editorial fix from a substantive draft. It also matches the convention the sibling Trust Tasks framework spec already uses via its target-framework-version declaration.

**Needs the group to confirm before applying:**
1. The MAJOR/MINOR/PATCH bump rule above.
2. How today's history maps onto it — I'd assume WD01 → `0.1.0`, WD02 → `0.2.0`, so WD03 becomes `0.3.0`, but that's worth saying out loud rather than assuming.

**Where this applies right now, concretely, in PR #47** (branch `feat/verifiable-statement-credential`), once confirmed:

| Location | Current text | Change |
|---|---|---|
| `spec/header.md:4` | `_Document Status:_ Working Draft 02` | `_Document Status:_ Working Draft 0.3.0` — this is the one that actually matters: the PR's own editor's notes already call themselves WD03 twice, but this line is never touched by the diff, so it would ship still saying "02" |
| `spec/body.md:861` | `> **Editor's note — WD03.** The VSC replaces... subtypes of Working Draft 02...` | Reads fine as informal shorthand once the header carries the real version — optionally spell out `WD 0.3.0` here too for consistency |
| `spec/body.md:947` | `for this Working Draft, the two core profiles that replace the WD02 VEC and VWC sections` | Same — optional spell-out, not load-bearing |
| `spec/body.md:5` | `the endorsement and witness credentials of Working Draft 02 are now its first two predicate profiles` | Same, references the *prior* draft (`0.2.0`) by design — no change needed once the convention is documented |

`specs.json` has no version field, so nothing to change there.

The one that actually blocks anything is `header.md:4` — everything else is cosmetic follow-through once the convention exists.

title: Adopt semantic versioning for Document Status, distinct from Version
body:
Addresses trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#51.

Companion PRs applying the same convention to the sibling DTGWG specs:
- Trust Tasks: trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#14
- VTI: trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#31

## Summary

`_Version:_` and `_Document Status:_` read as if they meant the same thing but didn't distinguish two different concerns. They now do:

- **`_Version:_`** stays `1.0` — the release this specification is converging toward, confirmed only when a wider body ratifies it as a Working Group Approved Deliverable or ToIP Approved Deliverable. It does not move with each Working Draft revision.
- **`_Document Status:_`** now reads `Working Draft 0.4.0` — this Working Draft's own semantic version, which editors and implementers use to coordinate day-to-day.

Also:
- Adds a **Compatibility Rules** subsection (adapted from the Trust Tasks specification's own versioning section) governing how Document Status increments and what holders/verifiers must accept across MINOR/PATCH changes.
- Fixes the minimum-compatible-version note on the `taskContext` binding: the citation-binding mechanism it depends on landed in Trust Tasks Document Status **0.4.0** (not 0.3 as previously stated), and now points at `dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec` since the content has migrated there from `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`.
- Notes how the historical "01"/"02" Working Draft ordinals map onto `Document Status`, so `0.4.0` isn't mistaken for `0.3.0` (which would collide with the pre-migration `v0.3` proposal draft this Working Draft supersedes).

Reviewed together with the companion PRs so the three specs land on consistent language.

title: Adopt semantic versioning for Document Status, distinct from Version (#54)
body:
Adopt semantic versioning for Document Status, distinct from Version (#54)

* Adopt Version/Document Status semantic versioning, aligned across DTGWG specs

Per issue #51: _Version:_ and _Document Status:_ read as if they meant
the same thing but didn't distinguish a rarely-changing target from an
incrementing draft number. They now do:

- _Version:_ stays 1.0 - the release this specification is converging
  toward, confirmed only when a wider body ratifies it as a Working
  Group Approved Deliverable or ToIP Approved Deliverable. It does not
  move with each Working Draft revision.
- _Document Status:_ carries this Working Draft's own semantic version
  (Working Draft 0.4.0), which editors and implementers use to
  coordinate day-to-day. A note explains how the historical "01"/"02"
  ordinals map onto it, so 0.4.0 isn't mistaken for 0.3.0 - which would
  collide with the pre-migration v0.3 proposal draft this Working Draft
  supersedes.

Adds a Compatibility Rules subsection - adapted from the Trust Tasks
specification's own versioning section, the DTGWG spec that has
thought hardest about this - governing how Document Status increments
and what holders/verifiers must accept across MINOR/PATCH changes.

Also fixes the minimum-compatible-version note on the taskContext
binding: the citation-binding mechanism it depends on landed in Trust
Tasks Document Status 0.4.0 (not 0.3 as previously stated), and points
at dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec now that the content has migrated there from
dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf.

Companion PRs apply the same Version/Document Status convention to the
sibling Trust Tasks and VTI specifications.

Signed-off-by: Brendan Miller <code+os@brendanmiller.com>

* Add pre-ratification SemVer escape clause and ratification lifecycle

geoffturk noted on #54 that the Compatibility Rules have no pre-1.0
escape clause: the next breaking change to this Working Draft would be
forced to bump Document Status straight to 1.0.0, colliding with the
number reserved for actual ratification. Fix it the way the Trust
Tasks specification already does for individual Trust Task specs at
`draft` status: a breaking change MAY stay MINOR while Document
Status's MAJOR component is 0, per SemVer 2.0.0 §4.

Also add a Ratification and the Stable Release Line subsection
answering the follow-up: once this specification IS ratified,
Document Status crosses into 1.x.x (the SemVer-correct trigger for
that crossing), _Version:_ confirms to match, and from then on the two
fields carry the same MAJOR.MINOR - only the status label differs -
until the next breaking change resumes the pre-ratification split by
advancing Document Status ahead to the next MAJOR while _Version:_
holds at the last-ratified release.

Full rationale lives in the companion Trust Tasks PR, which this
section links to as the canonical explanation shared across the
DTGWG's specifications.

Signed-off-by: Brendan Miller <code+os@brendanmiller.com>

title: docs: add an identity vetting predicate as a worked statement profile
body:
Builds on #47. A worked example of a community-defined predicate, added after **Community-Defined Predicates**.

**Why this replaces #49.** #49 profiled the VEC for identity vetting, with the reasoning "why a VEC and not a new credential type". That was wrong, and the objection is the obvious one: a *Verifiable Endorsement Credential* is for endorsing. A vetting statement is a record of a procedure — a named member checked an applicant's claimed identity, by a stated method, against stated classes of document, on a stated date. Pressing the endorsement envelope into that service is renaming, not modelling. #47 is exactly the mechanism that makes it unnecessary, so vetting becomes its own predicate instead. I'll close #49 in favour of this.

**What it adds.** One informative subsection. The payload #49 carried in the `endorsement` body moves unchanged into the statement's `object.value`: `community`, `method`, `documentClasses`, `claimsVerified`, `livenessConfirmed`, `identityCommitment`, `cardDigestMultibase`, `declaredRelationship`, `attestationTextDigest`. It states all nine items [Predicate Profiles](#predicate-profiles) requires, including what a pass does and does not establish — notably that it establishes nothing about whether the claimed identity is *true*, whether the vetter was eligible, or whether anyone has been admitted.

**A difficulty that dissolves.** #49 needed an editor's note asking whether a vetting exchange satisfies the VEC's "one party to a DTG edge" language, since vetter and applicant often share no edge and the applicant is not yet a member. A statement annotates a node, so the question no longer arises and the note is gone.

**Namespace.** The predicate sits in a community namespace (`https://vtc.example/vocab/vetting/v1#vetted`), matching the existing community-predicate example and the editor's note that this specification defines mechanisms rather than naming predicates. If more than one community adopts it, it is a candidate for promotion into the planned vocabulary — the path your note already describes.

**Validation.** `npm run render` completes cleanly and writes `docs/index.html`. The five dangling definitions it reports (CTA, PNV, personal trust network, relationship invitation, VTC trust anchor) are unreferenced on the base branch too, so they are not from this change. One term reference is used, `[[ref: VMC]]`.

**One observation, not addressed here.** Section links of the form `](#vsc-verifiable-statement-credential)` do not resolve: the renderer emits ids with the parentheses, `id="vsc-(verifiable-statement-credential)"`. Six such links already exist on the base branch, so my new link follows the same house form rather than diverging in one place. Worth a separate fix across the document if you agree.

Based on `feat/verifiable-statement-credential`, so it should merge after #47. Happy to rebase onto `main` instead if that lands differently.

title: Add a generic statement credential so new predicates do not each need a credential type
body:
## Summary

WD02 added two concrete subtypes, the VDC and the VAC. Both earned a section of their own. The next candidates will not: "I saw this person's passport", "I was at this event", "this document was presented to me", "this device was in my custody". Each is a signed claim that a verifier reads and either believes or does not. If every one of them becomes a `DTGCredential` subtype, the catalogue grows one section per predicate and the spec becomes a vocabulary list.

This issue proposes a single generic credential, working name **Verifiable Statement Credential (VSC)**, carrying a subject, a predicate term, and an object. Per-predicate constraints live in short **predicate profiles** rather than in new types. The VEC and the VWC become its first two profiles. The issue also proposes writing down the test the spec already applies implicitly, so future contributors know when a new predicate is a profile and when it is a new type.

## Why the DTG needs a statement primitive

The DTG is a graph of subject, predicate, object statements whose nodes are DIDs and whose edges are signed. That is the semantic web's model, with three things RDF never had:

- every statement has a signer, so "who says so" is intrinsic rather than metadata;
- a statement that needs both parties (membership, relationship, delegation) carries both parties' signatures, so consent is part of the edge rather than an assumption;
- node identifiers carry a [correlation scope](https://trustoverip.github.io/dtgwg-cred-spec/#correlation-scope), so the holder decides who may even name the node.

The semantic web could not express any of that in its data model. Its "Proof" and "Trust" layers were never built, and privacy was always added around the data rather than in it. Solid is the most serious attempt to add control, and it did so by putting access lists on the server that holds the data, keyed to a single public WebID. The DTG makes the opposite choice: policy lives inside the artifact and the identifier, and the holder presents rather than the server serves.

What the DTG has not yet taken from RDF is its one genuinely good primitive: a statement shape that carries *any* predicate. RDF gets away with a single shape because nothing ever acts on a triple. The DTG needs specialised types exactly where a verifier acts: delegation, authority, membership, invitation. Everywhere else, a signed statement whose meaning is fixed by a governed vocabulary is sufficient. The VEC is already that credential with the predicate hard-wired to "endorses" and the vocabulary handed to the governing VTC or VTN. This proposal generalises it.

## The test the spec already states

The [VDC section](https://trustoverip.github.io/dtgwg-cred-spec/#vdc-verifiable-delegation-credential) draws the line:

> A VDC differs from every other credential in this specification in kind, not only in payload. The VRC, VMC, VIC, VPC, VEC, and VWC all *attest* that something is true about the graph; a verifier evaluates each as a claim and asks whether it is true. A VDC establishes *representation* [...] and answering it requires steps that evaluating a claim does not: scope containment, chain resolution, invocation binding, and timely revocation.

That is the test. If verifying a credential means "check the signature, check the status, read the claim", it is a statement and can share one shape. If the verifier must do more (complete an edge, match a consent digest, resolve a chain, contain a scope, or hand the credential to a PEP that acts on it), it is a concrete subtype.

Applied to the current catalogue:

| Credential | Verdict | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| VRC, VMC | stays concrete | two halves complete an edge; consent digest |
| VDC | stays concrete | representation; chain, scope, invocation |
| VAC | stays concrete | authority; attenuation, chain |
| VIC | stays concrete | consumed by a PEP to admit a member |
| VPC | stays concrete for now | carries correlation semantics; revisit separately |
| VEC | becomes a profile | claim with a governed payload |
| VWC | becomes a profile | claim whose object is a credential digest |

The VWC fits despite the digest. [Digest Encoding](https://trustoverip.github.io/dtgwg-cred-spec/#digest-encoding) already sorts the digest-valued members into three roles: consent (VMC acknowledgement, VDC acceptance), attestation (VWC), and chain (VDC and VAC parents). Consent completes an edge and chain triggers resolution, so those stay in their types. Attestation is the one role where the verifier does nothing with the referenced credential except confirm it is the one named, a decode-and-compare the spec already defines generically. Everything else the VWC section requires (mandatory `taskContext`, subject must be the issuer of the referenced credential, witness identifier `directed` at minimum, the `witnessContext` payload, one credential per direction) is a constraint the profile states, not a new verification step.

## Proposed shape

A strawman, to be refined in the PR.

- `type` (array, REQUIRED): MUST include `"StatementCredential"`. A profile MAY register an additional type string so wallets and verifiers that dispatch on `type` keep working; `"WitnessCredential"` and `"EndorsementCredential"` would be retained this way.
- `issuer` (string, REQUIRED): DID of the party making the statement.
- `taskContext` (string, OPTIONAL unless the profile requires it).
- `credentialSubject` (object, REQUIRED):
  - `id` (string, REQUIRED): DID of the subject of the statement.
  - `predicate` (string, REQUIRED): a term from a governed vocabulary, expressed as an IRI or a CURIE resolvable through the DTG JSON-LD context. Core predicates defined by this spec would live under the DTG context (`dtg:endorses`, `dtg:witnessed`); community-defined ones under the community's own.
  - `object` (object, REQUIRED): exactly one of
    - `id` (string): a DID or other IRI, when the object is a party or a named thing;
    - `digestMultibase` (string): when the object is another credential, encoded per Digest Encoding;
    - `value` (any): a literal or structured payload, when the object is neither.
  - further members as the profile defines.

A **predicate profile** is a short normative block, in this spec for core predicates or in a governance framework for community ones, that fixes:

- the predicate term and its meaning;
- which object kind(s) are permitted;
- any relationship required between subject and object (for `dtg:witnessed`, the subject MUST be the issuer of the referenced credential);
- required and optional additional members and their schema;
- whether `taskContext` is REQUIRED;
- the minimum correlation scope the issuer may truthfully declare;
- who may issue (a member, a VTA under VTC policy, the subject itself).

Two guardrails, stated once for the type:

1. A statement credential attests; it never establishes. A verifier MUST NOT treat a statement as conferring representation, authority, membership, or admission, whatever its predicate says. Those are the concrete subtypes' job, and a predicate named `mayActFor` is just a string.
2. A statement credential is unilateral. If a predicate is only true when the counterparty agrees, it is an edge, and belongs in the edge category with an acknowledgement half, not in a profile.

The verifiability rule from the VEC carries over unchanged: the signature is verifiable; the truth of the statement is governed by whoever defines the vocabulary.

## Worked examples

An observation, issued by whoever inspected the document:

```json
{
  "type": ["VerifiableCredential", "DTGCredential", "StatementCredential"],
  "issuer": "did:key:z6Mk...observer",
  "validFrom": "2026-09-08T10:00:00Z",
  "credentialSubject": {
    "id": "did:key:z6Mk...subject",
    "predicate": "example:observedDocument",
    "object": { "value": { "documentType": "passport", "issuingCountry": "NL" } }
  }
}
```

Presence, self-issued:

```json
{
  "type": ["VerifiableCredential", "DTGCredential", "StatementCredential"],
  "issuer": "did:key:z6Mk...me",
  "validFrom": "2026-09-08T10:00:00Z",
  "credentialSubject": {
    "id": "did:key:z6Mk...me",
    "predicate": "example:attended",
    "object": { "id": "https://events.example/gdc-2026" }
  }
}
```

The WD02 VWC example re-expressed. Nothing a verifier checks has changed:

```json
{
  "type": ["VerifiableCredential", "DTGCredential", "StatementCredential", "WitnessCredential"],
  "issuer": "did:webvh:QmVzTd9hRkPqLu4WgXyN...:witness-service.example",
  "validFrom": "2026-01-06T10:00:00Z",
  "taskContext": "thread-abc-123",
  "credentialSubject": {
    "id": "did:key:z6MkpTHR8VNs...",
    "predicate": "dtg:witnessed",
    "object": { "digestMultibase": "zQmdfTbBqBPQ7VNxZEYEj14VmRuZBkqFbiwReogJgS1zR1n" },
    "witnessContext": {
      "event": "GDC 2026",
      "location": "Geneva",
      "method": "in-person-proximity"
    }
  }
}
```

## What would change in the spec

- A new section defining the statement credential and the profile mechanism, with the profile/type test stated in the taxonomy section. This reshapes the categorisation question in #28: the categories become edge credentials (VRC, VMC, VDC) and statement credentials (one type, N profiles), with VIC, VPC and VAC standing alone.
- VEC and VWC rewritten as the `dtg:endorses` and `dtg:witnessed` profiles, keeping their type strings as registered aliases so WD02 credentials remain recognisable. The VWC's per-direction and "make the referenced credential available" guidance moves into the profile and must not be lost.
- Digest Encoding's list of digest-valued members gains the statement `object` and loses the VWC line; the three-role explanation is unchanged.
- Trust Task Context Binding: "currently only the VWC" becomes "profiles that require it".
- One presentation circuit covers every profile, which simplifies the ZKP work in #9 rather than adding to it.
- Blinding under #38 has one more slot to cover, and one fewer credential type, since the witness digest and any future credential-valued object share the same member.

Edge credentials, the VIC, and the VAC are untouched.

## Open questions

1. **Name.** "Attestation" and "assertion" both collide with VAC; "predicate" collides with VPC. "Statement" is RDF's own word for the unit and is free. Other suggestions welcome.
2. **Predicate term form.** IRI/CURIE through the JSON-LD context (proposed, because it makes the credential a real RDF statement when expanded), or a plain string namespaced by the governing community?
3. **A registry.** Should ToIP host a registry of common predicates (observation, presence, document-presented) so communities converge rather than each minting their own, or is that a governance-framework matter?
4. **Sequencing.** Define the type and profiles in one PR with VEC and VWC migrated, or land the type first and migrate in a follow-on?
5. **VPC.** It is annotation-shaped but carries correlation semantics. Leave it concrete for WD03 and revisit, or fold it now?

title: Add the verifiable statement credential (VSC)
body:
## Summary

Adds the **Verifiable Statement Credential (VSC)**: one `StatementCredential` type carrying a subject, an absolute-IRI predicate drawn from a governed vocabulary, and an object. The WD02 `EndorsementCredential` and `WitnessCredential` subtypes become its first two **predicate profiles** (`dtg:endorses`, `dtg:witnessed`); future predicates are added as profiles, not types. Implements the design settled in #45, including the fail-closed rule, the "what does PASS mean" bound on every profile, and the predicate-handling rules raised in that thread, plus the unconditional VWC direction binding and the registry framing settled in review here.

Type count goes from eight to seven. The type strings `EndorsementCredential` and `WitnessCredential` are removed — a VSC carries exactly one channel of meaning, its `predicate`.

## What changed

- **New `VSC` section** (`spec/body.md`, replacing the VWC and VEC sections):
  - *Statements and Establishment* — the profile/type test, stated once; statements are evidence, governance turns evidence into establishment
  - Schema — `credentialSubject.id` / `predicate` / `object` (`id` | `digestMultibase` | `value`), the unilateral rule
  - *Predicate Handling* (normative) — reject anything not an absolute IRI; reject any predicate not in a configured vocabulary; no equivalence-following; NFC; identifier vs `rdfs:label`; resolve at configuration time, never at verification time; vocabularies immutable once published
  - *What Verification Establishes* (normative) — type-level bound (representation, authority, membership, admission, governed status, task completion) and the per-profile "establishes / does not establish" requirement; a profile classifies shape and narrows no cross-cutting obligation
  - *Predicate Profiles* (normative) — the nine things a profile MUST state; artifact rule; non-nested-task rule; editor's note on the **DTG Predicate Vocabulary**, a repo-driven registry per #52, which curates a default set and does not gate who may define or use a predicate
  - *Statements in the Graph* — the credential is the unit of attribution; informative RDF-reification note; editor's note on context terms (`predicate` as `@id`, `object.value` as `@json`)
  - `dtg:endorses` (VEC) and `dtg:witnessed` (VWC) profiles with PASS blocks; community-defined predicate example
- **Generic wording** in Digest Encoding (statement `object` replaces the VWC line; predicate named as a #38 blinding target), Trust Task Context Binding ("currently only the VWC" → profiles that require it), VDC "differs in kind" list, ZK predicate list, Security (#6 generalised, new #7 on predicate acceptance), Governance #4, Internationalization, Conformance targets, References
- **`intro.md` / `header.md`** — eight → seven; VEC/VWC listed as VSC profiles; DTG Predicate Vocabulary added to Related Specifications, described as a registry rather than a specification. `_Document Status:_` stays at Working Draft 02; the bump is #54's.
- **Glossary** — new VSC term; VEC, VWC and DTG annotation credential definitions updated

Renders cleanly with `npm run render`; no undefined terms or broken `[[ref]]`s.

## Judgment calls — please review these specifically

1. **Absolute IRIs only; no CURIEs on the wire.** The strawman allowed CURIEs. Dropping them removes the silent-failure case (undefined prefix → VC 2.0's issuer-dependent `@vocab`), makes predicate matching a byte comparison that needs neither `@context` nor a JSON-LD processor, and gives each predicate exactly one representation for digests and blinding. `dtg:` is declared as documentation notation only.
2. **Direction binding unconditional on every VWC.** WD02 required "subject = issuer of the referenced credential" only for bidirectional exchanges. The profile now states what `dtg:witnessed` *means* — the issuer observed the subject *issue* the named credential — so the binding is the shape of that meaning and a verifier can check it whenever it can check the digest. The WD02 "observed party" alternative is retired, not presented: the review cases (community-issued VMC, VDC, presentation/custody) showed it does not generalise. Witnessing a party *present* or *hold* a credential is a different predicate, `presented`, whose home is the registry (#52), not a third core profile. Settled with @bmiller59 in the thread below.
3. **VEC/VWC kept as the names of the two profiles** so existing prose (witness scope, DID methods, privacy) still reads; only the type strings are gone.
4. **VSC placed under Annotation Credentials provisionally.** It annotates a node, not an edge. Category reshaping is left to #28; editor's notes in the taxonomy and the section say so.
5. **Non-nested-task rule stated here** as a constraint on profiles, with nesting semantics deferred to the trust task spec (#11). Could equally live there.
6. **The two core profiles stay in this spec for this Working Draft** because they replace WD02 normative text and need a published home now, not because the registry does not yet exist. Presentation/custody replaces nothing, so it goes to the registry rather than becoming a third core profile. The editor's note says the two move once the registry has a release, and that nothing on the wire changes when they do.
7. **`specs.json` still says "seven"** — it was stale before and is now correct, so it's untouched.

## The DTG namespace is a placeholder — decided in #48

Mandating absolute IRIs means the core predicates are written out in full. This PR writes them under the existing context URL plus `#`, and the notation note in the VSC section says plainly that this is a placeholder:

```
https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1#witnessed
```

The final form is decided in #48, before the Implementers Draft. Two constraints from #52 already narrow it: the vocabulary namespace carries **no version segment**, because predicate IRIs are compared byte-exact and must not change when a term is added; and the namespace and the versioned `@context` IRI are therefore two different IRIs with different rules. Changing the placeholder later is a find-and-replace in the spec and, so long as it happens before credentials are issued under it, nothing more.

## Pre-existing issue noticed, not fixed here

spec-up-t generates heading ids with parentheses and percent-encoded colons (`vac-(verifiable-authority-credential)`) while every internal link in the spec uses GitHub-style slugs (`#vac-verifiable-authority-credential`). This predates the branch and affects all existing links; this PR follows the existing convention. Worth checking whether anchors resolve on the published site.

Refs #45, #28, #38, #11, #48, #52.

title: Create the DTG predicate vocabulary as a repo-driven registry
body:
## Summary

#47 introduces the verifiable statement credential (VSC), whose meaning is carried by a predicate from a governed vocabulary, and says that predicates beyond the two core profiles will be defined in a planned "DTG Predicate Vocabulary" specification. Review has already produced the first candidates (#50 identity vetting; presentation/custody in the #47 thread), and the question of where they go is blocking. This issue proposes the answer: **a repo-driven registry, on the model of the ToIP glossary, not a specification** — and lays out what the repository needs to contain so that it can be created and populated without further design work.

The proposal was discussed against the alternative of growing the credential spec, or a dedicated vocabulary spec, and rejected both on cadence: a ToIP specification moves WD → Implementers Draft → Approved Deliverable, and a vocabulary needs to add an entry the week a community needs it. A generated registry governed by pull request is the only shape that matches how the content changes.

Assumption for this issue: ToIP is amenable to hosting the namespace and the published artifacts, at least for now. The IRIs below are placeholders until #48 is decided.

## Three things that were being called "the vocabulary"

| | What it is | Nature | Home |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. The rules** | what a predicate definition must contain, how it is published, immutability, NFC, labels, admission criteria | normative, changes rarely | the credential spec's *Predicate Profiles* section for now (it already states the nine required members); split out into a small "DTG Vocabularies" spec if and when the definition format needs its own normative home |
| **B. WG-curated predicates** | `endorses`, `witnessed`, and whatever the WG agrees to define under the DTG namespace | content, grows one entry at a time | **this repository** |
| **C. Community predicates** | terms a VTC or VTN defines under a namespace it controls | content, not ours to hold | the community's own namespace, referenced from its governance framework; published in the same format as B so tooling works for both |

The credential spec's *Community-Defined Predicates* section keeps one illustrative example and no more; every real predicate goes to B or C.

## The repository

Proposed name: `trustoverip/dtgwg-predicate-vocab`. Same tooling philosophy as `ctwg-main-glossary`: one source file per entry, a generator, a published output, PR governance.

```
dtgwg-predicate-vocab/
├── README.md                     what this is, how to propose a predicate
├── GOVERNANCE.md                 admission criteria, review, statuses, versioning
├── predicates/                   one file per predicate — the source of truth
│   ├── endorses.jsonld
│   ├── witnessed.jsonld
│   ├── identity-vetting.jsonld   from #50
│   └── presented.jsonld          from the #47 review thread
├── schemas/                      JSON Schema for each predicate's `value` payload
│   └── identity-vetting.schema.json
├── meta/
│   ├── predicate.schema.json     the definition format (mirrors the nine points in the credential spec)
│   └── meta-context.jsonld       JSON-LD context for the definition files themselves
├── tools/                        generator: validates predicates/ against meta/, builds dist/
└── dist/                         generated, published at the namespace; never hand-edited
    ├── vocab.jsonld              all active and deprecated terms, additive
    ├── index.html                human-readable vocabulary document
    ├── accept-list.json          machine-readable list verifiers can import
    └── context/
        └── v1.jsonld             frozen context for the additional members of core profiles
```

## The definition format

One JSON-LD document per predicate. The members are the nine points a profile MUST state under *Predicate Profiles* in #47, plus registry metadata. `witnessed`, as it would appear:

```json
{
  "@context": "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab/meta-context.jsonld",
  "id": "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab#witnessed",
  "type": "Predicate",
  "status": "active",
  "since": "2026-10-01",
  "label": {
    "en": "witnessed",
    "de": "bezeugt",
    "nl": "getuige geweest van"
  },
  "definition": {
    "en": "The issuer observed the subject issue the credential the object names, under the conditions of a specific trust task exchange."
  },
  "classification": "evidence",
  "weighedBy": "The community whose witnessing policy the attestation is issued under.",
  "objectKind": ["digestMultibase"],
  "subjectObjectRelationship": "credentialSubject.id MUST be the issuer of the credential object.digestMultibase names; a verifier holding that credential MUST check it.",
  "additionalMembers": {
    "witnessContext": {
      "required": false,
      "schema": "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab/schemas/witness-context.schema.json"
    }
  },
  "taskContextRequired": true,
  "minimumIssuerScope": "directed",
  "issuer": "A member, or a VTA acting according to VTC policy.",
  "establishes": "That the issuer attests that, in the exchange identified by taskContext, it observed the subject issue the credential whose claims digest to object.digestMultibase.",
  "doesNotEstablish": [
    "that the referenced credential is currently valid or unrevoked",
    "that the referenced credential's claims are true",
    "that the exchange reached its terminal state (Outcome Interpretability applies)",
    "that the witness is a member of any community",
    "that any consequential action is authorized"
  ],
  "definedIn": "https://trustoverip.github.io/dtgwg-cred-spec/#the-dtgwitnessed-profile-vwc",
  "governedBy": null
}
```

The presentation/custody predicate from the #47 thread, showing the case where the observed party is the referenced credential's *subject*:

```json
{
  "@context": "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab/meta-context.jsonld",
  "id": "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab#presented",
  "type": "Predicate",
  "status": "proposed",
  "label": { "en": "presented" },
  "definition": {
    "en": "The issuer observed the subject present the credential the object names. The subject is the holder; the credential's issuer need not have been present."
  },
  "classification": "evidence",
  "objectKind": ["digestMultibase"],
  "subjectObjectRelationship": "credentialSubject.id MUST be the credentialSubject.id of the credential object.digestMultibase names.",
  "taskContextRequired": true,
  "minimumIssuerScope": "directed",
  "issuer": "A member, or a VTA acting according to VTC policy.",
  "establishes": "That the issuer attests that, in the exchange identified by taskContext, the subject presented the credential whose claims digest to object.digestMultibase.",
  "doesNotEstablish": [
    "that the presented credential is valid, unrevoked, or was issued to the subject",
    "that the presented credential's claims are true",
    "that the subject controls the presented credential's subject identifier",
    "that any consequential action is authorized"
  ]
}
```

A community predicate uses the same format under its own namespace, with `governedBy` pointing at the governance framework that defines who may issue it and how it is weighed. That is what makes one generator, one validator and one accept-list format serve both tiers.

## Generated outputs

| Artifact | Consumer | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `vocab.jsonld` | tooling, RDF consumers, `rdfs:label` lookups | additive; a term is never removed or altered once active, only deprecated |
| `index.html` | people | the human-readable vocabulary, one section per predicate, labels in every language supplied |
| `accept-list.json` | verifiers | the active IRIs with their machine-checkable constraints (object kinds, `taskContextRequired`, minimum scope, schema URLs), for import into verifier configuration at configuration time |
| `context/v1.jsonld` | credentials under core profiles | the JSON-LD terms for additional members such as `witnessContext`; frozen per version, as VC contexts must be |

An `accept-list.json` entry, so the shape is concrete:

```json
{
  "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab#witnessed": {
    "status": "active",
    "objectKind": ["digestMultibase"],
    "taskContextRequired": true,
    "minimumIssuerScope": "directed",
    "additionalMembers": { "witnessContext": { "required": false } }
  }
}
```

## Versioning and immutability — two different rules

This is the part that needs to be got right before anything is published, and it feeds #48.

- **Predicate IRIs are unversioned and term-immutable.** `…/vocab#witnessed` never changes meaning and is never deleted; adding `#presented` does not touch it. Versioning the namespace (`…/vocab/v1#witnessed` → `…/vocab/v2#witnessed`) would change every predicate's IRI whenever any predicate is added, and break byte-exact matching for every issued credential. So the namespace IRI decided in #48 **must carry no version segment**. The current placeholder in #47 (`https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1#witnessed`) has one and should not be the final form.
- **Contexts are versioned and frozen.** A JSON-LD context that credentials list must not change after publication, so `context/v1.jsonld` is frozen and additions go in `v2`. This is fine because credentials do not need the vocabulary context to carry a predicate — predicates are absolute IRIs — only to carry a core profile's additional members.

Releases are git tags. `dist/` at a tag is the published state; the namespace serves the latest tag's `vocab.jsonld` and `index.html`, and every `context/vN.jsonld` ever released.

## Governance

`GOVERNANCE.md`, drawing on the credential spec's rules:

- **Not a gate.** The registry curates a shared, trusted default set; it does not decide who may define or use a predicate. Because a predicate is an absolute IRI that a verifier accepts by configuration, resolved at configuration time and never at verification time (Predicate Handling in #47), a community that publishes a predicate under a namespace it controls can issue under it, and verifiers can accept it, without waiting on or ever seeking admission here. #50's identity vetting predicate already works this way. Admission is what a community seeks when it wants convergence — one identifier shared across communities — not what it needs in order to use the standard. The admission criteria below therefore bound what enters the DTG namespace, not what the mechanism permits. This is a stated design guarantee, mirrored in the credential spec's editor's note on where profiles live (#47), not an emergent property.
- **Admission to the DTG namespace.** A proposed predicate is accepted when it (1) is complete against `meta/predicate.schema.json`, including the establishes / does-not-establish block; (2) is on the *attests* side of the statement/establishment test — it is not a predicate whose PASS a verifier would act on as representation, authority, membership, admission, governed status or task completion; (3) is unilateral; (4) is not meaningful only inside one exchange; (5) has no existing term with the same meaning — one identifier per concept; (6) has an NFC IRI and at least an English label; and (7) is either needed by a DTG specification or in use, or credibly about to be, by more than one community.
- **Statuses.** `proposed` (merged, not yet in a release), `active`, `deprecated` (kept forever, marked, with a pointer to any replacement). Nothing is ever deleted.
- **Review.** Two WG approvals for a new `active` term; one for editorial changes to labels or definitions that do not alter meaning; meaning changes are not permitted — deprecate and add.
- **Equivalence.** The registry MAY record that a community term has the same meaning as a DTG term, as information for people configuring verifiers. Verifiers never follow it (Predicate Handling in #47).

## Relationship to the credential spec

- The credential spec keeps the statement mechanism, Predicate Handling, What Verification Establishes, Predicate Profiles (which is where the definition format's requirements live for now), and — for WD03 — the `endorses` and `witnessed` profiles, because they replace WD02 normative text and need a published home. Once this repository has a release, those two move here and the credential spec references them; nothing on the wire changes.
- The `dtg:` notation in the credential spec resolves to this repository's namespace once #48 is decided.
- *Related Specifications* in the credential spec should describe this as a registry, not a specification.
- #50 should target this repository rather than the credential spec's example section, as the first entry.
- #47's reviewer request for a core presentation/custody profile is answered by `presented.jsonld` above rather than by a third profile in the credential spec.

## Sequencing

1. Create the repository with `README.md`, `GOVERNANCE.md`, `meta/`, and an empty `predicates/`; decide #48 so the placeholder IRIs can be replaced.
2. Add the generator (validation against `meta/predicate.schema.json`, build of `dist/`), and CI that fails a PR whose definition is incomplete.
3. First entries: `identity-vetting` (#50), `presented`. Mirror `endorses` and `witnessed` as `proposed` so the format is exercised against the two real profiles.
4. First release once the credential spec reaches WD03; then move `endorses` and `witnessed` here for WD04 and update the credential spec's references.

## Open questions

- Which ToIP deliverable type a repo-driven registry is, and whether the glossary's process and tooling can be borrowed wholesale. (A question for ToIP staff.)
- Whether this repository should also carry the other community-defined vocabularies the DTG already depends on — VDC `scope` terms, VAC `actions`, the VEC endorsement vocabulary — since they are the same kind of thing with the same publication gap. If so, "DTG Vocabularies" is the better name. Flagged, not proposed here.
- Namespace and hosting: #48.

Refs #45, #47, #48, #50, #51.

title: Structural review: split Trust Contexts chapter, tighten Appendix E normativity, VTC cross-references
body:
## Summary

Structural review of the VTI spec (all 22 chapter files, ~4500 lines), done as the "review the VTI spec structure and suggest improvements if needed" action item. This is a structural review only — not a line-level correctness pass — and it also checked chapter organization against the sibling DTGWG specs (Credentials, Trust Tasks) for consistency.

**Overall verdict:** the structure is basically sound. The four-part organization (Foundations / Common Model / Nodes / System Properties) is coherent, the reading-guide table in the introduction is accurate, chapter ordering respects dependencies (contexts and authority before the things built on them, nodes after the common model, composition/operations last), and the ending convention (Considerations → Conformance → References → Appendix) matches both sibling specs exactly. No deeper reorganization is warranted. One finding below is worth real effort; the rest are small, targeted fixes.

## Findings

### 1. Split `03-trust-contexts.md` (626 lines) — it bundles four requirement areas into one chapter

The Conformance chapter's own area table treats `CTX`, `ACL`, `APV` (approvals/consent/step-up), and `AUD` (audit) as four separate requirement areas — exactly like every other area in the document gets its own chapter (`KEY`→04, `TRN`→05, `SES`→06, `CLT`→07, …). But all four currently live in one file titled "Trust Contexts and the Authority Model," which doesn't mention approvals or audit in its title and is 2–8x longer than any sibling chapter. A reader looking for step-up/consent rules or audit requirements has no reason to look here.

**Suggested fix:** split into at least four chapters matching the four requirement areas — Trust Contexts (`CTX`), Access Control and Authority (`ACL`), Approvals/Consent/Step-Up (`APV`), Audit (`AUD`) — consistent with how every other area in the document is organized.

### 2. Appendix E is labeled informative but two MUST requirements depend on it

VTI-CMP-002 requires a conformance claim to state evidence "recorded in Appendix E"; VTI-CMP-120 requires ownership classification/evidence/counter-cases to be recorded there. Both are normative obligations pointing at a section the document marks "This appendix is informative."

**Suggested fix:** either promote the specific record format to normative, or rephrase CMP-002/CMP-120 to point at a normative subsection rather than the whole appendix.

Related, flagging alongside rather than as a separate ask: VTI-CNF-006 requires every requirement to map to a conformance test, but `95-conformance.md` admits the test suite's location "is not yet settled" — a MUST resting on infrastructure that doesn't exist yet.

### 3. `11-vtc.md` (81 lines) is thin, and VTC's content is split across three files with no cross-pointer

VTA gets 166 lines; VTN — which has zero implementations and an explicitly open structural question — gets 304. VTC, one of only two node types with real implementations, has its real content split across `11-vtc.md`, `12-vtc-lifecycle.md`, and `13-registries.md`, with no forward-pointer between them. A reader following the "Implementing or operating a VTC" row in the intro's reading-guide table has to independently discover it needs all three.

**Suggested fix:** add a one-line "see also" at the top of `11-vtc.md` pointing to 12 and 13.

### 4. VTI is the only one of the three sibling specs split into per-chapter files

`dtgwg-cred-spec` and `dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec` each use a single `body.md`; VTI uses ~20 numbered files. Defensible given VTI's size (4500 vs. 600–1400 lines), but it means the intro's "Structure of this document" table and `specs.json`'s `markdown_paths` list are two places that must stay in sync as chapters move — a maintenance mode the siblings don't have.

**Suggested fix:** no code change needed — just worth this being a deliberate, acknowledged choice rather than an unexamined one. Flagging for awareness.

### 5. `11a-vtn.md` is the only lettered filename in an otherwise sequential scheme

Evidently VTN was inserted after 02–15 were already numbered. Harmless — chapter file numbers aren't the stable identifiers, `VTI-XXX-nnn` requirement IDs are, and those don't reference file numbers — but a small renumbering (VTN→12, shifting Membership/Registries/Composition/Operational down one) would remove the only rough edge in the numbering.

### 6. `VTI-SES-042` is defined out of order in `06-sessions-auth.md`

It appears after `VTI-SES-043` in the text. Cosmetic, but the document repeatedly states that identifiers are "allocated in order within its area," so this is a small inconsistency with its own stated convention.

## Priority

Finding 1 is the only one worth real effort. Findings 2 and 3 are quick, targeted fixes. Finding 4 is informational (no action needed unless the WG wants to reconsider the file-split approach). Findings 5 and 6 are cosmetic and can be batched into any of the other fixes' PRs.

title: feat(vtc): retry and discard a failed sync job from the console
body:
feat(vtc): retry and discard a failed sync job from the console

The queue became visible in #1487 and comparable against the registry in #1489,
and in both the answer to "so fix it" was: stop the daemon and run a CLI. The
mutation could not be a route, because binding a `spec/vtc/registry/…` Trust
Task URI ahead of its upstream specification is what `trust_task_manifest.rs`
refuses.

trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#460 specified the family and trust-tasks-rs
0.20.6 publishes it, so the four tasks bind and the buttons work:

- `GET  /v1/registry/sync-jobs`         `…/sync-jobs/list/0.1`
- `POST /v1/registry/sync-jobs/retry`   `…/sync-jobs/retry/0.1`
- `POST /v1/registry/sync-jobs/discard` `…/sync-jobs/discard/0.1`
- `GET  /v1/registry/records`           `…/records/list/0.1`

The offline `vtc sync-jobs` CLI stays. It is the break-glass path for a daemon
that will not start, which is exactly when an HTTP route is no use, and both
surfaces go through `sync_jobs_cli::requeue` and the same eligibility rule, so
"only a Failed row may move" is written once.

Where the two deliberately differ is in how they refuse. Retry *reports* an
ineligible row (`skipped`, with `notFailed` or `notFound`) rather than failing,
so one row the reconciler picked up cannot defeat a bulk retry, and a job swept
between the page load and the click is an ordinary race. Discard *raises*
409/404, because the request names exactly one job and there is no partial
outcome to describe. Bulk retry is `allFailed: true` rather than an omitted
`jobId` — a client bug that drops the identifier must not become a bulk
operation — and discard has no bulk form at all.

Two census gates caught real defects on the way, both worth recording:

- `generated_wire_types_census` rejected the two query structs I had written
  by hand. It was right: they restated `…/list/0.1`'s payload. The handlers now
  take the generated `Payload` as the `Query` extractor, and the OpenAPI
  parameters are declared inline rather than derived from a mirror.
- `every_bound_published_uri_has_a_witness` required a conformance fixture per
  bound URI. Added four, transcribed from what the handlers build — including
  that a failed job carries no `nextAttemptAt`, because it has no schedule and
  claiming one would be the response asserting something untrue.

Every `#[non_exhaustive]` generated enum is matched with an explicit refusal
rather than a catch-all that guesses. A future spec release naming a fourth
retry target must not be silently read as one of the existing two.

title: ci(release): skip the semver check whose baseline cannot be built
body:
#1491 got the Release PR job past the memory ceiling — it now runs 25 minutes
instead of being killed at 6 — and the wall behind that one is this:

    error: failed to build rustdoc for crate vti-secrets v0.3.7
    error[E0308]: expected `DocumentObject`, found `HashMap<String, Document>`
    error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `&_` not covered

`cargo-semver-checks` builds each crate's **published** baseline with all
features. `vti-secrets 0.3.7` on crates.io declares `aws-config` and
`aws-sdk-secretsmanager` and no `aws-smithy-types`: the `>=1.6.1, <1.7` bound
landed in #1485, *after* 0.3.7 was published. So the baseline resolves 1.7.0 and
`aws-smithy-json 0.63` does not compile against it — the same upstream break
#1485 fixed for this workspace, reaching us from a version that predates the
fix.

That is a deadlock rather than a defect: the baseline builds as soon as a
`vti-secrets` carrying the bound is published, and publishing needs the Release
PR this check was blocking.

## Scoped to one crate, and it expires

`vta-service` reaches `aws-config` too, and its baseline **does** build —
verified against a cold `cargo-semver-checks` cache, which matters: a warm cache
reuses baseline rustdoc from before 1.7.0 existed and hides this class of
failure completely. My first local run of `vta-service` "passed" that way and
was worth nothing. None of the other checked crates reach the AWS stack.

So `vta-service` keeps its check — the one with a real external consumer
(`openvtc-core`'s dev-dependency) — and this entry covers only the crate whose
baseline is unbuildable.

**Delete the entry after the first release that publishes `vti-secrets`.** The
baseline is then ≥ 0.3.8, carries the bound, builds, and the check works again.
The comment in `release-plz.toml` says so at the point someone will read it.

title: fix(enclave-proxy): re-lock affinidi-crypto version skew + CI coverage
body:
affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk 0.8.37 pulls didwebvh-rs 0.7.0, whose own manifest mixes affinidi-crypto 0.1.5 (via affinidi-secrets-resolver 0.5.5) and 0.2.6 (via affinidi-did-common 0.4.2) — E0308 in did_key.rs. Bumps affinidi-secrets-resolver to 0.5.11 and affinidi-did-resolver-traits to 0.1.3 (both already published, both within existing semver floors) to collapse onto one affinidi-crypto major. Lockfile-only.

Also adds a CI job for this standalone crate (excluded from the root workspace), since no existing job builds it — which is why this sat on main undetected until a downstream pipeline hit it.

Verified: `cargo build --release --locked` and the downstream Docker build both pass locally.
author: marat-affinidi

title: fix(enclave-proxy): re-lock affinidi-crypto version skew + CI coverage (#1490)
body:
fix(enclave-proxy): re-lock affinidi-crypto version skew + CI coverage (#1490)

* fix(enclave-proxy): re-lock affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk deps to close the affinidi-crypto version skew

affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk 0.8.37 pulled didwebvh-rs 0.7.0 (via
affinidi-did-common 0.4.2 -> affinidi-crypto 0.2.6) alongside
affinidi-did-resolver-traits 0.1.1 (via the older affinidi-did-common 0.3.3
-> affinidi-crypto 0.1.5), so two incompatible affinidi-crypto majors ended
up in the same build and didwebvh-rs's own code passed a type from one
across an API boundary expecting the other (E0308 in did_key.rs).

Bump affinidi-secrets-resolver 0.5.5 -> 0.5.11 and affinidi-did-resolver-traits
0.1.1 -> 0.1.3, both already on crates.io and both within their crates'
existing semver floors, so the whole graph resolves onto a single
affinidi-crypto 0.2.x. Lockfile-only change; `cargo build --release --locked`
now succeeds.

Signed-off-by: Marat Shakirov <marat.s@affinidi.com>

* ci: build deploy/nitro/enclave-proxy on every push/PR

deploy/nitro/enclave-proxy is a standalone crate (its own [workspace]
table, excluded from the root workspace because tokio-vsock is
Linux-only) with its own Cargo.lock. Every job in ci.yml — check, test,
clippy, fmt, msrv, lockfile-resolves — walks the root workspace, and
`affects` reasons about the root workspace's dependency graph, so none
of them ever touch this crate.

That gap is why the affinidi-crypto version-skew break (previous
commit) sat on main invisible to CI, surfacing only when a downstream
image build tried to compile this exact crate from a pinned commit —
a repo away from the change that caused it.

Add a job that builds it the way it's packaged downstream (cargo build
--release --locked) plus its unit tests, unconditionally on every
push/PR, so a break here is caught on the PR that causes it.

Signed-off-by: Marat Shakirov <marat.s@affinidi.com>

* fix(enclave-proxy): patch two live advisories in the standalone lock

The first cargo-deny run this crate has ever had (added in the next
commit) found two vulnerabilities and two yanked crates in its lock, all
of them already patched in the root workspace's:

  h2               0.4.14 -> 0.4.19   RUSTSEC-2026-0258, unbounded empty
                                      DATA frames: hyper queues them
                                      without limit, so an un-drained
                                      stream is unbounded memory or a
                                      length-overflow panic
  crossbeam-epoch  0.9.18 -> 0.9.21   RUSTSEC-2026-0204, invalid pointer
                                      dereference in `fmt::Pointer`
  chacha20         0.10.0 -> 0.10.2   yanked
  spin             0.9.8  -> 0.9.9    yanked

h2 is the one that matters here: this crate terminates TLS on the parent
instance and reaches h2 through reqwest on every DID resolution.

`cargo update` of exactly those four packages; 137 others stay put, and
the affinidi-crypto collapse this branch exists for is untouched.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* ci: fix the enclave-proxy cache-key collision and widen its coverage

Four corrections to the job added in the previous commit.

**The cache key collides with the `enclave` job.** restore-keys are
prefix matches, so `Linux-cargo-enclave-proxy-<hash>` is a hit for the
`enclave` job's `Linux-cargo-enclave-`. That job keys on
`hashFiles('**/Cargo.lock')`, which now includes this crate's lock, so it
falls through to its restore-key routinely — and GitHub hands back the
most recently created match, frequently this job's ~400-package registry
rather than the root workspace's. The `enclave` job then silently
re-downloads the difference. Same shape as #891, documented at the top of
this file. Renamed to `encproxy`, which nothing else prefixes.

**`cargo test --locked` compiled the whole graph a second time.**
`target/` is not cached, so the dev-profile test build shared nothing
with the release build above it — 399 packages twice, `aws-lc-sys` (a
cmake/C build) among them, inside `timeout-minutes: 20` on a cold runner.
Every step is `--release` now, which is also the profile the downstream
image ships. clippy builds dependencies with plain rustc, so it warms the
cache for the two steps after it rather than competing with them.

**`fmt` and `clippy` still never saw this crate.** `fmt --all` and
`clippy --workspace` reach workspace members only, and this crate is
excluded; this job is the one place either can run for it.

**Nor did `cargo-deny`.** The scan walks the root workspace, so a crate
with its own `[workspace]` and its own lock was never in frame — for as
long as it has existed. The first run found two live advisories (see the
previous commit). `--config deny.toml` is required: cargo-deny looks for
a config beside the manifest, finds none, and would otherwise fall back
to defaults that enforce none of the justified ignores.

The test step is `--test-threads=1`: `detect.rs` mutates `PATH` /
`NITRO_CLI` with `unsafe { set_var }`, and a `setenv` racing another
thread's `getenv` — libc's own included — is the unsoundness edition 2024
made that call unsafe for. 23 tests, so serialising costs nothing.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* style(enclave-proxy): rustfmt the crate

`cargo fmt --all` has never covered this crate — it walks the root
workspace, which excludes it. Mechanical; `rustfmt` output only, no
edits of my own. The previous commit adds the check that keeps it this
way.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* refactor(enclave-proxy): clear the six clippy lints the crate carries

`clippy --workspace` never reached this crate either. All six are
mechanical and none changes behaviour:

- three `collapsible_if` -> let-chains (the crate is edition 2024)
- `ptr_arg`: `write_did_log_file` took `&PathBuf`, so its own
  `unwrap_or(data_dir.as_path())` existed only to undo the borrow
- `type_complexity`: `Vec<(Vec<u8>, Vec<u8>)>` named as `KvPair`
- `trim_split_whitespace`: `split_whitespace` already skips the
  leading and trailing whitespace the `trim()` was removing, the
  CRLF of the CONNECT request line included

The `-D warnings` step added two commits back is what holds this.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* ci: pass --config to cargo-deny as a top-level flag, not a check one

The enclave-proxy deny step failed with `unexpected argument '--config'
found`. `--config` moved between cargo-deny releases: it sits under
`check` in 0.19, and is top-level in 0.20, which is what the action's
image ships. It was written against 0.19 because that is what was
installed locally — the version, not the invocation, was the difference
between the local run and CI.

Also corrects the reason given for passing it at all. It does not default
to a config beside the manifest; it defaults to `<cwd>/deny.toml`, so the
root config was always going to be found from this job's working
directory. Naming it explicitly is cheap insurance against that cwd
changing, which is a smaller claim than the one the comment made.

Verified against cargo-deny 0.20.2 — the exact build the pinned action
installs — with the full argv its entrypoint composes:
advisories ok, bans ok, licenses ok, sources ok.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Marat Shakirov <marat.s@affinidi.com>
Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
Co-authored-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: ci(release): give the semver check the memory it measurably needs
body:
The Release PR job has failed **sixteen consecutive times** since 2026-09-14
(first on #1470), so no Release PR has opened since — while the publish job
beside it stayed green and shipped `vta-sdk 0.38.1`. From outside that reads as
"release-plz is not firing", which is the wrong diagnosis: it fires, gets as far
as computing every next version, and is then killed.

    INFO determining next version for vta-service 0.27.1
    INFO Checking API compatibility with cargo-semver-checks...
    ##[error]Process completed with exit code 143.

That is the entire failure. No message, no crate named, no stack — six minutes
in, well inside the 30-minute `timeout-minutes`, so it does not read as a
timeout either.

## The measurement

`cargo semver-checks --package vta-service --baseline-version 0.27.0`, locally,
warm cache: **146 s and 5,311,905,792 bytes peak RSS**. An `ubuntu-latest`
runner has 7 GB, rustdocs the crate twice (current and baseline), and builds the
dependency graph cold first. 5.3 GB against that ceiling is the kill, and a
killed process is exactly what logs nothing.

`vta-service` is the only large crate still checked: `release-plz.toml` switches
the twelve subsystem crates off, and keeps this one because `openvtc-core`
dev-depends on it, so a silent break there reaches somebody.

## Swap, not a bigger runner

No workflow in this repo uses a larger-runner label, so that route is an
org-level change with billing attached; swap costs a few minutes of paging on
one job and nothing else. `ubuntu-latest` already has a 4 GB swapfile at
`/mnt/swapfile`, so it is replaced rather than added to — a second `swapon` on
the same file fails.

`free -h` is printed after, so the next person reads a real number instead of
assuming this step did its job.

If it stops being enough, the order is: larger runner, then `semver_check =
false` for `vta-service` — that last, because it is the one semver signal here
with a consumer who can act on it.

## For next time

An exit 143 with no output, in a step that builds something large, is the memory
ceiling until proven otherwise. The comment in the workflow says so at the point
where someone will be looking.
author: stormer78

    INFO Checking API compatibility with cargo-semver-checks...
    ##[error]Process completed with exit code 143.

That is the entire failure. No message, no crate named, no stack — six minutes
in, well inside the 30-minute `timeout-minutes`, so it does not read as a
timeout either.

## The measurement

`cargo semver-checks --package vta-service --baseline-version 0.27.0`, locally,
warm cache: **146 s and 5,311,905,792 bytes peak RSS**. An `ubuntu-latest`
runner has 7 GB, rustdocs the crate twice (current and baseline), and builds the
dependency graph cold first. 5.3 GB against that ceiling is the kill, and a
killed process is exactly what logs nothing.

`vta-service` is the only large crate still checked: `release-plz.toml` switches
the twelve subsystem crates off, and keeps this one because `openvtc-core`
dev-depends on it, so a silent break there reaches somebody.

## Swap, not a bigger runner

No workflow in this repo uses a larger-runner label, so that route is an
org-level change with billing attached; swap costs a few minutes of paging on
one job and nothing else. `ubuntu-latest` already has a 4 GB swapfile at
`/mnt/swapfile`, so it is replaced rather than added to — a second `swapon` on
the same file fails.

`free -h` is printed after, so the next person reads a real number instead of
assuming this step did its job.

If it stops being enough, the order is: larger runner, then `semver_check =
false` for `vta-service` — that last, because it is the one semver signal here
with a consumer who can act on it.

## For next time

An exit 143 with no output, in a step that builds something large, is the memory
ceiling until proven otherwise. The comment in the workflow says so at the point
where someone will be looking.

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.20.6
body:
### Added

- **vtc/registry**: An operator surface for the trust-registry reconciler ([#460](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/460))

A Verifiable Trust Community publishes its membership to a trust registry
  through a queue, because the registry is a separate party that can be
  unreachable, unauthorised, or running an incompatible version at the moment a
  member joins. Today there is no specified way to look at that queue, and no
  specified way to act on it — so a membership change that never landed is
  invisible, and stays invisible until someone reads a log.

  Four tasks, one family:

  - `vtc/registry/sync-jobs/list/0.1` — enumerate the queue: which member, which
    mutation, how many attempts, and the registry's own last answer verbatim.
    `attempts` discriminates the two unrelated failures that look identical from
    outside: a registry that answered and refused, versus one that never answered.
  - `vtc/registry/sync-jobs/retry/0.1` — requeue an abandoned job. The only thing
    that re-drives one: the audit position that produced it has long since moved
    past. Bulk retry is spelled `allFailed: true` rather than an absent `jobId`,
    so a client that drops the identifier cannot silently become a bulk operation.
  - `vtc/registry/sync-jobs/discard/0.1` — delete one without dispatching it.
    Destructive, single-target by construction: a bulk form would let one request
    erase every record of a systemic failure.
  - `vtc/registry/records/list/0.1` — enumerate the recognition graph itself,
    from the registry (`source: "registry"`) or from what the community believes
    it published (`source: "local"`). The two are different questions and the
    answer worth having is the difference, so a consumer must not serve the
    registry view from a local cache — a stale local answer presented as the
    registry's is the exact fault an operator is looking for.

  Recognition has been specified only as a per-DID probe, which is the right
  shape for a decision and the wrong one for an operator: it cannot show that a
  member is missing from the registry, because you have to already suspect the
  member to ask.

  Both list tasks state that a nullable response member may be sent as `null` or
  omitted and that a producer must treat the two identically. That is not
  pedantry — the generated Rust bindings skip `None`, so an implementation built
  on them omits where the prose would say null, and a consumer that distinguished
  them would break against a conforming producer.

  Bindings regenerated; 896 trust-tasks-rs tests pass.

title: feat(vtc): compare the registry mirror against the registry, and show it
body:
feat(vtc): compare the registry mirror against the registry, and show it

The `registry_records` keyspace has held what this community believes it
published since Phase 3. `RegistryRecord`'s own doc comment says it exists "so
the daemon can detect drift at boot". Nothing ever detected any: `list_records`
had no caller in the service, and the mirror was written on every successful
sync and never read.

That gap is why a lost write was invisible. The Recognition page carried three
signals and none of them answered the question that matters:

  registryStatus           does the registry respond?
  membership sync counters were our writes accepted?
  (nothing)                are they still there?

And the third outlives the second. A failed sync job is swept after 30 days;
the member stays unpublished, and at that point no surface in the service said
so at all.

- `registry::drift` compares the two views on its own timer (`[registry]
  drift_check_interval_seconds`, default 900, `0` disables). Its own timer and
  not the diagnostics handler, because enumerating the graph is several round
  trips and the console polls diagnostics every 15 seconds — on-demand would
  turn one open browser tab into steady load on a third party.
- A disagreement is reported in one of three directions, because they have
  opposite fixes: missing at registry (a lost write — the member is invisible
  to every other community), unknown locally (benign, so reported without being
  counted a fault), status mismatch (a removal that half-landed). Truncation
  sorts faults first, so a community with more benign extras than lost writes
  does not have the lost writes pushed off the end.
- A failed check annotates the last snapshot rather than replacing it. A
  registry that was briefly unreachable is not evidence that drift went away,
  and clearing a real finding on a transient error cancels an operator's alarm
  without fixing anything.
- Absent is not empty. `registryDrift` is omitted until a check completes, and
  the console renders "not checked yet" distinctly from "the two views agree" —
  a VTC whose check never ran must not look healthy.
- `TrustRegistryClient::list_records` defaults to a typed "cannot enumerate"
  rather than an error, so a REST-only transport reports unsupported rather
  than an outage. The messaging arm pages `record/query` and refuses to compare
  a partial enumeration: a short list against a complete mirror would invent a
  lost write for every member past the cap.

Rides in the diagnostics `ext` envelope, so no new canonical URI is bound —
`trust_task_manifest.rs` refuses one ahead of its upstream spec. The
corresponding online browse and retry surfaces are specified in
trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#460 and land here after a trust-tasks-rs bump.
