title: fix(tsp): every client seals Trust Tasks in the binding envelope
body:
#1478 gave the VTA's TSP receiver the published `trust-tasks-tsp` binding and
cut the browser wallet over with it. Every Rust client kept sealing the bare
document, so the VTA refused all of them:

    refused a TSP frame that is not a binding envelope
      reason=TSP payload is not a `…/binding/tsp/0.1/envelope` envelope
             (got `…/spec/messaging/ping/0.1`)

A TSP trust ping, and `keys/export-secret/0.1` from openvtc, are the two that
were reported; the cause is one missing call, in the send funnels every TSP
client in this workspace goes through — `TspSession::send_document` (so
`announce`, `request`, and the mobile approver), `DIDCommSession::
send_tsp_document` (so `request_tsp`, so every `VtaClient` trust task on TSP),
and the two `TspPingSession` probes behind `pnm health`.

## The binding is now one module, not one per crate

`messaging::tsp_binding` moved to `vta_sdk::tsp_binding`, which `vta-service`
uses in place of its own copy. Its header called it "a single fact about this
service", and that was the defect in miniature: a binding known to one side is
the private dialect it exists to end. `vta-sdk` is the leaf both sides already
depend on.

The receive halves open the envelope in the same one place, so a caller of
`receive_next` / `receive_next_tsp` still gets a document. A client *skips* a
frame that is not the binding rather than answering it, unlike the VTA: that
socket also carries mediator traffic, where "not our binding" means "not
addressed to this layer".

## What the mediator speaks, and why one send stays bare

The mediator's TSP management surface parses the bare document and claims it
only when the type is one it serves (`trust_tasks::parse_if_served`) — it has
no envelope to open, and would file a wrapped frame as mail with the account
ACL silently unset. So `acl_setup::set_client_acl_over_tsp` stays bare, named
in the census as the one peer that cannot read the binding.

## The VTC answers in the carriage it was addressed in

`handle_tsp` dispatched the raw payload and replied raw, so wrapping the
clients would have broken it twice over: an envelope reaching the spine is a
`malformedRequest` for a well-formed request, and a bare reply is one a
conformant client now skips. It opens the envelope when there is one — liberal,
as it already was for replies, because it answers peers it does not ship with —
and wraps its reply only when the request was wrapped.

## Tests

- `tests/e2e/tests/tsp_binding_pair.rs` — the pair, across the crate boundary:
  a real `TspSession` seals and routes through a real mediator, the frame is
  unpacked as the delivery layer unpacks it, and the bytes go into the VTA's own
  `tsp_inbound::dispatch_one`. Reverting the wrap reproduces the log line above
  verbatim. Nothing caught this before because `tsp_round_trip` and
  `tsp_dual_leg` send *and* receive through the SDK, and `tsp_inbound`'s unit
  tests frame their fixtures with the service's own wrapper: each side agreed
  with itself.
- `vta-sdk/tests/tsp_binding_census.rs` — for the send sites nobody has driven
  yet. Source-text, so it is feature-independent.
- `join_tsp` now submits in both carriages, so the VTC's liberality is exercised
  rather than asserted.

## A test that only held in a build without `tsp`

Reaching `tsp_inbound` from the e2e crate turns `tsp` on for `vta-service` in a
workspace build, and `a_tsp_only_peer_is_refused_naming_both_sides` panicked: a
build that *can* initiate TSP refuses nothing. The assertion was unconditional,
so it held only while nothing enabled the feature — and `cargo test -p
vta-service` has no `tsp` either, so the crate's own suite could not see it.
Gated, with the opposite arm asserted beside it.

title: feat(tsp): form relationships with XRFI/XRFA, which Rev 3 requires
body:
feat(tsp): form relationships with XRFI/XRFA, which Rev 3 requires

Rev 3 §7.2.2 turned relationships from bookkeeping into a precondition:
an endpoint SHOULD drop an application message from a VID it holds no
relationship with. Dropped, not refused — nothing comes back — so a
wallet that skips the handshake does not get an error, it gets a
30-second timeout and a transport that looks broken. The Rust SDK
defaults `tsp_relationship_gating` to true, so this is the live default
on the far side, not a setting someone might turn on.

vti-tsp-js gains the codec and the rules:

  - `packInvite` / `packAccept` / `packCancel`, and `unpack` returning a
    verified `control` message.
  - The §7.2.1 `TSP_Digest`, which is the substance of it: self-addressing
    over the message's own envelope and payload with its own slot filled
    by 33 dummy bytes, carried on the wire, recomputed by the receiver,
    and refused on a mismatch. Rev 2 correlated on a hash of the encrypted
    payload that was never transmitted and so could never be checked.
  - `relationship.ts` — the §7.2/§7.3 state machine, pure: state and event
    in, state or a refusal out, with no storage, clock or keys. That is
    the line between the two packages. `unpack` does not apply it, because
    a codec that mutated relationship state would make receiving a message
    a side effect, and a wallet must be able to look at an invite before
    answering it.

Two rules are encoded rather than commented. An accept's digests are
named `inReplyTo` and `digest` rather than the spec's `Digest` and
`Reply_Digest`, whose order is the reverse of how they read — affinidi-tsp
keeps the spec names and warns about it in a comment, and a name that
cannot spring the trap is stronger than a warning. And the §7.2.3 invite
race is decided on bytes alone: both sides keep the lexicographically
lower digest, because a timestamp or an "ours wins" tie-break would let
the two ends disagree and form two half-relationships.

pnm-core gains the handshake, shaped by what the far side actually does:

  - `ensureRelationship` invites before the first application message, at
    most once at a time — N concurrent first-sends would otherwise invite
    N times, which a peer's state machine refuses as repeated sendInvite
    from pending, failing every request after the first.
  - It is best-effort and never throws. A VTA that does not implement
    control messages never answers, and a wallet that waited for an accept
    before ever sending would have broken itself against every peer that
    does not gate — which is every peer running today.
  - A failed send clears the record. The far side's store is
    `InMemoryRelationshipStore` by default, so a VTA forgets every
    relationship when its process restarts; a wallet that kept believing
    its own record would post into silence indefinitely. Re-inviting costs
    one round trip and cannot go quietly wrong, so the default store here
    is deliberately no more durable than theirs.

Verified against the specification's three published control vectors,
which is what makes the digest derivation trustworthy: our decoder
recomputes the SAID and refuses on mismatch, so a vector that unpacks at
all is a derivation agreeing with the ToIP reference over the envelope,
both VIDs, the type code, the sender field, the nonce, the reply path,
the referral slot and the dummy bytes. The accept vector is checked
against the invite vector rather than itself, so the two-digest order is
pinned to external bytes. Both directions against affinidi-tsp again: an
invite and an accept packed here unpack there with matching digests.

Not implemented, deliberately: composing a referral (§7.2.5). Its
`Signature_new` covers the invite's digest, so composing one needs the
introduced VID's signing key at pack time, and a wallet holding another
VID's private key is not a shape to invite. Referrals are decoded and
exposed unverified, with `referralSignedData` for a caller that can
resolve `VID_new` and check.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: fix(mediator-transport): route long-framed TSP messages, which Rev 3 made real
body:
fix(mediator-transport): route long-framed TSP messages, which Rev 3 made real

The inbound demux classified TSP by `text.startsWith("-E")` — the qb64
spelling of the *short* `-E` count code. TSP spec Rev 3 widened that count
to cover all signable content, the ciphertext included, so any message past
4095 quadlets (~12 KB) is framed with the six-byte long count code instead
and its text starts `--E`. `"--E…".startsWith("-E")` is false, so every
large Rev 3 message went to the DIDComm unpacker.

The failure is silent in the worst direction. A TSP frame handed to
`unpackInbound` throws, is reported as a poison frame, and — because the
throw returns before `_dispatchTspFrame` — is never acked. The mediator
therefore keeps its copy and redelivers it on every reconnect, forever,
while the consumer that wanted it never hears. A message that loops is
harder to notice than one that errors.

Nothing could have caught this before Rev 3 existed: Rev 2's `-E` count
covered only the envelope header, a couple of dozen quadlets whatever the
message size, so it could not produce a long frame at all.

`src/tsp-frame.js` now owns the predicate — `isTspFrameText` for the qb64
form the mediator delivers, `isTspFrameBytes` for qb2 — rather than an
inline `startsWith`. It is a module because the rule is not obvious from
the expression and has a deliberate exclusion worth writing down: Rev 2's
long form `-0E…`, from a superseded draft of the CESR v2 tables, is not
matched, because nothing can emit it (reaching a long count under Rev 2's
header-only semantics would take ~12 KB of VIDs in one envelope) and
matching it would route a frame no implementation produces.

Reading Rev 2 is unaffected. Rev 2 messages are short-framed and start
`-E` exactly as they always did; the framing question and the revision
question are independent, and this library answers only the first — it is
key-blind for TSP and hands the bytes to a consumer that decides the rest.

The same predicate exists in the mediator (`affinidi_tsp::is_tsp`) and in
the wallet's codec (`@openvtc/vti-tsp-js`'s `isTsp`), both fixed for this
reason on their own branches. That is R4.1's situation, and deliberately
not solved by sharing code: they are independent implementations of one
wire contract, and a shared helper would only make them agree on a shared
mistake. CLAUDE.md records that a change to what counts as a TSP frame
lands in all three.

Test heads are bytes from real messages packed by vti-tsp-js 0.3.0, pinned
rather than imported so this library takes no dependency on the other
implementation. Reverting the predicate to `["-E"]` fails three of them —
the classifier test, the routing test, and the ack test, since routing a
frame without acking it still loses the message.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
author: stormer78

title: feat(tsp-js): pack TSP Rev 3, read Rev 3 and Rev 2
body:
feat(tsp-js): pack TSP Rev 3, read Rev 3 and Rev 2

The specification's Rev 3 changed the crypto mode, the version byte, the
long count-code prefix, the ciphertext code and layout, the `-E` count's
meaning, the signature code and every payload layout at once. Nothing a
Rev 2 peer packs can be unpacked by a Rev 3 one or the reverse, and the
protocol negotiates nothing.

The wire carries a version marker, so reading can be dual. `unpack` now
peeks it — a fixed offset, no keys, nine bytes — and dispatches. Packing
cannot be: an inbound message says what it is, an outbound one has to be
decided before a byte exists, and no field says what a peer can read. So
we pack Rev 3 only. A Rev 2 peer cannot read what we send; that is the
cutover, not a bug.

That asymmetry is what keeps this from being the compatibility fold
CLAUDE.md bans. There is no `if (rev === 2)` anywhere on the Rev 3 path.
Rev 2 is a frozen decode-only codec in `src/rev2/`, and it is deleted
whole — with its arm of the dispatcher — the day the last Rev 2 peer is
gone. CLAUDE.md now records why TSP is the one exception: it is a ToIP
specification with implementations nobody here controls, where the VTA
and the mediator cut over with us and other peers do not.

Wire changes, all of them Rev 3's:

  - HPKE-Auth -> HPKE-Base. The sender's key leaves the KEM, so `PackKeys`
    lost `senderEncryptionKey` outright and `UnpackKeys` keeps it as an
    optional Rev 2-only member — HPKE-Auth cannot *open* a message
    without it. `info` is the fixed code `YTSP-`; the AAD is the envelope
    fields, where Rev 2 passed the whole frame as `info` with empty AAD.
  - `YTSP-AAB` -> `YTSP-AAC`, MAJOR.MINOR. Only MAJOR gates, so any other
    MINOR at MAJOR 0 — upstream's `ABA` (64) included — reads as Rev 3.
  - Ciphertext `G` -> `F`, field `enc || ct`. A `C`-coded sealed box
    (§8.3) is recognised and refused by name, never as a corrupt `F`.
  - Long counts `-0X#####` -> `--X#####`.
  - The `-E` count covers all signable content, so the frame is finalized
    after sealing: `encodeEnvelope` is replaced by `encodeFields` +
    `finalizeFrame`, split exactly where the AAD boundary falls.
  - The `X 00 00` marker is deleted; the receiver field is always written.
  - Indexed signature `B#` under length-based counts `-C23 -K22`.
  - Payload frames carry an ESSR sender VID and a padding field, a direct
    body sits in a `-A` stream, `-J` counts bytes not VIDs, and a nested
    inner is raw — so it must be quadlet-aligned.

Two bugs fixed on the way, both latent:

  - `decodeCount` returned long-form counts with the identifier bits still
    in them, so every long-framed message decoded to a wrong length. The
    test covering it asserted the wrong behaviour deliberately, calling it
    "a reference quirk ... benign, TSP frames by cursor position and
    discards this value". Rev 3 makes it fatal: the `-E` and `-Z` counts
    are load-bearing lengths now. affinidi-tsp fixed the same bug
    independently.
  - `MAX_HOPS` was 16 when packing against a decoder that stopped at 10, so
    a 12-hop route packed cleanly and could not be read back here.

Checked three ways, because a round trip proves none of it — encoder and
decoder agree with each other whatever they both get wrong, which is
precisely what Rev 3's one-character changes produce:

  - The specification's own Appendix A vectors run as a suite. Every
    published vector is exercised or named as uncovered, so the list
    cannot quietly shrink.
  - Both directions against affinidi-tsp's `tsp-rev3` branch: its Rev 2
    vector unpacks here, and a message packed here unpacks there with a
    byte-identical thread digest.
  - Pinned bytes for the deterministic parts of what we emit, since a
    sealed message is not reproducible.

Not implemented, each for a stated reason rather than by omission: the
libsodium sealed box, the post-quantum suite, fillable padding, and the
relationship state machine. The last one matters for the cutover — Rev 3
gates application messages on a relationship by default, so a VTA
enforcing §7.2.2 will drop what we send until that layer exists.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
author: stormer78

title: vta-service-v0.27.1
body:
### Fixed

- **webvh**: Key records follow the document's verification-method ids, and a repair for the ones that don't ([#1466](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1466))

* fix(webvh): name a created DID's key records after the document it published

  A key record's id **is** a verification-method id. `save_entity_key_records`
  says so in its own name, and `vta_sdk::did_secrets::select_secret_kid` rule 1
  depends on it: the kid a mediator matches inbound JWE recipients against is the
  record id, on the reasoning that "the DID document decided what the key is
  called".

  Create never read the document to find out. It named the records `{did}#key-0`
  and `{did}#key-1` while the document was whatever the caller or the template
  said — and the `room` and `room-host` built-in templates number their methods
  from `#key-1`. So on every room and every room host this VTA has ever minted:

  - the document's `#key-1` is the **signing** key and the keystore's `#key-1` is
    the **x25519** one. One name, two keys, no error anywhere. Hand the id the
    document publishes to `keys/sign` — the natural thing to do, having read it
    off the document — and the oracle fetches an x25519 record for an EdDSA
    signature;
  - the document's `keyAgreement` (`#key-2`) matches no record at all, so an
    authcrypt message addressed to it finds no local secret. That is the storm.ws
    outage of #337 reached from the other side: there a decorative label
    overwrote the right kid, here the right kid was never stored;
  - `next_fragment_id` was stored as the constant 2, so the DID's first rotation
    allocates `#key-2` — over the id its key-agreement method is already
    published under.

  Room credentials still verify, which is why this stayed quiet: `RoomKeySigner`
  hardcodes `{room_did}#key-1` to match the template, and the public keys line up
  positionally, so the proof names a method that resolves to the key that signed
  it. Everything that addresses a key *by name* is what breaks.

title: vta-tee-v0.2.6
body:
### Fixed

- **pnm-cli**: Anchor TEE bootstrap connect by DID and PCR0 ([#1454](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1454))

* fix(pnm-cli): anchor TEE bootstrap connect by DID and PCR0

  Add mutually exclusive --vta-did and --vta-url targets. Resolve WebVH locally without guessing a URL on failure, preserve the advertised REST endpoint, and reject credentials for a different VTA DID.

  Accept a pinned PCR0 as the online connect trust anchor without requiring the server-generated digest or an opt-out warning. Preserve explicit digest opt-out warnings, conflicting-flag errors, and mandatory offline digest verification.

  Add regression tests for target selection, strict endpoint resolution, credential identity checks, and anchor combinations. Update the PNM quick start and TEE bootstrap guide.

- **webvh**: Clamp versionTime against the previous log entry ([#1456](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1456))

* fix(tee): backdate WebVH genesis versionTime

  The TEE genesis path used the library's current-time default while
  runtime updates used PR #600's backdated timestamps. This caused the
  first update to have a lower versionTime than genesis, making the DID
  unresolvable.

  Apply the shared PR #600 backdating policy to TEE genesis and move the
  helper into vta-support so both TEE and service paths use one implementation.
author: github-actions[bot]

title: pnm-cli-v0.16.4
body:
### Added

- **pnm**: Confirm before `vta remove`, with a --force opt-out ([#1457](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1457))

`pnm vta remove <slug>` deleted the stored VTA connection and its
  keyring credential with no prompt, and a mistyped slug is unrecoverable
  from the config file. It now prints what is about to go — name, DID, the
  credential, and whether the default VTA moves — and asks before doing
  it.

  The prompt reuses `vta_cli_common::commands::contexts::confirm_destructive`,
  so the wording matches `pnm contexts delete`. As there, a non-TTY stdin
  reads EOF and aborts, which is what `--force` is for: scripts that today
  call `pnm vta remove` (the `pnm setup --overwrite` hint points at it) pass
  the flag to keep their old behaviour.

title: feat(vtc): make a failed registry sync job visible and recoverable
body:
A `Failed` membership-sync job is terminal — the syncer skips it on every
tick, boot recovery rescues only `InFlight`, and nothing re-derives it — so
the row names a condition that never resolves on its own. The only operator
surfaces were a bare count on `/v1/health/diagnostics` and a line in the
service log, and there was no way at all to act on one: the member stayed
absent from the trust registry until the retention sweeper purged the row
~30 days later, clearing the failure without fixing it.

Worse, the page above the counter could say `active` throughout.

## What prompted it

A live community showed `STATUS active`, `FAILED 1`, `LAST FAILURE (none)`
on the Recognition page, with no way to find out more from the console. The
job had been refused with:

```
unsupportedType (unsupported type: https://trusttasks.org/spec/registry/record/put/0.1)
```

`registry/record/put/0.1` and `registry/record/query/0.1` arrived in
affinidi-trust-registry-rs **0.10.0** (#121) as a clean cutover with no
dual-accept — it removed `registry/record/{create,update,read,list}/0.1`. The
deployed registry predated it, so every call was being refused. The remedy is
to upgrade the registry; nothing about the community's configuration was
wrong, and nothing on the console could have said so.

The green status has its own cause. The liveness probe counts any correlated
reply as proof of life, including a rejection — and `record/query` is from the
same cutover, so the probe was being refused identically and reporting
`active`. `LAST FAILURE (none)` followed from the same gap: only the retriable
branch calls `RegistryHealth::record_failure`, so a permanent rejection never
touched the health state.

## Changes

**`RegistryError::Incompatible`** splits `unsupportedType` out of `Permanent`.
It is not a bad request; it says the registry does not route the task at all.
The probe fails on it — a registry that cannot answer the read we depend on
cannot answer the writes either — while an ordinary rejection still counts as
liveness, because that one really does prove the dispatcher read and routed our
document. Still re-falsifiable (R6.2): upgrade the registry and the next tick
flips back to `active`. The syncer also records it on the health signal at the
moment of failure rather than waiting a probe interval.

**`ext["org.openvtc"].failedJobs`** carries every failed row: member DID,
operation, attempts, the registry's verbatim error, and when the sweeper will
purge it. The plaintext member DID is the field the audit trail cannot give —
`RegistrySyncFailed` envelopes carry only `targetDidHash` (§11.1) — and it is
what turns "1 failed" into something actionable. Under `ext` because the
published response is `additionalProperties: false`. Capped at 50; the count
stays authoritative.

**`vtc sync-jobs {list,retry,discard}`** is the write half. `retry` is the only
thing that re-drives a failed row — the sync cursor passed the originating
audit envelope long ago — and it refuses anything the syncer still owns.

**Recognition page** lists the failed jobs under the counters and banners the
version-skew case, which an operator would not otherwise infer from a queue of
failures. `attempts: 1` is labelled "refused outright" to separate it from a
job that burned ~18h of backoff against silence.

## Why the mutation is a CLI and not a route

`vtc-service/tests/trust_task_manifest.rs` refuses a new `spec/vtc/registry/…`
URI bound ahead of its upstream specification — *"Author the spec upstream, or
bind an authority we control; raising this number is the wrong fix."* Offline
break-glass on a stopped daemon needs no wire contract, and `vta approvals` /
`vta policy` / `vta services` are the same shape for the same reason. It sits
beside `vtc acl` rather than under `vtc admin` because `admin` is gated on the
`setup` feature and queue triage should not vanish from a
`--no-default-features` build.

Putting it in the browser is a follow-up that starts with authoring the task in
dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — green
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean
- `npm run lint` in `admin-ui` (`wire:check` + `tsc -b`) — clean
- `openapi.json` and `wire.ts` regenerated; the manifest census is unchanged,
  because no new canonical URI is bound

New tests: `unsupported_type_is_incompatible_not_a_rejection` (the classify
split and both `is_retriable` / `is_incompatible` sides),
`failed_jobs_ride_in_the_openvtc_ext_namespace` (placement, plaintext member
DID, verbatim error, purge deadline, and absence from the top level),
`failed_jobs_is_an_empty_list_when_nothing_failed`, plus `requeue` coverage for
the dispatchable reset, the surviving `rtbf_batched` marker, and the
failed-only targeting.

Docs: `docs/03-vtc/trust-registry.md` gains a "Triaging a failed job" section
with the three error classes and what each one means.

title: fix(extension): emit no modulepreload links, which Chrome refuses to use
body:
Every generated wallet page carried a `<link rel="modulepreload" crossorigin>` for each shared chunk its entry imports, and Chrome declined all of them:

> A preload for 'chrome-extension://…/assets/bridge-protocol-….js' is found, but is not used because it is a cross-world extension resource mismatch.

The hint is fetched under a different resource world than the module graph that `<script type="module">` then loads, so the preloaded copy never matches the lookup and is discarded — each chunk fetched twice, and **18 warnings** across popup (4), options (6), confirm (4) and offscreen (4) on the `chrome://extensions` Errors page.

Nothing was broken by them; the script tag is what actually loads the graph. The cost is the page they filled. The Errors page is where a real fault has to be noticed, and a screenful of benign warnings is how one gets scrolled past — the same reasoning R7.2 applies to a lost prompt.

Preloading buys nothing here anyway: every asset is read from local disk, with no network latency to hide. `manager.html` never had any, because `codeSplitting: false` leaves the console no shared chunks to preload, and `background.js` is a single bundle with no HTML at all — so `vite.config.ts` is the one config that needed the option.

## Verification

Built both ways and counted the links:

| page | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| popup.html | 4 | 0 |
| options.html | 6 | 0 |
| confirm.html | 4 | 0 |
| offscreen.html | 4 | 0 |

The entry's own `<script type="module" crossorigin src="…">` is unchanged, which is the tag that actually loads.

- `npm run build --workspace @openvtc/pnm-extension` (all three configs) — clean
- `npm test --workspace @openvtc/pnm-extension` — 726 pass, 0 fail
- dist guards re-run locally: `background.js` has no dynamic `import()`; `acl/*`, `contexts/delete`, `keys/sign` and `persona/attribute/put` appear in no file but `manager.js`; no `vta/seeds/*` anywhere; no `manager-split-*.js`; packaged manifest has no `content_scripts`; no `chrome.cookies` in `dist/`

## Pre-merge checklist (vti-stack-development-guide.md)

- [x] No cross-service wire contract touched — this is a bundler output option only
- [x] No compatibility fold added
- [x] No new fetch, endpoint or error-matching path (R1.2 / R3.7 unaffected)
- [x] MV3 invariants intact: single `background.js` bundle, `codeSplitting: false` on the console build

title: fix(vetting): size a ticket's QR code to the space it has, and give it a screen of its own
body:
A ticket's QR code ran off the bottom of the panel, and scrolling did not rescue it.

## The bug

`qr_lines` chose a code by **width alone**. On a wide, short terminal that
picks the widest code — which is also the tallest — and it overflows. Scrolling
is not the answer even where it works: a scanner needs the whole code, finder
patterns and quiet zone included, in one view. Half a QR code is not a degraded
QR code, it is a picture of nothing, and a convincing one.

## The fix, in two parts

**Height is now a budget like width.** Both shrink the same two dials — the
error-correction level and the quiet zone — so the first combination that fits
is the strongest one that does, and a code that cannot fit is not drawn. The
refusal names the direction that is actually short, in rows the *window* needs
rather than rows the code needs (the code competes with everything else on the
panel):

> The QR code needs a window 6 rows taller — or copy the link with u.

**`⏎` on a ticket shows its code full-screen**, and this is the part that makes
the feature work rather than merely fail honestly. The desk header, the view
tabs, the ticket row and two key lines take about half the panel; on a maximised
132×41 terminal that leaves too few rows for the codes these links produce, so
sizing alone would have replaced a broken code with a "make your window taller"
message. Given the whole panel, the same code fits.

It is also the right screen for the job — someone else is pointing a phone at
it — so it holds the code, the characters to read aloud if the scan fails, and
nothing else:

```
Ticket   9ENN-8R76   webvh.storm.ws/@first-vtc

█▀▀▀▀▀█ ▀▄█▀▄ ▄█ █▀▀▀▀▀█
█ ███ █ ▄█▀ ▀█▄█ █ ███ █
█ ▀▀▀ █ █▄▀▄▀ ▄█ █ ▀▀▀ █
             …
Esc or Enter: back  (y: copy code  u: copy link)
```

Esc and Enter both close it — either is what a hand reaches for when the scan
is done.

## About the scrolling

Scrolling does work on that panel (PgUp/PgDn/Home/End, per the footer); ↑/↓ move
the ticket selection instead, which is probably what got tried. It is moot now:
a code that fits needs no scrolling, and one that does not fit is not drawn.

## Also

The content panel records its height for the frame alongside its width, carried
by the same thread-local mechanism and documented for the one consumer that
cannot scroll its content into view.

## Checks

`cargo test --workspace`, again with `--include-ignored`; clippy across all
targets; `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc`; `cargo fmt`.

New tests: a short window gets a shorter code or is told how much taller to be,
and the figure it names is enough; the wide-but-short case is refused rather
than overflowed; and — the one that caught a real off-by-one while I wrote it —
a real ticket link at 132×41 does *not* fit the list view but does fit the
full-screen view, whole, within the panel's rows.

title: fix(deps): bound aws-smithy-types below 1.7, which breaks aws-smithy-json 0.63 (#1485)
body:
fix(deps): bound aws-smithy-types below 1.7, which breaks aws-smithy-json 0.63 (#1485)

A fresh dependency resolution stopped compiling:

    error[E0308]: expected `DocumentObject`, found `HashMap<String, Document>`
      --> aws-smithy-json-0.63.0/src/codec/deserializer.rs:707:37
    error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `&_` not covered
      --> aws-smithy-json-0.63.0/src/serialize.rs:36:15

`aws-smithy-types` 1.7.0 changed `Document::Object` from
`HashMap<String, Document>` to a new `DocumentObject`, and added a variant
to an enum that is `#[non_exhaustive]` — a breaking change shipped as a
MINOR bump. `aws-smithy-json` 0.63.0 declares `aws-smithy-types = "^1.6.1"`,
which admits 1.7.0 and then does not compile against it.

Cargo unifies `aws-smithy-types` to one version across the graph but keeps
both `aws-smithy-json` 0.63 and 0.64 — 0.x minors are incompatible majors —
so the two coexist and only the 0.63 copy breaks. We have both because
`aws-sdk-secretsmanager` 1.116.0 moved to json `^0.64.0` while `aws-config`
1.12.0, its newest release, still wants `^0.63.0`. Both reach us:
`vti-secrets` behind `aws-secrets`, and `vta-tee` unconditionally, so a
plain `cargo build --workspace` is affected as well as the secrets path.

Cargo.lock already held 1.6.3, so committed builds were never affected and
only a lockless resolution broke — which is what `cargo install --path`
does unless given `--locked`. That is how this was met:

    cargo install --path vtc-service --no-default-features \
      --features setup,website,admin-ui,aws-secrets,tsp

`--locked` remains the right flag for a reproducible install. This bound is
what keeps `cargo update` and a lockless build honest too.

The bound is declared once in `[workspace.dependencies]` with the
reasoning, and referenced from the two crates that pull `aws-config` —
Cargo only honours a version requirement from a crate that declares it, so
a workspace entry alone would constrain nothing. Neither crate calls it.

`>= 1.6.1, < 1.7` rather than `= 1.6.3`: 1.6.1 is aws-smithy-json 0.63.0's
own floor, and the upper bound excludes the break without freezing out
patch releases in the working line. **Remove it when `aws-config` ships a
release on json 0.64.**

Verified, on this branch:

  - without the bound, a lockless resolve picks aws-smithy-types 1.7.0 with
    aws-smithy-json 0.63.0 AND 0.64.0 — the failing combination
  - with it, a lockless resolve picks 1.6.3, json 0.63.0 alone, and backs
    aws-sdk-secretsmanager off to 1.115.0
  - Cargo.lock moves by two lines, both dependency edges; no version churn
  - `cargo check -p vti-secrets --no-default-features --features aws-secrets`
    and `cargo check -p vtc-service --no-default-features --features
    setup,website,admin-ui,aws-secrets,tsp` both pass

title: fix(cli): validate the backup password at the import prompt too
body:
Every export prompt calls `validate_backup_password`; no import prompt did — `pnm backup import` on both the legacy and descriptor paths (`pnm-cli/src/commands/backup.rs`), and `cnm backup import` (`cnm-cli/src/backup.rs`).

The floor binds on the way in as well: the published `finalize-import/1.0` schema carries `minLength: 15` on `password`, and the legacy import op re-checks it server-side. So a short password was already refused either way — this does not change what is possible, only which error the operator reads.

Before, a mistyped or short restore password surfaced as either:

- a client-side `refusing to send a payload that does not conform to …/finalize-import/1.0 … The recipient would reject this as malformedRequest` (descriptor path, which is the default for `pnm backup import`), or
- a round trip to the VTA (legacy path).

After, both say `backup password must be at least 15 characters`. The prompt also states the minimum up front, as the three export prompts already do, so the constraint is visible before the operator types rather than after.

Noticed while reviewing #1480, which routes the descriptor flow through `dispatch_trust_task` and so makes the schema gate the first thing a short password hits. Not a regression from that PR — the gap predates it — so it is fixed separately rather than expanding that PR's scope.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p pnm-cli -p cnm-cli --no-fail-fast` — 123 passed, 0 failed
- `cargo clippy -p pnm-cli -p cnm-cli --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean

title: feat(vetting): one desk for vetting, headed by the credential that makes you a vetter
body:
Two questions from testing the vetting flow — "do I get a credential for being a vetter, and where do I see it?" and "why is the vetter profile hidden under Tickets?" — turned out to have the same answer.

## You do get a credential, and nothing drew it

A community naming you a vetter issues an `EndorsementCredential` with
`{type: "CommunityRole", role: "vetter", communityDid}`, a `validUntil` and a
status-list entry (design §10.3). The client stored it, gated the entire vetter
UI on it, and presented it to every applicant accepted — as `eligibilityVp`,
nonce-bound to their request. The applicant saw it verified. Its holder never
saw it at all: not its expiry, not which communities had granted it.

## Two tabs, not four

§12.3 asks for **Applications** and a **Vetter Desk** with sub-views. The
shipped page had flattened that into four siblings, which put a vetter's
inbound queue beside their outbound tickets as separate concerns, and parked
the vetter profile under Tickets — where it has nothing to do with tickets and
was reachable from nowhere else.

```
Applications (0)  │  Vetting desk (2)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
You vet for   ● Kernel Developers   until 2027-01-18    listed in the directory
              ● first-vtc           expires in 12 days  no profile sent
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Requests (2)   Tickets (1)   Issued (0)    ←/→

 ▸ Alice Example        accepted
   Bob Smith            awaiting session
```

- `←`/`→` move between the desk's views; `Tab` still switches tabs.
- `p` (profile) and `g` (ask for the credential again) are the **desk's**, so
  they work from all three views.
- The desk is shown **whether or not a grant is live**. §12.3 suggests hiding
  it unless the persona holds the role; that would take "ask for it again" away
  at exactly the moment a grant lapses.

## The header keeps what every other read drops

`vetter_standing` is the only vetter-side read that keeps a **lapsed** grant.
Everything else filters to a live one, which is right — a lapsed vetter can
hold no tickets and their requests are refused — and is precisely why a lapse
was invisible: the communities just stopped being listed. Now it reads
`expired 2026-09-01`, next to the key that asks for a new one.

## The other two surfaces

- **My Credentials → Membership** lists the vetter credential beside the VMC
  and role VEC from the same community, with its validity window and raw JSON.
  It is stored apart from them (§10.3 keeps it out of `CommunityRecord`, since
  it grants a role rather than membership) — that separation is right, and it
  is what left the one credential a vetter acts on unreadable.
- **Inbox** gains `VetterGrantExpiring`, raised by the hourly sweep. Nothing
  arrives to announce a lapse; the first sign is an applicant's request refused
  at *their* end as `notEligible`, for a reason they cannot act on and we never
  see. Said once per grant per state — approaching, then lapsed, which are
  different sentences — and recorded in the book, so a dismissed warning stays
  dismissed rather than returning hourly for something only the community can
  fix.

## One behaviour change to know about

**Esc now leaves the content panel** on the Vetting page. The desk consumes
`←`/`→` for its views, and those are how focus returns to the menu on every
other panel (`Tab` was already consumed here). Without Esc the desk would have
been a room whose door is bound to something else.

## Checks

`cargo test --workspace`, again with `--include-ignored`; clippy across all
targets; `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc`; `cargo fmt`.

New tests: the desk header renders the credential, the profile and a lapsed
grant, on every view; the no-grant desk explains itself rather than showing an
empty list; `p`/`g` reach the profile from all three views while each view
keeps its own keys; Esc leaves the panel from every tab and view; a lapsing
grant warns once per state, a renewed one can warn again later, and the
standing keeps what `vetter_grant` drops; the credential is listed under
Membership, including when its stored body is unreadable.

§12.3 and §10.3 updated with *as built* notes, including why the desk is always
shown.

title: feat(vetting): one desk for vetting, headed by the credential that makes you a vetter (#325)
body:
feat(vetting): one desk for vetting, headed by the credential that makes you a vetter (#325)

A community naming you a vetter issues a real credential — an
`EndorsementCredential` with `{type: CommunityRole, role: vetter}`, a
`validUntil` and a status list (design §10.3). It gates every ticket you can
hand out and is presented to every applicant you accept. It was visible to
those applicants and to nobody else, least of all its holder: the client
stored it, filtered the whole vetter UI on it, and never once drew it.

**The desk now answers "am I a vetter, for whom, until when".** Its header
lists each community that has named this persona, its grant's expiry, and what
that community holds of the vetter's profile. It is the only view that keeps a
*lapsed* grant. Everything else on the vetter side filters to a live one,
which is correct — a lapsed vetter can hold no tickets and their requests are
refused — and is exactly why a lapse was invisible: the communities simply
stopped being listed, with nothing saying why or that asking for it again is
the fix.

**Four tabs become two**, which is what §12.3 asked for: Applications, where
you are being vetted, and the Vetting desk, where you vet. The desk holds
Requests, Tickets and Issued as sub-views on `←`/`→`. The old layout put a
vetter's inbound queue beside their outbound tickets as if they were separate
concerns, and parked the vetter profile under Tickets, where it had nothing to
do with tickets and could be reached from nowhere else. `p` and `g` are now
the desk's, not one list's.

The desk is shown whether or not a grant is live. Hiding it, as §12.3
suggested, would take "ask for it again" away at precisely the moment it is
needed.

Esc now leaves the content panel. The desk takes `←`/`→` for its views, and
those are how focus returns to the menu everywhere else — consuming them
without offering another way out would have made the desk a room whose door is
bound to something else.

**Two more places the credential surfaces.** My Credentials → Membership lists
it beside the VMC and role VEC from the same community, with its window and
its raw JSON; it is stored apart from them, and that separation is right, but
it left the one credential a vetter acts on as the one they could not read.
And the hourly sweep raises an inbox task when a grant lapses or is about to —
nothing arrives to announce it, since the first sign is an applicant's request
refused at their end for a reason they cannot act on. Said once per grant per
state, recorded in the book, so a dismissed warning stays dismissed rather
than returning every hour for something only the community can fix.

title: refactor(webvh): one transport selector, so a TSP did-host is reached over TSP
body:
Follow-on to #1482, and the last redundant path in the outbound refactor.

## There were two transport selectors

The seam (`operations::outbound`) reads a peer's advertisement and picks TSP > DIDComm > REST. `operations/did_webvh/transport.rs` was the other one — its own copy of the service-type constants, its own precedence rule, and **no knowledge of TSP at all**:

```rust
if services.iter().any(|s| s.types().iter().any(is_didcomm)) {
    return Some(ResolvedTransport::DIDComm);
}
```

And it ran **first**. So for every webvh hosting server the choice was already made before the seam saw it, and a did-host advertising TSP was answered over DIDComm — not because anything decided that, but because the second selector could not express it. `PREFERENCE_ORDER` never got to speak.

`Outbound::didcomm_or_rest` was the same gap from the other end: it hardcoded `tsp: None`, so even once the arm reached the seam, TSP was removed from selection. Its own doc comment called it *"a limitation, not a decision"*. This takes that back.

## What changed

**The selector answers a narrower question** — *can the seam carry a Trust Task to this server at all?* — and `operations::outbound` picks from there. `ResolvedTransport::DIDComm` becomes `TrustTask`, matched on either `TSPTransport` or `DIDCommMessaging`.

**The constants now come from `vta_sdk::protocol::matching`**, the module the seam itself reads, and a test asserts that equality rather than leaving it to review. A local copy is exactly how this module came not to know about TSP; re-deriving it is the part that stops it happening again.

**`Outbound::from_parts` replaces `didcomm_or_rest`**, and the name is the point: a caller must now pass *something* for TSP, so `None` is visible at the call site instead of baked into a constructor.

**`WebvhTransport::DIDComm` becomes `TrustTask` and holds the client** rather than the three parts to rebuild one. Nine call sites destructured those parts and re-ran `WebvhDIDCommClient::new`; storing the client is what let a field be added without touching any of them — and is why this adds a transport without a nine-way edit.

## Two deliberate calls

**`TrustTaskHTTPS` is not a seam trigger.** Such a host *is* reachable by the seam over its REST binding, but routing there would swap the legacy WebVH REST API for the Trust-Task one **on the DID publish path** — live data, and not a change a transport selector should make on its own. A test pins the current answer.

It is also what keeps this caller's `ReplyTrust::TransportAuthenticated` honest, which is now noted in the code: DIDComm authcrypt and the TSP sender VID both authenticate the peer end to end, while TLS authenticates a *host*, not the DID that composed the reply.

**Nine `tsp: None` sites are real answers, not gaps.** CLI, setup wizard, TEE autogen, `ProtocolDeps`, provisioning, and `VtaState` — the DIDComm handler's own state — hold no mediator socket. The compiler required each to state its answer (a struct literal missing a field does not compile), which is why each carries a note rather than a default.

## Docs corrected, not just code

`webvh_didcomm.rs`'s header argued at length that it needed none of the REST client's signing identity, audience binding or typed-error machinery because DIDComm authcrypt supplied each. Sound — and the wrong shape since the outbound refactor: the module composes did-management documents and reads replies, and the transport is the seam's business. The reasoning is kept, scoped to the DIDComm leg where it still holds. Three `servers.rs` comments saying "DIDComm-only servers" were likewise corrected, since that arm now covers TSP.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` — **5991 passed, 0 failed**
- **The three new TSP tests confirmed non-vacuous**: restoring the DIDComm-only rule fails two of them with the intended messages
- All five `vta-service` feature combinations CI runs (including `--no-default-features --features rest` and `setup,keyring,rest,tsp,cli-synthesis`) — clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- Branch built on current `main`

## After this

Adding a transport is five deliberate places, each genuinely transport-specific: the `Protocol` enum and preference order, the capability reader, `OUTBOUND_SUPPORTED` plus a send arm, an inbound handler, and a binding envelope. The duplicated *selection* is gone, which was the part that made it more than that.

title: feat(manager): mint a DID from the whole task surface, and read its log
body:
The New DID form sent 3 of the 20 members `vta/webvh/dids/create/1.0`
accepts, and the DIDs pane showed `logEntryCount` with no way to read an
entry — a number with nothing behind it. Anything past a server id and
Portable meant leaving the console for the CLI.

## The form

Grouped by the decision each member makes rather than by the payload's field
order:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Where it is published** | server, `domain`, `label`, and the existing `PathPicker` with its live DID preview and the hosting server's own path rules |
| **What it commits to** | `portable` and `preRotationCount` as choices with their consequence beside them, since both are fixed in the first log entry |
| **Which keys it is built on** | `signingKeyId` / `kaKeyId`, offering only active keys of the right type in the right context |
| **What it advertises** | `addMediatorService` / `addTspService`, plus a structured id/type/endpoint editor for `additionalServices` |
| **What it is stamped from** | templates from `didTemplateList`, a field per `requiredVars`, `defaults` seeding the controls above |

`setPrimary` is now sent explicitly as `false`. The agent defaults it to
`true`, so the quiet path through the old form replaced the context's identity
on **every** mint — which anything resolving a context's DID to find its keys,
a room host at startup, would then follow.

`additionalServices` is validated here because the agent does not validate it:
it is written into the document verbatim, and the document is a log entry,
which is append-only. A bad entry is published, not refused. `http://` and
credentials-in-URL are rejected; `did:` endpoints are accepted, since a
mediator entry names a DID.

## Reading a log

Clicking the DID expands the row into `vta/webvh/dids/get` with `includeLog`,
fetched **on open** rather than with the listing — the log is the DID's whole
history, and a listing that pulled every one would be every history, to draw a
table. Each entry shows version id, time, proof count, parameters,
verification methods and services, with copy buttons at three levels: whole
log, one entry, the DID.

A response carrying no log is drawn as a refusal to read, never as an absence
of history: `includeLog`'s own spec says absence means it was not asked for.
One unreadable line is one unreadable entry, with its raw text still copyable,
rather than a blank panel.

## DID templates pane

Full CRUD; built-ins are inspect-only because the agent refuses the write and
a button that refuses first beats a refusal after the form was filled in.

Update is a **REPLACE**, so the editor carries `optionalVars` and `defaults` it
never draws — without that a save cleared them while the agent reported
success. *Render the stored version* calls `didTemplateRender` so the operator
sees the agent's own substitution rather than this console's guess at it; the
button says it renders the stored version, because `render` takes a name and
cannot see unsaved edits.

## Three defects the new tests caught before they shipped

1. **`templateDefaults` coerced its hint with `Number()`, and `Number(null)` is
   `0`** — a null `preRotationCount` hint would have silently switched
   pre-rotation off, the one setting that makes a stolen key unrecoverable.
2. **The agent answers a context-scoped template listing with global templates
   too**, so asking both namespaces listed every global template twice, under
   one React key. `mergeTemplates` keys on scope *and* name, which still keeps
   two genuinely different templates of one name apart.
3. **The key pickers said "Reading…" with no context selected**, when nothing
   had been asked for.

Reuse of a key is offered but never quiet: two DIDs publishing one key are
provably one holder, so the form says so when a key is chosen and clears the
choice after a mint — leaving it set would build the next DID on the same key
by inaction.

## Core

`webvhDidCreate` threads the members it was dropping. `pathMode` is exposed
without the bare `path` shorthand, because sending both is an error and one way
to say it cannot be said twice. `preRotationCount` and `addMediatorService` use
`!== undefined` rather than a truthy test: `0` and `false` are the caller's
answers, not absence.

## Guards

The four new `vta/did-templates/*` URIs join the admin guard in `ci.yml` —
operator surface outside that list is unchecked. Verified after a build that
all four appear only in `manager.js`, that the seeds guard is untouched, that
`manager.js` is still a single chunk, and that `background.js` still has no
dynamic `import()`.

## Second commit: a pre-existing CI race, fixed en route

The first push went red on both Node versions, and it was not this change —
the identical failure took out `main` at db16fbb on 2026-09-14.

`tests/task-surface-sync.mjs` drove `sync-task-surface.mjs` against a fixture
SDK, let it write the **real checked-in** `packages/core/task-surface.json`, and
restored the saved copy in a `finally`. That is a race rather than a cleanup:
`node --test` runs test *files* in parallel processes, and
`tests/task-surface.mjs` reads that same file at module scope. Watching the file
while the sync test ran against the original code:

```
task counts observed:  256  1  3  2  0
```

— which is exactly the two shapes CI reported: `task-surface.json looks
truncated` plus `implements 0 of 3 canonical task families` on one runner, and
`SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input` on the other. One cause, two
symptoms, which is why it read like a corrupt checkout. The blob is
byte-identical in the tree; I checked the remote SHA against local before
suspecting the tests.

It reproduces only where the two files overlap — rarely on a many-core dev
machine, often on a two-core runner — so `npm test` stayed green locally through
every one of these failures.

`sync-task-surface.mjs` now takes the output path as an optional second
argument and the fixture points it inside its own temp directory, so no test
opens the checked-in snapshot for writing. With the fix the same observation
loop sees only `256`. One assertion changed with it: *"the real snapshot is
untouched after a failed sync"* was the only statement available while the
fixture shared that file; with a path of its own, a stopped sync leaves no
snapshot at all, which says it directly.

**This bug is on `main` and will keep flaking other PRs until this merges.** If
you would rather it landed separately it lifts out cleanly — it is the last
commit and touches only those two files.

## Verification

`tsc -b` clean, **1452 tests pass / 0 fail** (77 new across 7 files), build
clean. Also driven in a real Chrome tab against a shim — confirmed the template
`defaults` seeding Portable + pre-rotation 3, the render round-trip, the log
expansion, and that the key pickers exclude an `x25519` key from the signing
list, a `revoked` key from both, and a key belonging to another context.

## Pre-merge checklist

```
- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) — no new fetch; every call goes through the console relay
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3) — n/a, no locks
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1) — all writes are single Trust Tasks; the form's own state is cleared only after the agent answers
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) — no retries added
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5) — n/a, no loops
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6) — n/a, inbound path untouched
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*) — no new wire types; existing spec members threaded with `===`-exact spelling, no compat folds
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*) — a key's absent `contextId` is read as restrictive, never as a wildcard; an unreachable template registry does not fall back to a compiled copy
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*) — a missing log is a refusal to read, not "no history"; a failed server/key/template listing says so rather than rendering empty
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1) — a serverless mint keeps its `logEntry` on screen after the form resets, because it is the only copy of the thing that must be served
- [ ] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers — none
```

title: feat(persona): choose the DID path, and name the row a refused profile is about
body:
Two things an operator could see but not act on.

## A persona DID's path was always the server's random mnemonic

The create-persona overlay gains a step between the label and the context:

```
Where should this persona's DID live on the hosting server?
The path is part of the DID, and cannot be changed afterwards.

▸ Server-assigned  (a random, unguessable path)
  My own path:  alice▎

  Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens; '/' separates segments.
↑/↓ choose   type: name the path   ⏎ next   esc back
```

Server-assigned is unchanged and still the default — it is what every persona
minted before this got. A typed path is a name that can be handed out and
recognised, at the cost of being a name: it can already be taken, and it is
public forever. The step says so.

Typing anywhere in the step picks the typed row and keeps the character, so the
key that starts the name is not swallowed. Esc now steps back one phase at a
time (context → path → label).

**Checked before anything is minted.** A standalone mint creates the VTA context
*first*, so a path the server was always going to refuse would otherwise cost an
empty orphan context before the operator hears about a typo.

**Why the rules are a copy.** They mirror
`did-hosting-common::server::mnemonic::validate_custom_path` rather than calling
it: that crate is published, but pins its own, older `vta-sdk`, so depending on
it would put two `vta-sdk` copies in the tree and fail on the shared auth types.
The hosting service stays authoritative — a name someone else has taken is still
refused at mint time, and that failure now names the path it asked for and
suggests another. `.well-known` is refused by name: it is the host's own root
DID slot, not a persona path.

**Back-compat.** The request carries the path in both `path_mode` and the legacy
`path` field. A VTA predating `path_mode` would otherwise ignore the field it
does not know and silently auto-assign a mnemonic — handing a random path to
someone who typed one. Both come from `to_request_path()`, so they cannot
disagree, and auto-assign still omits `path` entirely (a present-but-empty one
is `e.p.did.path-invalid`).

The join flow's mid-join mint is untouched and still auto-assigns.

## A refused vetter profile did not say which row it was about

A country written `USA` was refused as

> the community would refuse this: breaks its published schema: doesn't match pattern "^[A-Z]{2}$"

while the cursor sat eleven rows away on "How to get a ticket", with nothing
tying the two together. Now:

> Country: write it as a two-letter code, like US or CZ — not the country's name

and the cursor moves to the Country row. Every refusal of a typed value names
its row in the form's own label (`Languages:`, `Documents I accept:`, `I vet:`,
`First day`, …) across all three vetting forms — profile, event, directory
filter. Country gets its own sentence rather than the schema's wording, because
the pattern is true and no help to someone who has to work out that it wants
`US`.

Two things kept the jump honest:

- The labels are **one array per form**, read by the renderer *and* by the
  cursor jump. A label that drifted between the message and the renderer would
  move the cursor to the wrong row — worse than not moving it at all.
- An event's refusal is **wrapped**, not passed up. The profile and the event
  form both have a "Country" row and they are not the same row; a profile
  resolving the inner label against its own rows would land on the wrong one.
  The wrapper carries the event's index, so the profile puts the cursor on that
  event's row instead.

A payload-wide refusal (an event ending before it starts) keeps the old
unlabelled wording and leaves the cursor alone — there is no single row at
fault.

## Checks

- `cargo test --workspace`, and again with `--include-ignored` so the MockVta
  e2es ran
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets`
- `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` (caught three
  doc-link breaks)
- `cargo fmt --all`

New tests: the path grammar and its refusals; the overlay's path phase keys and
that both rows plus the key line fit on screen; the phase walk and back-stepping;
that every row a refusal can name resolves to the row the form actually draws
there; and that an event's refusal reports the event, not a profile row.

Not done: the mint cannot check availability before it runs — `vta-sdk` exposes
the `did/check-name/0.1` task constant but no client method for it, so a taken
path is still a mint-time failure.

title: feat(trust-tasks): correlate replies in the spine, so TSP can initiate
body:
The last piece of the transport-agnostic outbound seam. **TSP was in `Protocol::PREFERENCE_ORDER` and could never be selected** — `OUTBOUND_SUPPORTED` did not name it, because there was nowhere to put the waiter for a reply. This adds that, and a VTA now reaches a peer over its highest-preference transport instead of falling through to DIDComm or REST.

## Why an agent needs a registry at all

TSP has no request/response. `trust-tasks-tsp` is `pack` and `unpack` and nothing else — deliberately, because correlation belongs to the document layer (SPEC §4.9 `threadId`). So "send a Trust Task over TSP and get the answer" is not one call on a transport; it is a send now, and later an inbound document that threads back to it. Without somewhere to hold the waiter between those two events, a VTA can only *receive* over TSP.

## Why it lives in the spine, not in the TSP transport

Correlation is a fact about the **document**, and `dispatch_trust_task_inner` is the one place this service reads documents — the property `only_the_spine_parses_a_trust_task_document` (#1479) already guards exactly that. A transport that correlated for itself would be parsing, and would have to be written again for the next transport.

Putting it in the spine means **every transport gets reply correlation at once**. TSP is what needed it; nothing about it is TSP-specific, which is why `AppState::pending_replies` is deliberately **not** feature-gated.

The check runs **before authorization and before dispatch**, because that is what a reply is: it carries no authority and asks for nothing, so running it through the request pipeline would at best refuse it and at worst execute it. A claimed document returns `204 No Content` — the "nothing goes back" signal the transports already understand.

## The bug this found: the key is `threadId ?? id`

`trust-tasks-rs` builds every response — `respond_with` and `build_error_response` alike — with:

```rust
let thread_id = self.thread_id.clone().or_else(|| Some(self.id.clone()));
```

Keying the registry on the request's `id` works **only** for a request that opens its own thread. A request already inside a thread is answered *in that thread*: its waiter is never woken, the reply falls through to the dispatcher as an unsolicited request, and the sender waits out its full timeout for a document that already arrived.

`reply_thread_of` is a function rather than an expression written twice, so both sides of the registry read one rule. Its tests assert against a **real `respond_with` / `reject_with`** rather than a hand-written expectation — the framework owns this rule, so the test has to ask the framework, or it passes forever while the rule moves underneath it.

## Two deliberate asymmetries

- **`complete` matches on `threadId` only, with no `id` fallback.** An ordinary request whose `id` collided with an outstanding thread would otherwise be swallowed as a reply — a document that *disappears* rather than one that is refused. Pinned by a test that constructs exactly that collision.
- **A waiter whose receiver was dropped still claims the document.** Returning `false` would hand a reply to the dispatcher to execute as a request. Dropping a late answer is much the lesser outcome.

## `Outbound`'s fields are now private

A struct literal is how a caller silently opts out of a transport. `webvh_didcomm` built one, so adding `tsp` broke it at compile time — which was luck; the next field added would have broken it the same way, or been given a plausible default that quietly removed a transport from selection.

`didcomm_or_rest` is named for what it gives up. That caller has no `AppState` (its client is constructed deep inside the webvh transport enum), so it passes up TSP for want of plumbing — **a limitation, not a decision**, recorded as such. Threading `AppState` through `WebvhTransport` removes the constructor. A did-host advertises TSP and now serves the full Trust-Task surface on it (affinidi-webvh-service#183), so this is a real transport being left on the table.

## Ordering

The waiter is registered **before** the frame is sealed. A reply arriving in between would find nothing waiting, be dispatched as a request, and be refused — while this call sat until timeout. The window is small and the mediator is fast, which is exactly the combination that makes it rare enough to survive testing. Every failure path abandons the entry; leaving one would hold it until the process restarted, and a much later reply would find a receiver nobody reads.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` — **5986 passed, 0 failed**
- **The six new tests confirmed non-vacuous**: reverting `reply_thread_of` to `id` fails two of them with the intended messages
- All five `vta-service` feature combinations CI runs — including `--no-default-features --features rest` and `setup,keyring,rest,tsp,cli-synthesis` — clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- Branch built on current `main`; diff touches five files plus the new module

title: docs(build): every documented build and install passes --locked
body:
## The failure this prevents

A host build of `vtc-service` failed with three `E0308`/`E0004` errors **inside `aws-smithy-json 0.63.0`** — a file nobody in this workspace wrote:

```
error[E0308]: mismatched types
   --> .../aws-smithy-json-0.63.0/src/codec/deserializer.rs:707:37
    |    Ok(Document::Object(map))
    |       expected `DocumentObject`, found `HashMap<String, Document>`
```

**The lockfile was not at fault.** `Cargo.lock` on `main` pins `aws-smithy-types` 1.6.3 and exactly one copy of `aws-smithy-json` (0.63.0). The failing build compiled **both 0.63.0 and 0.64.0** — a combination that exists in no commit. It had re-resolved and ignored the lock.

The break itself is upstream and cannot be fixed from here: `aws-smithy-types` **1.7.0 replaced `Document::Object`'s payload** (`HashMap<String, Document>` → `DocumentObject`) in a *minor* release, while `aws-smithy-json` 0.63.0 — reached through the latest `aws-config` — declares `aws-smithy-types = "1.6.1"` and is therefore considered compatible with it. Confirmed here:

```console
$ cargo update --dry-run -p aws-smithy-types
    Updating aws-smithy-types v1.6.3 -> v1.7.0
```

Any resolution that floats past the lockfile picks 1.7.0 and stops compiling.

## What changed

`cargo build` and `cargo test` already honour `Cargo.lock`, so `--locked` on those is a statement rather than a behaviour change — it turns a silently stale lock into an error.

**`cargo install` is the actual trap: it ignores `Cargo.lock` by default.** That is exactly the command someone reaches for when putting a binary on a box, and the one place this repo said nothing at all.

The Dockerfiles already got this right (`cargo build --release --locked`). What did not:

| File | Command |
|---|---|
| `README.md` | quick-start `cargo build --workspace` |
| `docs/03-vtc/feature-flags.md` | four `vtc-service` build lines |
| `docs/03-vtc/trust-registry-deployment.md` | `--bin trust-registry` |
| `docs/02-vta/data-rooms.md` | `-p room-host` |
| `docs/02-vta/examples/agent-memory-with-vta-mcp.md` | `-p vta-mcp` |
| `deploy/nitro/README.md` | enclave proxy build; the `affinidi-did-resolver-cache-server` install (×3) |
| `deploy/nitro/deploy-enclave.sh` | same two, in the script that actually runs |
| `vta-mobile-core/scripts/{build-mobile,package-ios}.sh` | four `cargo build` lines |

For the crates.io install of `affinidi-did-resolver-cache-server`, `--locked` takes **that crate's** published lockfile — the same protection, against the same class of upstream break, on a command that runs mid-deploy.

The README carries the reasoning beside the quick-start command rather than a bare instruction, because "pass `--locked`" without the failure it prevents is advice that gets dropped the first time someone is in a hurry on a box.

## Verification

Run exactly as documented:

- `cargo build --workspace --locked` — Finished
- `cargo build --release --locked --package vtc-service --features aws-secrets` — Finished
- `bash -n` clean on all three edited shell scripts

Docs and scripts only; no Rust source or manifest changes.

title: test(trust-tasks): keep the inbound path single as transports are added
body:
Stacked on #1478. Last of the series. **No behaviour changes** — this pins a property that is already true, because nothing else does.

## What is already true

The three transports converge on `dispatch_trust_task_core`, and each does only what its own binding requires on the way: REST's binding is the request path, DIDComm's is the message `type`, TSP's is the payload wrapper. A sweep of `messaging/` and `routes/` finds exactly **one** Trust-Task parse outside `trust_tasks/`, and it is a documented pre-login exception.

I had planned this PR as "merge three unwrappings onto one spine". Investigating showed there is nothing to merge — the inbound side is already the shape the outbound side has just been refactored into. Doing a merge anyway would have been manufacturing work, so what it became is the guard.

## The failure it is for

A fourth transport is meant to be a binding module plus a thin entry. The way that goes wrong is undramatic and does not look like a mistake at the time: someone deserialises the document in their handler to read one field — a type, a recipient — then branches on it, and a second dispatch path grows with its own idea of validation, replay and signing. Each step is small and reasonable. By the time the divergence is visible it is a rewrite.

That is not hypothetical here. **This whole stack exists because it already happened on the outbound side** — four hand-rolled carriages, two of them silently disagreeing about whether a reply is evidence (#1474). The inbound side is one guard away from the same drift.

## Why source-level

The property is about *where* parsing happens, which a behavioural test cannot see: a second spine performing all the same checks passes every round-trip test there is. Same reasoning as `the_spine_signs_every_response_it_returns` beside it, and `vta-sdk`'s `connect_with_transport` body check.

## The allowlist

`routes/auth.rs` parses documents in three places, legitimately: pre-login `auth/{challenge,authenticate,refresh}` carry no session, so they cannot pass `AuthClaims` through the dispatcher's extractor and are served as dedicated REST routes. `REST_ROUTED_URIS` is the canonical list and names exactly these.

The entry carries that reason, and the test fails if it ever stops being needed — so the list can only shrink, like the served-URI debt list next door.

## Verified non-vacuous, both ways

- Adding a plausible *"just peek at one field"* parse to `messaging/tsp_inbound.rs` fails it, naming file and line.
- Pointing the allowlist at a different file makes `routes/auth.rs` fail it — which is what says the entry is load bearing rather than decorative.

A first probe was worthless and was redone rather than counted: removing the parse from `auth.rs` broke compilation, so the test never ran.

## Checks

`cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — **exit 0, 4300 pass**, zero faults. Clippy and fmt clean.

* docs(outbound): say what the seam is not for, so a device push is not folded into it

The push path (`step_up::try_push_over_tsp` and the DIDComm fallback) also puts
Trust Tasks on a wire, and reads like an omission from this module unless the
reason is written down.

It is a different operation. Selection cannot be by advertisement — a device is
a wallet behind a mediator whose DID often advertises nothing dialable, so the
push chooses on *learned reachability* (`tsp_reach`, recorded from inbound
frames), which is a different question from what a peer says it accepts. There
is no reply to correlate. And delivery is durable with a doorbell: a buffered
`PendingResponse` and a gateway wake, neither of which means anything for a
request whose answer the caller is waiting on.

Absorbing that would need a no-reply mode and a pluggable selection strategy,
which makes this function less clear about what it does rather than more.

What the two paths do share is the part that matters for adding a transport: the
binding. Both go through `messaging::tsp_binding` for TSP, and both would go
through the next one the same way.

is gated on `tsp` — so in the default build nothing uses it, and `-D warnings`
turns that into a failed Clippy job rather than a lint nobody reads.

Mine, from #1478, and it is on `main`: everything stacked there inherits the
failure. The gate goes on the re-export so it travels with the consumer, which

title: feat(tsp): carry Trust Tasks in the TSP binding envelope
body:
Stacked on #1477. The VTA half of a coordinated wire change — wallet half is OpenVTC/vta-browser-plugin#246. **They land together.**

## What we were speaking

Over TSP this service sealed and parsed the **bare document**, and said so: `tsp_inbound`'s header called the payload *"identical to the REST body"*, and the wallet's `tsp-channel.ts` carried *"TSP plaintext = the Trust-Task envelope JSON (no binding wrapper)"*. The two agreed with each other and with nothing else.

The published binding specifies `{"type": …/binding/tsp/0.1/envelope, "document": <TrustTask>}`, and `trust-tasks-tsp`'s `unpack_trust_task` refuses anything else with `WrongEnvelopeType`.

**The reason to fix it is not conformance for its own sake.** While the wire is a private shape, `trust-tasks-tsp` can never be used — which is exactly what makes *"adding a transport is adding a binding"* untrue in practice rather than in principle. Every transport after this one would hit the same fork.

## Why TSP needs a wrapper when the others don't

Each binding must say *"this payload is a Trust Task"* somewhere readable before parsing. HTTPS says it with the request path; DIDComm with the message `type`. A TSP frame has neither — sender VID, recipient VID, opaque bytes — so the binding puts it in the JSON. Not ceremony; the only place TSP has.

## One module, both directions

`messaging::tsp_binding` wraps outbound and opens inbound, so the binding is one fact about this service rather than a convention each path remembers.

`try_push_over_tsp` — shared by step-up and task-consent — goes through it too. A push is still a Trust Task on a TSP wire, and sending one bare would leave **exactly one frame** in the system speaking the old dialect, which is the hardest kind to find later.

`vault::unseal_tsp_secret` deliberately does *not* change: it unseals a vault secret, not a Trust Task.

## The refusal names the carriage, not the document

Worth review. The obvious implementation routes a rejected frame through `reject_trust_task`, which re-parses the body and — on failure — **discards the caller's reason**, substituting *"body did not parse as a Trust Task document"*.

But here the document is usually well formed and merely unwrapped, so that message sends the sender to inspect the one thing that is fine. During a binding cutover it's the most misleading sentence this service could say. `malformed_request_response` keeps the caller's wording, and a test pins that the refusal names the *envelope*.

## A feature gate that moved silently

Adding the module placed `tsp_binding` under the `#[cfg(feature = "tsp")]` belonging to `tsp_inbound`, so a build **without** that feature compiled `tsp_inbound` against two modules that weren't there. Every `cargo check --features tsp` passed — only the full-workspace run, which builds some crates without it, caught it. Noted because it's the second time in this stack that a green targeted check hid a real break.

## Checks

`cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — **exit 0, 4299 pass**, zero overflows. Clippy and fmt clean. Ten tests across the two TSP modules, including a bare document being refused *for the right reason* and a wrong-binding envelope naming what arrived.

body:
feat(tsp): carry Trust Tasks in the TSP binding envelope (#1478)

* refactor(webvh): the did-hosting client builds documents; the seam carries them

`webvh_didcomm` was the second of the workspace's hand-rolled carriages: it
packed a DIDComm envelope, awaited the correlated reply, and mapped a
problem-report, for one peer. All three are now `operations::outbound`'s, and
this client keeps only what is actually did-management's — the document it
builds and the reply it reads.

The measure of the change is that **the module no longer names a transport or a
message type anywhere**. Removing the last one produced an `unused import` on
`ENVELOPE_TYPE`, which is a better proof than any assertion: there is nothing
left here that could send.

## `build_outbound` is gone, and that is the point

It returned the DIDComm message type alongside the document, and its own note
explained why: the type "is the value this entire change exists to get right,
and a wrong one fails *silently*", so it had to come from somewhere a test could
look at. That care was real and it was **local** — the same care had to be taken
again by the next client.

`operations::outbound::DIDCOMM_MESSAGE_TYPE` now names it once for every caller,
with the assertion that went with it. A caller has no argument that could carry
a message type, so the mistake stops being prevented by discipline and starts
being unrepresentable.

## `TransportAuthenticated`, and why this is a disclosure rather than a change

This client has never verified a reply's proof. Routing it through the seam made
that an argument that has to be written down, and the honest value today is
`TransportAuthenticated`: over the DIDComm binding the peer is authenticated end
to end by the authcrypt envelope, and these replies confer nothing — a reserved
path, an availability answer, an acknowledgement.

Whether it *should* be `SignedByRecipient` is a real question, and it is one to
ask of did-hosting (whether it signs these replies at all) rather than to assume
here. What has changed is that the question is now visible at the call site
instead of being the silent consequence of nobody having added a check.

## What this does not finish, and why the blocker is not here

The eight REST arms in `did_webvh`'s transport enum stay. They cannot move,
because did-hosting's Trust-Task HTTPS endpoint does not serve the verbs the VTA
sends it: `build_dispatcher` registers `acl/{grant,revoke,change-role,show,list}`
and `trust-task-discovery`, and nothing else. The did-management verbs travel
over the DIDComm envelope path or the legacy JWT `/api/...` routes.

So completing the single path for did-hosting needs a change in
`affinidi-webvh-service` — serving those verbs over `/api/trust-tasks` — after
which the legacy REST client and this enum both delete. Recorded here so the
next person reads it as a far-side gap rather than an unfinished refactor.
