body:
Stacked on #1476. Fourth of the series. `webvh_didcomm` was the second of the workspace's hand-rolled carriages — it packed a DIDComm envelope, awaited the correlated reply, and mapped a problem report, all for one peer. Those three are now `operations::outbound`'s, and this client keeps only what is actually did-management's: the document it builds and the reply it reads.

## The measure of it

**The module no longer names a transport or a message type anywhere.** Removing the last one produced an `unused import` on `ENVELOPE_TYPE` — a better proof than any assertion, because it means there is nothing left here that could send.

## `build_outbound` is gone, and that is the point

It returned the DIDComm message type alongside the document, and its own note explained why: the type *"is the value this entire change exists to get right, and a wrong one fails silently"*, so it had to come from somewhere a test could look at. That care was real, and it was **local** — the next client had to take it again.

`operations::outbound::DIDCOMM_MESSAGE_TYPE` now names it once for every caller, with the assertion that went with it. A caller has no argument that could carry a message type, so the mistake stops being prevented by discipline and becomes unrepresentable.

## `TransportAuthenticated` is a disclosure, not a change

This client has never verified a reply's proof. Routing it through the seam turned that into an argument that has to be written down, and the honest value today is `TransportAuthenticated`: over the DIDComm binding the peer is authenticated end to end by the authcrypt envelope, and these replies confer nothing — a reserved path, an availability answer, an acknowledgement.

Whether it *should* be `SignedByRecipient` is a real question, and one to ask of did-hosting — whether it signs these replies at all — rather than to assume here. What changed is that the question is now visible at the call site instead of being the silent consequence of nobody having added a check.

## A stack overflow this introduced, and how it was caught

Worth reading, because it presented as flakiness and was not.

The full-workspace suite aborted with `SIGABRT` in `mock_vta` — **no test failed**, 4256 passed, and it hit a *different* test each run, never when that binary ran alone. Every signal said resource pressure. The one that did not: both tests ran through code this PR changes.

The parent commit runs the same suite at **exit 0 with zero overflows**. So it was this PR.

`Outbound::send` is a large future — DID resolution, transport round trip, proof verification, each with sub-futures — and in a debug build the compiler inlines all of it into the **caller's** frame. `webvh_didcomm` sits under `create_did_webvh`, already several awaits deep, and that overflowed the 2MB stack a `#[tokio::test]` worker gets.

`send` now boxes its body into `send_inner`. Deliberately in the seam rather than at the call site: the size is this function's, a caller cannot know it has grown too large to inline, and the next caller added would otherwise rediscover it the same expensive way. The comment records how it presented, so the next person seeing a `mock_vta` SIGABRT does not have to re-derive that it is not flakiness.

## What this does not finish, and why the blocker is elsewhere

The eight REST arms in `did_webvh`'s transport enum stay. They cannot move: did-hosting's Trust-Task HTTPS endpoint does not serve the verbs the VTA sends it. `build_dispatcher` registers `acl/{grant,revoke,change-role,show,list}` and `trust-task-discovery`, and nothing else — the did-management verbs travel over the DIDComm envelope path or the legacy JWT `/api/…` routes.

Completing the single path for did-hosting therefore needs a change in `affinidi-webvh-service`, serving those verbs at `/api/trust-tasks`; after that the legacy REST client and this enum both delete. Recorded in the module so the next reader takes it as a far-side gap rather than an unfinished refactor.

## Checks

`cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — **exit 0, 4299 pass, zero overflows**. Clippy `--all-targets` clean, fmt clean.

title: feat(templates): a did-host advertises where it accepts Trust Tasks
body:
Stacked on #1475. Third of the series. #1475 taught the SDK to discover a Trust-Task endpoint by its binding type; this makes the did-hosting templates actually advertise one, so there is something to discover.

## The claim that was never made

The `did-host-*` templates advertised `WebVHHosting` and nothing else a Trust-Task consumer could use. `WebVHHosting` says **where DID documents are served**. It is not a claim to accept documents posted to it — and this VTA posts Trust Tasks there anyway.

It works because the same host happens to serve both. That is the kind of working that stops without warning, and it is exactly the conflation `TrustTaskHTTPS` exists to end.

## Why the base is `{URL}/api`, with evidence

Not a guess:

- `did-hosting-control` nests its whole API under `/api` off the origin root (`routes/mod.rs`).
- The live deployment confirms it: `https://webvh.storm.ws/api/health` answers **200**, from the same origin the hosting URL names.

A deployment serving its control plane on a *different* origin from its hosting URL must edit this entry, and the template description now says so rather than leaving it to be found the hard way.

This is also the concrete case HTTPS binding 0.2 §6 was written to settle: the path was fixed while what it was relative to was not, so this control plane composed `/api/trust-tasks` and the VTA composed `/trust-tasks` — and both were right.

## Tests

The composition test is **updated, not relaxed**: it asserted "exactly two entries", and now asserts *which* entry is which and why the second one exists.

The new test is the one that matters. It renders each `did-host-*` template and puts it through the **real `ServiceCapabilities` matcher**, asserting it resolves to the Trust-Task base. Reading the array back would only have tested that I wrote what I wrote; resolving it tests that a consumer finds it, which is the part that was broken.

`cargo test -p vta-sdk` — 338 pass. Clippy `--all-targets` clean, fmt clean.

## What this unlocks

With #1474 (the seam), #1475 (discovery) and this, a did-hosting server is reachable through the single outbound path over **any** transport it advertises, with no product knowledge in the sender. The next PR can then delete `webvh_didcomm`'s bespoke client and the `did_webvh` enum that hand-matches 8 verbs × 2 transports — they have nothing left to do.

body:
feat(templates): a did-host advertises where it accepts Trust Tasks (#1476)

* refactor(vta): one outbound path for Trust Tasks, chosen from what a peer advertises

Adding an external service should be choosing a task URI and a recipient DID.
It was not. `room_host` hand-rolled REST, `webvh_didcomm` hand-rolled DIDComm,
`did_webvh` hand-matched eight verbs across two transports, and the device-push
path picks TSP-or-DIDComm inline — four carriages for one wire contract, and a
fifth service would have been a fifth.

This lands the seam and moves the first caller onto it. The rest follow.

## The cost was not duplication

Duplication is cheap. What it bought was **divergence nobody could see**: the two
existing paths disagreed about whether a reply is evidence. `room_host` verified
the proof and bound the signer to the party it had addressed, with a comment
explaining why that is not optional. `webvh_didcomm` verified nothing at all.
Both are defensible inside their own file and only one of them can be right, and
the difference was invisible because there was nowhere the question got asked
once.

So `ReplyTrust` is an argument. `SignedByRecipient` is what anything acted on
needs; `TransportAuthenticated` is available for a reply that confers nothing,
and a caller choosing it has to write it down. The weaker answer stops being the
silent consequence of nobody having added a check.

## What moved, and what deliberately did not

Moved: transport selection, the refusal naming both sides, the REST and DIDComm
carriages, and reply verification.

Stayed in `room_host`: the document, the refusal to write to a host caught
contradicting itself, and reading a room reply's three outcomes apart. None of
that is about transports.

Signing stays too, and cannot move — `VtaClient` signs from a `ClientIdentity`
holding a raw `private_key_multibase`, and a VTA never holds its own keys in
that shape. The caller signs; only bytes travel.

Interpretation stays with the caller as well. The seam returns the verified
reply *document*: what a given `#response` means is the caller's family to read,
and a shared reader would have to know every family to do it.

## DIDComm was never missing

`OUTBOUND_SUPPORTED` held REST alone, on a comment saying initiating DIDComm
"needs a correlated reply this service does not yet keep". That was already
untrue when it was written: `DIDCommBridge::send_and_wait` sends to an arbitrary
DID and awaits the reply the delivery layer demuxes by thread id, and
`webvh_didcomm` has been sending Trust Tasks that way for some time. Nothing was
missing but a caller. It is now `[Didcomm, Rest]`, so a room host that publishes
DIDComm at a mediator is reachable without opening an HTTP port.

**TSP is genuinely absent, and the header now says why properly.** Its binding
(`trust-tasks-tsp`) offers `pack` and `unpack` and nothing else, by design —
correlation is a document concern (SPEC §4.9 `threadId`), not a transport one.
So reaching it is not building request/reply over `send_routed`: it is teaching
`messaging::tsp_inbound::dispatch_one` that a document threading to one we sent
is a reply rather than a request, which it does not do — it authorizes every
frame and dispatches it as a request. Naming TSP in `OUTBOUND_SUPPORTED` before
that exists would send a request that is never answered: worse than the refusal,
because it would time out instead of saying why.

## Tests

Nine in the seam. Two are the reply-trust ones lifted from `room_host` — they
were always testing this, not rooms — and one asserts what the weaker level
*does*, so it cannot drift into "verify anyway" or the reverse unnoticed.

`preference_comes_from_preference_order_not_from_this_list` guards the thing
most likely to rot: `OUTBOUND_SUPPORTED` is a membership set, and its own order
is deliberately the opposite of the winning one, so anything that starts reading
it as a preference list trips immediately.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(outbound): the seam compiles in a build without DIDComm

`AppState::didcomm_bridge` is gated on `didcomm` (or `tsp`), and the room call
sites named it unconditionally — so every feature combo without DIDComm stopped
compiling. CI's `Feature combos` job found it; the default-feature build, the

Three things move together, because they are one fact:

- the `bridge` field exists only under `didcomm`,
- so does the arm that sends on it,
- so does its entry in `OUTBOUND_SUPPORTED`, which is now a slice rather than a
  fixed-length array. Naming a protocol this build cannot initiate would turn a
  compile-time absence into a runtime "named in OUTBOUND_SUPPORTED but has no

body:
Stacked on #1474. Second of the series collapsing this repo onto one protocol-agnostic Trust-Task path — this is the *discovery* half, and it removes the last thing that would have forced per-service knowledge back into the seam.

## The conflation

`REST_SERVICE_TYPES` held `VTARest` and `TRQPRest`. Neither says *"I accept Trust Task documents"*; they say *"a VTA's REST API is here"* and *"a Trust Registry's TRQP surface is here"*. Those coincide with accepting Trust Tasks only because every Trust-Task server in this workspace happens to be one of those two products.

**It is already biting.** This VTA posts Trust Tasks to a `WebVHHosting` endpoint — and `WebVHHosting` advertises *where DID documents are served*. We are posting documents to an endpoint that never agreed to accept them. It works because the same host happens to serve both, which is the kind of working that stops without warning.

## The type that states the interface

`TrustTaskHTTPS` (HTTPS binding 0.2 §6.2), whose `serviceEndpoint` is the **Trust-Task base**, with the request URL `base + "/trust-tasks"`.

Binding 0.2 had to settle that because the path was fixed while what it was relative to was not — so two conformant implementations composed `/api/trust-tasks` and `/trust-tasks`, and both were right. That is precisely the divergence between this VTA and the did-hosting control plane today, and it is why the did-hosting client could never have been folded into the shared path while discovery went by product type.

The browser plugin has implemented this since its #125 (`vta/endpoint.ts`); this is the Rust side catching up. The constant names that file so the two stay in step.

The product types stay accepted, and stay second — every VTA advertises `VTARest` today and its endpoint *is* the Trust-Task base (#125 made vta-service 0.18.0 a floor for exactly that). They are a compatibility reading of a claim that was never quite the one being made, and a party that wants to be found should advertise the binding type.

## Rank, not position

The REST winner is now chosen by **which type it is**. `get_or_insert` took the first usable entry in *document order*, so a party advertising both the binding type and a product type got whichever it happened to list first — and only one of them actually claims to accept Trust Tasks.

Best rank wins, ties going to document order. It is the same wherever-it-sits rule DIDComm already follows in this module, applied to the case that now has more than one candidate. The new test lists the binding type **last** on purpose: position must not be what decides it.

## Checks

`cargo test -p vta-sdk protocol::matching` — 12 pass. Clippy `-p vta-sdk -p vta-service --all-targets` clean, fmt clean.

- **did-hosting** should advertise `TrustTaskHTTPS` with base `{url}/api` (a PR against `affinidi-webvh-service`). Until it does, it stays discoverable over DIDComm, which is what the VTA uses for it today anyway.
- **Then** `webvh_didcomm` and the `did_webvh` transport enum — 8 verbs × 2 transports, hand-matched — collapse onto the seam with no product knowledge in it.

existing paths disagreed about whether a reply is evidence. `room_host` verified
the proof and bound the signer to the party it had addressed, with a comment
explaining why that is not optional. `webvh_didcomm` verified nothing at all.
Both are defensible inside their own file and only one of them can be right, and
the difference was invisible because there was nowhere the question got asked
once.

So `ReplyTrust` is an argument. `SignedByRecipient` is what anything acted on
needs; `TransportAuthenticated` is available for a reply that confers nothing,
and a caller choosing it has to write it down. The weaker answer stops being the
silent consequence of nobody having added a check.

## What moved, and what deliberately did not

Moved: transport selection, the refusal naming both sides, the REST and DIDComm
carriages, and reply verification.

Stayed in `room_host`: the document, the refusal to write to a host caught
contradicting itself, and reading a room reply's three outcomes apart. None of
that is about transports.

Signing stays too, and cannot move — `VtaClient` signs from a `ClientIdentity`
holding a raw `private_key_multibase`, and a VTA never holds its own keys in
that shape. The caller signs; only bytes travel.

Interpretation stays with the caller as well. The seam returns the verified
reply *document*: what a given `#response` means is the caller's family to read,
and a shared reader would have to know every family to do it.

## DIDComm was never missing

`OUTBOUND_SUPPORTED` held REST alone, on a comment saying initiating DIDComm
"needs a correlated reply this service does not yet keep". That was already
untrue when it was written: `DIDCommBridge::send_and_wait` sends to an arbitrary
DID and awaits the reply the delivery layer demuxes by thread id, and
`webvh_didcomm` has been sending Trust Tasks that way for some time. Nothing was
missing but a caller. It is now `[Didcomm, Rest]`, so a room host that publishes
DIDComm at a mediator is reachable without opening an HTTP port.

**TSP is genuinely absent, and the header now says why properly.** Its binding
(`trust-tasks-tsp`) offers `pack` and `unpack` and nothing else, by design —
correlation is a document concern (SPEC §4.9 `threadId`), not a transport one.
So reaching it is not building request/reply over `send_routed`: it is teaching
`messaging::tsp_inbound::dispatch_one` that a document threading to one we sent
is a reply rather than a request, which it does not do — it authorizes every
frame and dispatches it as a request. Naming TSP in `OUTBOUND_SUPPORTED` before
that exists would send a request that is never answered: worse than the refusal,
because it would time out instead of saying why.

## Tests

Nine in the seam. Two are the reply-trust ones lifted from `room_host` — they
were always testing this, not rooms — and one asserts what the weaker level
*does*, so it cannot drift into "verify anyway" or the reverse unnoticed.

`preference_comes_from_preference_order_not_from_this_list` guards the thing
most likely to rot: `OUTBOUND_SUPPORTED` is a membership set, and its own order
is deliberately the opposite of the winning one, so anything that starts reading
it as a preference list trips immediately.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(outbound): the seam compiles in a build without DIDComm

`AppState::didcomm_bridge` is gated on `didcomm` (or `tsp`), and the room call
sites named it unconditionally — so every feature combo without DIDComm stopped
compiling. CI's `Feature combos` job found it; the default-feature build, the
workspace test run and clippy all passed.

Three things move together, because they are one fact:

- the `bridge` field exists only under `didcomm`,
- so does the arm that sends on it,
- so does its entry in `OUTBOUND_SUPPORTED`, which is now a slice rather than a
  fixed-length array. Naming a protocol this build cannot initiate would turn a
  compile-time absence into a runtime "named in OUTBOUND_SUPPORTED but has no
  send path" — a worse way to find out.

`Outbound::from_app_state` replaces five struct literals. Without it each call
site carries the same `cfg`, and the next one added omits it and breaks a build
nobody runs locally — which is exactly what happened here. Same reason
`WebvhDeps::from_app_state` exists.

title: feat(tsp): carry Trust Tasks in the TSP binding envelope
body:
The wallet half of a coordinated wire change. VTA half: OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure (stacked after #1477). **They land together.**

## What we were speaking

Over TSP this wallet sealed the **bare document**, and said so in its own comments — `tsp-channel.ts`: *"TSP plaintext = the Trust-Task envelope JSON (no binding wrapper)"*; `tsp-inbound.ts`: *"over TSP the plaintext is the document, with no wrapper"*. The VTA parsed exactly that.

The two agreed with each other and with nothing else. The published binding (`https://trusttasks.org/binding/tsp/0.1`) specifies `{"type": …/envelope, "document": <TrustTask>}`, and `trust-tasks-tsp`'s `unpack_trust_task` refuses anything else with `WrongEnvelopeType`.

So a conformant peer would have rejected every frame we sent, and we all of theirs. More to the point: **neither side could ever have used the binding library** — which is what makes "adding a transport is adding a binding" untrue in practice rather than in principle. That is the reason to fix it now, ahead of anything that would build on TSP.

## Why TSP needs a wrapper when the others don't

Each binding has to say *"this payload is a Trust Task"* somewhere a reader sees before parsing. HTTPS says it with the request path; DIDComm with the message `type`. A TSP frame has neither — sender VID, recipient VID, opaque bytes — so the binding puts it in the JSON. The wrapper isn't ceremony; it's the only place TSP has.

## One module, both directions

`tsp-binding.ts` wraps outbound and opens inbound, so the binding is one fact about this package rather than a convention each path remembers. The next transport should be a module beside it, not an edit spread across every sender and receiver.

The wrapper goes on **after** signing, and must: the proof is taken over the document, so reshaping it during wrapping would invalidate every signature while looking identical.

A payload that isn't an envelope, or carries another binding's type, is refused rather than read as a document — and the refusal **names what arrived**, so a peer still sending the old shape can see which half is wrong. Accepting a bare one "just in case" would keep the dialect alive as long as anything spoke it.

## The test change that matters most

The simulated VTA in `tsp.channel.mjs` now speaks the binding in both directions. That's more important than the assertions around it: a stub that kept accepting a bare document would let this wallet regress to the old dialect with every test still green.

`npm test` — **1352 pass, 0 fail**. Build clean.

title: test: the vetting ceremony end to end, over a real mediator
body:
`src/vetting/tests.rs` walks this sequence already — handing each message
straight to the handler. But `openvtc-core/tests/` had **nothing** for vetting,
so the wire was untested for it while join, community context, relationships and
agent names each have an e2e over the in-process mediator.

This is the same walk with DIDComm underneath: ticket → request → acceptance
with the vetter's grant → session → signed card → attestation → statement. Every
document is packed, sent through the mediator, and unpacked before the
production handler sees it.

Alice and Bob are the mediator's two profiles, because the DID that signs a
vetting document has to be the DID that sends it: `wire::open` refuses a document
whose issuer is not the DIDComm sender, and refuses a proof signed by anyone
else. In-process, that pairing is asserted by the test itself rather than by the
transport.

## What it covers that the unit tests cannot

- **The largest payloads OpenVTC sends peer to peer.** A signed Vetting Card
  carries the applicant's released claims and a proof; a signed Vetting Statement
  carries an endorsement credential. A size limit silently dropping a join
  submission has happened here before (#137), and nothing in-process would have
  caught it — so the test asserts the request and the card arrive byte-identical
  to what was sent.
- **The thread surviving the round trip**, which is what correlates a session's
  card with the statement that follows it.
- **The match code both sides derive**, from the session document that actually
  crossed rather than one built beside the assertion.

A second test is the anti-spam gate over the wire: a ticket the vetter never
issued opens no desk and records nothing.

## Notes

Both parties are `did:peer`, which `TrustTaskVmResolver::did_key_only` resolves
with no I/O — the name is about the network, not the method — so the proofs
verify offline. The community is a `did:key` and never joins the mediator: its
manifest and the vetter's role credential are replies authenticated by their
transport, not peer traffic, so they are handed in as setup rather than sent.

`#[ignore]`d with the rest of the integration suite (mediator boot ~1s); CI's
coverage job runs it with `--include-ignored`.

**Verified to bite:** signing the request with the wrong party's key fails the
test at the acceptance assertion rather than passing quietly.

## Checks

- `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast -- --include-ignored` — all green,
  including the two new tests
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps -p openvtc-core` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean

Nothing was needed on the infrastructure side: `sign_card`, `sign_statement` and
the resolver's offline `did:peer` path already carry it.

title: security(deps): take rustls 0.23.45 for RUSTSEC-2026-0285
body:
`cargo deny check advisories` fails on **main**, and has since the advisory was
published — no commit made it red. Reproduced on a clean checkout, so every open
branch inherits it, including #322.

## The advisory

[RUSTSEC-2026-0285](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0285): rustls
accepted TLS 1.3 handshake messages sent at the wrong encryption level when they
followed a key-changing message in the same record — a plaintext
`EncryptedExtensions` packed into the same record as the `ServerHello` was taken,
where RFC 8446 §5.1 requires the connection be closed with `unexpected_message`.

The transcript stays authenticated, so this does not let a network-position
attacker alter or complete a handshake; the effect is that a peer can send in
plaintext what should have been encrypted. Functionally the same bug as Go's
CVE-2025-61730.

## The fix

The advisory names **>= 0.23.45**. rustls is transitive here — through
`affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk`, the messaging SDK and `vta-sdk` — and the
graph's requirement already admits it, so only the lockfile moves: `0.23.44 →
0.23.45`, one package, no manifest change.

0.23.45 is also what the infrastructure resolves: VTI took it in
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1468 for this same advisory. This keeps
the two trees on one rustls rather than picking the newest thing on crates.io.

No stale `advisory-not-detected` entries to prune here — unlike the VTI side, the
ignore list still matches the tree.

## Checks

- `cargo deny check advisories bans sources licenses` — clean, no warnings
  (it was `advisories FAILED`)
- `cargo metadata --locked` — resolves
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` — green

Unblocks the red Cargo Deny job on #322, which changes no dependency.

title: fix(vtc-admin-ui): the flow chart grows downwards, so it fits the panel it lives in
body:
Reported from a live console: the chart renders into a tangle — endings clipped
at the right edge, labels running across their neighbours. Two causes, both mine
from #1472.

## A column per depth, in the narrow half of the layout

The decision policy sits in the right-hand panel, ~600px wide. The chart gave
each level of the tree its own 250px column, so the join policy — four questions
deep once vetting is not required — wanted about a thousand, and its endings ran
off the edge.

Depth is now an **indent of 26px** and each node owns a **row**, so the width is
fixed and the height grows. A panel can give height; it cannot give width.

## Nothing cut a label to its box

*"…and the requirements also demand an invitation"* is three times the width of
the box it was drawn in, so it ran across whatever sat beside it — and the branch
labels did the same to the boxes below them.

Labels are cut to their box now, with the whole text kept in a `<title>`. The
tooltip is what makes truncating acceptable rather than a second way to mislead.

## Why this will not recur quietly

One row per node makes overlap *impossible* rather than unlikely: nothing is
positioned relative to another node's text. And the invariant is asserted rather
than eyeballed —

```
every box starts at x ≥ 0 and ends at x ≤ WIDTH
no two boxes share vertical space
```

— because "looks right on my screen" is exactly what shipped the bug.

Also drops the 620px floor the chart had, which is what turned the overflow into
a horizontal scrollbar instead of a visible mistake.

- `npx vitest run` — 141 passed (17 files), 4 new on the geometry and truncation
- `npm run lint`, `npm run build` — clean

Three existing tests in this file changed with it: truncation and the tooltips
mean a whole-document text match no longer finds a drawn label, so they query the
`<text>` nodes themselves. No daemon change.

title: feat(vtc-admin-ui): chart what a policy decides, by evaluating it rather than reading it
body:
The console could only draw a policy it had authored itself. Both visual views
read the `@vtc-rule-ir` header, so a hand-written module — most of what an
operator uploads, and every policy predating the editor — had exactly one view:
its own Rego.

The obvious fix is a Rego parser, and it is the wrong one. It would cover the
subset we happened to think of, and a partial parser that quietly mis-draws a
policy is worse than no picture, because an operator would believe it.

## So the Flow tab evaluates the policy instead of reading it

A ceremony manifest already declares the inputs its dry-run can vary, so their
combinations are a finite space. Evaluate the policy at every point of it
(`POST /v1/policies/{id}/test` — the daemon's own evaluator) and the result is a
decision table; a decision table induces a flow chart. **24 evaluations for
join.**

This renders **any** policy. It is also more truthful than the authored view for
policies that *do* carry an IR: the header is a claim its author maintains by
hand, and the shipped `join.rego` has already drifted from its own — the header
says the invitation route admits as `member`, the body admits at `invited_role`
from the invitation's scopes. Plain English shows the header. The chart shows
what runs.

## How the chart is built

- It asks the input that separates the endings best, **weighted by how much of
  the space each branch covers**. Weighting is load-bearing: summing branches
  unweighted penalises a five-way question for having five branches, and the
  chart then opens with a toggle that settles almost nothing. (It did, until a
  test caught it.)
- A question whose every answer leads to the same ending is **dropped** — once
  the vetters verified different identities, nothing about an invitation changes
  the outcome, so nothing about an invitation is asked.
- Where the probes disagree and no declared input separates them, the chart says
  **varies** rather than picking one. That is the policy reading a fact the
  ceremony does not expose; hiding it would be the same lie as the partial
  parser.
- `probeSpace` **refuses** a space larger than the cap instead of truncating it.
  A chart drawn from part of the space is wrong about the rest, silently.

Inline SVG in the console's own tokens, like the pipeline strip above it — no
diagramming dependency, no second visual language, and a surface the dry-run can
point at: set the simulator's inputs and the chart lights the path they take.

## Tests

The property that matters: **the chart never disagrees with the evaluations it
was built from.** For every probe, walking the chart with those inputs reaches
the ending the policy gave. A chart that is merely plausible is the failure this
replaces.

- `npx vitest run` — 137 passed (17 files), 13 new across the induction and the
  drawing
- `npm run lint`, `npm run build` — clean
- No daemon change; `openapi.json` and `wire.ts` untouched.

Follows #1471, which gave the join dry-run the inputs this probes across. The
mock that settled the direction is in the thread.

Not exercised against a live daemon — component tests only. Worth a look at the
Flow tab on a real community before trusting the chart for anything load-bearing.

title: feat(webvh): dispatch realign-keys as a Trust Task
body:
Follow-up to #1466, which added the `realign-keys` repair as a REST route and a `pnm` command. This makes it reachable from every surface that speaks Trust Tasks.

## Why it needs to be a task

The browser console's bridge carries a task `type` and `payload` and nothing else — deliberately, so that a page or an extension surface cannot drive arbitrary REST at the agent. A REST-only operation is therefore not addressable from it at all, and the console is exactly where an operator looking at a DID would want to repair it.

`vta/webvh/dids/realign-keys/1.0`, specified upstream at trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#456 and published in `trust-tasks-rs` 0.20.5.

The handler is thin, because the operation already exists and already takes only what it reads (two keyspaces and the audit sink, not `WebvhDeps`). This adds the URI, the request body, the dispatch arm, the conformance witness, and the two classifications a new task owes.

## Three judgements worth reviewing

**Dispatch table: `Mutating`, not `Destructive` — unlike both of its neighbours.** `dids/update` and `dids/rotate-keys` are destructive because they retire key material. A realign renames records: the same private halves remain, reachable under the names the document publishes for them, which is the state they were supposed to be in all along. Classing it with the other two would say a repair is as dangerous as the thing it repairs.

**`vta-mcp` guard: `Mutating`, beside `rename`** — the same act, one record at a time. Deliberately *not* `Sensitive`, which is the call worth questioning: `keys/set-exportability` earns that class because a caller chooses the direction and one of them lets a protected key out. Here the caller chooses nothing — the payload is a DID and a boolean, and every target name is derived by the agent from that DID's own log. The worst a blanket `vta_call` approval can do is move records into agreement with the document they were always meant to match. No secret is emitted either: the response carries verification-method ids and the *public* halves behind them, both already world-readable in the DID document.

**Retry safety: `RetrySafe`, where `update` and `rotate-keys` are `Keyed`.** Those append a log entry, so a second execution leaves a second durable artefact. A realign appends nothing — it re-derives its plan from the document current at execution time — so a repeat finds every record already aligned and moves none. `a_second_run_has_nothing_left_to_do` is that property, pinned in #1466.

**The conformance witness carries the interleaved response** — one record's destination is the other's current name — rather than a tidy one. That is the shape the specification exists for, and the one that broke the first draft of the operation's own conflict check in #1466.

## The floor

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.20.4 → 0.20.5. Recorded beside the two floors already documented there, with the difference stated: those are floors on a *response member* (emit it against an older schema and a success comes back `500 responseSchemaViolation`). This one is a floor on **serving at all** — `every_served_uri_has_a_published_spec_or_is_tracked_debt` fails on a dispatched URI the registry has no schema for, so below 0.20.5 the task is not a degraded feature, it is a build that does not pass.

That guard is also what proved this change could not be merged before the release: it failed on exactly this URI, with a message saying that growing the debt allowlist is the wrong fix. Written against a local `[patch.crates-io]` while the spec was in review, and re-verified here against the published crate.

## Checks

- `cargo test -p vta-service --lib trust_tasks::` — 251 pass against the real 0.20.5 (both conformance sweeps and the dispatch guard)
- `cargo test -p vta-mcp` — 36 pass · `cargo test -p vta-sdk retry_safety` — 8 pass
- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — running; 0 failures at time of writing
- `cargo clippy -p vta-service -p vta-sdk --all-targets` clean, `cargo fmt --all --check` clean

The first push of this branch failed CI on `every_dispatchable_uri_has_a_known_verb`: I had verified with `-p vta-service` and a workspace `cargo check`, which compiles tests without running them. Both censuses are now classified, and I swept every enumerator of the task catalog rather than fixing the one that fired.

Console side: OpenVTC/vta-browser-plugin#245 (merged, and depends on this).

title: feat(vtc-admin-ui): let the join dry-run reach the vetting routes it cannot test
body:
The Join ceremony's simulator offered one control — *presented credential is
trusted* — so of the shipped policy's eight routes it could reach two. Every
vetting route and the invitation route were unreachable, which means the routes
that decide a **vetted** admission could not be dry-run at all: the only way to
learn what the policy does was to run a real applicant through a real vetting
session with a real second person.

## What the dry-run can now set

| Control | Fact |
|---|---|
| Presents a valid invitation | `evidence.invitation` — verified, trusted, unconsumed. Absent unless set: "no invitation" and "an invitation that fails" are different questions. |
| Peer identity vetting | `evidence.vetting` — *not required · not enough statements yet · vetters verified different identities · vetters not independent enough · requirements met* |
| …and the requirements also demand an invitation | `evidence.vetting.invitation_required`, shown only once the statements are in |

Vetting is **one select, not five toggles**. The host derives `satisfied` from
the others, so separate switches would let an operator assemble a fact set the
host can never produce and then draw a conclusion from it. For *not required*,
`evidence.vetting` is omitted entirely — that absence is exactly what
`vetting_ok` reads.

## Two directives grew

Both in the materializer the admin UI already had:

- `$if` takes an optional `eq`, the comparison `showWhen` already speaks. Bare
  truthiness cannot read a five-way select: every non-empty option is truthy.
- A branch that names nothing now drops its key instead of writing `null`,
  because `not input.evidence.vetting` is how "this criterion does not vet" is
  asked, and `null` answers it wrongly.

## Tests

A Rust test checks the simulator against the shipped `join.rego` itself: every
`input.evidence.vetting.*` member the policy reads must be one the template can
set. A rename on either side fails there, rather than quietly making a route
untestable again.

Also caps blurbs in a unit test: `ceremonies/list/0.1` allows 256 characters,
and the response validator turns an over-long blurb into a **500 for the whole
listing** — every ceremony page blank, not just the one whose text grew. The
integration test caught mine while I was writing this; this catches the next one
a layer earlier.

- `cargo test -p vtc-service --lib routes::ceremonies` — 6 passed
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --test ceremonies_list --test openapi_snapshot` — 6 passed
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check` — clean
- `npx vitest run` — 124 passed (15 files), 7 new for the materializer
- No schema change: `FieldDef`/`ShowWhen` are untouched and the directives live inside `facts_template`, so `openapi.json` and `wire.ts` are unchanged.

Next: the decision-cascade rendering, so the policy reads as a flow rather than
a stack of cards — and so a dry-run can highlight the route that fired.

title: feat(manager): realign a DID's key records from the console
body:
Completes the chain that started with the rename bug in #243. Drives `vta/webvh/dids/realign-keys/1.0` from the DIDs pane.

**Depends on OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1470** (the dispatch arm). Merge that first — this snapshot claims the task is in `vta-sdk`, and until #1470 lands that is true only on its branch.

## The dry run is the diagnosis, not a courtesy

Nothing on this screen tells an operator whether a DID needs realigning: the answer lives in the agent's key store and the DID's published log, and comparing them is precisely what the task does. So the preview *is* the feature — a consistent DID says so, and one that isn't lists every rename before any of them happen.

Which is why the action is offered on **every** DID rather than only where the console thinks it's needed. Deciding that here would mean a second, client-side copy of the comparison, and a copy that disagreed with the agent's would be invisible to the operator.

## A repair is not a destruction

`Destructive` was the obvious home — already ask-then-confirm, and it already routes a consent refusal to the ceremony instead of a red string. But its voice is deletion throughout: a danger button, *"what this would destroy"*, a danger note. A realign renames records and leaves key material untouched, and drawing that in red is the lie `manager-theme.css` forbids, where `--w-danger` is one of three colours that mean something.

So the shape of the decision stays shared and the voice became a parameter: `nature: "corrective"` asks what would *change* and draws in the accent. No force tick, because there's no refusal to override. A second component would have been a second place for the consent-refusal handling to be forgotten.

## The three outcomes are kept apart

`moved` empty with `unmatched` non-empty is **not** "nothing to change" — it's an agent that cannot finish the repair, because it holds no key for a method the document publishes. Both have an empty `moved`, and the reassuring reading is the wrong one. Six rendered tests assert each outcome against the words on screen, including that the repair is never dressed as a destruction.

## The snapshot moves more than this task

`task-surface.json` re-syncs 0.35.0 → 0.38.0, and the coverage expectation with it, 204 → 205. The canonical **total** jumps 227 → 235, and only one of those eight is this task.

The other seven were always in the SDK and invisible to the old scanner, which matched only string literals while `vta-sdk` increasingly derives a constant from the generated payload type. #244 taught it to resolve those. So this is not the agent growing seven families — it's a denominator that had been under-counting the very gap this number exists to keep reviewable. Nothing is lost in the resync: all 245 tasks in the old snapshot survive.

## Checks

`npm test` — 1352 across the workspace, 0 failures. `npm run build` clean.

## The chain, for the record

dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#456 (spec) → #457 (unblocked its CI) → releases 0.20.5 / 0.19.5 → VTI#1466 (create fix + repair) → VTI#1470 (dispatch) → #244 (scanner) → this.

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.20.5
body:
### Added

- **vta/webvh/dids/realign-keys**: A DID's key records follow the methods it publishes ([#456](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/456))

A key record's identifier *is* a verification-method identifier: it is what a
  mediator matches an inbound JWE recipient against, and what a caller reading a
  DID document would naturally hand to a signing task. An agent that names a
  record when it mints a key — rather than reading the document it has just
  published — names it correctly only for documents shaped the way it assumed.
  A document supplied by a caller or rendered from a template is free to identify
  its methods any way it likes, and then the agent holds a key the document
  addresses under a name the agent does not answer to.

  `keys/rename` cannot repair that, and should not be able to: its identifier gate
  exists so that a rename is not a way to write verification-method-shaped or
  namespace-colliding names into a key store. So the repair has to be a task whose
  **request carries no names at all** — the producer identifies a DID, and every
  identifier in the outcome is derived by the recipient from that DID's own
  published document. That is the whole design, and it is why this is a Trust Task
  rather than a parameterised rename.

  Three things the conformance section pins that an implementer would otherwise
  get wrong:

  - **Match records to methods by key material, never by position or by a `#key-N`
    pattern.** A record is what it is because of the key it holds; its current name
    is the thing being repaired and so cannot be an input to deciding what it
    should be. This is also what lets the repair reach a record someone has already
    renamed away from its method identifier, which is otherwise unreachable.
  - **All or nothing.** The renames interleave — one record's destination is
    another's current name — and in the general case form a cycle, so an
    implementation that requires each destination to be free before moving
    anything refuses the very shape the task exists for. The response example
    shows that case rather than a tidy one.
  - **A method whose key the recipient does not hold is reported, not an error.**
    "Nothing to move" and "that key is not here" are different answers and only
    the first means the DID is now consistent.

  Sits in the `vta/webvh/dids/*` family beside `rotate-keys`, and squarely in the
  "genuinely VTA-side" row of the two-ends-of-one-wire question: a hosting server
  has no notion of the key custody this renames, so there is no `did-management/*`
  counterpart to reuse.

  Bindings regenerated for both libraries.

title: fix(core): the task-surface scanner resolves computed constants, or stops
body:
## The bug, and why it was worth chasing

`sync-task-surface.mjs` only ever matched a string literal. `vta-sdk` increasingly doesn't write one — it derives the constant from the generated payload type, so the URI appears nowhere in the source:

```rust
pub const JOIN_REQUEST_MANIFEST_TYPE: &str =
    <manifest::v0_1::Payload as trust_tasks_rs::Payload>::TYPE_URI;
```

**Nineteen** constants are already in that form. The scanner saw none of them, and the *way* it failed is what makes this worth fixing rather than noting: the task was simply absent from the snapshot, and `tests/task-surface.mjs` reports any URI this library calls that's missing from it as a task **the SDK does not have** — its wording for a typo or a dropped task.

So a scanner limitation is indistinguishable from a live version-left-behind. It was mistaken for one, by me, earlier today: `vtc/join-requests/manifest/0.1` in `vtc/membership.ts` read as a dead call. It isn't — vta-sdk still exports it and vtc-service still dispatches it (`ManifestVersion::V0_1`, `trust_tasks/mod.rs:226`). The next `tasks:sync` would have produced the same false finding again.

## Resolving

Follows `pub use trust_tasks_rs::specs::…` within a file and reconstructs the URI from the module path: segments snake_case → kebab-case (`join_requests` → `join-requests`), `v0_1` → `0.1`. Braced groups resolve each name, including across the wrap rustfmt applies to a long one.

A `pub use` reaching *inside* a version module is importing types, not aliasing a spec — `…::manifest::v0_2::{VettingRequirements, Branding}` names two structs — so a path carrying a `vN_M` segment registers no aliases. Without that rule those struct names become spec modules and resolve to invented URIs.

## Stopping

The more important half. A `&str` constant the script cannot turn into a URI is now **fatal**, naming the file, the declaration line and the constant:

```
Cannot resolve 1 `&str` constant(s) to a task URI:
  src/p.rs:2  ORPHAN_TYPE — no `pub use trust_tasks_rs::specs::…` in this file brings `nowhere` into scope
```

Writing the snapshot without it is what turned a limitation into something that read as a finding. Refusing to write is the scanner saying *"I do not understand this"*, which is the true statement. `include_str!` / `concat!` constants are recognised as not-a-task so the stop doesn't fire on them.

## The check that says the resolver is right

Re-syncing the **same SDK the committed snapshot came from** loses nothing — all 245 tasks survive — and gains eleven, ten of which are genuine SDK additions since 0.35 (the vetting family, `audit/verify/0.1`, `join-requests/manifest/0.2`). Agreeing with the literal era across 245 entries is stronger evidence than any fixture: it says the resolver reproduces what a human wrote by hand, rather than merely producing plausible strings.

`task-surface.json` is deliberately untouched here. The snapshot is of a *published* vta-sdk and refreshing it is its own deliberate act; this commit only makes that act correct when someone performs it.

## Tests

Eight, driving the script as a subprocess against fixture SDK trees — what went wrong was end-to-end (what lands in the file, and what the exit code is), and neither is visible from importing a helper. They cover the resolution forms, the version-module rule, literal constants with and without a wrap and a `#[deprecated]`, and the stop itself — including that a failed run leaves the existing snapshot on disk untouched.

`npm test --workspace @openvtc/pnm-core` — 649 pass.

## [0.20.5](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/compare/trust-tasks-rs-v0.20.4...trust-tasks-rs-v0.20.5) — 2026-09-14 ### Added - **vta/webvh/dids/realign-keys**: A DID's key records follow the methods it publishes ([#456](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/456)) A key record's identifier *is* a verification-method identifier: it is what a mediator matches an inbound JWE recipient against, and what a caller reading a DID document would naturally hand to a signing task. An agent that names a record when it mints a key — rather than reading the document it has just published — names it correctly only for documents shaped the way it assumed. A document supplied by a caller or rendered from a template is free to identify its methods any way it likes, and then the agent holds a key the document addresses under a name the agent does not answer to. `keys/rename` cannot repair that, and should not be able to: its identifier gate exists so that a rename is not a way to write verification-method-shaped or namespace-colliding names into a key store. So the repair has to be a task whose **request carries no names at all** — the producer identifies a DID, and every identifier in the outcome is derived by the recipient from that DID's own published document. That is the whole design, and it is why this is a Trust Task rather than a parameterised rename. Three things the conformance section pins that an implementer would otherwise get wrong: - **Match records to methods by key material, never by position or by a `#key-N` pattern.** A record is what it is because of the key it holds; its current name is the thing being repaired and so cannot be an input to deciding what it should be. This is also what lets the repair reach a record someone has already renamed away from its method identifier, which is otherwise unreachable. - **All or nothing.** The renames interleave — one record's destination is another's current name — and in the general case form a cycle, so an implementation that requires each destination to be free before moving anything refuses the very shape the task exists for. The response example shows that case rather than a tidy one. - **A method whose key the recipient does not hold is reported, not an error.** "Nothing to move" and "that key is not here" are different answers and only the first means the DID is now consistent. Sits in the `vta/webvh/dids/*` family beside `rotate-keys`, and squarely in the "genuinely VTA-side" row of the two-ends-of-one-wire question: a hosting server has no notion of the key custody this renames, so there is no `did-management/*` counterpart to reuse. Bindings regenerated for both libraries.

title: fix(core): the task-surface scanner resolves computed constants, or stops
body:
fix(core): the task-surface scanner resolves computed constants, or stops

`sync-task-surface.mjs` only ever matched a string literal:

    pub const TASK_ACL_GRANT_0_1: &str = "https://trusttasks.org/spec/acl/grant/0.1";

`vta-sdk` increasingly does not write one. It derives the constant from the
generated payload type instead, so the URI appears nowhere in the source:

    pub const JOIN_REQUEST_MANIFEST_TYPE: &str =
        <manifest::v0_1::Payload as trust_tasks_rs::Payload>::TYPE_URI;

Nineteen constants are already in that form. The scanner saw none of them, and
the way it failed is the reason this is worth fixing rather than noting: the
task was simply **absent** from the snapshot, and `tests/task-surface.mjs` then
reports any URI this library calls that is missing from it as a task *the SDK
does not have* — which is its wording for a typo or a task that was dropped.

So a scanner limitation is indistinguishable from a live version-left-behind.
It was mistaken for one: `vtc/join-requests/manifest/0.1` was read as a dead
call in `vtc/membership.ts`, and it is not — vta-sdk still exports it and
vtc-service still dispatches it (`ManifestVersion::V0_1`). The finding cost an
investigation before it was recognised as a false one, and the next `tasks:sync`
would have produced it again.

## Resolving

The scanner now follows `pub use trust_tasks_rs::specs::…` within a file and
reconstructs the URI from the module path: segments snake_case → kebab-case
(`join_requests` → `join-requests`), `v0_1` → `0.1`. Braced groups resolve each
name, including across the wrap rustfmt applies to a long one.

A `pub use` that reaches *inside* a version module is importing types, not
aliasing a spec — `…::manifest::v0_2::{VettingRequirements, Branding}` names two
structs — so a path carrying a `vN_M` segment registers no aliases. Without that
rule those struct names become spec modules and resolve to invented URIs.

## Stopping

The other half, and the more important one: a `&str` constant this script cannot
turn into a URI is now **fatal**, naming the file, the declaration line and the
constant. Writing the snapshot without it is what turned a limitation into
something that read as a finding; refusing to write is the scanner saying "I do
not understand this", which is the true statement. `include_str!` and `concat!`
constants are recognised as not-a-task so the stop does not fire on them.

## What it changes, checked against the old snapshot

Re-syncing the same SDK the committed snapshot came from loses **nothing** —
every one of its 245 tasks survives — and gains eleven, ten of which are real
SDK additions since 0.35 (the vetting family, `audit/verify/0.1`,
`join-requests/manifest/0.2`). That is the check that says the resolver agrees
with the literal era rather than merely producing plausible strings.

`task-surface.json` itself is deliberately untouched here: the snapshot is of a
*published* vta-sdk and refreshing it is its own deliberate act, which this
commit only makes correct when someone does it.

Eight tests drive the script as a subprocess against fixture SDK trees, because
what went wrong was end-to-end — what lands in the file, and what the exit code
is — and neither is visible from importing a helper.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: fix(deps): take the patched rustls, and record clear_on_drop as unfixable here
body:
`cargo deny` is red on `main` right now. Nothing changed — the advisory database moved since main last ran on 11 September, and two findings landed on the existing tree. They want opposite treatments, which is the only interesting thing about this PR.

**RUSTSEC-2026-0285 (rustls) — fixed.** Rustls accepted TLS 1.3 handshake messages sent at the wrong encryption level when they followed a key-changing message in the same record (a plaintext `EncryptedExtensions` packed into the same record as the `ServerHello`, say). There is a patched release, so the lockfile takes it rather than the ignore list: `rustls` 0.23.40 → 0.23.45, pulling `rustls-webpki` 0.103.15 and `aws-lc-rs` 1.18.1. Note 0.23.43 is **not** enough — still flagged.

**RUSTSEC-2026-0283 (clear_on_drop) — ignored, with the reason recorded.** The advisory is explicit: *"No safe upgrade is available"*. 0.2.5 is the last release and the replacement is a different crate with a different API (`zeroize`'s `Zeroizing`). It arrives by the same chain the existing h2 0.3 entry already describes — `ssi-jws 0.3.1` → `ssi-dids-core 0.1.3` → `affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk` — and so reaches crates we publish (`trust-tasks-tsp` via `affinidi-tsp`, and `trust-tasks-proof`) as a normal dependency, not a dev one. Our requirement on the resolver SDK is already open and every 0.8.x pulls the same `ssi-dids-core`, so there is nothing here to shorten. Maintenance status, no CVE.

## Checks

- `cargo deny check` — advisories ok, bans ok, licenses ok, sources ok
- `cargo check --workspace` — clean

Found while opening #456, whose `cargo deny` job fails for this reason and not for anything in that PR — verified by running the check against unmodified `origin/main`, which fails identically.

title: feat(vta/webvh/dids/realign-keys): a DID's key records follow the methods it publishes
body:
Adds `vta/webvh/dids/realign-keys/1.0`, beside `rotate-keys` in the same family.

## The problem it specifies a repair for

A key record's identifier **is** a verification-method identifier — it is what a mediator matches an inbound JWE recipient against, and what a caller reading a DID document would naturally hand to a signing task.

An agent that names a record when it mints a key, rather than reading the document it has just published, names it correctly only for documents shaped the way it assumed. A document supplied by a caller or rendered from a template is free to identify its methods any way it likes. The result is an agent holding a key that the document addresses under a name the agent does not answer to — and, where the numbering merely shifts, *one name meaning two different keys*: the signing key to every resolver, a key-agreement key to the agent holding it.

(Found in the wild: `vta-sdk`'s `room` and `room-host` templates number their methods from `#key-1` while the create path stored records from `#key-0`. Fix and repair: OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1466.)

## Why it is a task, and not a parameterised rename

`keys/rename` cannot do this, and should not be able to: its identifier gate exists so that a rename is not a way to write verification-method-shaped or namespace-colliding names into a key store. A caller who can write `{someone-elses-did}#key-0` as a store key can squat the kid of a DID that has not minted its keys yet.

So the request **carries no names at all**. The producer identifies a DID; every identifier in the outcome is derived by the recipient from that DID's own published document. That is the whole design — and it has a pleasant side effect on authorization: an administrator of one context cannot name a method belonging to a DID in another, because they cannot name anything. (The role check still stands. This narrows what a mistake can reach, not who may ask.)

## Three conformance rules an implementer would otherwise get wrong

- **Match records to methods by key material** — never by position, never by a `#key-N` pattern. A record is what it is because of the key it holds; its current name is the thing being repaired, so it cannot be an input to deciding what it should be. This is also what reaches a record someone has already renamed away from its method identifier, which no other call can name again.
- **All or nothing.** The renames interleave — one record's destination is another's current name — and in the general case form a cycle. An implementation that requires each destination to be free before moving anything refuses the very shape this exists for, so the response example shows that case rather than a tidy one.
- **A method whose key the recipient does not hold is reported, not an error.** "Nothing to move" and "that key is not here" are different answers, and only the first means the DID is now consistent.

`dryRun` is echoed in the response because a plan and a receipt are otherwise the same shape, and a reader who has to remember which one they asked for will eventually be wrong about it.

## On §B

This sits squarely in the *"likely genuinely VTA-side"* row of the two-ends-of-one-wire question in the consumer's reduction plan: a hosting server has no notion of the key custody being renamed, so there is no `did-management/*` counterpart to reuse and nothing here forecloses that decision for the rest of the family.

## Checks

- `npm run build` — 438 specs validated, 647 example documents against the envelope schema, no new warnings
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` + `cargo fmt --all`, `npm run build-ts-bindings` — both binding sets regenerated and committed
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --all-features` — green; 3 generated tests for this spec, including `rejects_invalid_examples` over the five fixtures in `payload.invalid-examples.json`

The invalid-example fixtures are worth a look in review: two of them (a caller-supplied target name, and `dryRun` as the string `"true"`) are the mistakes that would quietly undo the design rather than fail loudly.

No version bump or CHANGELOG entry, per CONTRIBUTING-SPECS → release-plz.

title: Decide the home of the DTG namespace before the Implementers Draft
body:
## Summary

#47 makes VSC predicates absolute IRIs on the wire, so the core predicates are now written out in full. The PR writes them under the existing context URL plus `#`:

```
https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1#endorses
https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1#witnessed
```

That is a default inherited from the `@context` requirement in Base Structure, not a decision anyone has made. The namespace is where every predicate this WG defines will live, it is the prefix communities will copy when they define their own vocabularies, and it is what the planned DTG Predicate Vocabulary specification will be published under. It needs an owner.

## Why it has to be decided early

Changing the namespace later is a find-and-replace in the spec but a migration for every credential issued under it: a predicate IRI is compared byte-exact (Predicate Handling in #47), so a credential issued under the old namespace does not match a verifier configured for the new one. That cost is zero today and grows with every issued credential. **This should be settled as soon as possible, and at the latest before the specification bumps to an Implementers Draft**, since that is the point at which implementations start issuing credentials that have to keep verifying.

The same question applies to the `@context` IRI itself, which Base Structure already requires and which is not yet published either; the two should be decided together.

## Options

1. **Keep `https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1#`.** No change to the spec. The vocabulary — and the context — are then hosted and controlled by First Person, and the DTG Predicate Vocabulary spec, if it becomes a ToIP deliverable, would define terms under a namespace ToIP does not control.
2. **Move to a ToIP-controlled IRI.** For example under `https://trustoverip.org/...` or another origin the Foundation administers. The context and vocabulary are then governed with the specification. Requires ToIP to agree to host and maintain the resources, and a find-and-replace in the spec before any credential is issued.

## What the decision needs to cover

- The namespace IRI for DTG-defined predicates.
- The `@context` IRI (currently `https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1`), and whether the namespace is that URL plus `#` or a separate IRI.
- Who administers the origin, and the commitment that published context and vocabulary versions are immutable (a requirement in #47).
- Versioning: whether `v1` in the path is the context version, the vocabulary version, or both.

## Proposed resolution

Decide at the next editors' call, record the answer here, and apply it to #47 before merge or in a follow-up PR before the Implementers Draft.

Refs #45, #47.

title: feat(vtc-admin-ui): write admission criteria and statement types from the console
body:
Turning vetting on took two calls no interface could make. **Vetting →
Requirements** read the join manifest and said so in its own header — *"read-only
on purpose: this console has no criteria editor"* — and `cnm` has no schema-store
command either, so the first thing an operator has to do was the one thing
nothing could help them do. The two steps also fail in the wrong order: a
criterion naming an unregistered `statementType` is refused, so the missing
endorsement-type registration surfaces as a refusal of the *criterion*.

The panel now writes what it used to only show.

## What changed

- **Criteria** — add, edit and remove (`/v1/schemas/accepts`). The form writes
  the `vetting` object member by member: statements required, methods, per-method
  floors, vetter role, claims verified, statement age, documentation floor,
  independence caps, invitation, deadlines, governance link. The DCQL query is
  its own field, starting from the shape a vetting criterion uses and kept
  verbatim on an existing criterion.
- **Statement types** — register them (`/v1/endorsement-types`), with one button
  for the identity-vetting type when the community has none: the prerequisite on
  the page that needs it, before the refusal it causes.
- **The rules are not written twice.** `validateRequirements` already mirrored
  the daemon's checks for the read-only view. A draft is converted to a
  requirements object and answered with those same sentences; the daemon runs all
  of them again on save. A count that is not a number becomes `NaN`, which the
  existing rule refuses in the existing words.
- **Two things the form does that a JSON body cannot.** A per-method minimum is
  only offered for a method the criterion accepts, so the commonest refusal
  cannot be written. And "each vetter decides what documentation they accept" is
  a switch separate from the list, because an absent `acceptedDocumentClasses`
  and an empty one mean opposite things to a vetter (D16) and look almost
  identical in JSON.
- Before saving, the page says in sentences what applicants will be told, reusing
  `summarizeRequirements`.

`api.ts` gains `postJsonExempt` / `deleteJsonExempt` beside the existing
`putJsonExempt` — the schema store is one of the daemon's Trust-Task-exempt
routes, named at the call site like the rest of that carve-out. `AcceptsCriterion`,
`EndorsementType` and their bodies are aliased from the generated wire types
rather than described again.

No daemon change: every route this uses already exists, so `openapi.json` and
`wire.ts` are untouched.

## Checks

- `npm run lint` (wire:check + `tsc -b --noEmit`) — clean
- `npm run build` — clean
- `npx vitest run` — 100 passed (12 files), including 18 new: the editor's body
  on save, the refusals it will not send, the documentation-floor distinction,
  the per-method offer, criterion removal behind its confirmation, statement-type
  registration, and the draft ⇄ wire round trip.

Not exercised against a live daemon; the panels are covered by DOM tests only.

## Follow-ups, deliberately not here

- The policy upload form's placeholder is `package vtc.${purpose}`, so for
  `vetterEligibility` it prints `package vtc.vetterEligibility` while the daemon
  requires `vtc.vetter_eligibility` (`PolicyPurpose::expected_package`).
  `validate_purpose_package` refuses it with a clear message, so it costs a round
  trip rather than a silent misfire — but it hands the operator the wrong package
  at the moment they need the right one. `pkgFor()` beside it has the same
  omission. Separate one-line fix.
- The visual rule editor has conditions only for join, removal, directory and
  roleChange, so authoring a `vetterEligibility` policy still means writing Rego
  by hand.

title: feat(vtc-admin-ui): author the vetter-eligibility policy, in the package the daemon requires
body:
Who the automatic sweep names a vetter is a Rego policy, and the console let an
admin reach it but not write it. `canAuthor` was `CEREMONY_PURPOSES.includes()`,
so `vetterEligibility` — which has no ceremony — got the raw textarea, and that
textarea's placeholder printed `package vtc.${purpose}`: `vtc.vetterEligibility`,
which `validate_purpose_package` refuses. The console pointed at the policy, then
handed over a wrong package name and a blank box.

## The package

`pkgFor` moves to `policies-api.ts`, beside the purposes it describes, and
derives the package rather than special-casing one purpose: every shipped policy
in `policies/default/` is the snake_case of its camelCase purpose. The upload
placeholder now uses it, which also corrects `roleChange`, `roleDefinitions` and
both cross-community purposes.

A test reads the daemon's own `.rego` files and asserts every purpose maps to a
package one of them declares — so the console's idea of where a policy lives is
the daemon's, not a list kept in parallel.

## The vocabulary

A `vetterEligibility` block: membership active, admission under review or not,
how they were admitted, tenure in days, vetting depth from a founding member,
roles held. Enough to author the policy the shipped default's own comment
suggests, by clicking.

Three things it deliberately does **not** do, each because the sweep's input is a
member record rather than somebody's request:

- **The shared conditions are withheld.** `actor_is_admin` and its siblings read
  `input.actor` / `input.subject` / `input.state`, none of which exist here — so
  every one would be false. Offering them would be offering a trap.
- **Only `allow` and `deny` are offered**, named "Name a vetter" / "Do not name a
  vetter". `refer` and `request_more` are logged as undecided and act on no one,
  so authoring one would author a policy that quietly does nothing.
- **A blank policy starts at `deny`** — the posture the daemon ships, and the
  only backstop the sweep acts on.

## Arguments that must match

`admittedVia` is compared exactly, so a typo compiles cleanly and matches nobody.
The IR's argument spec gains `options` (rendered as a choice) and `kind: "number"`
(compiled unquoted), and the editor will not add a condition whose argument is
empty, not a whole number, or not one of the choices. The compiler stays total
regardless: a count that is not a number is emitted quoted, which Rego compares
across types and finds false, rather than as text that would not compile.

`ConditionDef` also gains an optional `phrase`, so a parametrised condition reads
as a sentence — "is at most 2 vetting hops from a founding member" rather than
"is within vetting hops of a founding member 2" — in both the route card and the
plain-English view, which now agree. `effectToEnglish` takes the purpose for the
same reason.

## Checks

- `npm run lint` (wire:check + `tsc -b --noEmit`) — clean
- `npm run build` — clean
- `npx vitest run` — 99 passed (12 files), 17 of them new: the compiler against
  the documented example policy, the package mapping against the shipped `.rego`
  files, the withheld conditions and effects, and the editor's argument gating.

No daemon change; `openapi.json` and `wire.ts` untouched. Not exercised against a
live daemon — the editor is covered by DOM tests only.

Follow-up to #1465, which made the Requirements panel write what it showed. The
two touch different files apart from one line each in `docs/03-vtc/vetting.md`.

title: fix(webvh): key records follow the document's verification-method ids, and a repair for the ones that don't
body:
Found from the browser plugin's Keys pane: a room host's keys were listed as `#key-0` / `#key-1` while its published DID document declares `#key-1` / `#key-2`.

## The defect

A key record's id **is** a verification-method id. `save_entity_key_records` says so in its own name, and `vta_sdk::did_secrets::select_secret_kid` rule 1 depends on it — the kid a mediator matches inbound JWE recipients against is the record id, on the reasoning that "the DID document decided what the key is called".

Create never read the document to find out. It named records `{did}#key-0` / `{did}#key-1` while the document was whatever the caller or the template said — and `room.json` and `room-host.json` number their methods from `#key-1`. On every room and room host this VTA has minted:

| | signing (ed25519) | key agreement (x25519) |
|---|---|---|
| published document | `#key-1` | `#key-2` |
| key records | `#key-0` | `#key-1` |

- **`#key-1` names two different keys.** The signing key to every resolver; the x25519 key to the agent holding it. Hand the id the document publishes to `keys/sign` — the natural thing, having read it off the document — and the oracle fetches an x25519 record for an EdDSA signature.
- **The published `keyAgreement` matches no record.** An authcrypt message addressed to `#key-2` finds no local secret: the storm.ws outage of #337 reached from the other side. There a decorative label overwrote the right kid; here the right kid was never stored.
- **`next_fragment_id` was the constant 2**, so a room's first rotation allocates `#key-2` — over the id its key-agreement method is already published under.

Room credentials still verify, which is why this stayed quiet: `RoomKeySigner` hardcodes `{room_did}#key-1` to match the template and the public keys line up positionally, so the proof names a method that resolves to the key that signed it. Everything that addresses a key **by name** is what breaks.

(`ai-agent-peer.json` also numbers from 1 and is correct — `did:peer` fragments are 1-based by spec. Only the two `webvh` room templates are affected.)

## Commit 1 — create reads the document it just published

`document::minted_vm_ids` matches methods to the minted keys on `publicKeyMultibase` and takes the ids it finds. Matching on key material rather than position or a `#key-N` shape is what makes it total: right for a template numbering from 1, for `vta-admin` (method id `{DID}#{SIGNING_KEY_MB}`), and for a hand-written document.

Renumbering the two templates instead would have been smaller and wrong twice: `RoomKeySigner`'s hardcoded `#key-1` would then name a method the new documents lack, and the next custom template reintroduces the whole thing.

Also: `next_fragment_id` comes from the document's highest `#key-N`, and delete cleans up every `#key-N` the record allocated instead of exactly two — which had been leaking the records of every rotated DID too.

## Commit 2 — a repair for the DIDs already out there

`keys/rename` cannot do it, deliberately: its gate exists so a rename is "not a back door into VM-shaped or namespace-colliding names" (`rename_key_rejects_separator_shaped_new_key_id` pins it), and the reason is real — a caller who can write `{someone-elses-did}#key-0` as a store key can squat the kid of a DID that has not minted its keys yet. An operator attempting the obvious repair is told their new name is 86 bytes against a limit of 64, with no second attempt that works. Worse, the rename that *is* accepted detaches the record from the document permanently, because the id it had cannot be given back.

So the agent computes the names: `POST /webvh/dids/{did}/realign-keys` (admin, scoped to the DID's context), `pnm did-mgmt dids realign-keys <did> [--dry-run]`. Every target comes from the DID's own log — read locally, because a repair that depends on the network cannot run when the network is what is broken — and records are matched to methods by `publicKeyMultibase`. No caller-supplied string becomes a store key, which is what makes this safe where widening `keys/rename` would not be. Matching on key material also recovers a key already renamed away from its method id, which nothing else can name again.

It plans, then applies: nothing is written until every move is known safe. The moves **interleave** — `#key-0` → `#key-1` and `#key-1` → `#key-2`, so one destination is held by the other record in the same plan, and the general case is a cycle — so the conflict check refuses a target held by a key that is *not* moving, rather than any occupied target. Destinations are written before sources are dropped, so an interrupted run leaves a duplicate the next run collapses, never a key whose record is gone.

REST-only, and the client method says so rather than timing out on a DIDComm message nothing answers.

## Checks

- `cargo test -p vta-service --lib` — **1119 passed**, 0 failed
- `cargo test -p vta-keys` — 42 passed
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all`

15 new tests. The five on `minted_vm_ids` run against the **real** built-in templates rather than a fixture — the defect was not misreading a document, it was never reading one, so a fixture of my own choosing would have agreed with the broken code — and are verified non-vacuous: three fail against the old behaviour while the builder and fallback tests stay green. Two of the ten realign tests are cases that would otherwise be found in production: the interleaved move (which the first draft of the conflict check refused outright — the tests caught it) and a key already renamed away from its method id.

## Companion

Plugin-side: OpenVTC/vta-browser-plugin#243, merged — the console now applies the agent's identifier rule before sending a rename, so this refusal arrives as a sentence under the field instead of a raw `malformed request`.

* fix(webvh): name a created DID's key records after the document it published

from `#key-1`. So on every room and every room host this VTA has ever minted:

- the document's `#key-1` is the **signing** key and the keystore's `#key-1` is
  the **x25519** one. One name, two keys, no error anywhere. Hand the id the
  document publishes to `keys/sign` — the natural thing to do, having read it
  off the document — and the oracle fetches an x25519 record for an EdDSA

`document::minted_vm_ids` matches methods to the minted keys on

a template that numbers from 1, for `vta-admin` (whose method id is

Renumbering `room.json` / `room-host.json` to `#key-0` / `#key-1` would have

builder's own `#key-0` / `#key-1` and the no-such-key fallback stay green,
which is what says the change is narrow.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(webvh): realign a DID's key records with the methods it publishes

The previous commit fixes DIDs minted from now on. Every room and room host
already published carries records the document does not name, and there is no
caller-facing call that can repair one.

`keys/rename` cannot, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight — its
gate exists so that a rename is "not a back door into VM-shaped or
namespace-colliding names", with `rename_key_rejects_separator_shaped_new_key_id`
pinning it. The reason is real: a caller who can write `{someone-elses-did}#key-0`
as a store key can squat the kid of a DID that has not minted its keys yet. So
an operator who tries the obvious repair — rename the record to the id the
document publishes — is told their new name is 86 bytes against a limit of 64,
and there is no second attempt that works.

*is* accepted (`vdr-host-key-2`, say) detaches the record from the document for
good, because the id it had cannot be given back.

## So the agent computes the names

can name it again.

**It plans, then applies.** Nothing is written until every move is known to be
safe, so a conflict leaves the keystore exactly as it was rather than
half-moved. `--dry-run` returns that plan without applying it.
